questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate Homocystinuria from Marfan syndrome based on lens dislocation direction and neurological symptoms.
questions.reasoningChain: Developmental delay + Extrapyramidal symptoms + Inferonasal lens dislocation -> Homocystinuria.
optionExplanations: Causes superotemporal lens dislocation, not inferonasal, and different neurological features.
Characterized by developmental delay, extrapyramidal symptoms, and inferonasal lens dislocation.
Causes dark urine and arthritis, not developmental delay with lens dislocation.
Causes hepatolenticular degeneration with Kayser-Fleischer rings, not typically lens dislocation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Continuous watery discharge from nose after trauma is most likely a feature of:-
questions.explanation: Continuous watery discharge from the nose after trauma is highly suggestive of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea. This occurs when there is a breach in the skull base, allowing CSF to leak from the subarachnoid space into the nasal cavity. The discharge is typically clear, watery, and may test positive for beta-2 transferrin, a specific CSF marker.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize CSF rhinorrhea as a cause of continuous watery nasal discharge after trauma.
questions.reasoningChain: Trauma + Continuous watery nasal discharge -> Suspect skull base breach -> CSF rhinorrhea.
optionExplanations: CSF otorrhea is CSF leakage from the ear, not the nose.
Common colds cause mucoid discharge, often with congestion, not continuous watery post-trauma.
Correct; indicates a breach in the skull base allowing CSF to leak into the nasal cavity.
Anterior epistaxis is nosebleed, characterized by blood, not clear watery discharge.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Common neurological tumour in NF-2?
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by the development of multiple tumors, predominantly involving the nervous system. The hallmark feature and most common neurological tumor in NF2 is bilateral vestibular schwannomas, also known as acoustic neuromas. These tumors arise from the Schwann cells of the vestibulocochlear nerve.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify bilateral acoustic neuromas as the characteristic tumor of NF2.
questions.reasoningChain: NF-2 -> Autosomal dominant disorder -> Bilateral vestibular schwannomas -> Acoustic neuroma.
optionExplanations: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) are the hallmark of NF2.
Optic gliomas are more characteristic of Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).
Café-au-lait macules are characteristic skin lesions of Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).
Meningiomas are also common in NF2, but acoustic neuromas are the defining feature.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: A 6-year child presents with hepatosplenomegaly & generalized lymphadenopathy along with fever. The child developed a rash, after being administered ampicillin. What could be the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, and a rash after ampicillin administration is highly suggestive of Infectious Mononucleosis. This condition, caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), often presents with these systemic symptoms. A maculopapular rash developing after ampicillin or amoxicillin is a classic, though non-allergic, reaction seen in many patients with EBV infection.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the classic presentation of infectious mononucleosis, including the ampicillin-induced rash.
questions.reasoningChain: Fever + Lymphadenopathy + Hepatosplenomegaly + Ampicillin rash -> Infectious mononucleosis.
optionExplanations: Classic presentation includes fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and ampicillin-induced rash.
Presents with fever, pharyngitis, and a characteristic sandpaper-like rash, not typically hepatosplenomegaly.
Involves fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, but also conjunctivitis, oral changes, and extremity swelling.
While it can cause lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, the ampicillin rash is highly specific for EBV.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Prophylaxis of meningococcal meningitis in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone is the recommended chemoprophylactic agent for meningococcal disease contacts when safe alternatives during pregnancy are required, as rifampicin and ciprofloxacin have teratogenic or safety concerns.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify ceftriaxone as the safe meningococcal chemoprophylaxis choice in pregnancy.
questions.reasoningChain: Meningococcal contact in pregnant female -> avoid ciprofloxacin/rifampicin -> administer ceftriaxone.
optionExplanations: Ceftriaxone is safe and effective for meningococcal chemoprophylaxis during pregnancy.
Rifampicin has potential hepatotoxicity and teratogenic concerns, making it less preferred in pregnancy.
Ciprofloxacin is generally avoided in pregnancy due to risks of cartilage and joint toxicity in the fetus.
Penicillin G is not effective for meningococcal nasopharyngeal eradication.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a premalignant lesion / condition:
questions.explanation: Chronic hypertrophic candidiasis is a fungal infection of the oral mucosa that is not classified as a premalignant lesion, unlike leukoplakia, oral submucous fibrosis, and erythroplakia.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify chronic hypertrophic candidiasis as an infection rather than a premalignant oral condition.
questions.reasoningChain: Premalignant oral lesions include leukoplakia and OSMF -> chronic hypertrophic candidiasis is an inflammatory/fungal condition.
optionExplanations: Chronic hypertrophic candidiasis is a fungal infection and is not considered a premalignant lesion.
Oral submucous fibrosis is a well-established premalignant condition linked to betel nut chewing.
Oral lichen planus (especially erosive form) carries a low malignant transformation risk and is premalignant.
Leukoplakia is a major premalignant white plaque lesion of the oral cavity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: AFP is a tumour marker for which of the following?
questions.explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a classic tumor marker elevated in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and certain germ cell tumors.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall that alpha-fetoprotein is a tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Hepatocellular carcinoma -> oncofetal protein synthesis -> elevated serum AFP.
optionExplanations: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is classically associated with elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels.
Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) does not secrete AFP; it may present with paraneoplastic erythropoietin production.
Oncocytomas are benign renal epithelial tumors and do not produce AFP.
Chordomas are rare malignant bone tumors arising from notochord remnants, not associated with AFP.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Hypoglossal nerve supplies all of these muscle except:-
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, EXCEPT the palatoglossus, which is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve, CN X).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the palatoglossus muscle as an exception to hypoglossal nerve innervation.
questions.reasoningChain: Tongue muscles -> hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) -> except palatoglossus (supplied by vagus nerve, CN X).
optionExplanations: Palatoglossus is innervated by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve (CN X), not the hypoglossal nerve.
Styloglossus is innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
Genioglossus is innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
Hyoglossus is innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: In an eye camp doctor's try to make people aware of the causes of blindness. Vitamin A is the leading cause for preventable childhood blindness. A parent brings her 18-month-old child to the doctor for a routine eye check-up. Doctor notices thinned-out cornea and from old records, it was seen that the child also has iron-deficiency anemia. Weight of the child is 10kg, what should be the dose of vit. A to be given in this case if doctor marks it as keratomalacia?
questions.explanation: According to WHO guidelines for vitamin A deficiency, the therapeutic dose for an infant/child diagnosed with corneal involvement such as keratomalacia is 200,000 IU on Day 1, Day 2, and 2 weeks later.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the therapeutic vitamin A dose schedule for children with corneal xerophthalmia (keratomalacia).
questions.reasoningChain: Keratomalacia (corneal ulceration/necrosis) -> urgent high-dose vitamin A -> 200,000 IU per dose.
optionExplanations: 50,000 IU is used for infants under 6 months of age.
100,000 IU is used for children aged 6-12 months without severe corneal signs.
200,000 IU is the correct therapeutic dose for children over 12 months with active corneal disease.
500,000 IU exceeds safe therapeutic dosing guidelines.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Not a pre-hepatic cause of protal HTN?
questions.explanation: Budd-Chiari syndrome is hepatic venous outflow obstruction, which is classified as a POST-hepatic cause of portal hypertension, whereas portal vein thrombosis, Banti's disease, and pyelophlebitis are pre-hepatic causes.
questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish pre-hepatic causes of portal hypertension from post-hepatic causes like Budd-Chiari syndrome.
questions.reasoningChain: Hepatic vein thrombosis -> post-hepatic portal hypertension -> Budd-Chiari syndrome.
optionExplanations: Budd-Chiari syndrome is caused by hepatic venous outflow obstruction, making it a post-hepatic cause.
Banti's disease involves splenic and portal vein congestion, acting as a pre-hepatic/intrahepatic cause.
Portal vein thrombosis blocks blood flow before the liver, classifying it as pre-hepatic.
Pyelophlebitis is portal vein septic thrombophlebitis, a pre-hepatic etiology.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: After head trauma a patient in unable to smell coffee but can smell ammonia. Which of the following statements is true about the patient?
options: Ammonia is used for testing olfactory nerve
The olfaction system is not damaged
questions.explanation: Inability to smell coffee (anosmia) indicates olfactory nerve (CN I) damage, whereas perceiving pungent odors like ammonia demonstrates intact trigeminal nerve (CN V) intranasal nociceptive pathways.
questions.educationalObjective: Explain that ammonia stimulates the trigeminal nerve rather than testing true olfaction.
questions.reasoningChain: Head trauma -> olfactory nerve sheared (anosmia to coffee) -> trigeminal nerve intact (detects ammonia irritation).
optionExplanations: Ammonia is an irritant that stimulates intranasal free nerve endings of the trigeminal nerve, not CN I.
The olfactory system is indeed damaged for aromatic scents like coffee.
Ammonia irritates the trigeminal nerve (CN V), explaining why patients can still sense it despite anosmia.
All of the above is correct because statements A, B, and C collectively explain the clinical phenomenon.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Prophylactic dose of Oseltamivir for infants is?
questions.explanation: The standard prophylactic weight-based dose of oseltamivir for infants (aged less than 1 year) is 3 mg/kg twice daily (or total 3-6 mg/kg/day depending on guidelines; standard pediatric recall keys list 3 mg/kg/day or specific weight tiers).
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the prophylactic dosing of oseltamivir for infants.
questions.reasoningChain: Infant influenza exposure -> antiviral chemoprophylaxis -> oseltamivir at 3 mg/kg/day.
optionExplanations: 1 mg/kg/day is insufficient for effective influenza prophylaxis in infants.
3 mg/kg/day is the standard guideline-recommended dosing for infant oseltamivir prophylaxis.
5 mg/kg/day exceeds standard infant prophylactic dosing recommendations.
7 mg/kg/day is excessive and increases toxicity risks.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Pheochromocytoma produces all except?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine-secreting tumors of chromaffin cells that can also secrete various peptides such as calcitonin or VIP, but they do not secrete secretin, which is produced by S-cells of the duodenum.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify secretin as a gastrointestinal hormone not produced by pheochromocytomas.
questions.reasoningChain: Pheochromocytoma -> neural crest origin -> secretes catecholamines, calcitonin, and VIP -> does not secrete secretin.
optionExplanations: Nor-epinephrine is a primary catecholamine secreted by pheochromocytomas.
Secretin is a duodenal hormone and is not produced by adrenal chromaffin tumors.
Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) can occasionally be secreted by pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas.
Calcitonin is frequently co-secreted by neuroendocrine tumor cells in pheochromocytoma/MEN2 settings.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Which of the following is an accessory masticatory muscle?
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is often considered an accessory muscle of mastication because it assists in keeping food between the teeth during chewing by pressing the cheeks against the teeth. The primary muscles of mastication are the masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, and lateral pterygoid, all innervated by the mandibular nerve (V3).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify accessory masticatory muscles assisting the primary muscles of chewing.
questions.reasoningChain: Primary mastication muscles include masseter, temporalis, and pterygoids -> Buccinator aids chewing by keeping food on occlusal surfaces -> Therefore, buccinator acts as an accessory masticatory muscle.
optionExplanations: Buccinator assists chewing by pressing cheeks against teeth, acting as an accessory masticatory muscle.
Masseter is a primary, major muscle of mastication closing the jaw.
Medial pterygoid is a primary muscle of mastication helping in elevation and side-to-side movement.
Lateral pterygoid is a primary muscle of mastication primarily responsible for jaw depression and protrusion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Cut off for diagnosis of Priapism is?
questions.explanation: Priapism is defined clinically as a prolonged penile erection lasting longer than 4 hours that continues beyond or is unrelated to sexual stimulation, requiring urgent intervention.
questions.educationalObjective: State the 4-hour time threshold for defining clinical priapism.
questions.reasoningChain: Prolonged erection -> exceeds 4 hours -> ischemic tissue damage risk -> defines priapism.
optionExplanations: 1 hour is too short; normal erections can occasionally persist longer without ischemic injury.
2 hours is insufficient to meet the standardized diagnostic cutoff for priapism.
3 hours approaches but does not meet the strict 4-hour clinical definition.
4 hours is the established medical cutoff defining pathological priapism requiring urgent management.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: A term neonate was born to G2P1 mother and initial measures were done by your senior resident and he asked you a question "A new born loses maximum heat from?
questions.explanation: Neonates have a high surface-area-to-mass ratio and relatively large head size with prominent blood supply, resulting in the head being the primary site of maximum heat loss.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the head as the primary site of heat loss in a newborn infant.
questions.reasoningChain: Newborn anatomy -> large head surface area -> maximum heat loss occurs from the head.
optionExplanations: The head represents the largest relative surface area in neonates, accounting for maximum heat loss.
The abdomen contributes less to total relative surface area heat dissipation.
Palms and soles have lower relative surface-area-to-mass contributions for total neonatal heat loss.
The neck has minimal surface area compared to the neonatal head.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Glucose is reabsorbed in which part?
questions.explanation: Glucose is almost entirely reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the nephron. This process primarily occurs in the early PCT via secondary active transport, involving SGLT2 co-transporters on the apical membrane and GLUT2 transporters on the basolateral membrane. This ensures that essential glucose is conserved and not excreted in urine under normal physiological conditions, preventing glucosuria.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the primary site and mechanism of glucose reabsorption in the kidney.
questions.reasoningChain: Glucose is vital -> Kidney reabsorbs it -> PCT is the primary site -> Early PCT has high capacity.
optionExplanations: The primary site for nearly complete glucose reabsorption, utilizing SGLT2 and GLUT2 transporters.
Primarily involved in water and ion reabsorption, not significant glucose reabsorption.
Regulates final urine concentration and pH, with no role in glucose reabsorption.
Primarily reabsorbs sodium, chloride, and calcium, not glucose.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: 6-year-old with fever for 3 days with pain in right hypochondrium. On examination tenderness is noted in Right upper quadrant. What is the next best investigation?
questions.explanation: A 6-year-old with fever, right hypochondrium pain, and RUQ tenderness suggests potential hepatobiliary pathology, such as acute cholecystitis, hepatitis, or liver abscess. Ultrasound (USG) is the initial investigation of choice due to its non-invasiveness, lack of radiation, and ability to visualize the gallbladder, bile ducts, and liver parenchyma effectively. It can detect gallstones, wall thickening, or fluid collections.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the initial diagnostic imaging for RUQ pain in a child.
questions.reasoningChain: Child with RUQ pain + fever -> Suspect hepatobiliary issue -> USG is safe, quick, and effective first-line imaging.
optionExplanations: Non-invasive, readily available, and excellent for visualizing the gallbladder, bile ducts, and liver parenchyma.
Useful for specific infections (e.g., hepatitis viruses) but not the immediate best first-line for structural assessment.
Blood tests indicating liver function or damage, but do not provide anatomical information.
More radiation exposure and typically reserved for complex cases or when USG is inconclusive.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Recommended daily dose of Iodine in a child is?
questions.explanation: The recommended daily allowance (RDA) of iodine varies by age. For children aged 6-12 years, the recommended daily intake is generally 90-120 μg. Adequate iodine intake is crucial for thyroid hormone synthesis, which is essential for normal growth, neurodevelopment, and metabolic regulation in children. Deficiency can lead to goiter and impaired cognitive function.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the recommended daily iodine intake for children.
questions.reasoningChain: Iodine is essential for thyroid -> Thyroid needs specific daily amount -> Children have specific needs.
optionExplanations: This range is higher than the general recommendation for children, closer to adult needs.
This range aligns with the generally accepted daily iodine recommendation for school-aged children.
This range is typically too low for adequate iodine intake in children, risking deficiency.
This dose is significantly higher than the recommended daily intake for children and could be excessive.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following is not seen in Horner syndrome?
questions.explanation: Horner syndrome results from damage to the sympathetic pathway to the eye and face. Its classic triad includes ptosis (drooping eyelid), miosis (constricted pupil), and anhidrosis (decreased sweating) on the affected side. Mydriasis, which is pupil dilation, is a feature of sympathetic activation, not sympathetic denervation, and therefore is not seen in Horner syndrome.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the clinical features of Horner syndrome.
questions.reasoningChain: Horner syndrome = sympathetic denervation -> Sympathetic denervation causes specific signs -> Mydriasis is sympathetic activation.
optionExplanations: Mydriasis (pupil dilation) is caused by sympathetic stimulation, not denervation, so it is not seen in Horner syndrome.
Ptosis (drooping of the upper eyelid) is a classic feature due to paralysis of the superior tarsal muscle.
Anhidrosis (decreased sweating) on the affected side of the face is a common sign of sympathetic denervation.
Enophthalmos (sunken eye appearance) is often described, though it is usually a pseudo-enophthalmos due to ptosis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old female comes to the OPD for well-care visits. The patient is completely well and eats a balanced diet. She never smokes or drinks alcohol and has no significant past medical history. On examination, her vitals are normal. The patient tells the physician that next week she will go on a trip to an island and is worried about motion sickness. Which of the following drugs may be considered first-line therapy for this patient's prophylaxis of motion sickness?
questions.explanation: For prophylaxis of motion sickness, antihistamines with anticholinergic properties are considered first-line. Promethazine, a first-generation H1 antihistamine, is highly effective due to its potent anticholinergic and sedative effects, which help to suppress vestibular stimulation and the vomiting center. It should be taken before travel for optimal effect. Other options are generally not first-line for prophylaxis.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify first-line prophylactic medication for motion sickness.
questions.reasoningChain: Motion sickness prophylaxis -> Antihistamines with anticholinergic effects are first-line -> Promethazine fits this profile.
optionExplanations: A first-generation antihistamine with strong anticholinergic and sedative effects, making it first-line for motion sickness prophylaxis.
An antiemetic primarily acting on 5-HT3 receptors, effective for chemotherapy-induced nausea, but not first-line for motion sickness.
A prokinetic and antiemetic, primarily dopamine receptor antagonist, not typically used for motion sickness prophylaxis.
A peripheral dopamine receptor antagonist, primarily used for nausea and vomiting, but not first-line for motion sickness.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following is not correct about Defibrillation?
options: Decrease in success rate with delay in initiation
questions.explanation: Defibrillation is a critical intervention for life-threatening arrhythmias like ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT). It is not easy for untrained persons to perform correctly, and delays significantly decrease success rates and prognosis. Current guidelines recommend immediate defibrillation with minimal interruptions, and subsequent shocks should be delivered rapidly if needed, without a 1-minute gap, as continuous chest compressions are prioritized.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the principles and guidelines for defibrillation.
questions.reasoningChain: Defibrillation is emergency -> Timely and correct application is key -> Delays and interruptions are detrimental.
optionExplanations: Defibrillation requires training for proper pad placement, safety, and rhythm interpretation, making it not easy for untrained persons.
Delay in initiating defibrillation for VF/pVT significantly reduces the chances of successful resuscitation and survival.
Prompt and effective defibrillation is crucial for terminating life-threatening arrhythmias and improving patient outcomes.
Current guidelines emphasize continuous chest compressions and rapid sequential shocks if needed, not a 1-minute gap between shocks.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Exenatide is a new drug used in diabetes mellitus. Mechanism of action of this drug is:
options: Release of insulin via acting as agonist of GLP-1 receptors
questions.answer: Release of insulin via acting as agonist of GLP-1 receptors
questions.explanation: Exenatide is an incretin mimetic, specifically a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist. It mimics the action of natural GLP-1, leading to glucose-dependent insulin release from pancreatic beta cells, suppression of glucagon secretion, slowed gastric emptying, and increased satiety. These actions collectively help to lower blood glucose levels in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the mechanism of action of GLP-1 receptor agonists like Exenatide.
questions.reasoningChain: Exenatide is a GLP-1 mimetic -> GLP-1 agonists stimulate insulin release -> This lowers blood glucose.
optionExplanations: This describes the mechanism of action for DPP-4 inhibitors, a different class of antidiabetic drugs.
Exenatide acts as an agonist at GLP-1 receptors, stimulating glucose-dependent insulin secretion.
This describes the mechanism of action for alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, which reduce carbohydrate absorption.
This describes the mechanism of action for thiazolidinediones (glitazones), which improve insulin sensitivity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: The compound prostaglandin has been indicated in multiple conditions is actually a derivative of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Prostaglandins are a group of lipid compounds derived enzymatically from fatty acids. Specifically, they are synthesized from arachidonic acid, a 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid, through the cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway. Arachidonic acid is released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2 and then converted into various prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and prostacyclins, which act as local mediators.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the precursor molecule for prostaglandin synthesis.
questions.reasoningChain: Prostaglandins are lipid mediators -> They are derived from fatty acids -> Arachidonic acid is the primary precursor.
optionExplanations: Stearic acid is a saturated fatty acid, not the direct precursor for prostaglandin synthesis.
Arachidonic acid is the primary 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid precursor for prostaglandin synthesis.
Linoleic acid is an essential omega-6 fatty acid, but it is not the direct precursor for prostaglandins.
Linolenic acid is an essential omega-3 fatty acid, not the direct precursor for prostaglandins.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Which of the following drug is contraindicated in a pregnant female?
questions.explanation: Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic that is contraindicated in pregnancy due to its known ototoxic effects on the fetus, potentially causing permanent congenital deafness. It belongs to pregnancy category D. Erythromycin, Amoxicillin, and Ceftriaxone are generally considered safer options during pregnancy, falling into categories B or C, with better safety profiles.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify antibiotics contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal harm.
questions.reasoningChain: Antibiotics in pregnancy -> Some are teratogenic -> Streptomycin causes ototoxicity.
optionExplanations: Generally considered safe in pregnancy (Category B), often used for various infections.
A penicillin antibiotic, widely considered safe for use during pregnancy (Category B).
A third-generation cephalosporin, generally considered safe in pregnancy (Category B).
An aminoglycoside antibiotic, contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal ototoxicity (Category D).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Mediastinal surface of the right lung is related to? A. The Azygos vein B. The Right Lymphatic Duct C. The Aorta D. The Trachea
questions.explanation: The mediastinal surface of the right lung is intimately related to several structures within the mediastinum. The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung and then descends along the right side of the vertebral column, making it a key relation. The trachea is also related to the right lung's mediastinal surface, particularly superiorly. The right lymphatic duct is more superior and anterior, while the aorta is primarily related to the left lung.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the anatomical relations of the mediastinal surface of the right lung.
questions.reasoningChain: Right lung mediastinal surface -> Identify adjacent structures -> Azygos vein and trachea are key relations.
optionExplanations: The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung and descends along its mediastinal surface.
The right lymphatic duct is more superior and anterior, not a primary mediastinal surface relation. The trachea is related.
The aorta is primarily related to the mediastinal surface of the left lung, not the right.
Both the azygos vein and the trachea are significant relations to the mediastinal surface of the right lung.
questions.reviewNote: The provided answer 'A only' is incorrect. Both the Azygos vein and the Trachea are related to the mediastinal surface of the right lung. The prompt's options format (A only, B & D only, C only, A & D only) implies that 'A & D only' would be the most accurate choice if 'D. The Trachea' is considered. The explanation reflects the correct anatomical relationships.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Sternum is attached to scapula via?
questions.explanation: The sternum does not directly articulate with the scapula. Instead, the sternum articulates with the clavicle (collarbone) at the sternoclavicular joint. The clavicle then articulates with the scapula at the acromioclavicular joint. Therefore, the clavicle serves as the bony link between the sternum and the scapula, providing the only bony attachment of the upper limb to the axial skeleton.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the bony connections between the sternum and scapula.
questions.reasoningChain: Sternum and scapula connection -> No direct articulation -> Clavicle acts as the intermediary bone.
optionExplanations: The manubrium is the superior part of the sternum, articulating with the clavicle, but not directly with the scapula.
The clavicle articulates with both the sternum (sternoclavicular joint) and the scapula (acromioclavicular joint), linking them.
The first rib articulates with the manubrium of the sternum, but not directly with the scapula.
The second rib articulates with the sternum, but not directly with the scapula.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of methyl dopa?
questions.explanation: Methyldopa is an antihypertensive drug that acts as a prodrug. It is metabolized to alpha-methylnorepinephrine in the brain, which then acts as an alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist. Stimulation of presynaptic alpha-2 receptors in the central nervous system leads to a reduction in sympathetic outflow from the brainstem, resulting in decreased peripheral vascular resistance and heart rate, thereby lowering blood pressure.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the mechanism of action of methyldopa.
questions.reasoningChain: Methyldopa is an antihypertensive -> It's a prodrug -> Metabolized to alpha-methylnorepinephrine -> Agonizes central alpha-2 receptors.
optionExplanations: This describes the mechanism of beta-blockers, not methyldopa.
Agonism of beta-2 receptors would cause bronchodilation and vasodilation, not the primary antihypertensive effect of methyldopa.
Methyldopa's active metabolite acts as an agonist at central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, reducing sympathetic outflow.
Blockade of alpha-2 receptors would increase sympathetic outflow, which is contrary to methyldopa's hypotensive effect.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Retraction of scapula at sternoclavicular joint is done by?
questions.explanation: Retraction of the scapula at the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints is principally executed by the trapezius muscle, assisted by the rhomboids.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the trapezius muscle as responsible for scapular retraction.
questions.reasoningChain: Pulling scapula back toward the spine -> trapezius muscle contraction -> scapular retraction.
optionExplanations: Serratus anterior protracts and rotates the scapula upward.
Trapezius retracts, elevates, and depresses the scapula.
Subscapularis is a rotator cuff muscle that internally rotates the arm.
Supraspinatus initiates arm abduction at the shoulder joint.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A 5-year-old male child is brought to the ophthalmology clinic by his mother with complaints of blurring of vision for one week. The patient further explains that he only has blurring of the far vision and has no problem in his near vision. The patient gives a history of no other abnormalities. For a detailed examination of the eye, the doctor uses a short-acting topical medication which also has a cycloplegic effect. Which of the following drug was used by the doctor in this case?
questions.explanation: Tropicamide is a short-acting topical anticholinergic eye drop that induces mydriasis and cycloplegia for brief ocular examinations in children and adults.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify tropicamide as a short-acting mydriatic and cycloplegic eye drop.
questions.reasoningChain: Short examination needed -> topical antimuscarinic -> tropicamide eye drops provide quick cycloplegia.
optionExplanations: Atropine oral is inappropriate and has prolonged duration.
Atropine eye ointment has an overly prolonged duration of action lasting several days to weeks.
Tropicamide eye drops provide rapid-onset, short-duration mydriasis and cycloplegia ideal for exams.
Phenylephrine causes mydriasis via alpha-1 agonism but lacks significant cycloplegic effect.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Winging of Scapula is due to paralysis of?
questions.explanation: Winging of the scapula is caused by paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle resulting from injury to the long thoracic nerve, leading to the medial border of the scapula protruding posteriorly.
questions.educationalObjective: Link scapular winging to paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle.
questions.reasoningChain: Long thoracic nerve injury -> serratus anterior paralysis -> medial scapular winging.

Serratus anterior paralysis causes the classic winging of the scapula when pushing against a wall.
Latissimus dorsi paralysis affects arm extension, adduction, and medial rotation.
Pectoralis major paralysis affects shoulder adduction and internal rotation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Identify the marked bony process?
questions.explanation: The provided elbow radiograph highlights the proximal end of the radius, specifically identifying the radial head articulating with the capitulum.

Trochlea is the spool-shaped articular surface of the distal humerus articulating with the ulna.
Radial head is the marked structure articulating with the capitulum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: A 6-months-old infant presents to the emergency department with bilious emesis. On further investigation, it is found that the cecum remains fixed in the right upper quadrant due to peritoneal bands. The infant is diagnosed with intestinal malrotation. Which of the following is the correct statement regarding the midgut rotation during embryological development?
questions.explanation: During normal embryological development, the midgut undergoes a total 270-degree rotation in an anticlockwise (counterclockwise) direction around the superior mesenteric artery axis.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall that midgut rotation during embryogenesis is 270 degrees anticlockwise.
questions.reasoningChain: Midgut physiological herniation -> rotation around SMA -> 270-degree anticlockwise return to abdominal cavity.
optionExplanations: 270-degree clockwise is incorrect; the physiological rotation direction is anticlockwise.
270-degree anticlockwise represents the correct embryological midgut rotation angle and direction.
360-degree rotation is abnormal and does not reflect normal embryogenesis.
360-degree anticlockwise rotation exceeds the normal physiological developmental parameters.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: A research article is published about vasa brevia and its branches and course. Concerning the anatomy of vasa brevia, a first-year surgery resident is asked a question by a senior surgeon; the question appears like vasa brevia is the other name for which of the following arteries is carried by the gastrosplenic ligament.
questions.explanation: The vasa brevia are alternate anatomical names for the short gastric arteries, which travel within the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the gastric fundus.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify vasa brevia as another name for the short gastric arteries.
questions.reasoningChain: Gastrosplenic ligament -> carries gastric branches from splenic artery -> short gastric arteries (vasa brevia).
optionExplanations: Long gastric arteries is not the standard anatomical term for these vessels.
Short gastric arteries are synonymous with vasa brevia within the gastrosplenic ligament.
Ileal vasa recta supply the small intestine mesentery, not the stomach.
Jejunal vasa recta supply the jejunum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Identify the marked artery originating from celiac trunk territory?
questions.explanation: The gastroepiploic artery runs along the greater curvature of the stomach within the greater omentum, originating from the celiac trunk via the gastroduodenal artery (right) and splenic artery (left).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the gastroepiploic artery on a celiac trunk vascular diagram.
questions.reasoningChain: Arrow points to vessel along greater curvature -> gastroepiploic artery.
optionExplanations: Splenic artery travels along the superior border of the pancreas toward the spleen.
Gastroepiploic artery runs along the greater curvature of the stomach as indicated by the arrow.
Gastroduodenal artery branches downward posterior to the pylorus.
Left gastric artery ascends along the lesser curvature of the stomach.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: In a healthy adult female, the tail of pancreas lies in lienorenal ligament derived from peritoneum. This is another name for which of the following ligaments?
questions.explanation: The lienorenal ligament, which attaches the spleen to the left kidney and contains the tail of the pancreas and splenic vessels, is also known as the splenorenal ligament.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that lienorenal ligament is synonymous with splenorenal ligament.
questions.reasoningChain: Lienorenal ligament -> connects spleen and kidney -> also called splenorenal ligament.
optionExplanations: Hepatogastric ligament connects the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach.
Hepatoduodenal ligament connects the liver to the duodenum and contains the portal triad.
Gastrosplenic ligament connects the stomach to the spleen and contains short gastric vessels.
Splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament connects the spleen to the posterior abdominal wall/kidney.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Bleeding vessel in hemorrhoids is?
questions.explanation: Internal hemorrhoids originate above the pectinate line and bleed from the superior rectal vein plexus, presenting as painless bright red rectal bleeding.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the superior rectal vein as the bleeding vessel source in internal hemorrhoids.
questions.reasoningChain: Above pectinate line -> internal hemorrhoid -> superior rectal vein plexus involvement -> bleeding.
optionExplanations: Superior rectal artery supplies blood flow, but the dilated venous plexus is the bleeding source.
Superior rectal vein is the primary vascular source of bleeding in internal hemorrhoids.
Middle rectal artery contributes systemic arterial flow but is not the primary hemorrhoidal bleeding source.
Middle rectal vein drains lower pelvic viscera but internal hemorrhoids drain via superior rectal veins.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Foot eversion is caused by?
questions.explanation: Foot eversion is primarily produced by the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis muscles located in the lateral compartment of the leg, innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the peroneus longus muscle as a prime mover for foot eversion.
questions.reasoningChain: Lateral leg compartment -> tendon passes posterior to lateral malleolus -> peroneus longus everts foot.
optionExplanations: Extensor digitorum longus extends toes and assists in ankle dorsiflexion.
Peroneus longus is a primary evertor of the foot.
Tibialis anterior is a primary ankle dorsiflexor and foot invertor.
Tibialis posterior is a primary foot invertor and plantarflexor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Tibial and common peroneal nerve supplies the muscle?
questions.explanation: The biceps femoris muscle has a dual innervation: its long head is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, and its short head is supplied by the common peroneal (fibular) division.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the biceps femoris muscle as receiving supply from both tibial and common peroneal nerves.
questions.reasoningChain: Posterior thigh compartment -> biceps femoris -> long head (tibial) and short head (common peroneal).
optionExplanations: Gracilis is innervated exclusively by the obturator nerve.
Biceps femoris receives dual innervation from both tibial and common peroneal nerves.
Adductor longus is innervated by the obturator nerve.
Adductor magnus has dual innervation (obturator and tibial parts), but biceps femoris is the classic dual-nerve thigh exam answer.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Pilocarpine produces:
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine is a direct-acting muscarinic agonist that contracts the circular smooth muscle of the iris sphincter (sphincter pupillae), producing active miosis (pupillary constriction).
questions.educationalObjective: Understand that pilocarpine causes active miosis via muscarinic receptor stimulation.
questions.reasoningChain: Pilocarpine -> muscarinic agonist -> sphincter pupillae contraction -> active miosis.
optionExplanations: Active miosis results from direct cholinergic stimulation of the iris sphincter muscle.
Active mydriasis is produced by sympathomimetic agents contracting the dilator pupillae.
Miosis induced by pilocarpine is an active, receptor-mediated contraction, not passive.
Passive mydriasis occurs due to withdrawal of parasympathetic tone or sympathetic overactivity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: Drugs Affecting Blood and Blood formation
questions.prompt: Which of the following drugs is a direct inhibitor of clotting factor Xa?
questions.explanation: Apixaban is a direct, oral, active-site inhibitor of coagulation factor Xa, used for stroke prevention and thromboembolism prophylaxis.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify apixaban as a direct oral inhibitor of factor Xa.
questions.reasoningChain: Direct oral anticoagulant -> targets factor Xa active site -> apixaban.
optionExplanations: Apixaban is a direct, oral inhibitor of coagulation factor Xa.
Argatroban is a direct, parenteral thrombin (factor IIa) inhibitor.
Fondaparinux is an indirect, injectable factor Xa inhibitor requiring antithrombin III.
Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent inhibiting cyclooxygenase-1.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Which of the following drug is a protein synthesis inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Linezolid is an oxazolidinone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit, preventing formation of the initiation complex.
questions.educationalObjective: Classify linezolid as an antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis.
questions.reasoningChain: Oxazolidinone class -> binds 50S ribosomal subunit -> inhibits bacterial protein synthesis.
optionExplanations: Linezolid is a protein synthesis inhibitor acting on the 50S ribosomal subunit.
Nevirapine is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor targeting HIV, not bacterial protein synthesis.
Indinavir is an HIV protease inhibitor.
Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Drug of choice for prophylaxis of meningococcal meningitis in a pregnant female after contact with a case is:-
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone is the drug of choice for meningococcal chemoprophylaxis in pregnant women, avoiding the teratogenic and safety concerns associated with rifampicin and ciprofloxacin.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall ceftriaxone as the preferred meningococcal chemoprophylaxis agent in pregnancy.
questions.reasoningChain: Pregnant contact of meningococcal meningitis -> safe prophylaxis needed -> ceftriaxone injection.
optionExplanations: Ciprofloxacin is avoided during pregnancy due to potential cartilage toxicity in the fetus.
Ceftriaxone is the safe drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis in pregnant women.
Cefalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin not indicated for meningococcal prophylaxis.
Rifabutin is less preferred than ceftriaxone for meningococcal prophylaxis in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Purpose of adding zinc to insulin in commercial preparations for treatment of diabetes mellitus is:-
options: Addition of zinc make the insulin effective orally
questions.explanation: Zinc is added to commercial insulin preparations (e.g., Lente, Ultralente) to form stable complexes that decrease solubility and slow absorption, thereby making the insulin formulation long-acting.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the pharmacological purpose of adding zinc to insulin preparations to prolong duration of action.
questions.reasoningChain: Insulin + zinc ions -> crystal/complex formation -> slower subcutaneous absorption -> long-acting insulin.
optionExplanations: Addition of zinc decreases absorption rate, successfully creating long-acting insulin preparations.
Zinc slows absorption, so it is not used to make insulin short-acting.
Fast-acting insulins (e.g., Lispro, Regular) minimize or omit zinc additives to ensure rapid monomer dissociation.
Insulin is a peptide destroyed by gastrointestinal enzymes and cannot be made effective orally by adding zinc.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: . A 40-year-old patient is undergoing surgery. He is given anesthesia. Some other agents are used to aid anaesthesia or to prevent adverse effects of anaesthesia. Which of the following is the shortest-acting muscle relaxant and is considered for rapid sequence induction?
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker with a rapid onset (under 1 minute) and extremely short duration of action (~5-10 minutes), making it ideal for rapid sequence intubation.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify succinylcholine as the shortest-acting neuromuscular blocker used for rapid sequence induction.
questions.reasoningChain: Rapid intubation required -> depolarizing blocker -> ultra-short duration -> succinylcholine.
optionExplanations: Tubocurarine is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker with a longer duration of action.
Succinylcholine is a rapid-onset, ultra-short-acting depolarizing muscle relaxant used for rapid sequence induction.
Pancuronium is a long-acting non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker.
Atracurium is an intermediate-acting non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker cleared by Hofmann elimination.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: The drug that causes fall in elderly patients with postural hypotension is:-
questions.explanation: Prazosin is an alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist that can cause pronounced first-dose orthostatic hypotension and dizziness, predisposing elderly patients to falls.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize prazosin as an alpha-blocker prone to causing postural hypotension and falls in the elderly.
questions.reasoningChain: Alpha-1 blockade -> vasodilation -> postural blood pressure drop -> falls in elderly patients.
optionExplanations: Metformin is an oral biguanide anti-diabetic drug that does not typically cause acute postural hypotension.
Prazosin is an alpha-1 blocker well known for inducing orthostatic hypotension and falls, especially in elderly patients.
Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor causing gastrointestinal side effects, not postural hypotension.
Nor-adrenaline is an endogenous vasopressor that raises blood pressure, rather than causing hypotensive falls.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A 23 year old female presented with burning pain during micturition. On investigations, she is found to be suffering from co-infection with chlamydia and gonococcus. Drug of choice for treatment of this female is:-
questions.explanation: In co-infections with Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, treatment guidelines recommend combination therapy or a regimen covering both organisms, with a single 1g dose of azithromycin covering chlamydia alongside ceftriaxone for gonorrhea.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify azithromycin as part of the recommended regimen for treating chlamydial co-infection.
questions.reasoningChain: Chlamydia and gonorrhea co-infection -> azithromycin covers chlamydia -> ceftriaxone covers gonorrhea.
optionExplanations: Azithromycin is the drug of choice for treating Chlamydia trachomatis.
Ceftriaxone treats Neisseria gonorrhoeae, but azithromycin is specifically paired to cover Chlamydia co-infection.
Fluconazole is an antifungal agent, useless against bacterial sexually transmitted infections.
Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibiotic used for anaerobic and gram-positive infections, not standard for chlamydia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A patient was given anti-cancer therapy and developed neutropenia. Which of the following drug can be used to prevent neutropenia in next cycle of chemotherapy?
questions.explanation: Filgrastim is a recombinant granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) used to stimulate neutrophil production and shorten the duration of chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify filgrastim as a G-CSF analog used to prevent or treat chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.
questions.reasoningChain: Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia -> administer G-CSF -> stimulates bone marrow neutrophil production -> filgrastim.
optionExplanations: Filgrastim (G-CSF) stimulates neutrophil recovery to prevent chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.
Prednisolone is a corticosteroid used as an anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressant.
Vitamin B12 treats megaloblastic anemia, not acute chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.
Folic acid is used to prevent neural tube defects and folate-deficiency anemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: The following image shows?
questions.explanation: The barium swallow image shows simultaneous, uncoordinated, non-peristaltic contractions giving a 'corkscrew' or 'rosary bead' esophagus appearance, which is classic for diffuse esophageal spasm.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the corkscrew esophagus appearance on barium swallow as diagnostic of diffuse esophageal spasm.
questions.reasoningChain: Barium swallow -> simultaneous non-peristaltic contractions -> corkscrew esophagus -> diffuse esophageal spasm.
optionExplanations: Achalasia cardia presents with a smooth 'bird's beak' tapering of the lower esophageal sphincter.
Diffuse esophageal spasm shows repetitive, simultaneous contractions producing a classic corkscrew esophagus.
Carcinoma esophagus typically shows an irregular filling defect, shouldering, and mucosal destruction.
Schatzki's ring presents as a thin, smooth, web-like stricture at the gastroesophageal junction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following is not done in Carcinoma Oesophagus?
questions.explanation: Esophageal pH-metry is used to evaluate gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and acid exposure, whereas carcinoma esophagus is diagnosed and staged using biopsy, CT chest, and PET scans.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that pH-metry is not part of the standard diagnostic workup for esophageal carcinoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Esophageal cancer workup -> needs tissue diagnosis (biopsy) and staging (CT/PET) -> pH-metry is for GERD.
optionExplanations: Biopsy is essential for histopathological confirmation of esophageal carcinoma.
pH-metry assesses acid reflux for GERD and is not indicated for staging or diagnosing esophageal cancer.
CT chest is crucial for staging local invasion and distant metastasis in esophageal cancer.
PET scan evaluates metabolic activity and distant metastasis in staging esophageal cancer.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following features are true about Allergic Broncho Pulmonary Aspergilloma? 1. Distal bronchiectasis 2. Serum precipitins to Aspergillus 3. increased lgE Levels 4. Seen in asthmatics
questions.explanation: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is characterized by asthma, proximal (not distal) bronchiectasis, elevated serum IgE, peripheral eosinophilia, and positive serum precipitins to Aspergillus.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the diagnostic features of ABPA including proximal bronchiectasis, elevated IgE, and Aspergillus precipitins.
questions.reasoningChain: Aspergillus hypersensitivity in asthmatics -> elevated IgE + serum precipitins -> proximal bronchiectasis.
optionExplanations: 1 is incorrect because bronchiectasis in ABPA is characteristically proximal, not distal.
Serum precipitins to Aspergillus are a key diagnostic criterion present in ABPA.
Elevated total and specific IgE levels are a hallmark laboratory finding in ABPA.
ABPA characteristically occurs in patients with underlying asthma or cystic fibrosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Correct about marble Schonberg disease is?
questions.explanation: Albers-Schönberg disease (marble bone disease) is an older eponym for autosomal dominant osteopetrosis, a genetic bone disorder characterized by defective osteoclast function leading to dense, brittle bones.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Albers-Schönberg disease as a synonym for osteopetrosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Marble bone disease / Albers-Schönberg disease -> defective osteoclasts -> osteopetrosis.
optionExplanations: Osteopetrosis is also known as Albers-Schönberg disease or marble bone disease.
Osteomalacia involves defective bone mineralization due to vitamin D deficiency.
Osteosclerosis refers to increased bone density, which is a sign rather than the specific syndrome name.
Osteonecrosis is bone infarction due to interrupted blood supply.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Why Covid-19 a major global concern despite the property of influenza spreading faster than COVID-19?
options: Median incubation period is more in influenza
Serial interval is 5-6 days in influenza
Reproductive number for Influenza is more
questions.explanation: COVID-19 became a major global concern because its basic reproduction number ($R_0$) of approximately 2.0 to 2.5 combined with significant presymptomatic transmission and high morbidity/mortality made containment challenging compared to seasonal influenza.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the epidemiological parameters (like $R_0$) that drove the global impact of COVID-19.
questions.reasoningChain: High transmission potential ($R_0$ 2-2.5) + severe clinical outcomes -> global public health concern.
optionExplanations: Influenza has a shorter median incubation period, not longer.
A reproduction number for COVID-19 of 2-2.5 drives sustained community transmission and pandemic spread.
Serial interval of influenza is relatively short, but does not explain COVID-19 severity concerns.
Influenza often has a lower baseline $R_0$ than emerging pandemic strains, but COVID-19's impact stems from naive populations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Mental retardation is seen in?
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, leading to accumulation of phenylalanine and severe intellectual disability (mental retardation) if untreated from infancy.
questions.educationalObjective: Link phenylketonuria to phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency and resulting mental retardation.
questions.reasoningChain: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency -> toxic phenylalanine accumulation -> irreversible brain damage and mental retardation.
optionExplanations: Phenylketonuria classically results in intellectual disability/mental retardation if dietary phenylalanine is not restricted.
Alkaptonuria causes homogentisic acid accumulation leading to ochronosis and arthritis without mental retardation.
Albinism results in lack of melanin pigmentation without primary cognitive impairment.
Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) causes neurodegeneration and ketoacidosis due to branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase defect.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Reversible dementia is seen in?
questions.explanation: Subacute combined degeneration (SACD) of the spinal cord is caused by vitamin B12 deficiency and presents with neurological deficits and dementia that can be reversible with timely vitamin B12 replacement.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify subacute combined degeneration as a treatable, reversible cause of dementia.
questions.reasoningChain: Vitamin B12 deficiency -> SACD -> cognitive impairment and spinal cord demyelination -> reversible with treatment.
optionExplanations: Subacute combined degeneration (SACD) is a classic reversible cause of vitamin B12 deficiency-related dementia.
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive, irreversible neurodegenerative dementia.
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a rapidly progressive and fatal prion disease.
Pick's disease (frontotemporal dementia) is a progressive and irreversible neurodegenerative condition.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding Parkinson disease?
options: Usage of Carbidopa leads to on and off phenomenon
Slight tremor in the hand or foot followed by jaw
Cog wheel rigidity or lead pipe rigidity is seen
questions.answer: Usage of Carbidopa leads to on and off phenomenon
questions.explanation: The 'on-off' phenomenon is a motor fluctuation commonly seen with long-term levodopa therapy in Parkinson's disease, not carbidopa. Carbidopa is combined with levodopa solely to inhibit peripheral decarboxylation.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify that the on-off phenomenon is associated with chronic levodopa therapy rather than carbidopa.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic levodopa therapy -> wearing off and on-off motor fluctuations -> carbidopa inhibits peripheral metabolism but does not cause the phenomenon.
optionExplanations: Manganese toxicity can indeed cause secondary Parkinsonism (basal ganglia damage).
The on-off phenomenon is a complication of long-term levodopa therapy, making the statement attributing it solely to carbidopa incorrect.
Parkinson's disease classically presents with resting tremor (e.g., pill-rolling) starting in the hand or foot.
Cogwheel and lead pipe rigidity are hallmark extrapyramidal signs of Parkinson's disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: The following patient has presented after chest trauma. On examination crepitus is felt. The clinical diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of chest trauma accompanied by palpable crepitus (crackling sensation under the skin) indicates air dissecting into the subcutaneous tissues, known as subcutaneous emphysema.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize palpable crepitus following chest trauma as a sign of subcutaneous emphysema.
questions.reasoningChain: Chest trauma -> air leakage from lung/airway -> tracking into subcutaneous fat -> subcutaneous emphysema with crepitus.
optionExplanations: Subcutaneous emphysema is characterized by crepitus upon palpation due to air in the soft tissues.
Gas gangrene is caused by bacterial infection (e.g., Clostridium perfringens) producing tissue gas without acute chest trauma.
Acute tubular necrosis is a form of intrinsic acute kidney injury.
Hyperbaric decompression sickness occurs due to rapid ascent from high-pressure environments.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Commonest on the diagnosis of the image shown:
questions.explanation: The erect chest X-ray demonstrates free air under the right hemidiaphragm (pneumoperitoneum), appearing as a crescent-shaped radiolucency, which is indicative of hollow viscus perforation.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify pneumoperitoneum (free air under the diaphragm) on an erect chest radiograph.
questions.reasoningChain: Erect chest X-ray -> crescentic radiolucency beneath diaphragm -> free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum).
optionExplanations: Pneumoperitoneum is demonstrated by free air beneath the diaphragmatic shadow on an erect radiograph.
Pneumothorax shows visceral pleural lines and absent lung markings at the periphery.
Eventration of the diaphragm shows elevation of an intact diaphragmatic leaflet.
Pneumomediastinum shows air outlining mediastinal structures and great vessels.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Mark the true statements? 1. MEN 2B is also known as Sipple syndrome 2. MEN 1 is also known as Werner syndrome 3. Marfanoid Habitus is a feature of MEN 2B 4. MEN 4 is a/w CDKN1B
questions.explanation: MEN 1 is known as Werner syndrome (not MEN 2B, which is Wermer's vs Sipple's: MEN 2A is Sipple syndrome, MEN 1 is Wermer syndrome; note: Werner syndrome is adult progeria, whereas Wermer syndrome is MEN 1). Marfanoid habitus and mucosal neuromas are features of MEN 2B, and MEN 4 is associated with germline mutations in CDKN1B.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify correct associations among multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes (MEN 2B features marfanoid habitus, MEN 4 involves CDKN1B).
questions.reasoningChain: MEN 2B -> marfanoid habitus; MEN 4 -> CDKN1B gene mutation -> statements 3 and 4 are correct.
optionExplanations: Statement 1 is incorrect (Sipple syndrome is MEN 2A, not MEN 2B).
Statement 2 is often a naming confusion (Wermer syndrome is MEN 1, whereas Werner syndrome is adult progeria).
Statements 3 and 4 correctly pair MEN 2B with marfanoid habitus and MEN 4 with CDKN1B.
Statements 1 and 2 contain eponym nomenclature inaccuracies regarding Sipple and Werner syndromes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Among the following options, which of them is present in the least concentration in intracellular fluid (ICF)?
questions.explanation: Intracellular fluid (ICF) has high concentrations of potassium, magnesium, and proteins, whereas extracellular fluid (ECF) has high sodium, chloride, and calcium. Calcium is maintained at extremely low ionized concentrations within the cytoplasm of cells to prevent unwanted precipitation and to serve as a vital secondary messenger.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the relative concentrations of intracellular versus extracellular ions.
questions.reasoningChain: Intracellular fluid is rich in potassium, magnesium, and proteins -> Calcium acts as an intracellular messenger and is actively extruded -> Calcium exists in the lowest concentration inside the cell.
optionExplanations: Calcium is maintained at very low concentrations within the ICF to function effectively as a signaling molecule.
Magnesium is the second most abundant intracellular cation, present in much higher amounts than calcium.
Potassium is the principal intracellular cation, present in very high concentrations.
Proteins are abundant intracellularly, contributing significantly to the intracellular osmolarity and buffer systems.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: In good pasture syndrome, which organ is involved apart from lung?
questions.explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is an autoimmune disorder characterized by autoantibodies against type IV collagen, classically resulting in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (kidney involvement) and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (lung involvement).
questions.educationalObjective: Recall that Goodpasture syndrome involves both the lungs and the kidneys.
questions.reasoningChain: Anti-GBM antibodies -> pulmonary hemorrhage + renal glomerulonephritis -> kidney and lung involvement.
optionExplanations: The kidney is one of the two primary target organs involved in Goodpasture syndrome.
The liver is not a primary target organ in Goodpasture syndrome.
The spleen is not involved in the pathogenesis of Goodpasture anti-GBM disease.
The heart is not targeted by anti-type IV collagen antibodies in this syndrome.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Resistance against passive stretch is called?
questions.explanation: Muscle tone is defined clinically and physiologically as the resistance of muscle to passive stretch or elongation at rest.
questions.educationalObjective: Define muscle tone as the resistance against passive stretch.
questions.reasoningChain: Passive stretch applied to resting muscle -> reflex resistance -> muscle tone.
optionExplanations: Tone represents the baseline resistance of a muscle to passive stretch.
Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes.
Rigidity is a velocity-independent resistance to passive movement throughout the range of motion.
Paratonia (Gegenhalten) is an inability to relax muscles, seen in frontal lobe dysfunction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Enterokinase is an activator of?
questions.explanation: Enterokinase (enteropeptidase), an enzyme located on the brush border of the duodenal mucosa, cleaves trypsinogen into its active form, trypsin, which in turn activates other pancreatic zymogens.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify enterokinase as the intestinal brush border enzyme that activates trypsinogen.
questions.reasoningChain: Duodenal brush border -> enterokinase -> converts trypsinogen to active trypsin.
optionExplanations: Trypsinogen is the zymogen substrate activated directly by enterokinase.
Trypsin is the active enzyme produced after enterokinase cleavage.
Chymotrypsinogen is activated by trypsin, not directly by enterokinase.
Antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor, not an activated digestive enzyme.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a component of child pugh Classification?
questions.explanation: The Child-Pugh score assesses chronic liver disease severity using five parameters: total bilirubin, serum albumin, prothrombin time (INR), ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. SGOT (AST) is not a component.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the components of the Child-Pugh classification and recognize SGOT as an excluded parameter.
questions.reasoningChain: Child-Pugh score components -> Bilirubin, Albumin, PT/INR, Ascites, Encephalopathy -> SGOT is not included.
optionExplanations: SGOT (AST) is a transaminase and is not included in the Child-Pugh scoring system.
Bilirubin is a primary component assessing liver excretory function in Child-Pugh.
Albumin measures hepatic synthetic function and is part of the Child-Pugh score.
Prothrombin time / INR evaluates coagulation factor synthesis and is a Child-Pugh parameter.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Which structure connects the Broca's area and Wernicke area?
questions.explanation: The arcuate fasciculus is a crucial bundle of association fibers connecting the posterior temporoparietal junction (Wernicke's area), responsible for language comprehension, to the frontal lobe (Broca's area), involved in speech production. This pathway is essential for integrating these two areas, particularly for tasks like repeating spoken words. Damage to this tract can result in conduction aphasia, where repetition is impaired despite relatively preserved comprehension and fluency.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the arcuate fasciculus as the primary connection between Broca's and Wernicke's areas.
questions.reasoningChain: Broca's and Wernicke's areas are language centers; their functional connection is mediated by the arcuate fasciculus.

Anterior commissure connects the temporal lobes and amygdalae, involved in pain and memory.
Corpus callosum is a large commissural tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.
Fornix is a C-shaped fiber bundle involved in memory formation, part of the limbic system.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Fulminant diabetes mellitus is seen in?
questions.explanation: Fulminant type 1 diabetes mellitus is a distinct, rapidly progressive form of diabetes characterized by abrupt onset of hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis, often without typical autoimmune markers. It is strongly associated with viral infections, particularly Coxsackie B virus, which is believed to trigger acute destruction of pancreatic beta-cells. This rapid and severe presentation differentiates it from classic autoimmune type 1 diabetes.
questions.educationalObjective: Associate Coxsackie B virus with the etiology of fulminant type 1 diabetes mellitus.
questions.reasoningChain: Fulminant diabetes has rapid onset and severe beta-cell destruction; viral infections like Coxsackie B are known triggers.
optionExplanations: Diabetic ketoacidosis is a complication of diabetes, not a cause of fulminant diabetes itself.
Coxsackie B virus is a recognized trigger for the rapid onset of fulminant type 1 diabetes.
Non-ketotic hyperosmolar coma is a complication of type 2 diabetes, not a cause of fulminant diabetes.
Autoimmune pancreatitis is a distinct inflammatory condition of the pancreas, not directly causing fulminant diabetes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Calcium-binding proteins are proteins that participate in calcium cell signaling pathways by binding to Ca2+, which plays an important role in many cellular processes. Which of the following is not a calcium-binding protein?
questions.explanation: Clathrin is a protein involved in forming clathrin-coated vesicles, essential for endocytosis and intracellular trafficking. It does not directly bind calcium as part of a calcium signaling pathway. In contrast, calbindin, calmodulin, and troponin are well-known calcium-binding proteins. Calbindin buffers calcium, calmodulin mediates many calcium-dependent cellular processes, and troponin regulates muscle contraction by binding calcium.
questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate clathrin from common calcium-binding proteins involved in cell signaling.
questions.reasoningChain: Calcium-binding proteins mediate calcium signaling; clathrin's primary role is vesicle formation, not calcium binding.
optionExplanations: Calbindin is a calcium-binding protein that buffers intracellular calcium levels.
Calmodulin is a ubiquitous calcium-binding protein that mediates many calcium-dependent cellular processes.
Troponin is a calcium-binding protein crucial for regulating muscle contraction in striated muscle.
Clathrin is a protein involved in forming coated vesicles for endocytosis, not a calcium-binding protein.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 6 year presents with low grade fever for 7 days and on examination has enlarged cervical lymph nodes with palpable spleen tip. He was given ampicillin followed by development of extensive rash all over the body. Diagnosis is?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of low-grade fever, enlarged cervical lymph nodes, and palpable spleen tip in a 6-year-old is highly suggestive of infectious mononucleosis, typically caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). A classic clue for this diagnosis is the development of an extensive rash after administration of ampicillin (or amoxicillin), which occurs in a high percentage of patients with EBV infection treated with these antibiotics.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the classic triad of infectious mononucleosis and the characteristic rash with ampicillin.
questions.reasoningChain: Fever, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly suggest mononucleosis; ampicillin-induced rash confirms it.
optionExplanations: Infectious mononucleosis presents with fever, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and ampicillin rash.
Scarlet fever presents with a sandpaper-like rash, pharyngitis, and strawberry tongue, not splenomegaly.
Kawasaki disease involves fever, conjunctivitis, rash, lymphadenopathy, but not typically splenomegaly or ampicillin rash.
Hodgkin's lymphoma is a malignancy, less likely to present acutely with an ampicillin-induced rash.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Histamine is secreted by?
questions.explanation: Histamine is primarily secreted by enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the gastric mucosa. These cells are stimulated by gastrin and acetylcholine to release histamine, which then acts on H2 receptors on parietal cells to stimulate gastric acid secretion. While parietal cells respond to histamine, they do not secrete it. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, and oxyntic cells are another name for parietal cells.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells as the primary source of histamine in the stomach.
questions.reasoningChain: Histamine stimulates acid secretion; enterochromaffin-like cells are the source of gastric histamine.
optionExplanations: Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the gastric mucosa are the primary secretors of histamine.
Parietal cells (also called oxyntic cells) secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, not histamine.
Oxyntic cell is another name for a parietal cell, which secretes acid, not histamine.
Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase, not histamine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which is correct about rheumatoid nodules?
options: Tender, located on extensor surface and seen with arthritis
Non tender, located on extensor surface and seen with arthritis
Non tender, located on flexor surface and seen with arthritis
Tender, located on flexor surface and seen with arthritis

questions.explanation: Rheumatoid nodules are a characteristic extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis, typically found in patients with severe, long-standing disease. They are classically described as firm, non-tender, subcutaneous nodules. Their most common location is over extensor surfaces, particularly around the elbows, but they can also occur in other pressure areas or internal organs. Their presence is often associated with more aggressive disease.
