questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Narrowest part of airway in infant:
questions.explanation: In infants and young children, the narrowest part of the airway is the subglottis, specifically at the level of the cricoid cartilage. In contrast, the narrowest part of the adult airway is the glottis (rima glottidis).
questions.educationalObjective: The subglottis is the narrowest portion of the pediatric airway.
questions.reasoningChain: Pediatric airway anatomy -> cricoid ring is rigid and narrowest -> Subglottis.
optionExplanations: Supraglottis is wider and includes the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds.
Glottis is the narrowest part in adults, formed by the vocal cords.
Subglottis is the narrowest airway segment in infants and children.
Epiglottis is a leaf-shaped elastic cartilage protecting the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A 15 year old male patient presented with nasal mass reaching upto cheek and causing unilateral obstruction with intermittent epistaxis. Most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a benign, highly vascular tumor that typically affects adolescent males. It presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent, profuse epistaxis.
questions.educationalObjective: JNA is a vascular tumor in adolescent males causing nasal obstruction and epistaxis.
questions.reasoningChain: Adolescent male + unilateral nasal mass + recurrent epistaxis -> Juvenile angiofibroma.
optionExplanations: Angiofibroma is the classic diagnosis for a vascular nasal mass in adolescent males with epistaxis.
Nasal polyp presents with pale, non-tender masses causing obstruction without severe epistaxis.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is more common in adults and associated with EBV and cervical nodes.
Inverted papilloma typically presents with unilateral obstruction and friable mucosal lesions in older adults.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: High Tracheostomy is done in which of the following?
questions.explanation: A high tracheostomy is performed above the isthmus of the thyroid gland, typically indicated in cases of laryngeal pathology such as carcinoma of the larynx where the lower trachea is clear.
questions.educationalObjective: High tracheostomy is indicated in laryngeal carcinoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Carcinoma of larynx -> obstructs upper airway -> requires tracheostomy above thyroid isthmus (high tracheostomy).
optionExplanations: Laryngeal papilloma often requires conservative endoscopic management rather than high tracheostomy.
Carcinoma larynx is a classic indication for high tracheostomy.
Bilateral vocal fold palsy can be managed with various airway procedures depending on urgency.
Laryngomalacia is managed conservatively as it usually resolves spontaneously.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: All are parts of Hypopharynx except
questions.explanation: The hypopharynx (laryngopharynx) extends from the superior border of the epiglottis to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage and includes the pyriform sinus, posterior pharyngeal wall, and post-cricoid area. The vallecula is located in the oropharynx at the base of the tongue.
questions.educationalObjective: The vallecula is part of the oropharynx, not the hypopharynx.
questions.reasoningChain: Hypopharynx subdivisions -> pyriform sinus, post-cricoid, posterior wall -> vallecula is in oropharynx.
optionExplanations: Posterior pharyngeal wall forms part of the hypopharynx.
Pyriform sinus is a mucosal recess located in the hypopharynx.
Post cricoid area is situated in the anterior wall of the hypopharynx.
Vallecula is located at the base of the tongue within the oropharynx.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A 3 yrs old child presented with profound Sensorineural deafness, not responding to hearing aids with intact auditory nerve function. Which of the following procedures is preferred in this patient?
questions.explanation: A child with profound sensorineural hearing loss who does not benefit from conventional hearing aids but has an intact auditory nerve is the ideal candidate for a cochlear implant to directly stimulate the spiral ganglion cells.
questions.educationalObjective: Cochlear implants are indicated for profound sensorineural hearing loss with an intact cochlear nerve.
questions.reasoningChain: Profound sensorineural deafness + hearing aid failure + intact auditory nerve -> Cochlear implant.
optionExplanations: Hearing aids are insufficient for profound hearing loss as stated in the prompt.
BAHA (Bone Anchored Hearing Aid) is used for conductive or mixed hearing loss or single-sided deafness.
Cochlear implant is the preferred treatment for profound sensorineural hearing loss with intact nerve.
Auditory brainstem implant is reserved for patients with absent or damaged cochlear nerves (e.g., neurofibromatosis type 2).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A patient presented with a 2 day history of fever and difficulty in swallowing. On examination there was swelling seen in the oropharynx pushing tonsil to midline and swelling over the upper part of neck. What is the most likely diagnosis:
questions.explanation: Parapharyngeal abscess presents with fever, dysphagia, swelling in the oropharynx pushing the tonsil medially, and swelling in the neck (superior/inferior to the hyoid), distinguishing it from peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) which lacks external neck swelling.
questions.educationalObjective: Parapharyngeal abscess involves both oropharyngeal and neck swelling with medial tonsillar displacement.
questions.reasoningChain: Oropharyngeal swelling with medialized tonsil + neck swelling -> Parapharyngeal abscess.
optionExplanations: Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) causes medial tonsil displacement without external neck swelling.
Parapharyngeal abscess presents with both oropharyngeal and prominent neck swelling.
Retropharyngeal abscess presents with posterior pharyngeal wall bulging and dysphagia.
Tonsillitis causes bilateral or unilateral tonsillar inflammation without deep fascial space abscess formation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Deep lobe of parotid gland swelling presents at
questions.explanation: The parotid gland is divided by the facial nerve into superficial and deep lobes. Tumors or swellings originating in the deep lobe of the parotid gland typically expand medially and present as a swelling in the parapharyngeal space or as a bulge in the lateral pharyngeal wall/soft palate.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the anatomical presentation of deep lobe parotid gland lesions.
questions.reasoningChain: Deep lobe of parotid gland lies medial to the facial nerve -> Expansion grows medially toward the upper pharynx -> Presentation typically manifests as a parapharyngeal space mass.
optionExplanations: Swelling below the ear lobe is characteristic of superficial parotid gland lesions or tail of the parotid.
Cheek swellings are generally associated with superficial parotid tumors or Stensen's duct pathology.
Temporal lobe is an intracranial structure and not a direct site for parotid swelling presentation.
Parapharyngeal space is where deep lobe parotid tumors characteristically present and bulge.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Which of the following muscles is the life saving muscle of larynx that pulls back vocal cords in order for breathing to take place
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle is the sole abductor of the vocal cords. By rotating the arytenoid cartilages laterally, it widens the rima glottidis, serving as the critical life-saving muscle for respiration.
questions.educationalObjective: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle responsible for vocal cord abduction.
questions.reasoningChain: Abduction of vocal cords -> opening airway -> Posterior cricoarytenoid muscle action.
optionExplanations: Cricothyroid muscle tensor of the vocal cords, innervated by the superior laryngeal nerve.
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor and life-saving muscle of the larynx.
Lateral cricoarytenoid adducts the vocal cords.
Transverse arytenoid adducts the vocal cords by approximating the arytenoid cartilages.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Rodent ulcers are which type of malignancy
questions.explanation: Rodent ulcer is the classic clinical term for nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC) of the skin, characterized by a slow-growing, pearly papule with telangiectasias that eventually undergoes central ulceration with rolled borders.
questions.educationalObjective: Rodent ulcer is synonymous with basal cell carcinoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Nodular skin lesion with rolled border and central ulceration -> rodent ulcer -> Basal cell carcinoma.
optionExplanations: Squamous cell carcinoma presents as scaly, hyperkeratotic plaques with potential for metastasis.
Basal cell carcinoma is commonly known as a rodent ulcer due to its locally destructive nature.
Malignant melanoma is an aggressive pigmented tumor arising from melanocytes.
Adenocarcinoma is a glandular malignancy, uncommon as a primary cutaneous rodent ulcer.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: What is the most common cause of deafness in a patient of Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma:
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma frequently originates near the fossa of Rosenmüller, obstructing the pharyngeal opening of the Eustachian tube. This leads to negative middle ear pressure and the accumulation of fluid, causing serous otitis media and conductive hearing loss.
questions.educationalObjective: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma causes serous otitis media by obstructing the Eustachian tube.
questions.reasoningChain: Nasopharyngeal mass -> Eustachian tube obstruction -> negative middle ear pressure -> serous otitis media.
optionExplanations: Metastasis to the temporal bone is uncommon as the primary cause of early deafness in NPC.
Middle ear infection is secondary, but the primary fluid accumulation is sterile serous otitis media.
Serous otitis media is the most common cause of conductive hearing loss in nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Direct tumor infiltration of the middle ear is rare compared to Eustachian tube dysfunction.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Most Common Presenting Complaint of Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma often presents insidiously with painless upper cervical lymphadenopathy due to early metastasis to the deep cervical lymph nodes, even before primary mucosal symptoms appear.
questions.educationalObjective: Cervical lymphadenopathy is the most frequent presenting sign of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Nasopharyngeal malignancy -> early lymphatic spread -> painless cervical lymphadenopathy as most common presentation.
optionExplanations: Cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common presenting complaint of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Hearing loss due to serous otitis media is a frequent but secondary presentation.
Airway obstruction occurs in advanced stages of tumor growth.
Epistaxis is common but typically manifests as blood-tinged nasal discharge rather than the primary complaint.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Structures not seen in indirect laryngoscopy?
questions.explanation: During indirect laryngoscopy, the anterior commissure of the vocal folds is often difficult to visualize completely due to the angle of the laryngeal mirror and the overhang of the epiglottis.
questions.educationalObjective: The anterior commissure is frequently obscured during indirect laryngoscopy.
questions.reasoningChain: Indirect laryngoscopy view -> anterior laryngeal structures obscured by epiglottis -> Anterior commissure poorly seen.
optionExplanations: Anterior commissure is notoriously difficult to visualize fully on indirect laryngoscopy.
Posterior commissure is easily visualized in the posterior aspect of the laryngeal view.
Epiglottis is prominently seen at the top of the laryngeal view.
False vocal cords are readily observed lateral to the true vocal cords.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Earliest symptoms of vocal fold growth is?
questions.explanation: The earliest symptom of any mass or lesion on the vocal folds (such as nodules, polyps, or early carcinoma) is a change in voice quality, most commonly hoarseness.
questions.educationalObjective: Change of voice is the earliest symptom of vocal fold lesions.
questions.reasoningChain: Vocal fold lesion -> disrupts normal mucosal vibration -> early change of voice (hoarseness).
optionExplanations: Cough is a non-specific airway symptom, not the earliest primary sign of a vocal fold growth.
Change of voice (hoarseness) is the earliest and most sensitive symptom of vocal cord pathology.
Fatigue of voice occurs with prolonged speaking but follows initial hoarseness.
Pain is a late symptom indicating deep invasion or cartilage involvement.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Parotid gland is supplied by which nerve
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic secretomotor innervation to the parotid gland is provided by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). Preganglionic fibers travel via the tympanic plexus and lesser petrosal nerve to synapse in the otic ganglion.
questions.educationalObjective: The parotid gland receives parasympathetic secretomotor supply from the glossopharyngeal nerve.
questions.reasoningChain: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) -> lesser petrosal nerve -> otic ganglion -> auriculotemporal nerve -> parotid gland.
optionExplanations: Facial nerve runs through the parotid gland but supplies muscles of facial expression, not parotid secretion.
Glossopharyngeal nerve provides parasympathetic secretomotor innervation to the parotid gland.
Vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to thoracic and abdominal viscera.
Hypoglossal nerve supplies intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: Grounds of divorce:
questions.explanation: Under Hindu Marriage Act and general legal jurisprudence regarding matrimonial remedies, impotence existing at the time of marriage and continuing until the institution of the suit is a ground for nullity. Impotence developing *after* marriage is generally not recognized as a statutory ground for divorce.
questions.educationalObjective: Impotence existing prior to and at marriage is a ground for nullity, whereas impotence developing after marriage is not typically a statutory ground.
questions.reasoningChain: Matrimonial law -> impotence must exist at marriage -> post-marriage impotence is not a standard statutory ground.
optionExplanations: Sterility (inability to conceive) is distinct from impotence and is not a statutory ground for divorce.
Frigidity alone without specific legal provisions is generally not a direct statutory ground for divorce.
Impotence developing after marriage is legally not considered a ground for divorce in traditional jurisdictions.
Poverty is never a legal ground for divorce.
questions.reviewNote: Review note: The prompt's keyed option 'Impotence developing after the marriage' is legally incorrect in standard jurisdictions (impotence must be incurable and exist *prior* to marriage). However, keeping historical exam key compliance in mind, the question is flagged for legal inaccuracy.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: What is the IPC section for causing abortion without a woman's consent?
questions.explanation: Under the Indian Penal Code (IPC), Section 312 deals with causing miscarriage without consent, Section 313 deals with causing miscarriage without woman's consent (where the woman is not necessarily pregnant with quicking in older terminology), and Section 314 deals with death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage.
questions.educationalObjective: IPC Section 313 defines punishment for causing an abortion without the woman's consent.
questions.reasoningChain: Causing abortion -> without consent -> IPC Section 313.
optionExplanations: IPC 312 deals with causing miscarriage with consent (when not done in good faith to save life).
IPC 313 deals specifically with causing miscarriage without the woman's consent.
IPC 314 deals with death caused by an act done with intent to cause miscarriage.
IPC 315 deals with acts done with intent to prevent a child being born alive or to cause it to die after birth.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: In corrosive acid case stomach is opened along
questions.explanation: In forensic autopsies involving suspected poisoning or corrosive acid ingestion, the stomach is incised along its greater curvature. This prevents artifactual damage to lesions and ulcers typically located along the lesser curvature.
questions.educationalObjective: The stomach is opened along the greater curvature during forensic autopsies to preserve lesser curvature lesions.
questions.reasoningChain: Corrosive acid poisoning -> lesions/perforations occur on lesser curvature -> stomach opened along greater curvature to protect pathology.
optionExplanations: Lesser curvature is the common site of peptic ulcers and corrosive pooling, so cutting it would destroy evidence.
Greater curvature is the standard site for incision to preserve lesser curvature pathology.
Vertical incision is not the standard forensic protocol for gastric examination.
Pylorus is a sphincter region, not the line of incision.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: Inhaling the cloth soaked in drug is
questions.explanation: Inhalant abuse terminology distinguishes between methods: 'huffing' involves soaking a rag or cloth in the volatile substance and holding it to the mouth or nose, whereas 'sniffing' involves inhaling directly from the container.
questions.educationalObjective: Inhaling a drug from a soaked cloth is termed huffing.
questions.reasoningChain: Drug-soaked cloth -> inhaled -> terminology is huffing.
optionExplanations: Bagging involves inhaling fumes from a substance placed inside a plastic or paper bag.
Spraying involves aerosolizing a substance directly into the nose or mouth.
Huffing specifically refers to inhaling from a soaked cloth or rag placed over the face.
Sniffing involves direct inhalation from the container or a surface.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: One of the victims of the fire which had destroyed 6 huts in a nearby slum has decided to give a dying declaration. The doctor was called in as part of the team to record the statement. Which among the following is the role of the doctor?
options: To record statement even in presence of magistrate
Put person under oath before declaration
questions.explanation: When a doctor is called to record a dying declaration, their primary medicolegal duty is to examine and certify whether the patient is in a fit mental state (compos mentis) to make a reliable statement.
questions.educationalObjective: The doctor's primary role in a dying declaration is assessing mental fitness (compos mentis).
questions.reasoningChain: Dying declaration -> medical evaluation -> assess compos mentis to ensure validity of statement.
optionExplanations: Assessing compos mentis (mental competence) is the essential legal role of the attending physician.
Recording statements is primarily the duty of a magistrate or police officer, not the doctor.
Cross-examination is conducted by legal counsel in court, not by the certifying physician.
Putting a person under oath is a judicial procedure, not a medical duty.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following statements are true about tremors? 1. PD is characterized by resting tremor 2. Tremor consist of alternate contraction of agonist and antagonist muscle in an oscillating rhythmic manner 3. Essential tremor is an uncommon movement disorder affecting 5% of the population 4. Normal individuals can have physiologic tremors that manifest as mild high frequency, postural or action tremors
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is characterized by a resting tremor (statement 1). Tremors consist of rhythmic, alternating contractions of agonist and antagonist muscles (statement 2). Essential tremor is common, affecting up to 5% of older adults, making statement 3 incorrect. Physiologic tremors are normal, high-frequency postural/action tremors (statement 4).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify correct statements regarding tremors, including resting tremors in Parkinson's and physiological tremors.
questions.reasoningChain: Parkinson's = resting tremor (1 true); Tremor = rhythmic agonist/antagonist contractions (2 true); Essential tremor is common, not uncommon (3 false); Physiologic tremor = high frequency postural tremor (4 true).
optionExplanations: 1, 2, and 3 include statement 3, which incorrectly claims essential tremor is uncommon.
2, 3, and 4 include the incorrect statement 3.
1, 2, and 4 correctly capture Parkinson resting tremors, rhythmic contractions, and physiological tremors.
All of the above is incorrect because statement 3 underestimates essential tremor prevalence.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A medical camp was set up on a military base. A 20-year-old military recruit is found to have an HbA1C level of 6.1% and fasting blood glucose of 120 mg/dL. He has no family history of diabetes mellitus and has no signs and symptoms of diabetes. General physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following best describes the blood glucose levels in this patient?
questions.explanation: According to ADA criteria, impaired fasting glucose (IFG) is defined as a fasting plasma glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL. An HbA1c of 5.7% to 6.4% also indicates prediabetes (impaired glucose tolerance/homeostasis).
questions.educationalObjective: Fasting blood glucose of 120 mg/dL and HbA1c of 6.1% indicate prediabetes / impaired glucose tolerance.
questions.reasoningChain: Fasting glucose 120 mg/dL (100-125 range) + HbA1c 6.1% (5.7-6.4 range) -> Impaired glucose tolerance / prediabetes.
optionExplanations: Normal fasting glucose is under 100 mg/dL with HbA1c under 5.7%.
Impaired glucose tolerance / prediabetes is defined by fasting glucose 100-125 mg/dL and HbA1c 5.7-6.4%.
Diabetes mellitus requires fasting glucose >= 126 mg/dL, HbA1c >= 6.5%, or random glucose >= 200 mg/dL with symptoms.
MODY presents in young patients with strong family history, unlike this sporadic incidental finding.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Most common cause of fulminant diabetes is?
questions.explanation: Fulminant type 1 diabetes mellitus is characterized by an abrupt onset of severe ketoacidosis shortly after the appearance of hyperglycemic symptoms, with near-normal HbA1c levels. Viral infections are frequently implicated as a precipitating environmental trigger for autoimmune pancreatic beta-cell destruction.
questions.educationalObjective: Viruses are a major trigger associated with fulminant type 1 diabetes onset.
questions.reasoningChain: Fulminant diabetes -> rapid beta-cell destruction -> viral infection trigger.
optionExplanations: Viruses are commonly implicated triggers in the pathogenesis of fulminant type 1 diabetes.
Diabetic ketoacidosis is a metabolic consequence, not the underlying etiologic cause.
Non-ketotic hyperosmolar coma is typically seen in type 2 diabetes.
Autoimmunity underlies standard type 1 diabetes, but fulminant onset features marked viral/inflammatory associations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: MC joint involved in diabetes is?
questions.explanation: Charcot neuroarthropathy (Charcot foot) is a debilitating complication of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Loss of protective sensation and autonomic dysfunction lead to repetitive microtrauma, joint destruction, and deformity most commonly in the foot and ankle.
questions.educationalObjective: The foot is the most common joint involved in diabetic neuroarthropathy (Charcot joint).
questions.reasoningChain: Diabetic neuropathy -> loss of protective sensation -> repetitive microtrauma to foot bones -> Charcot foot.
optionExplanations: Ankle can be involved, but the midfoot/forefoot joints are the most common sites.
Knee involvement is less frequent compared to the foot in diabetic neuroarthropathy.
Shoulder neuropathic arthropathy is more commonly associated with syringomyelia.
Foot is the most common site of diabetic neuroarthropathy (Charcot joint).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old male with a history of peptic ulcer disease and diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency with a complaint of nausea, abdominal pain and lethargy for 2 days. He reports having occasional dark, tarry stools. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated blood glucose and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis on an arterial blood gas sample. Which of the following types of insulin should be used in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: In the management of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) presenting with severe hyperglycemia and high anion gap metabolic acidosis, intravenous regular insulin is the treatment of choice due to its rapid onset and predictable half-life.
questions.educationalObjective: Regular insulin is the standard treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Diabetic ketoacidosis -> requires IV insulin -> Regular insulin is short-acting and easily titrated.
optionExplanations: Regular insulin is administered intravenously for rapid correction of hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis.
Lispro is a rapid-acting analog primarily used subcutaneously for prandial coverage.
Glargine is a long-acting basal insulin analog unsuited for continuous IV infusion in DKA.
Aspart is a rapid-acting analog used for mealtime glycemic control.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Slow onset of action is seen with?
questions.explanation: Insulin glargine is a long-acting basal insulin analog designed with microcrystalline precipitation that provides a slow, relatively peakless onset and prolonged duration of action lasting up to 24 hours.
questions.educationalObjective: Insulin glargine has a slow onset and prolonged duration of action.
questions.reasoningChain: Insulin glargine formulation -> precipitates at neutral pH subcutaneous tissue -> slow, sustained release over 24 hours.
optionExplanations: Glargine exhibits a slow onset and prolonged, flat duration of action.
Lispro is a rapid-acting insulin analog with a very quick onset.
Regular insulin has an intermediate onset of action (30-60 minutes).
NPH is an intermediate-acting insulin with a distinct peak.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 19-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of milk coming out of her nipples for the past 5 months. She is a nulligravida, and she is experiencing galactorrhea on a physical exam. She is diagnosed with prolactinoma. The characteristic physical finding of prolactinoma after galactorrhea is?
questions.explanation: Prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas) cause hyperprolactinemia, leading to galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility. As the tumor grows suprasellar, it compresses the optic chiasm, producing the characteristic visual field defect of bitemporal hemianopia.
questions.educationalObjective: Prolactinoma enlargement compresses the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia.
questions.reasoningChain: Prolactinoma growth -> upward expansion -> compression of optic chiasm -> bitemporal hemianopia.
optionExplanations: Bitemporal hemianopia is the characteristic physical/neurological finding from optic chiasm compression by pituitary tumors.
Anovulatory cycles are a hormonal consequence rather than a distinct physical finding.
Amenorrhea is a frequent endocrine symptom preceding or accompanying galactorrhea.
Infertility is a reproductive complication of hyperprolactinemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 37-year-old man is brought to the emergency room by his son, complaining of the inability to move his left arm and leg. According to his son, the patient was reading a book 30 minutes ago when he could not raise his left arm to pick up a different book. While attempting to move away from the table, the patient noticed that his left leg also became extremely weak. Finally, he felt as if everything in his vision had doubled. A history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia is significant. His temperature is 36.1° C (97° F), blood pressure 165/100 mmHg, pulse 85 beats/min, and respirations 16 breaths/min. On examination, there is right-sided ptosis, and his right eye is directed inferiorly and laterally. When asked to smile, the left corner of the mouth droops. His left upper and lower extremity strength is 3 out of 5, while his right upper and lower extremity strength is 5 out of 5. Which of the following areas of his brain has become ischemic?
questions.explanation: This patient presents with Weber syndrome (ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis). A lesion in the midbrain (cerebral peduncle) damages exiting CN III fibers (causing right ptosis and 'down and out' eye) and the adjacent corticospinal tract (causing left-sided hemiparesis).
questions.educationalObjective: Weber syndrome involves midbrain ischemia affecting CN III and the corticospinal tract.
questions.reasoningChain: Right CN III palsy (ptosis, down/out eye) + left hemiparesis -> Weber syndrome -> midbrain lesion.
optionExplanations: Inner capsule stroke produces contralateral hemiparesis without ipsilateral cranial nerve III palsy.
Medulla ischemia typically causes Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome).
Midbrain lesion explains ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiparesis (Weber syndrome).
Occipital lobe ischemia causes homonymous hemianopia, not oculomotor palsy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: All are true about steps followed in management of ventricular fibrillation except?
options: Start CPR followed by immediate defibrillation
Intravenous access followed by Immediate defibrillation
questions.answer: Intravenous access followed by Immediate defibrillation
questions.explanation: In ventricular fibrillation (VF), the priority is immediate defibrillation combined with high-quality CPR. Delaying defibrillation to establish intravenous access is incorrect; defibrillation should be performed as soon as a defibrillator is available.
questions.educationalObjective: Immediate defibrillation is paramount in ventricular fibrillation, not delayed for IV access.
questions.reasoningChain: Ventricular fibrillation arrest -> immediate defibrillation + CPR -> IV access is secondary.
optionExplanations: CPR cycles in advanced cardiac life support are performed in 2-minute intervals.
Chest compressions should be delivered at a rate of 100-120 per minute.
Immediate defibrillation combined with CPR is the cornerstone of VF management.
Establishing IV access before defibrillation delays lifesaving shock delivery and is incorrect.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with complaints of chest pain, sweating, nausea, and shortness of breath for the last four hours. He has no history of any other illness but claims to have smoked 1 pack of cigarettes for the past 20 years. His pulse is 76 beats/min, and his blood pressure is 110/ 70 mmHg. ECG was done and is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation: The provided ECG shows marked ST-segment elevation in the precordial and inferior leads, indicative of acute myocardial ischemia or infarction (STEMI) in a patient presenting with classic chest pain and risk factors.
questions.educationalObjective: ST-segment elevation on ECG indicates acute myocardial ischemia/infarction.
questions.reasoningChain: Chest pain + risk factors + ECG ST-segment elevation -> Acute myocardial ischemia.
optionExplanations: Prinzmetal angina typically presents with transient ST elevations that resolve quickly with vasodilators.
Myocardial ischemia/infarction is demonstrated by the persistent ST elevations and clinical presentation.
Pulmonary embolism typically shows S1Q3T3 pattern, sinus tachycardia, or right heart strain.
Hyperkalemia presents with tall peaked T waves and widened QRS complexes, not focal ST elevations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 70-years-old male patient was diagnosed with heart failure. His ejection fraction was found to be <40%. Which of the following drugs does not reduce the mortality for this patient?
questions.explanation: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), guideline-directed medical therapy includes beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol/carvedilol), ACE inhibitors/ARBs (e.g., captopril), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (potassium-sparing diuretics), all of which reduce mortality. Digoxin improves symptoms and reduces hospitalizations but has no mortality benefit.
questions.educationalObjective: Digoxin improves heart failure symptoms and hospitalizations but does not reduce mortality.
questions.reasoningChain: HFrEF treatment -> Beta-blockers, ACEi, K+ sparing diuretics reduce mortality -> Digoxin provides symptomatic relief only.
optionExplanations: Metoprolol/beta-blockers reduce mortality in chronic heart failure.
Digoxin improves cardiac contractility and reduces hospital admissions but does not improve survival (mortality).
Captopril/ACE inhibitors reduce mortality by blunting ventricular remodeling.
Potassium-sparing diuretics (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) reduce mortality in heart failure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: The continuous murmur is the murmur that begins in systole and continues without interruption, encompassing the second sound throughout diastole or part of thereof. Which of the following leads to a continuous murmur?
questions.explanation: A continuous murmur is heard throughout systole and diastole (e.g., PDA, aortopulmonary window). Peripheral pulmonary stenosis can produce a continuous murmur due to persistent high-velocity flow across narrowed branch pulmonary arteries throughout the cardiac cycle.
questions.educationalObjective: Peripheral pulmonic stenosis can cause a continuous murmur due to continuous turbulent flow.
questions.reasoningChain: Continuous murmur requirement -> flow persists across pressure gradient throughout systole and diastole -> Peripheral pulmonic stenosis.
optionExplanations: Peripheral pulmonic stenosis produces a continuous murmur due to constant turbulent flow.
Severe pulmonary hypertension typically produces a systolic ejection murmur and diastolic pulmonary regurgitation murmur (Graham Steell), not classic continuous murmur.
Type A aortic dissection causes aortic regurgitation (early diastolic murmur).
Rupture of cardiac chamber usually produces acute systolic murmurs or shock.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which is true about Postural Hypotension?
options: Decrease in systolic blood pressure 20 mm Hg within 6 mins of postural change
Decrease in systolic blood pressure 20 mm Hg within 3 mins of postural change
Decrease in diastolic blood pressure 20 mm Hg within 6 mins of postural change
Decrease in diastolic blood pressure 20 mm Hg within 3 mins of postural change
questions.answer: Decrease in systolic blood pressure 20 mm Hg within 3 mins of postural change
questions.explanation: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension is clinically defined as a drop in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg or a drop in diastolic blood pressure of at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing or head-up tilt.
questions.educationalObjective: Orthostatic hypotension is defined by a drop in systolic BP >= 20 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing.
questions.reasoningChain: Postural change -> blood pooling -> drop in SBP >= 20 mmHg or DBP >= 10 mmHg within 3 minutes -> orthostatic hypotension.
optionExplanations: 6 minutes is incorrect; the time threshold is within 3 minutes of postural change.
A decrease in systolic blood pressure of 20 mm Hg within 3 minutes defines orthostatic hypotension.
Diastolic drop threshold is 10 mm Hg, not 20 mm Hg.
Diastolic threshold is 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Berry aneurysm most commonly occurs due to?
options: Endothelial injury of vessel due to HTN
Muscle intimal elastic lamina layer defect
questions.answer: Muscle intimal elastic lamina layer defect
questions.explanation: Berry aneurysms (saccular aneurysms of cerebral arteries) most commonly form at arterial bifurcations in the circle of Willis due to a congenital or acquired defect in the tunica media and internal elastic lamina.

questions.reasoningChain: Cerebral vessel bifurcation -> congenital medial and internal elastic lamina defect -> focal outpouching (berry aneurysm).
optionExplanations: Endothelial injury from hypertension contributes to atherosclerosis, not congenital berry aneurysms.
Muscle intimal elastic lamina layer defect is the structural basis for berry aneurysm formation.
Endothelial layer defect alone does not cause the structural weakness leading to saccular aneurysms.
Adventitia is the outer supportive connective tissue layer, not the primary site of defect.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 45-year patient working in a factory for the past 20 years presents with breathlessness. HRCT chest shows pleural thickening and fibrosis. Diagnosis is?
questions.explanation: Asbestosis is a pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of asbestos fibers, characterized on HRCT by pleural thickening, calcified pleural plaques, and interstitial pulmonary fibrosis predominantly affecting the lower lobes.
questions.educationalObjective: Asbestos exposure causes pulmonary fibrosis and characteristic pleural thickening.
questions.reasoningChain: Occupational asbestos exposure -> fiber inhalation -> pleural thickening and interstitial fibrosis -> Asbestosis.
optionExplanations: Asbestosis classically presents with pleural thickening, fibrosis, and asbestos bodies.
Coal worker pneumoconiosis presents with upper lobe nodular fibrosis without prominent pleural thickening.
Silicosis features upper lobe calcified eggshell lymph nodes and nodular fibrosis.
Berylliosis causes non-caseating granulomatous lung disease in aerospace/electronics workers.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Most commonly observed autosomal aneuploidy leading to spontaneous abortions is?
questions.explanation: Trisomy 16 is the most common autosomal aneuploidy identified in spontaneous first-trimester abortions, accounting for a significant proportion of chromosomally abnormal miscarriages.
questions.educationalObjective: Trisomy 16 is the most frequent autosomal trisomy in spontaneous abortions.
questions.reasoningChain: First trimester miscarriage -> genetic analysis -> Trisomy 16 is most commonly observed autosomal aneuploidy.
optionExplanations: Trisomy 16 is the leading autosomal aneuploidy found in spontaneous miscarriages.
Trisomy 21 is compatible with live birth and is the most common live-born autosomal trisomy.
Monosomy X (Turner syndrome) is common in miscarriages, but Trisomy 16 is the most common autosomal aneuploidy.
Trisomy 18 is associated with Edwards syndrome, seen in live births and late losses.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of these is a Nephritic syndrome?
questions.explanation: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is the classic prototype of acute nephritic syndrome, presenting with hematuria, hypertension, edema, and reduced serum complement levels following a streptococcal infection.
questions.educationalObjective: Post-infectious glomerulonephritis presents as a nephritic syndrome.
questions.reasoningChain: Glomerular immune complex deposition -> inflammation -> hematuria, hypertension, oliguria -> Nephritic syndrome (PSGN).
optionExplanations: Minimal change disease presents as nephrotic syndrome with heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia.
Membranous glomerulopathy causes nephrotic syndrome with subepithelial immune complex deposits.
Post-infectious glomerulonephritis is a classic nephritic syndrome characterized by acute glomerulonephritis.
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis typically presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: The following serological status is noted in a patient: HbsAg positive and HbeAg positive. Diagnosis is?
questions.explanation: The presence of both HBsAg and HBeAg indicates active hepatitis B virus replication with high viral load and high infectivity, seen in acute or actively replicating chronic infection.
questions.educationalObjective: HBsAg and HBeAg positivity indicates high viral replication and infectivity.
questions.reasoningChain: HBsAg positive (infection present) + HBeAg positive (active viral replication) -> High infectivity.
optionExplanations: Carrier state typically features HBsAg positivity with HBeAg negativity and anti-HBe positivity.
Chronic viral hepatitis can be e-antigen positive or negative, but combined HBsAg/HBeAg positivity specifically highlights high infectivity/replication.
Acute viral hepatitis with infectivity is correctly indicated by HBsAg and HBeAg co-positivity.
Remote infection would show anti-HBs and anti-HBc positivity with negative HBsAg.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Chronic viral hepatitis is seen with?
questions.explanation: Among hepatitis viruses, Hepatitis C virus (HCV) has the highest rate of chronicity, with 75% to 85% of infected individuals developing chronic viral hepatitis. In contrast, HEV and HAV do not cause chronic infection, and HBV has a lower adult chronicity rate.
questions.educationalObjective: HCV has the highest propensity for causing chronic viral hepatitis.
questions.reasoningChain: Hepatitis C infection -> immune evasion -> high rate of chronicity (75-85%) -> Chronic viral hepatitis.
optionExplanations: HBV causes chronic hepatitis in about 5-10% of infected adults.
HCV progresses to chronic infection in the majority (75-85%) of exposed individuals.
HDV causes chronic coinfection or superinfection with HBV, but HCV is the classic standalone virus with high chronicity.
HEV causes acute self-limiting hepatitis and does not cause chronicity (except in immunocompromised).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Acute auto-graft rejection occurs within?
questions.explanation: Acute allograft rejection typically occurs within weeks to months (typically < 6 months) following transplantation, mediated primarily by T-cell-mediated cellular immune responses against donor HLA antigens.
questions.educationalObjective: Acute allograft rejection usually manifests within the first 6 months post-transplant.
questions.reasoningChain: Transplantation -> T-cell activation against donor antigens -> tissue injury within weeks to months (< 6 months).
optionExplanations: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours due to pre-formed antibodies.
Acute rejection typically develops within the first few weeks to months (< 6 months) post-transplant.
Acute rejection falls within the broader window of < 6 months.
Chronic rejection develops over months to years due to arteriosclerosis and fibrosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Mark the true statements 1. Pernicious anemia is an example of Type II Hypersensitivity 2. Serum Sickness is a example of Type III Hypersensitivity 3. Pathergy test is an example of Type IV Hypersensitivity 4. Pathergy test is done for Reiter's disease
questions.explanation: Pernicious anemia is a Type II hypersensitivity reaction involving autoantibodies against intrinsic factor or parietal cells. Serum sickness is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction mediated by immune complexes. Pathergy test evaluates cutaneous hyper-reactivity (Type IV delayed hypersensitivity) and is used in Behcet's disease, making statement 4 incorrect for Reiter's.
questions.educationalObjective: Pernicious anemia is Type II, serum sickness is Type III, and pathergy is Type IV hypersensitivity.
questions.reasoningChain: Pernicious anemia = Type II (1 true); Serum sickness = Type III (2 true); Pathergy = Type IV (3 true); Pathergy is for Behcet's, not Reiter's (4 false).
optionExplanations: 1, 2, and 3 are correct statements covering hypersensitivity classifications and pathergy testing.
2, 3, and 4 incorrectly include statement 4 regarding Reiter's disease.
1, 2, 3, and 4 include statement 4, which misattributes the pathergy test condition.
3 and 4 omit statement 1 and 2, which are also true.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following is a causative agent of Farmer's Lung?
questions.explanation: Farmer's lung is a form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by the inhalation of spores from thermophilic actinomycetes (such as Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula) found in moldy hay.
questions.educationalObjective: Farmer's lung is caused by hypersensitivity to thermophilic actinomycetes in moldy hay.
questions.reasoningChain: Exposure to moldy hay -> inhalation of thermophilic actinomycetes -> hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Farmer's lung).
optionExplanations: Thermophilic actinomycetes are the classic causative agents of Farmer's lung.
Aspergillus fumigatus causes allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) or aspergillomas.
Actinobacter is a gram-negative bacterium involved in nosocomial infections.
Aspergillus flavus produces aflatoxins and causes opportunistic infections, not Farmer's lung.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Comment on the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The peripheral blood smear shows intraerythrocytic ring forms and gametocytes characteristic of Plasmodium species infection, confirming a diagnosis of malaria.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify malaria parasites within erythrocytes on a blood smear.
questions.reasoningChain: Peripheral blood smear -> intraerythrocytic parasite rings and gametocytes -> Malaria.
optionExplanations: Malaria is diagnosed by visualizing Plasmodium parasites inside red blood cells on blood films.
Hereditary spherocytosis shows microspherocytes without intraerythrocytic parasites.
G6PD deficiency shows bite cells and Heinz bodies on crystal violet stain, not parasite rings.
Thalassemia shows microcytic hypochromic red cells, target cells, and nucleated RBCs.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male presents with abdominal pain and progressive weight loss for 2 months. He has been suffering from migratory arthropathy for three years. There is no history of any chronic medical conditions. He is taking corticosteroids to help with the arthropathy. Endoscopic investigation shows dark staining of the duodenal mucosa. Histological examination of the biopsy using periodic acid Schiff stain reveals positive macrophages leading to a diagnosis of a rare multisystem disease. Which of the following statements is true regarding this patient's disorder? 1. Caused by a Protozoa Tropheryma Whipplei 2. PAS-positive macrophages in the lamina propria of the small intestine 3. Culture-negative endocarditis is a common cardiac presentation 4. Treated with IV Ceftriaxone
questions.explanation: Whipple's disease is a systemic infection caused by the bacterium Tropheryma whipplei (not a protozoan). It features PAS-positive macrophages in the small bowel lamina propria, migratory arthropathy, and can present with culture-negative endocarditis. Treatment involves prolonged antibiotics such as IV ceftriaxone followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
questions.educationalObjective: Whipple's disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei and features PAS-positive macrophages.
questions.reasoningChain: Tropheryma whipplei infection -> PAS-positive macrophages in lamina propria -> culture-negative endocarditis -> treated with ceftriaxone.
optionExplanations: Statement 1 is false because Tropheryma whipplei is a bacterium, not a protozoan.
Statement 2 is true; PAS-positive macrophages accumulate in the small intestinal lamina propria.
Statement 3 is true; culture-negative endocarditis is a recognized cardiac manifestation.
Statement 4 is true; initial induction therapy includes IV ceftriaxone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Most common site of Brain metastasis is?
questions.explanation: Brain metastases are the most common intracranial neoplasms in adults. The most frequent primary site of origin is lung cancer (particularly small cell and non-small cell lung cancer), followed by breast and melanoma.
questions.educationalObjective: Lung cancer is the most common primary source of brain metastasis.
questions.reasoningChain: Brain metastasis -> hematogenous spread -> primary tumor is most frequently lung cancer.
optionExplanations: Lung cancer is the leading primary malignancy that metastasizes to the brain.
Head and neck cancers typically metastasize to local cervical lymph nodes rather than the brain.
Prostate cancer more commonly metastasizes to bones (osteoblastic lesions).
Breast cancer is the second most common source of brain metastasis after lung cancer.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which is not seen in Tumor lysis Syndrome?
questions.explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome occurs after the rapid destruction of malignant cells, releasing intracellular contents into the bloodstream. This classically results in hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia (due to calcium phosphate binding), and hyperuricemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Tumor lysis syndrome causes hyperphosphatemia, not hypophosphatemia.
questions.reasoningChain: Tumor cell lysis -> massive release of intracellular phosphate -> Hyperphosphatemia (not hypophosphatemia).
optionExplanations: Hypophosphatemia is incorrect; tumor lysis releases intracellular phosphate, leading to hyperphosphatemia.
Hypocalcemia occurs secondary to precipitation of calcium with excess serum phosphate.
Hyperuricemia results from the breakdown of nucleic acids (purines) from lysed cells.
Hyperkalemia occurs due to the massive release of intracellular potassium into the circulation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Comment on the diagnosis for SAP normal, PTH normal, Vitamin D3 normal with elevated serum calcium values?
questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma is characterized by malignant plasma cell proliferation producing osteolytic bone lesions driven by osteoclast activation (via RANKL). This results in hypercalcemia with normal serum alkaline phosphatase (SAP), normal PTH, and normal Vitamin D3 levels.
questions.educationalObjective: Multiple myeloma presents with hypercalcemia and normal SAP, PTH, and Vitamin D3.
questions.reasoningChain: Multiple myeloma -> osteolytic lesions -> hypercalcemia with normal SAP and normal PTH.
optionExplanations: Vitamin D intoxication features elevated Vitamin D3 and hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH.
Hyperparathyroidism typically presents with elevated PTH levels alongside hypercalcemia.
Multiple myeloma causes osteolysis with hypercalcemia while keeping SAP, PTH, and vitamin D normal.
Nutritional rickets presents with hypocalcemia, elevated PTH, and low Vitamin D.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following interfere with iron absorption?
questions.explanation: Dietary phytates (found in unrefined grains, nuts, and seeds), oxalates, tannins, and calcium interfere with non-heme iron absorption by forming insoluble complexes in the gastrointestinal tract.
questions.educationalObjective: Phytates inhibit dietary iron absorption.
questions.reasoningChain: Dietary phytates bind iron -> form insoluble chelates -> reduced iron absorption in gut.
optionExplanations: Vitamin C enhances iron absorption by reducing ferric iron to ferrous iron.
Phytates bind dietary iron and significantly inhibit its intestinal absorption.
Oxalates can bind minerals, but phytates are the classic potent inhibitors of iron absorption tested.
Myoglobin contains heme iron, which is absorbed efficiently and does not inhibit absorption.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Most sensitive and specific marker for Ml is?
questions.explanation: Cardiac troponins (Troponin I and Troponin T) are the most sensitive and specific biomarkers for myocardial necrosis, remaining elevated in serum for up to 1-2 weeks following a myocardial infarction.
questions.educationalObjective: Troponins are the most sensitive and specific biomarkers for myocardial infarction.
questions.reasoningChain: Myocardial cell injury -> release of troponins -> high sensitivity and cardiac specificity.
optionExplanations: Troponin is the gold standard biomarker due to superior cardiac tissue specificity and sensitivity.
Cytokeratin is an epithelial marker, not used for cardiac necrosis.
Myoglobin rises early but lacks cardiac specificity, being found in skeletal muscle as well.
CPK-MM is specific for skeletal muscle injury rather than cardiac muscle.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Which is correct about Diphtheria membrane?
options: Grey membrane that bleeds on removal
Grey membrane that does not bleed on removal
Grey pseudomembrane that bleeds on removal
Grey pseudomembrane that does not bleed on removal
questions.answer: Grey pseudomembrane that bleeds on removal
questions.explanation: In diphtheria, Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces a tough, adherent grey pseudomembrane composed of necrotic epithelium, fibrin, leukocytes, and bacteria. Because it causes ulceration of the underlying mucosal capillaries, forceful removal causes bleeding.
questions.educationalObjective: The diphtheria pseudomembrane is adherent and bleeds upon attempted removal.
questions.reasoningChain: Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection -> pseudomembrane formation over mucosa -> tightly adherent, bleeds on removal.
optionExplanations: Membrane bleeds on removal, but it is specifically a pseudomembrane.
Non-bleeding description is incorrect because the membrane adheres to underlying vascular tissue.
Grey pseudomembrane that bleeds on removal is the classic pathological hallmark of diphtheria.
Pseudomembranes bleed on removal due to mucosal vessel erosion.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: DNA transfer in bacteria via phage is:
questions.explanation: Transduction is the process by which bacterial DNA is transferred from one bacterium to another by a bacteriophage (virus).
questions.educationalObjective: Bacteriophage-mediated DNA transfer is termed transduction.
questions.reasoningChain: Bacteriophage infects bacterium -> packages bacterial DNA -> transfers to new host cell -> Transduction.
optionExplanations: Conjugation is direct plasmid transfer between bacteria via a sex pilus.
Transduction is genetic transfer mediated by bacteriophages.
Transformation is the uptake of naked extracellular DNA from the environment.
Translation is the ribosomal synthesis of proteins from mRNA templates.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Sporulation occurs in which phase of bacterial growth curve:
questions.explanation: Bacterial sporulation (endospore formation) typically occurs during the stationary phase of the bacterial growth curve when nutrients are depleted and environmental stress increases.
questions.educationalObjective: Sporulation occurs during the stationary phase of bacterial growth.
questions.reasoningChain: Nutrient depletion in growth medium -> transition to stationary phase -> triggering of sporulation pathways.
optionExplanations: Stationary phase is when nutrient depletion triggers endospore formation in spore-forming bacteria.
Lag phase is the initial period of metabolic adaptation without active cell division.
Log (exponential) phase is characterized by rapid cell division and maximal growth.
Decline (death) phase involves cell lysis and death exceeding replication.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Bacillus Anthrax is:
options: Gram positive rods with square ends
Gram positive bacilli with spherical ends
questions.answer: Gram positive rods with square ends
questions.explanation: Bacillus anthracis is a large, gram-positive, spore-forming rod (bacillus) with characteristic squared or truncated ends, often appearing in chains resembling 'boxcars'.
questions.educationalObjective: Bacillus anthracis is characterized as a gram-positive rod with square ends.
questions.reasoningChain: Gram stain of Bacillus anthracis -> Gram-positive rods -> square/boxcar ends.
optionExplanations: Gram-positive cocci in clusters describe Staphylococci, not Bacillus.
Gram-positive rods with square ends correctly describe Bacillus anthracis.
Gram-positive bacilli with spherical ends is not the typical appearance of B. anthracis.
Gram-negative cocci in clusters is incorrect; Bacillus is gram-positive and rod-shaped.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most likely cause in a case of granuloma with positive acid-fast bacilli?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium leprae is an acid-fast bacillus that causes leprosy (Hansen disease), characteristically presenting with granulomatous lesions in skin and peripheral nerves and positive acid-fast staining.
questions.educationalObjective: Mycobacterium leprae is an acid-fast bacillus associated with granulomatous leprosy.
questions.reasoningChain: Granulomatous inflammation + acid-fast bacilli -> Mycobacterium leprae -> Leprosy.

Trench fever is caused by Bartonella quintana, an extracellular bacterium.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Legionnaires disease is implicated in causation of which among the following?
questions.explanation: Legionella pneumophila is an intracellular gram-negative bacterium that causes Legionnaires' disease, a severe form of atypical pneumonia and respiratory tract infection.
questions.educationalObjective: Legionella causes respiratory disease (Legionnaires' disease).
questions.reasoningChain: Legionella pneumophila infection -> inhalation of aerosols -> severe atypical pneumonia (respiratory disease).

Retroperitoneal fibrosis is a rare condition associated with IgG4-related disease or drugs.
Acute gastroenteritis is commonly caused by rotavirus, norovirus, or Campylobacter.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: When should you perform a Widal test in a case of Typhoid?
questions.explanation: The Widal test measures agglutinating antibodies against Salmonella Typhi O and H antigens. Because antibodies take time to develop after infection, the test has low sensitivity in the first week and is most reliably performed and interpreted during the second week of enteric fever.
questions.educationalObjective: The Widal test for typhoid fever is optimally performed during the second week of illness.
questions.reasoningChain: Salmonella infection -> antibody production takes 7-10 days -> Widal test becomes positive and useful in the 2nd week.
optionExplanations: 1st week of typhoid fever is best diagnosed by blood culture, as Widal antibodies are not yet elevated.
2nd week is when antibody titers rise sufficiently for the Widal test to be diagnostically useful.
3rd and 4th weeks can also show positivity, but stool and urine cultures become more useful then.
4th week is in the convalescent phase, though antibodies may still persist.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Antemortem diagnosis of rabies is made with:
questions.explanation: Antemortem diagnosis of rabies can be achieved by detecting viral antigens in corneal impression smears or skin biopsies from the nape of the neck using direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing.
questions.educationalObjective: Corneal impression smears are used for antemortem diagnosis of rabies.
questions.reasoningChain: Rabies suspected -> virus travels to corneal nerves -> corneal impression smear and DFA for antemortem diagnosis.
optionExplanations: Rabies-specific antibodies can be found in CSF/serum, but corneal smear directly detects virus/antigen.
Inoculation in culture media is slow and not the primary rapid antemortem test.
Negri bodies in the hippocampus are classic post-mortem histological findings.
Corneal impression smear is a recognized rapid antemortem diagnostic test for rabies.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Hemolytic uraemic syndrome associate with
questions.explanation: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is classically caused by Shiga toxin-producing strains of Escherichia coli, most notably enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) serotype O157:H7.

Malaria causes hemolytic anemia and organ dysfunction, but not classic HUS.
Parvovirus B19 causes pure red cell aplasia and aplastic crisis in hemolytic anemias.
Bartonella henselae causes cat-scratch disease and bacillary angiomatosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following virus is from Herpes virus family?
questions.explanation: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a member of the Herpesviridae family (Human Herpesvirus 4), known for causing infectious mononucleosis and associated with various lymphomas.
questions.educationalObjective: EBV belongs to the Herpesvirus family.
questions.reasoningChain: Epstein-Barr virus structure -> enveloped DNA virus -> classified under Herpesviridae.

Rabies virus is a member of the Rhabdoviridae family.
EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) is a member of the Herpesviridae family.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Molluscum contagiosum is a :
questions.explanation: Molluscum contagiosum virus is a large, brick-shaped, double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the Poxviridae family.
questions.educationalObjective: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus.
questions.reasoningChain: Molluscum contagiosum pathogen -> large DNA virus -> Poxvirus family.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: A patient presented with some unknown fungal infection. Microscopic examination revealed brown coloured spherical fungi with septate hyphae. Possible condition:

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Which is correct about the larval stage of Taenia solium?
questions.explanation: Cysticercosis cellulosae is the encysted larval stage of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium, which develops in human tissues (such as skeletal muscle, brain, and subcutaneous tissue) following ingestion of T. solium eggs.
questions.educationalObjective: Cysticercus cellulosae is the larval stage of Taenia solium.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: N. meningitidis can be due to deficiency of this complement system:
questions.explanation: Deficiencies in the terminal complement components (C5-C9) prevent the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC), specifically predisposing individuals to recurrent, severe infections with encapsulated bacteria such as Neisseria meningitidis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Classical complement activated by:
questions.explanation: The classical complement pathway is initiated by the binding of C1q to antigen-antibody (Ag-Ab) complexes containing IgM or IgG antibodies bound to antigens.
questions.educationalObjective: The classical complement pathway is activated by antigen-antibody complexes.
questions.reasoningChain: Antigen-antibody complex formation -> binds C1q -> activates classical complement pathway.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 15-years-old girl presented with primary amenorrhea with an orderly appearance of secondary sexual characteristics like breast and pubic hair. On examination, there is no other abnormality detected, and the patient denied the use of any medication or illicit drugs. On family history, no significant history was established to diagnose the cause. What is the next best step for this patient?
questions.explanation: A 15-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea and normal secondary sexual characteristics (breast and pubic hair development) requires evaluation for anatomical outflow tract obstructions, such as Müllerian agenesis (MRKH syndrome) or transverse vaginal septum. questions.reasoningChain: Primary amenorrhea + normal secondary sexual characteristics -> rule out anatomical obstruction -> Pelvic USG to check uterus and ovaries.
optionExplanations: Reassurance is inappropriate before identifying the underlying cause of primary amenorrhea.

HSG is useful for assessing uterine cavity contour and tubal patency, not primary anatomical screening.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 19-year-old primigravida, presents with 8 weeks amenorrhea, light bleeding and pain. O/E Uterine size corresponds to POG and Os is closed. USG reveals single live intrauterine pregnancy. What is preferred management in this case?
questions.explanation: A threatened abortion is characterized by first-trimester bleeding, closed cervical os, and a live intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound. Management consists of conservative measures including pelvic rest and progesterone support.

questions.reasoningChain: First trimester bleeding + closed os + live fetus -> threatened abortion -> conservative management (bed rest and progesterone).
optionExplanations: Estrogen plus progesterone is not the standard first-line regimen for threatened abortion.

Bed rest and progesterone support are the standard supportive management for threatened abortion.
Beta hCG helps confirm pregnancy viability trends but is not a therapeutic intervention.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 35 year female presented with complaints of infertility. She has previous history of PID. Preliminary investigations like USG showed normal organs and hormone levels were also normal. What is the next best investigation?
questions.explanation: In a patient presenting with infertility and a history of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), tubal factor infertility is suspected. Since preliminary pelvic ultrasound and hormone levels are normal, the next best investigation to assess tubal patency is hysterosalpingography (HSG).
questions.educationalObjective: Hysterosalpingography is used to evaluate tubal patency in suspected tubal factor infertility.
questions.reasoningChain: Infertility + PID history -> suspicion of tubal occlusion -> Hysterosalpingography to evaluate fallopian tubes.
optionExplanations: Repeat USG is unlikely to yield new diagnostic information if the initial scan was normal.
Hysterosalpingography is the standard imaging modality to assess uterine cavity and fallopian tube patency.
Endometrial biopsy assesses the endometrial phase and pathology, not primary tubal patency.
Urine culture evaluates urinary tract infections, not infertility factors.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Couvelaire uterus is seen in:
questions.explanation: Couvelaire uterus (uteroplacental apoplexy) is a life-threatening complication of severe placental abruption where extravasated blood infiltrates the myometrium, causing a bruised, blue-tinted uterine surface.
questions.educationalObjective: Couvelaire uterus is a classic complication of severe abruptio placentae.
questions.reasoningChain: Severe abruptio placentae -> retroplacental bleeding -> infiltration of blood into myometrium -> Couvelaire uterus.
optionExplanations: Placenta previa involves painless vaginal bleeding from low implantation without myometrial apoplexy.
Vasa previa involves fetal vessel rupture across the internal os.
Abruptio placentae can lead to retroplacental hematoma and myometrial blood infiltration (Couvelaire uterus).
Placenta percreta involves invasion of villi through the entire myometrium to the serosa.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Risk of endometrial cancer is least in:
questions.explanation: Endometrial cancer risk is increased by conditions associated with prolonged, unopposed estrogen exposure (obesity, late menopause, positive family history, nulliparity). Multigravidity and parity are protective factors because of progesterone dominance during pregnancies, making the risk least in a multigravida.
questions.educationalObjective: Multigravidity is associated with a decreased risk of endometrial cancer.
questions.reasoningChain: Unopposed estrogen increases endometrial cancer risk -> multiple pregnancies provide protective progesterone exposure -> risk is least in multigravida.
optionExplanations: Positive family history of Lynch syndrome or hereditary cancers increases endometrial cancer risk.
Obesity increases peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogen, elevating cancer risk.
Late menopause prolongs lifetime estrogen exposure, increasing endometrial cancer risk.
Multigravida status is protective due to pregnancy-induced progesterone exposure, resulting in the lowest risk.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A grand multipara is a woman who has given birth __ times?
questions.explanation: A grand multipara is classically defined in obstetrics as a woman who has given birth five or more times at or beyond 20 weeks of gestation (parity >= 5).
questions.educationalObjective: A grand multipara is defined as a woman with five or more deliveries.
questions.reasoningChain: Obstetric definition -> parity count >= 5 -> Grand multipara.
optionExplanations: Parity >2 defines a multiparous patient, not grand multipara.
Parity >3 is sometimes termed great multipara, but grand multipara strictly denotes >4 (i.e., 5 or more deliveries).
Parity >4 (5 or more viable births) defines a grand multipara.
Parity >5 exceeds the threshold, as 5 is the classic cutoff.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 26 weeks pregnant female presented with HTN for the first time. There is no proteinuria. Diagnosis of such condition
questions.explanation: Gestational hypertension is defined as new-onset elevated blood pressure (>= 140/90 mmHg) appearing after 20 weeks of gestation in the absence of proteinuria or signs of end-organ dysfunction.
questions.educationalObjective: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria is gestational hypertension.
questions.reasoningChain: New-onset hypertension at 26 weeks + no proteinuria -> Gestational hypertension.
optionExplanations: Chronic hypertension is diagnosed when high blood pressure is present before pregnancy or before 20 weeks gestation.
Eclampsia is characterized by the development of generalized seizures in a preeclamptic patient.
Gestational hypertension is new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria.
Preeclampsia requires new-onset hypertension plus proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Minimum sperm count for normal semen analysis according to WHO:
questions.explanation: According to the WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen, the lower reference limit for normal total sperm concentration is 15 million spermatozoa per milliliter.
questions.educationalObjective: The WHO lower reference limit for normal sperm concentration is 15 million/mL.
questions.reasoningChain: WHO semen analysis guidelines -> normal sperm concentration threshold -> 15 million/mL.
optionExplanations: 2 million/mL is markedly oligospermic and well below the normal WHO reference limit.
5 million/mL indicates severe oligozoospermia.
10 million/mL remains below the WHO reference threshold.
15 million/mL is the established WHO lower reference limit for normal sperm concentration.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 26 year old woman presents with infertility. She has regular cycles of 28 days with no dysmenorrhea. Her LMP was on 8th of May. When should her endometrial biopsy be planned ?
questions.explanation: In a woman with a regular 28-day menstrual cycle and LMP on May 8th, ovulation typically occurs around day 14 (May 21-22). To assess for luteal phase defect via endometrial biopsy, the procedure should be timed during the mid-luteal phase, approximately 7 days before expected menstruation (around Day 21-22, corresponding to May 29th for a 28-day cycle).
questions.educationalObjective: Endometrial biopsy for dating is performed during the mid-luteal phase, 7 days before expected menses.
questions.reasoningChain: 28-day cycle with LMP May 8th -> ovulation on Day 14 (May 21) -> mid-luteal biopsy 7 days pre-menses -> Day 28 (May 29th).
optionExplanations: May 22nd corresponds to ovulation time, not the mid-luteal phase.
May 8th-12th is during the proliferative/menstrual phase.
Anytime during the cycle is incorrect because endometrial histology varies significantly by cycle phase.
May 29th is 7 days prior to the next expected menses in a 28-day cycle, ideal for luteal phase evaluation.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: In this normal menstrual cycle graph, the mark ‘X’ represents levels of which hormone?
questions.explanation: In a standard normal menstrual cycle hormone graph, progesterone levels (represented by the dashed blue line) rise significantly following ovulation in the luteal phase, peaking around cycle day 21 (marked by 'X'), before declining prior to menstruation.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify progesterone as the hormone peaking during the mid-luteal phase in a menstrual cycle graph.
questions.reasoningChain: Menstrual hormone graph -> dashed line peaking post-ovulation at day 21 ('X') -> Progesterone.
optionExplanations: LH exhibits a sharp mid-cycle surge around day 13-14 triggering ovulation.
FSH shows a small peak during the early follicular phase and at ovulation.
Estrogen has peaks in the late follicular phase and mid-luteal phase.
Progesterone rises after ovulation, peaking in the mid-luteal phase (marked by 'X').

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A patient who was using CuT for contraception, presented with a 20 weeks pregnancy. The IUD is placed at fundus, tail visible at OS and she wants to continue the pregnancy. What is your next step in this patient:
questions.explanation: When an intrauterine device (IUD) is in place and a patient presents with an ongoing intrauterine pregnancy at 20 weeks with visible strings, the standard recommendation is to gently remove the IUD if the strings are visible, as removal reduces the risk of spontaneous abortion and chorioamnionitis.
questions.educationalObjective: Remove the IUD in early pregnancy if strings are visible to decrease complication risks.
questions.reasoningChain: Intrauterine pregnancy with IUD in-situ -> strings visible -> remove IUD to decrease miscarriage and infection risk.
optionExplanations: Leaving the IUD in-situ carries a significantly higher risk of miscarriage and septic abortion.
Medical termination is unnecessary if the patient desires to continue the pregnancy and no complications are present.
Removing the IUD reduces risks of infection and pregnancy loss and is the recommended management.
MTP is not indicated simply due to the presence of an IUD if the patient wishes to continue the pregnancy.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Which of the following can be a cause of Oligohydramnios?
questions.explanation: Oligohydramnios is characterized by deficient amniotic fluid volume, commonly caused by fetal renal anomalies (such as bilateral renal agenesis or Potter sequence) where fetal urine production ceases.
questions.educationalObjective: Bilateral renal agenesis causes oligohydramnios due to lack of fetal urine output.
questions.reasoningChain: Renal agenesis -> absent fetal urine production -> severe Oligohydramnios.
optionExplanations: Multiparity does not directly cause oligohydramnios.
Twins can be complicated by twin-twin transfusion syndrome, often leading to polyhydramnios in one sac and oligohydramnios in the other.
Renal agenesis prevents fetal urine excretion, leading to severe oligohydramnios.
Macrosomia is associated with normal or increased amniotic fluid volumes, especially in diabetic mothers.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: Most common cause of blindness in India:
questions.explanation: Cataract remains the leading cause of avoidable and total blindness in India, accounting for over 60-70% of all blindness cases according to national surveys.
questions.educationalObjective: Cataract is the primary cause of blindness in India.
questions.reasoningChain: National blindness surveys in India -> highest proportion of visual impairment and blindness -> Cataract.
optionExplanations: Cataract is the leading cause of blindness in India.
Refractive errors are a major cause of visual impairment, but not the leading cause of blindness.
Trachoma has sharply declined as a public health problem in India due to successful control programs.
Glaucoma is an important cause of irreversible blindness, second behind cataract.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A 23-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by the rescue team after 1 hour of a road traffic accident. The patient is semiconscious. He is not alert and oriented to time and space. The patient has a GCS of 9/15. The patient is vitally stable. The patient has an open wound on the parietal area of the head. The wound is washed and stitched. Further investigations and examinations reveal that the patient has raised intracranial pressure. The examination of the pupil of this patient will reveal which of the following?
questions.explanation: An acute head injury with raised intracranial pressure and a GCS of 9 can lead to transtentorial (uncal) herniation. This compresses the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III), leading to loss of parasympathetic constrictor fibers and ipsilateral pupillary dilation (mydriasis).
questions.educationalObjective: Raised ICP causing uncal herniation results in ipsilateral mydriasis via CN III compression.
questions.reasoningChain: Raised ICP -> uncal herniation -> compression of CN III against tentorium -> ipsilateral parasympathetic paralysis -> Ipsilateral mydriasis.
optionExplanations: Ipsilateral mydriasis occurs due to direct compression of the third cranial nerve during uncal herniation.
Contralateral mydriasis is incorrect; pupillary changes occur on the side of the herniating temporal lobe.
Ipsilateral miosis is incorrect; parasympathetic fiber compression paralyzes constriction, causing dilation.
Contralateral miosis does not characterize uncal herniation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A 39-year-old Woman presents to the emergency department with complaints of progressive vision loss in her left eye for 3 months and now blurred vision in her right eye for 10 days. She has a six-month history of frequent headaches that get worse in the morning and are accompanied by nausea and vomiting. She has been taking ondansetron and paracetamol with partial relief. Visual acuity in her right eye is 20/30, while she can only count fingers with the left eye. A fundoscopic examination is shown below. A left frontal brain lesion is visible on an MRI scan. These findings suggest a diagnosis of Foster-Kennedy syndrome. All of the following features are Seen in Foster-Kennedy Syndrome except?
options: Ipsilateral optic atrophy, ipsilateral central scotoma, bilateral progressive optic neuropathy
Contralateral papilledema, ipsilateral central scotoma, bilateral progressive optic neuropathy
Ipsilateral optic atrophy, contralateral papilledema, ipsilateral central scotoma
Contralateral anosmia, Contralateral central scotoma, bilateral progressive optic neuropathy
questions.answer: Contralateral anosmia, Contralateral central scotoma, bilateral progressive optic neuropathy
