questions.explanation: Foster-Kennedy syndrome is characterized by ipsilateral optic atrophy (due to direct compression by a frontal lobe mass), contralateral papilledema (due to raised intracranial pressure), and ipsilateral central scotoma. Contralateral anosmia is not part of the classic triad; instead, ipsilateral anosmia from olfactory tract compression can occur.
questions.educationalObjective: Foster-Kennedy syndrome features ipsilateral optic atrophy, contralateral papilledema, and scotoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Frontal lobe tumor -> direct pressure on one optic nerve (atrophy) + raised ICP (papilledema on other side) -> Foster-Kennedy syndrome.
optionExplanations: Ipsilateral optic atrophy and central scotoma with bilateral progressive neuropathy is a recognized feature.
Contralateral papilledema combined with ipsilateral optic atrophy is classic.
Ipsilateral optic atrophy, contralateral papilledema, and ipsilateral central scotoma form the classic triad.
Contralateral anosmia is incorrect because olfactory nerve compression occurs on the same side as the frontal mass (ipsilateral).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A 42-year-old man presented to the ER with multiple knife wounds, one of which penetrated the right eye creating a 20 mm full-thickness laceration of the upper lid and a 12 mm superonasal full-thickness scleral laceration. The laceration extended radially back towards the optic nerve with prolapse of the intraocular contents. On admission, the patient underwent Evisceration of his right eyeball. Out of the given choices, Which layer of the eyeball is removed during evisceration?
questions.explanation: During an evisceration procedure of the eyeball, the contents of the globe (cornea, iris, lens, retina, choroid, and vitreous) are removed, leaving behind the outer sclera and the extraocular muscles attached to it.
questions.educationalObjective: Evisceration removes the middle (uvea) and inner (retina) layers of the eye, leaving the outer sclera intact.
questions.reasoningChain: Evisceration surgical step -> removal of intraocular contents -> outer sclera remains -> middle and inner layers removed.
optionExplanations: Middle (uvea/choroid) and inner (retina) layers are removed during evisceration.
Outer layer (sclera and cornea) is preserved in evisceration to support an orbital implant.
Outer and inner layer removal is anatomically incorrect.
All layers of the eyeball are removed during enucleation, not evisceration.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: The following image shows:
questions.explanation: The fluorescein-stained corneal image demonstrates a classic branching dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbous knobs, which is pathognomonic for epithelial herpes simplex keratitis (viral keratitis).
questions.educationalObjective: Dendritic corneal ulcers stained with fluorescein indicate viral (herpes simplex) keratitis.
questions.reasoningChain: Corneal stain -> branching dendritic pattern -> herpes simplex virus -> Viral keratitis.
optionExplanations: Bacterial keratitis typically presents with a dense, opaque stromal infiltrate and hypopyon.
Fungal keratitis often presents with feathery borders, dry-appearing infiltrates, and satellite lesions.
Viral keratitis (HSV) classically shows dendritic epithelial ulceration on fluorescein staining.
Syphilitic keratitis (interstitial keratitis) presents with deep stromal vascularization without primary dendritic ulcers.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: Drug contraindicated in keratitis
questions.explanation: Topical corticosteroids are strictly contraindicated in active infectious keratitis (particularly herpes simplex epithelial keratitis and fungal keratitis) because they suppress the local immune response, promote viral/fungal replication, and can cause corneal melting and perforation.
questions.educationalObjective: Topical steroids are contraindicated in infectious keratitis due to risk of exacerbation and perforation.
questions.reasoningChain: Infectious keratitis -> application of topical steroids -> decreased local immunity -> worsening infection and corneal perforation.
optionExplanations: Tear drops (artificial tears) provide lubrication and are safe and helpful.
Steroids are contraindicated in active corneal infections due to risk of exacerbation and perforation.
Cycloplegics are used to relieve painful ciliary spasm and prevent posterior synechiae in keratitis.
Timolol is used to lower intraocular pressure if secondary glaucoma develops.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is seen retinitis pigmentosa?
questions.explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa is a group of inherited retinal dystrophies characterized by progressive loss of photoreceptors. Fundoscopic findings classically include bone-spicule pigmentation, waxy pallor of the optic disc, and marked retinal arteriolar attenuation.
questions.educationalObjective: Retinitis pigmentosa fundoscopic findings include arteriolar attenuation and bone-spicule pigmentation.
questions.reasoningChain: Retinitis pigmentosa -> photoreceptor degeneration -> retinal vasoconstriction -> arteriolar attenuation.
optionExplanations: Arteriolar attenuation is a classic hallmark triad finding in retinitis pigmentosa.
Neovascularization is typical of proliferative retinopathies such as diabetic retinopathy.
Retinal artery thrombosis causes sudden, profound painless vision loss with a cherry-red spot.
Papilledema is swelling of the optic disc secondary to raised intracranial pressure.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: Not used for color vision testing:
questions.explanation: Color vision testing is performed using tools such as Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates, Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue test, and Holmgren wool test. The Ames test is a bacterial mutagenicity assay for chemical carcinogens, not a color vision test.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify standard color vision tests (Ishihara, FM 100-Hue, Holmgren) vs. Ames test.
questions.reasoningChain: Color vision tests -> Ishihara, Holmgren, FM 100 Hue -> Ames test is a bacterial mutagenicity assay.
optionExplanations: Holmgren wool test is a classical color matching test for color blindness.
Ishihara chart is the most widely used screening test for red-green color vision deficiency.
Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue test evaluates fine color discrimination.
Ames test is an assay used to test the mutagenic potential of chemical compounds, unrelated to vision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: Where is the lesion that produces the visual field defect shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The visual field defect shown is a contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky' defect). This results from a lesion affecting Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe.
questions.educationalObjective: Meyer's loop lesions in the temporal lobe cause contralateral superior quadrantanopia.
questions.reasoningChain: Superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky') -> lesion in Meyer's loop -> Temporal lobe.
optionExplanations: Craniopharyngioma typically compresses the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia.
Meningioma can cause various compressive optic neuropathy or chiasmal defects depending on location.
Pituitary adenoma causes bitemporal hemianopia via optic chiasm compression.
Temporal lobe lesion damages Meyer's loop, producing a contralateral superior quadrantanopia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: Which of the following field defects occurs due to a lesion at the optic chiasma?
questions.explanation: A lesion at the optic chiasma, such as a pituitary pituitary macroadenoma, typically compresses the crossing nasal retinal fibers from both eyes. These fibers convey information from the temporal visual fields, resulting in bitemporal hemianopia (loss of vision in the outer half of both visual fields).
questions.educationalObjective: Correlate optic chiasm lesions with the resulting visual field defect.
questions.reasoningChain: Optic chiasm contains crossing nasal fibers from both retinas -> Lesion at this site damages these fibers -> Results in loss of temporal visual fields known as bitemporal hemianopia.
optionExplanations: Bitemporal hemianopia is the classic visual field defect caused by compression at the optic chiasma.
Unilateral blindness results from a complete lesion of a single optic nerve prior to the chiasm.
Pie on the floor defect is caused by a lesion of the temporal radiation (Meyer's loop involvement causes pie in the sky).
Bilateral homonymous macular defect typically arises from lesions involving the visual cortex or posterior cerebral artery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: In which of the following condition there is ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia and facial palsy of upper motor neuron?
questions.explanation: Weber syndrome is characterized by ipsilateral oculomotor (3rd) nerve palsy combined with contralateral hemiplegia and contralateral upper motor neuron facial palsy. It is typically caused by a midbrain stroke involving the cerebral peduncle and exiting fascicles of the third cranial nerve.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose brainstem stroke syndromes based on cranial nerve and motor deficits.
questions.reasoningChain: Ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia defines midbrain ventral lesion -> This classic constellation constitutes Weber syndrome.
optionExplanations: Weber syndrome presents with ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiplegia.
Terson syndrome refers to intraocular hemorrhage associated with intracranial hemorrhage or subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Millard-Gubler syndrome involves ipsilateral CN VI and VII palsies with contralateral hemiplegia (pontine lesion).
Foville syndrome involves ipsilateral CN VI and VII palsies along with horizontal gaze palsy and contralateral hemiplegia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: All among the following are incorrect statements regarding lens induced glaucoma except :
options: Phacomorphic glaucoma is an open angle glaucoma
In phacolytic glaucoma lens capsule is intact.
Phacomorphic glaucoma has a deep anterior chamber
Mature cataract is an example of phacolytic glaucoma
questions.answer: In phacolytic glaucoma lens capsule is intact.
questions.explanation: Phacolytic glaucoma is an open-angle glaucoma caused by leakage of high-molecular-weight lens proteins through an intact but hypermature (or mature) cataract lens capsule, which block the trabecular meshwork and cause secondary elevation of intraocular pressure.
questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate the pathophysiological features of lens-induced glaucomas.
questions.reasoningChain: Phacolytic glaucoma involves leaking proteins -> Lens capsule remains microscopically intact -> Hypermature cataract allows leakage without capsule rupture.
optionExplanations: Phacomorphic glaucoma is a secondary angle-closure glaucoma, not open-angle.
In phacolytic glaucoma, the lens capsule is intact, permitting leakage of liquefied lens proteins.
Phacomorphic glaucoma features a shallow anterior chamber due to a swollen intumescent lens pushing forward.
Mature or hypermature cataract is associated with phacolytic glaucoma, while Morgagnian cataract is a specific sub-type.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old man reported within 6 weeks after sustaining a penetrating accidental injury to his left eye with a wooden stick. On examination, there is a marked diminution of vision in the right eye associated with pain, redness and photophobia. The first sign, the attending doctor can see on a fundus examination if it is a case of sympathetic ophthalmitis is:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic ophthalmitis is a bilateral granulomatous uveitis occurring after penetrating ocular trauma to one eye. The earliest sign visible on slit-lamp or fundus examination in the sympathizing (uninjured) eye is a subtle retrolental flare or cells in the anterior vitreous, representing early breakdown of the blood-ocular barrier.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the earliest clinical signs of sympathetic ophthalmitis in the uninjured eye.
questions.reasoningChain: Penetrating trauma leads to immune reaction -> Sympathizing eye shows earliest inflammatory breakdown -> Retrolental flare/cells represent the earliest objective finding.
optionExplanations: Circumcorneal congestion is a general sign of inflammation, not the earliest specific fundoscopic finding.
Hypopyon is a later and more severe sign of intraocular inflammation.
Retrolental flare represents the earliest slit-lamp sign of sympathetic ophthalmitis in the uninjured eye.
Iris nodules (such as Koeppe or Busacca) develop later in the granulomatous inflammatory course.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: A 6-year-old child is suspected with supracondylar fracture of right hand, complaining of pain and swelling. X-ray of right elbow was not significant. What is the next best step in this case?
options: Compare with X-ray of left hand
Closed reduction with K wire fixation Cast
questions.explanation: In a pediatric patient with suspected supracondylar fracture presenting with pain and swelling where initial X-rays are normal or inconclusive (often due to occult fractures or displacement), the standard management in an acute trauma setting with clinical symptoms is immobilization with a splint/slab to prevent displacement, followed by further imaging or specialist review.
questions.educationalObjective: Manage suspected pediatric supracondylar fractures when initial imaging is equivocal.
questions.reasoningChain: Child presents with signs of supracondylar fracture -> X-ray negative but pain/swelling persist -> Clinical suspicion dictates protective immobilization using a closed reduction and slab.
optionExplanations: Comparing with the uninjured side may help, but immediate supportive immobilization is priority for acute pain and stability.
Closed reduction and slab provides necessary stabilization for potential occult fractures with significant swelling.
K-wire fixation is reserved for displaced fractures confirmed on imaging, not occult or non-displaced cases.
A full cast is avoided initially in acute trauma with swelling due to the high risk of compartment syndrome.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: A 39-year-old male presents to the clinic for a routine checkup. Except for the mild generalized weakness, he does not have any symptoms. On assessment following findings are noted. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the above findings? Parameters Values ALP Normal Calcium High Phosphate High PTH Normal
questions.explanation: In Vitamin D toxicity, excessive vitamin D leads to increased intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, resulting in hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. Due to suppressed parathyroid hormone (PTH) via negative feedback from high calcium levels and normal alkaline phosphatase (ALP) in uncomplicated toxicity, this metabolic profile points directly to Vitamin D intoxication.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose vitamin D toxicity based on serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH profiles.
questions.reasoningChain: High calcium and phosphate with normal PTH and ALP -> Indicates exogenous or excess vitamin D intake -> Matches Vitamin D toxicity profile.
optionExplanations: Vitamin D toxicity causes high calcium, high phosphate, normal PTH, and normal ALP.
Hyperparathyroidism typically presents with high calcium, low phosphate, and high PTH.
Osteoporosis typically shows normal serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and ALP levels.
Osteomalacia typically presents with low calcium, low phosphate, and high PTH and ALP.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: Three point bony relationship has diagnostic value in:
questions.explanation: The three-point bony relationship of the elbow involves the medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, and the tip of the olecranon process. In normal extension, these form a straight line; in flexion, they form an equilateral triangle. This relationship is disrupted in elbow fractures and dislocations.
questions.educationalObjective: Utilize the three-point bony relationship for clinical assessment of elbow injuries.
questions.reasoningChain: Elbow landmarks comprise medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, and olecranon -> Their spatial alignment forms a diagnostic relationship -> Used specifically in evaluating elbow fractures and dislocations.
optionExplanations: Elbow fracture and dislocation are diagnosed by assessing the altered three-point bony relationship.
Monteggia fracture involves proximal ulnar fracture with radial head dislocation, requiring specific forearm evaluation.
Galeazzi fracture involves distal radial shaft fracture with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint.
Colles' fracture is a distal radius fracture evaluated via dinner-fork deformity and wrist examination.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: Management of Olecranon fracture as seen in the image is?
options: Close reduction with Tension band wiring
Open reduction with Tension band wiring
questions.answer: Open reduction with Tension band wiring
questions.explanation: Olecranon fractures involve the articular surface of the elbow joint and disrupt the extensor mechanism of the triceps. Displaced olecranon fractures require open reduction and internal fixation, most commonly using tension band wiring to restore articular congruity and stable fixation.
questions.educationalObjective: Determine the definitive surgical management for displaced olecranon fractures.
questions.reasoningChain: Olecranon fracture disrupts the articular surface and tension mechanism -> Requires anatomical reduction -> Open reduction with tension band wiring is the standard procedure.
optionExplanations: Above elbow plaster slab is insufficient for displaced intra-articular olecranon fractures requiring anatomic reduction.
Below elbow plaster slab does not immobilize the triceps pull or maintain reduction of the olecranon fragment.
Closed reduction is generally inadequate for achieving exact intra-articular alignment in displaced olecranon fractures.
Open reduction with tension band wiring accurately restores the articular surface and counteracts tensile forces.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: The diagnosis of the given image
questions.explanation: Scapholunate dissociation is identified on a plain wrist radiograph by widening of the scapholunate joint space (greater than 3 mm), often referred to as the 'signet ring sign' of the scaphoid or the 'Terry Thomas sign' due to the distinct gap between the scaphoid and lunate bones.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify scapholunate instability on wrist radiographs.
questions.reasoningChain: Widened gap between scaphoid and lunate on PA wrist radiograph -> Represents disruption of the scapholunate interosseous ligament -> Classic feature of scapholunate instability.
optionExplanations: Scapho-lunate instability is demonstrated by widened interosseous space between the scaphoid and lunate bones.
Lunate injury or dislocation typically shows altered triangular or triangular-to-trapezoidal shape of the lunate on lateral/PA views.
Distal radioulnar joint instability is assessed clinically and via dedicated views showing subluxation of the ulna.
Wrist dislocation encompasses broader carpal alignments, whereas isolated widening points to ligamentous dissociation.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: Diagnosis of Gout is confirmed by which test?
questions.explanation: The definitive diagnosis of gout is confirmed by synovial fluid analysis via polarizing light microscopy, which demonstrates negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals. While serum uric acid can be elevated, it is not diagnostic on its own during an acute flare.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the gold standard diagnostic test for confirming gout.
questions.reasoningChain: Clinical suspicion of gout requires crystal visualization -> Joint aspiration yields synovial fluid -> Polarized light microscopy reveals negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals.
optionExplanations: Serum uric acid levels can be normal during an acute gout attack and do not definitively confirm the diagnosis.
Synovial fluid analysis showing negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals confirms gout.
Urine uric acid levels assess overproduction versus underexcretion but do not confirm acute joint crystal deposition.
X-ray changes in gout appear late (e.g., punched-out erosions with overhanging edges) and are not used for early confirmation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Berry aneurysm most commonly occurs due to?
options: Endothelial injury of vessel due to HTN
Muscle intimal elastic lamina layer defect
questions.answer: Muscle intimal elastic lamina layer defect
questions.explanation: Berry aneurysms (saccular aneurysms of cerebral arteries, commonly in the circle of Willis) typically develop due to a congenital or acquired structural defect in the tunica media and internal elastic lamina at arterial branch points, which lack adequate smooth muscle support.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the congenital or structural wall defect responsible for berry aneurysms.
questions.reasoningChain: Circle of Willis branch points lack a complete muscular coat -> Defect in the media and internal elastic lamina occurs -> Hydrostatic pressure leads to saccular outpouching.
optionExplanations: Endothelial injury due to hypertension contributes to atherosclerosis, not classical saccular berry aneurysms.
Muscle and internal elastic lamina layer defect represents the characteristic structural weakness leading to berry aneurysms.
Muscle and adventitial layer defects do not describe the specific media-elastic lamina gap characteristic of cerebral aneurysms.
Adventitial defects alone are insufficient to cause the high-pressure ballooning seen in cerebral berry aneurysms.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A 45-year patient working in a factory for the past 20 years presents with breathlessness. HRCT chest shows pleural thickening and fibrosis. What is the person suffering from?
questions.explanation: Asbestosis is a pneumoconiosis caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers, classically presenting in workers with long-term industrial exposure. HRCT chest findings typically reveal lower lobe-predominant interstitial fibrosis and pleural plaques/thickening.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the clinical and radiological features of asbestosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Factory worker with long-term exposure and pleural thickening with fibrosis -> Points to asbestos exposure -> Diagnosis is asbestosis.
optionExplanations: Asbestosis characteristically causes pleural thickening, pleural plaques, and lower lobe pulmonary fibrosis.
Coal worker's pneumoconiosis presents with upper lobe nodular fibrosis without prominent pleural thickening.
Silicosis presents with upper lobe calcified eggshell nodes and progressive massive fibrosis, lacking prominent pleural plaques.
Berylliosis causes non-caseating granulomas resembling sarcoidosis due to beryllium exposure.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Correct about of Anaemia of chronic disease
options: Increased percentage of saturation of transferrin
questions.explanation: Anemia of chronic disease (ACD), also known as anemia of inflammation, is characterized by elevated levels of hepcidin induced by inflammatory cytokines. This traps iron within reticuloendothelial macrophages, leading to low serum iron, low transferrin, low total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and characteristically high or normal serum ferritin levels.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the iron profile associated with anemia of chronic disease.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic inflammation upregulates hepcidin -> Iron is sequestered in macrophages -> Serum ferritin is high while serum iron and transferrin saturation are low.
optionExplanations: High ferritin is a hallmark of anemia of chronic disease due to iron sequestration in storage depots.
Percentage saturation of transferrin is typically low or normal in anemia of chronic disease.
Transferrin levels are typically low or normal, unlike iron deficiency anemia where transferrin/TIBC is high.
Serum iron is low because iron is trapped inside reticuloendothelial macrophages by hepcidin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Which of these is Nephritic syndrome?
questions.explanation: Post-infectious glomerulonephritis (PIGN) is the classic prototype of acute nephritic syndrome, typically presenting following a group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection with hematuria, edema, hypertension, and oliguria. On histology, it shows diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with subepithelial humps.
questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate nephritic glomerulonephropathies from nephrotic entities.
questions.reasoningChain: Post-infectious glomerulonephritis presents with acute hematuria, hypertension, and edema -> These are hallmark features of nephritic syndrome.
optionExplanations: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, presenting with heavy proteinuria.
Membranous glomerulopathy is a primary cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, characterized by subepithelial immune deposits.
Post-infectious glomerulonephritis is a classic acute nephritic syndrome characterized by immune complex deposition.
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis typically presents with nephrotic syndrome and resistance to corticosteroid therapy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: The following serological status is noted in a patient: HbsAg positive and HbeAg positive. Diagnosis is?
questions.explanation: The presence of both Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) in serum indicates active viral replication and high infectivity, pointing to an active hepatitis B infection state (either acute or chronic exacerbation).
questions.educationalObjective: Interpret Hepatitis B serological marker combinations.
questions.reasoningChain: HBsAg positive indicates active infection -> HBeAg positive indicates high viral replication and infectivity -> Reflects high viral load and transmission risk.
optionExplanations: Acute viral hepatitis typically shows IgM anti-HBc alongside HBsAg and HBeAg, but HBeAg specifically highlights viral load.
Chronic viral hepatitis can show HBeAg, but acute phase with high infectivity is also directly denoted by HBeAg positivity.
Acute viral hepatitis with infectivity is precisely indicated by the presence of HBsAg and HBeAg.
Remote infection would show negative HBsAg with positive anti-HBs and anti-HBc antibodies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Chronic viral hepatitis is seen with all of the following viruses, except?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a single-stranded RNA virus transmitted via the enteral (fecal-oral) route. It typically causes acute self-limiting hepatitis and does not establish chronicity, unlike HBV, HCV, and HDV which frequently cause chronic viral hepatitis.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify hepatitis viruses capable of causing chronic infection.
questions.reasoningChain: Hepatitis E is transmitted enterically -> Causes acute self-limiting infection -> Does not lead to chronic viral hepatitis.
optionExplanations: HBV is a DNA virus well-known for causing chronic viral hepatitis.
HCV is an RNA virus with a very high rate of chronicity.
HDV is a defective satellite virus that requires HBV co-infection or superinfection and causes severe chronic disease.
HEV causes acute viral hepatitis and does not cause chronic hepatitis in immunocompetent individuals.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Acute graft rejection occurs within?
questions.explanation: Acute graft rejection typically occurs from 1 week up to 6 months post-transplantation, driven primarily by cellular immune responses (T-cell mediated) against donor human leukocyte antigens (HLAs).
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the timeline for acute transplant rejection.
questions.reasoningChain: Acute rejection is mediated by T-cells and host immunity against graft -> Occurs days to months after transplant -> Typically within 6 months.
optionExplanations: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours due to pre-existing donor-specific antibodies.
Acute cellular and antibody-mediated rejections typically manifest within days to less than 6 months post-transplant.
Acute rejection occurs within less than 6 months of transplantation.
Chronic rejection develops over months to years due to arteriosclerosis and fibrosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Type II Hypersensitivity is seen in?
questions.explanation: Type II hypersensitivity reactions involve antibody-mediated (IgG or IgM) destruction of cells via complement activation, opsonization, or antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity. Pernicious anemia is a classic example where autoantibodies target intrinsic factor or gastric parietal cells.
questions.educationalObjective: Classify pernicious anemia within the Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity framework.
questions.reasoningChain: Pernicious anemia involves autoantibodies against intrinsic factor/parietal cells -> Antibodies bind cell surfaces leading to destruction -> This represents a Type II hypersensitivity reaction.
optionExplanations: Pernicious anemia is mediated by antibodies directed against cellular antigens, classifying it as Type II hypersensitivity.
Serum sickness is an immune complex-mediated condition, classified as Type III hypersensitivity.
Arthus phenomenon is a localized immune complex-mediated vasculitis, classified as Type III hypersensitivity.
Pathergy phenomenon is a non-specific hyper-reactivity of the skin seen in Behçet's disease, not a standard hypersensitivity type.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A stable 25 years old farmer was admitted with acute onset of fever, cough, and dyspnea. Chest radiograph showed findings of pneumonia for which he was treated with antibiotics; showed good response. After 1 month he again presented in the hypoxemic state with progressive dyspnea. CT chest showed diffuse ground glass changes. Transbronchial biopsies showed numerous small granulomas and marked lymphocytosis. Which of the following is a causative agent for a given disease?
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis) occurs due to repeated inhalation of organic antigens, such as thermophilic actinomycetes found in moldy hay (farmer's lung). It presents subacutely or chronically with dyspnea, lymphocytic alveolitis, and non-caseating granulomas.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the etiology of farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis).
questions.reasoningChain: Farmer exposed to organic dust presents with recurrent respiratory symptoms and granulomas -> Classic presentation of farmer's lung -> Caused by Thermophilic Actinomycetes.
optionExplanations: Thermophilic Actinomycetes (e.g., Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula) causes farmer's lung hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Aspergillus fumigatus causes allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) or aspergilloma, not typical farmer's lung.
Actinobacter is a bacterial pathogen associated with nosocomial infections.
Aspergillus flavus produces aflatoxins and causes invasive infections or aspergillomas, not typical hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Most sensitive indicator for Iron deficiency anaemia?
questions.explanation: Serum ferritin reflects total body iron stores and is the most sensitive and reliable non-invasive indicator for diagnosing iron deficiency anemia, as stores deplete before the development of overt microcytic anemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Determine the most sensitive diagnostic marker for iron deficiency.
questions.reasoningChain: Iron stores deplete first in iron deficiency -> Serum ferritin directly correlates with iron storage -> Makes it the most sensitive indicator.
optionExplanations: Serum ferritin directly measures iron stores and decreases earliest in iron deficiency anemia.
TIBC increases in iron deficiency but is less sensitive than ferritin levels.
Percentage saturation of transferrin drops in iron deficiency but ferritin drops earlier.
Bone marrow iron staining is the gold standard for iron assessment but is invasive, not the most sensitive clinical blood indicator.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Whipple's disease is caused by.
questions.explanation: Whipple's disease is a systemic infectious condition caused by the Gram-positive bacterium Tropheryma whipplei. It classically presents with malabsorption, diarrhea, weight loss, and arthralgias, with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive macrophages in the lamina propria.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the causative infectious agent category of Whipple's disease.
questions.reasoningChain: Whipple's disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei -> Tropheryma whipplei is a bacterium -> Therefore, the disease is caused by bacteria.
optionExplanations: Bacteria (specifically Tropheryma whipplei) is the causative pathogen of Whipple's disease.
Viruses are not the etiologic agents responsible for Whipple's gastrointestinal pathology.
Protozoa are not responsible for Whipple's disease, though other parasites cause malabsorption.
Helminths do not cause Whipple's disease or the characteristic PAS-positive macrophage infiltration.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Most common primary for brain metastasis is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumors in adults. The most frequent primary source for brain metastasis is lung cancer (particularly small cell and non-small cell lung carcinomas), followed by breast cancer and melanoma.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the most frequent primary malignancy metastasizing to the brain.
questions.reasoningChain: Intracranial metastases most frequently originate from systemic tumors -> Lung cancer has the highest propensity to metastasize to the brain -> Makes lung cancer the most common primary.
optionExplanations: Lung cancer is the single most frequent primary malignancy that metastasizes to the brain.
Head and neck cancers rarely metastasize to the brain compared to lung and breast primaries.
Prostate cancer frequently metastasizes to bone, though brain metastases can occur less commonly.
Breast cancer is a common cause of brain metastasis, but second in frequency behind lung cancer.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Which is not seen in Tumor lysis Syndrome?
questions.explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome occurs due to massive destruction of malignant cells releasing intracellular contents into the bloodstream. This leads to hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, secondary hypocalcemia (due to calcium phosphate precipitation), and hyperuricemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the biochemical electrolyte disturbances seen in tumor lysis syndrome.
questions.reasoningChain: Rapid lysis of tumor cells releases intracellular ions -> Potassium, phosphate, and uric acid increase -> Calcium binds excess phosphate, causing hypocalcemia.
optionExplanations: Hypophosphatemia is incorrect; phosphate is released intracellularly in large amounts, causing hyperphosphatemia.
Hypocalcemia occurs secondary to binding of calcium by the released high levels of phosphate.
Hyperuricemia occurs due to rapid breakdown of cellular nucleic acids (purines into uric acid).
Hyperkalemia results from the massive release of intracellular potassium into the extracellular space.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A 12-year-old boy presents to the clinic complaining of severe abdominal pain and headache for the past two days. He has a history of myalgia and several episodes of vomiting. His parents self-medicated with paracetamol, but the patient had no relief. A dengue NS -1 antigen test was ordered which came out positive. What is the first line of defence of the body in the given scenario?
questions.explanation: Natural killer (NK) cells are part of the innate immune system and serve as the rapid first line of cellular defense against viral infections and intracellular pathogens prior to the adaptive T-cell response.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the primary innate immune effector cells acting as the first line of defense against viral infections.
questions.reasoningChain: Viral infection (such as dengue) triggers innate immunity -> Natural killer cells act immediately to lyse infected cells -> NK cells represent the first cellular defense.
optionExplanations: Natural killer cells provide immediate innate defense against virally infected cells before adaptive immunity takes over.
T cells belong to the adaptive immune system and take days to weeks to fully expand and clear infections.
Histiocytes are tissue macrophages involved in phagocytosis, serving later in antigen presentation and clearance.
Macrophages act primarily in phagocytosis and antigen presentation during the innate-to-adaptive transition.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Which of the following interfere with iron absorption?
questions.explanation: Dietary iron absorption in the duodenum is enhanced by reducing substances like Vitamin C and inhibited by chelating substances such as phytates (found in grains), oxalates (found in spinach), tannins (tea), and calcium.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify dietary factors that inhibit iron absorption.
questions.reasoningChain: Dietary components bind iron in the intestinal lumen -> Phytates form insoluble complexes preventing uptake -> Inhibits iron absorption.
optionExplanations: Vitamin C enhances iron absorption by maintaining iron in the ferrous state.
Phytates bind iron in the gastrointestinal tract, significantly interfering with and inhibiting its absorption.
Oxalates bind divalent cations like iron and calcium, reducing their bioavailability and absorption.
Myoglobin is a source of heme iron, which is absorbed efficiently and does not inhibit iron uptake.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Most sensitive and specific marker for myocardial infarction is?
questions.explanation: Cardiac troponins (specifically Troponin I and Troponin T) are the most sensitive and specific biomarkers for myocardial necrosis and myocardial infarction, remaining elevated for up to 1-2 weeks after an ischemic event.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the preferred biomarker for diagnosing myocardial infarction.
questions.reasoningChain: Myocardial injury releases structural proteins -> Troponins are highly specific to cardiac muscle tissue -> Troponins serve as the most sensitive and specific markers.
optionExplanations: Troponin is the most sensitive and specific biochemical marker for myocardial infarction.
Cytokeratin is a general epithelial marker, not specific to cardiac muscle necrosis.
Myoglobin is sensitive and rises early, but lacks cardiac specificity as it is also found in skeletal muscle.
CPK-MM is found predominantly in skeletal muscle and lacks cardiac specificity compared to CK-MB or troponin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Antecedent diagnosis of Group A streptococcal infection in Acute rheumatic fever can be made by?
questions.explanation: Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer is the classic serological test used to document a preceding Group A Streptococcus (GAS) infection when establishing the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever according to the Jones criteria.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the serological test confirming antecedent streptococcal infection in rheumatic fever.
questions.reasoningChain: Acute rheumatic fever requires evidence of preceding GAS infection -> ASO antibodies develop against streptolysin O -> ASO titer serves as the primary serological proof.
optionExplanations: ASO titer confirms recent Group A streptococcal infection as part of diagnosing acute rheumatic fever.
CRP is an acute-phase reactant indicating active systemic inflammation, not specific to streptococcus.
ESR elevation reflects systemic inflammation non-specifically.
Low C3 levels are characteristic of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, not rheumatic fever.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Most common anterior mediastinal tumour?
questions.explanation: Thymoma is the most common primary tumor of the anterior mediastinum in adults, often associated with autoimmune paraneoplastic syndromes such as myasthenia gravis.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the most common anterior mediastinal tumor.
questions.reasoningChain: Anterior mediastinum is the most frequent site for thymic neoplasms -> Thymoma represents the most prevalent primary tumor in this location.
optionExplanations: Thymoma is the most common primary neoplasm of the anterior mediastinum.
Neurofibroma typically arises in the posterior mediastinum along nerve roots.
Pericardial cyst is a benign middle/anterior mediastinal lesion but less frequent than thymoma.
Bronchogenic cyst is typically located in the middle or posterior mediastinum near airways.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Most characteristic finding of diabetic nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease (nodular glomerulosclerosis) is the pathognomonic and most characteristic histopathological finding of diabetic nephropathy, characterized by ball-like mesangial matrix accumulations in the glomeruli.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the pathognomonic renal lesion of diabetic nephropathy.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic diabetes mellitus leads to glomerular microvascular damage -> Nodular mesangial sclerosis develops -> Termed Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions.
optionExplanations: Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions (nodular glomerulosclerosis) are the pathognomonic hallmark of diabetic nephropathy.
Diffuse glomerulosclerosis is also seen in diabetic nephropathy but is less specific than nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions.
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is a primary glomerular disease causing nephrotic syndrome, not specific to diabetes.
Armani-Ebstein change refers to glycogen accumulation in renal tubular epithelial cells in severe untreated diabetes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Comment on the diagnosis for an individual serum alkaline phosphatase normal, PTH normal, Vitamin D3 normal with elevated serum Calcium values?
questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma frequently presents with hypercalcemia due to osteoclast activation by tumor cytokines (like RANKL). Unlike primary hyperparathyroidism or vitamin D toxicity, multiple myeloma features normal PTH, normal vitamin D3, and normal alkaline phosphatase because bone formation is suppressed while resorption is driven by lytic lesions.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose the cause of hypercalcemia with normal PTH and alkaline phosphatase.
questions.reasoningChain: Elevated calcium with normal PTH and normal vitamin D3 -> Suggests malignancy-driven bone resorption -> Multiple myeloma matches this profile with normal ALP.
optionExplanations: Vitamin D intoxication causes elevated calcium and high/normal vitamin D metabolites, but usually suppressed PTH.
Hyperparathyroidism is characterized by elevated calcium coupled with elevated PTH levels.
Multiple myeloma causes hypercalcemia via osteolytic bone destruction with normal PTH and normal alkaline phosphatase.
Nutritional rickets presents with low or normal calcium, low phosphate, and elevated PTH and ALP.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old patient presents in an emergency with complaints of severe headache, body aches, irregular fever during day and night, nausea and vomiting and loss of taste. He was successfully treated for malaria two months back when he had similar symptoms in the past, and his blood smear shows in the exhibit. On examination, he has hepatosplenomegaly and is jaundiced. He feels dizzy and weak during the examination and in severe distress. His platelet count is also decreased, and his LFTs are also deranged. What is the most common cause of recurrent malaria in this patient?
questions.explanation: Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale are characterized by the presence of dormant liver-stage parasites known as hypnozoites, which reactivate weeks to months after the initial infection, causing frequent relapses of malaria.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the mechanism and species responsible for relapsing malaria.
questions.reasoningChain: Recurrent malaria months after treatment implies dormant liver forms -> Hypnozoites are characteristic of Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale -> P. vivax is the most common cause.
optionExplanations: Plasmodium falciparum causes recrudescence due to persistent low-level blood parasitemia, not true hepatic relapses.
Plasmodium vivax forms dormant hypnozoites in the liver, leading to frequent clinical relapses.
Heterozygous sickle cell trait confers resistance against severe malaria rather than causing relapses.
Babesia is a tick-borne piroplasm causing babesiosis, not classic malarial relapses.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: MC cause of atypical pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the single most common cause of community-acquired atypical pneumonia, particularly in young adults and school-aged children, often presenting with insidious onset, persistent dry cough, and cold agglutinins.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the most frequent pathogen responsible for atypical pneumonia.
questions.reasoningChain: Atypical pneumonia is characterized by mild systemic symptoms and interstitial infiltrates -> Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the most frequent causative agent.
optionExplanations: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the leading cause of atypical pneumonia across outpatient populations.
Klebsiella pneumoniae is a classic cause of typical lobar pneumonia, particularly in alcoholics and hospitalized patients.
Haemophilus influenzae typically causes typical bacterial pneumonia or exacerbations of chronic bronchitis.
Chlamydia pneumoniae is another atypical pathogen, but less frequent than Mycoplasma.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: A 3-year-old child with a weight of 12 kg is having loose motions. He is thirsty, drinks eagerly, tears are absent and skin pinch goes back slowly. What is the best treatment plan for this child?
options: 300 ml ORS per episode of loose stool
questions.explanation: According to WHO IMNCI guidelines, a child with sunken eyes, eager drinking, and slow skin pinch is classified as having 'Some Dehydration' (Plan B). The recommended treatment is administration of 75 ml/kg of ORS over a 4-hour period (for a 12 kg child, approximately 900 ml of ORS).
questions.educationalObjective: Calculate the correct ORS rehydration volume and plan for pediatric dehydration.
questions.reasoningChain: Child exhibits signs of some dehydration -> IMNCI Plan B applies -> Calculate ORS dose (75 ml/kg for 12 kg = 900 ml over 4 hours).
optionExplanations: 1200 ml of RL over 12 hours is incorrect; IV fluids are reserved for severe dehydration under Plan C.
600 ml of RL over 6 hours is incorrect fluid type and duration for 'some' dehydration management.
900 ml of ORS over 4 hours is the correct WHO Plan B protocol for a 12 kg child with some dehydration.
300 ml per episode is used for maintenance or mild diarrhea without moderate dehydration signs (Plan A).

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Wide open posterior fontanelle ,large tongue ,rough dry skin with constipation is seen in?
questions.explanation: Congenital hypothyroidism presents with characteristic features including a wide-open posterior fontanelle, macroglossia (large tongue), dry rough skin, umbilical hernia, sluggishness, and prolonged constipation.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation of congenital hypothyroidism in infants.
questions.reasoningChain: Infant with wide posterior fontanelle, large tongue, and constipation -> Classic triad of congenital hypothyroidism -> Requires prompt thyroid hormone replacement.
optionExplanations: Pellagra presents with the 3 Ds (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia) due to niacin deficiency.
Down syndrome features hypotonia, upward slanting palpebral fissures, and single transverse palmar crease.
Congenital hypothyroidism classically manifests with wide fontanelles, macroglossia, dry skin, and constipation.
Nutritional rickets presents with craniotabes, widened wrists, and rachitic rosary due to vitamin D/calcium deficiency.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Neonatal jaundice becomes detectable at serum bilirubin exceeding?
questions.explanation: Neonatal jaundice becomes visibly noticeable on clinical inspection (scleral and dermal icterus) when the serum total bilirubin concentration exceeds approximately 5 mg/dL.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the threshold serum bilirubin level for visible neonatal jaundice.
questions.reasoningChain: Clinical jaundice appears when bilirubin accumulates in skin and sclera -> Threshold for visibility is approximately 5 mg/dL.
optionExplanations: 2 mg% is below the typical threshold for clinical detection of jaundice in newborns.
3 mg% is below the minimum serum bilirubin level required for visible cutaneous icterus.
4 mg% is close to but still slightly below the standard clinical detection threshold.
5 mg% is the recognized serum bilirubin level at which neonatal jaundice becomes clinically detectable.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: A professor explains the pathophysiology of a “tet spell” and that it is due to a decrease in systemic vascular resistance that leads to more shunting of blood from right to left, causing an overload on the left side of the heart and decreasing the amount of blood reaching the lungs. Which of the following options determines the severity of the cyanotic spells?
options: Size of the ventricular septal defect (VSD)
questions.explanation: In Tetralogy of Fallot, hypercyanotic ('tet') spells are triggered by a reduction in systemic vascular resistance or spasm of the infundibular pulmonary outflow tract. The anatomical feature that primarily dictates the baseline severity and risk of cyanotic spells is the degree of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (degree of pulmonary stenosis).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the primary determinant of symptom severity in Tetralogy of Fallot.
questions.reasoningChain: Tetralogy of Fallot pathophysiology centers on right-to-left shunting -> Shunt magnitude depends on pulmonary outflow resistance -> Degree of pulmonary stenosis dictates clinical severity.
optionExplanations: Size of the VSD is typically large (non-restrictive) in TOF, so it does not limit the shunt.
Overriding of the aorta is a fixed anatomical finding that contributes to anatomy but not dynamic severity.
Degree of RVH is a secondary compensatory response to the outflow obstruction, not the primary determinant.
Degree of pulmonary stenosis determines the amount of pulmonary blood flow and severity of cyanotic spells.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Infant is admitted with respiratory distress and prolonged expiration with rhonchi in chest. CXR shows hyperinflation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute bronchiolitis is a common lower respiratory tract infection in infants, characterized by respiratory distress, expiratory wheezing, rhonchi, and hyperinflation on chest radiography, most commonly caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV).
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose acute bronchiolitis in infants based on clinical and radiological findings.
questions.reasoningChain: Infant presents with respiratory distress, prolonged expiration, and hyperinflation -> Findings are classic for acute bronchiolitis.
optionExplanations: Pneumonia typically presents with focal crackles and focal consolidation rather than generalized hyperinflation and wheezing.
Croup presents with a characteristic barking cough and inspiratory stridor due to upper airway narrowing.
Asthma is less common in very young infants and typically presents with recurrent episodes of wheezing.
Bronchiolitis presents with expiratory wheezing, rhonchi, and hyperinflation in infants under 2 years of age.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: 6th day disease is?
questions.explanation: Exanthema subitum (Roseola infantum), caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), is often referred to as the 'sixth disease'. It is characterized by high fever for 3-5 days followed by sudden defervescence and the appearance of a blanching maculopapular rash.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the classic eponym/number designation for roseola infantum.
questions.reasoningChain: Classic childhood exanthems are numbered historically -> Roseola infantum corresponds to exanthema subitum -> Known as the sixth disease.
optionExplanations: Erythema infectiosum is known as fifth disease, caused by Parvovirus B19.
Exanthema subitum (roseola infantum) is classically known as the sixth disease.
Erythema marginatum is a characteristic rash associated with acute rheumatic fever.
Erythema nodosum represents painful subcutaneous nodules on shins, seen in sarcoidosis or streptococcal infections.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Shortest acting corticosteroid is?
questions.explanation: Hydrocortisone is a short-acting systemic corticosteroid with a biological half-life of 8-12 hours and prominent mineralocorticoid activity, making it structurally identical to endogenous cortisol.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the relative duration of action of systemic corticosteroids.
questions.reasoningChain: Corticosteroids are categorized by duration of action -> Hydrocortisone has a short biological half-life -> Shortest acting among the options.
optionExplanations: Dexamethasone is a long-acting corticosteroid with high potency and no mineralocorticoid activity.
Hydrocortisone is a short-acting corticosteroid with a biological half-life of 8-12 hours.
Triamcinolone is an intermediate-acting corticosteroid commonly used in dermatology and intra-articular injections.
Deflazacort is an intermediate-acting oxazoline derivative of prednisolone with bone-sparing properties.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old female presents to the clinic. She is a known epileptic patient, and she wants to get pregnant. Which of the following antiepileptic drugs has the highest teratogenic potential and is not prescribed to pregnant women?
questions.explanation: Sodium valproate is associated with the highest teratogenic potential among commonly used antiepileptic drugs, carrying a significant risk of neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida), craniofacial abnormalities, and cognitive impairment when taken during pregnancy.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the antiepileptic drug with the highest teratogenic risk.
questions.reasoningChain: Woman of childbearing age requires safe AED -> Valproate carries high risk of neural tube defects -> Contraindicated or avoided in pregnancy.
optionExplanations: Valproate has the highest teratogenic potential, notably causing neural tube defects and developmental delay.
Carbamazepine is teratogenic (associated with neural tube defects), but has a lower overall risk than valproate.
Phenytoin is teratogenic (fetal hydantoin syndrome), but valproate carries a higher risk profile.
Lamotrigine is considered one of the safer antiepileptic drugs during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: You, being an ardent researcher in the field of vaccine production, are the in-charge of preparing samples to make a vaccine against the new variant of SARS-CoV 2. After getting satisfactory results in preclinical studies, you seek approval to do clinical studies, which requires healthy volunteers. Which of the following phases does this refer to?
questions.explanation: Clinical trials are divided into phases. Phase 1 trials are the first stage of clinical testing in humans, conducted on a small group of healthy volunteers primarily to evaluate safety, pharmacokinetics, and toxicity.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the objectives of Phase 1 clinical trials.
questions.reasoningChain: Initial clinical evaluation of a new vaccine in healthy human volunteers -> Focuses primarily on safety and dosage -> Defines Phase 1 clinical trials.
optionExplanations: Phase 1 trials involve healthy human volunteers to evaluate safety, toxicity, and pharmacokinetics.
Phase 2 trials involve patients with the target condition to assess preliminary efficacy and optimal dosing.
Phase 3 trials involve large-scale randomized controlled trials to confirm therapeutic efficacy and monitor adverse effects.
Phase 4 trials are post-marketing surveillance studies conducted after drug approval.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Long term use of which of the following drug is most likely associated with development of tremors?
questions.explanation: Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist. Stimulation of beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle leads to increased intracellular cAMP and tremors (fine skeletal muscle tremors), which is a common dose-dependent adverse effect of long-term or excessive use.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the mechanism of tremors associated with beta-2 agonists.
questions.reasoningChain: Salbutamol stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors -> Causes skeletal muscle stimulation -> Results in fine tremors as a common side effect.
optionExplanations: Salbutamol causes fine tremors due to beta-2 receptor-mediated stimulation in skeletal muscle tissue.
Propofol is an intravenous anesthetic agent used for sedation and induction, not associated with tremors.
Betaxolol is a cardioselective beta-blocker used in glaucoma or hypertension.
Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker used primarily in ophthalmology for glaucoma.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is a long acting bronchodilator?
questions.explanation: Formoterol is a long-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist (LABA) with a rapid onset of action, used for long-term maintenance bronchodilation in asthma and COPD.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify long-acting bronchodilator agents.
questions.reasoningChain: Bronchodilators include short and long-acting agents -> Formoterol provides prolonged beta-2 agonism -> Classified as a long-acting bronchodilator.
optionExplanations: Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) used for acute rescue bronchodilation.
Terbutaline is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used for acute bronchospasm or to suppress premature labor.
Adrenaline is a non-selective adrenergic agonist used for acute anaphylaxis and resuscitation.
Formoterol is a long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA) providing sustained bronchodilation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Drug of choice for neurogenic diabetes insipidus is:
questions.explanation: Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a synthetic analog of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin) with enhanced V2 receptor specificity and a longer duration of action, making it the drug of choice for central (neurogenic) diabetes insipidus.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the drug of choice for neurogenic diabetes insipidus.
questions.reasoningChain: Neurogenic diabetes insipidus involves deficient ADH -> Desmopressin acts as a synthetic ADH analog -> Drug of choice for central DI.
optionExplanations: Conivaptan is a vasopressin V1a/V2 receptor antagonist used for euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia.
Vasopressin is short-acting and causes significant vasoconstriction via V1 receptors, making it less ideal for chronic use.
Terlipressin is a vasopressin analog used primarily for bleeding esophageal varices and hepatorenal syndrome.
Desmopressin is the drug of choice for central diabetes insipidus due to its specific V2 agonism and long duration.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Which of the following inhalational anesthetic agents can cause hepatitis on repeated use?
questions.explanation: Halothane is an inhalational anesthetic agent historically associated with a rare but severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity known as halothane hepatitis, which can occur upon repeated exposure due to immune-mediated destruction of trifluoroacetylated hepatocytes.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the hepatotoxic potential of repeated halothane exposure.
questions.reasoningChain: Repeated exposure to halothane -> Undergoes hepatic metabolism to reactive intermediates -> Can cause severe immune-mediated hepatitis.
optionExplanations: Halothane is well-known for causing idiosyncratic post-operative hepatitis upon repeated administration.
Isoflurane undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism and has an extremely low risk of hepatotoxicity.
Sevoflurane is a modern fluorinated ether anesthetic with an excellent hepatic safety profile.
Ether is an older volatile anesthetic agent not associated with this specific immune-mediated hepatitis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Preferred drug for the treatment of ventricular tachycardia is
questions.explanation: Lignocaine (lidocaine) is a Class Ib antiarrhythmic drug and is the historical preferred agent for the acute management and termination of ventricular arrhythmias, such as ventricular tachycardia, particularly in the setting of acute myocardial ischemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify antiarrhythmic agents used in acute ventricular tachycardia.
questions.reasoningChain: Ventricular tachycardia requires prompt antiarrhythmic therapy -> Lignocaine blocks cardiac sodium channels -> Effective choice for ischemic ventricular tachycardia.
optionExplanations: Digoxin is used for heart rate control in atrial fibrillation and heart failure, not ventricular tachycardia.
Propranolol is a beta-blocker used for supraventricular tachyarrhythmias or blood pressure control.
Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used for supraventricular tachycardias.
Lignocaine is a sodium channel blocker historically utilized for acute ventricular arrhythmias.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a history of severe pain and swelling of her left great toe. She has had similar episodes sporadically over the past 3 years. She drinks 6 beers daily. She does not smoke or use illicit drugs. She is allergic to hydrochlorothiazide and glipizide. Examination shows erythema, warmth, and tenderness of the left first metatarsophalangeal joint and a nodule over the right elbow. Which of the following drugs below is the first choice for chronic gout?
questions.explanation: Allopurinol, a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, is the first-line urate-lowering therapy recommended for the chronic management of gout to prevent recurrent flares and reduce tophaceous deposits.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the first-line pharmacotherapy for chronic gout management.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic gout requires urate-lowering therapy -> Xanthine oxidase inhibitors reduce uric acid synthesis -> Allopurinol is the established first-choice agent.
optionExplanations: Allopurinol is the first-choice xanthine oxidase inhibitor for chronic urate-lowering therapy in gout.
Febuxostat is an alternative xanthine oxidase inhibitor, often reserved for patients intolerant to allopurinol.
Probenecid is a uricosuric agent used as a second-line option for patients with under-excretion of uric acid.
Sulfinpyrazone is another older uricosuric agent, rarely used as first-line therapy due to toxicity risks.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is used for day care surgery?
options: Etomidate Drugs used in day care surgery
questions.explanation: Propofol is an intravenous anesthetic agent characterized by rapid onset and rapid recovery due to swift redistribution and clearance, making it the preferred agent for day-care (ambulatory) surgery.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify intravenous anesthetics suitable for ambulatory surgery.
questions.reasoningChain: Day-care surgery requires rapid recovery and minimal hangover effect -> Propofol provides fast onset and quick clear-headed recovery -> Ideal for outpatient procedures.
optionExplanations: Ketamine causes dissociative anesthesia and prolonged recovery with emergence delirium, less ideal for rapid outpatient discharge.
Thiopentone has a slower recovery profile due to accumulation in fat stores with repeated doses.
Propofol offers rapid clearance and quick recovery, making it ideal for day-care anesthesia.
Etomidate provides stable hemodynamics but can cause adrenal suppression and prolonged myoclonic movements.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A female with 20 weeks of pregnancy presents with fever and dysuria. A preliminary diagnosis of cystitis was made. Which of the following drugs will be safe to use for this patient?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin is a penicillin antibiotic that is considered safe for use during pregnancy for treating susceptible urinary tract infections, whereas tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and certain sulfa drugs carry significant fetal risks.
questions.educationalObjective: Select safe antibiotic therapy for cystitis during pregnancy.
questions.reasoningChain: Pregnant female with cystitis requires safe antimicrobial therapy -> Penicillins like amoxicillin have established safety profiles in pregnancy -> Safe choice.
optionExplanations: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone that carries risks of cartilage and joint damage in developing fetuses.
Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside associated with fetal ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity risks.
Cotrimoxazole contains trimethoprim, which can cause folate antagonism, especially during the first trimester.
Amoxicillin is safe and effective for treating urinary tract infections during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Praziquantel is used for the treatment of
questions.explanation: Praziquantel is an anthelmintic medication that increases cell membrane permeability to calcium in trematodes and cestodes, leading to rapid muscular contraction, paralysis, and death. It is the drug of choice for treating schistosomiasis (bilharziasis).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the clinical indication and antiparasitic spectrum of praziquantel.
questions.reasoningChain: Schistosomiasis is caused by blood flukes (trematodes) -> Praziquantel targets trematodes effectively -> Drug of choice for schistosomiasis.
optionExplanations: Strongyloidiasis is treated with ivermectin or albendazole, not praziquantel.
Trichomoniasis is a protozoal infection treated with nitroimidazoles like metronidazole.
Schistosomiasis is successfully treated using praziquantel.
Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by a protist (Rhinosporsee), treated surgically or with antimicrobials.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A young male presents with reduced sleep, hyperactivity and elevated mood. He has a family history of mania. Which of the following drug should be used for long term treatment of this patient?
questions.explanation: Lithium carbonate is a mood-stabilizing agent used as the gold standard for the long-term prophylactic maintenance treatment of bipolar affective disorder, reducing the frequency and severity of manic and depressive episodes.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the long-term maintenance drug of choice for bipolar disorder.
questions.reasoningChain: Patient presents with manic symptoms and family history of mania -> Requires long-term mood stabilization -> Lithium carbonate is the primary prophylactic agent.
optionExplanations: Sodium valproate is an effective mood stabilizer, but lithium remains the classic gold-standard agent for long-term prophylaxis.
Lithium carbonate is the established drug of choice for long-term maintenance and prevention of manic episodes.
Carbamazepine is used as an alternative mood stabilizer, particularly in rapid-cycling or mixed bipolar states.
Barbiturates are sedative-hypnotic drugs with high dependence potential, not used for mood stabilization.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Drug of choice for nasal carriers of MRSA is:
questions.explanation: Mupirocin nasal ointment is the gold-standard topical antibiotic used to eradicate nasal carriage of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) to prevent endogenous autoinfection and nosocomial spread.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the drug of choice for eradicating nasal MRSA carriage.
questions.reasoningChain: Nasal carriage of MRSA serves as an infection reservoir -> Topical mupirocin effectively eliminates nasal colonization -> Drug of choice.
optionExplanations: Vancomycin is administered intravenously for systemic MRSA infections, not topical nasal decolonization.
Teicoplanin is a parenteral glycopeptide antibiotic used for systemic resistant gram-positive infections.
Mupirocin is the preferred topical agent for eradicating nasal carriage of MRSA.
Linezolid is an oral/IV oxazolidinone used for resistant gram-positive pneumonia and skin infections.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Anti-depressant drug which is used for smoking cessation is?
questions.explanation: Bupropion is an atypical antidepressant (norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor) that is also approved under the trade name Zyban as an effective pharmacotherapy to aid in smoking cessation by reducing nicotine cravings and withdrawal symptoms.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify antidepressant medications utilized for smoking cessation.
questions.reasoningChain: Smoking cessation requires pharmacotherapy to reduce cravings -> Bupropion acts on dopamine and norepinephrine pathways -> Used successfully for smoking cessation.
optionExplanations: Venlafaxine is an SNRI used for depression and generalized anxiety disorders, not smoking cessation.
Topiramate is an anticonvulsant used for migraine prophylaxis and alcohol dependence.
Bupropion is an antidepressant that effectively aids in smoking cessation.
Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant used for neuropathic pain and depression.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of worsening pain and swelling in her left knee. She has a history of peptic ulcer disease, for which she takes cimetidine. Examination shows palpable crepitus and limited range of motion of the left knee. Which is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation: This patient has osteoarthritis and a history of peptic ulcer disease (taking cimetidine). Traditional NSAIDs pose a high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding and ulcer recurrence. A COX-2 selective inhibitor (coxib), such as etoricoxib, provides pain relief with a significantly lower incidence of gastroduodenal ulcers compared to non-selective NSAIDs.
questions.educationalObjective: Select appropriate analgesic therapy for osteoarthritis in patients with peptic ulcer disease.
questions.reasoningChain: Patient has OA and peptic ulcer disease -> Traditional NSAIDs risk GI bleeding -> COX-2 selective inhibitors like etoricoxib offer GI-sparing analgesia.
optionExplanations: Ketorolac is a potent non-selective NSAID with high GI toxicity, contraindicated in active PUD.
Etoricoxib is a COX-2 selective inhibitor providing pain relief with a reduced risk of gastroduodenal ulceration.
Piroxicam is a long-acting non-selective NSAID carrying high gastrointestinal ulcer risk.
Ibuprofen is a traditional non-selective NSAID that can exacerbate peptic ulcer disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Aerosol drug used for the treatment of RSV infection in a child is?
questions.explanation: Ribavirin is a synthetic nucleoside analog administered as an aerosol for the treatment of severe lower respiratory tract infections caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in infants and young children.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the aerosolized antiviral agent used for RSV infection.
questions.reasoningChain: Severe RSV infection in children -> Requires antiviral therapy -> Aerosolized ribavirin is specifically indicated.
optionExplanations: Indinavir is a protease inhibitor used in antiretroviral therapy for HIV.
Amantadine is an older antiviral agent used for Influenza A, though largely abandoned due to resistance.
Ribavirin is administered as an aerosol for severe Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) infections.
Tenofovir is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor used for HIV and Hepatitis B.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Drug of choice for treatment of Alzhiemer's disease is:
questions.explanation: Donepezil is a centrally acting, reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used as first-line pharmacotherapy for the symptomatic management of mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease to enhance cholinergic neurotransmission.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the drug of choice for managing Alzheimer's disease symptoms.
questions.reasoningChain: Alzheimer's disease involves central cholinergic deficit -> Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors improve cognitive function -> Donepezil is the standard first-line agent.
optionExplanations: Donepezil is a central acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used as first-line therapy for Alzheimer's disease.
Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist used to block cholinergic overactivity, opposite of the desired effect.
Physostigmine is a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor but has systemic side effects and a short half-life compared to donepezil.
Fluoxetine is an SSRI antidepressant used for mood disorders.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Mechanism of action of atropine in treatment of organophosphate poisoning is?
options: It is reactivation of acetylcholinesterase enzyme
It is agonist of acetylcholine receptors
questions.explanation: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to an excessive accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Atropine acts as a competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reversing the muscarinic manifestations of poisoning.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the mechanism of atropine in organophosphate poisoning.
questions.reasoningChain: Organophosphate poisoning causes acetylcholine excess -> Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors -> Antagonizes muscarinic symptoms of toxicity.
optionExplanations: Atropine does not inhibit acetylcholine secretion; it blocks the receptors where acetylcholine acts.
Reactivation of acetylcholinesterase is performed by oximes like pralidoxime, not atropine.
Atropine exhibits potent competitive antimuscarinic activity at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors.
Atropine is an antagonist, not an agonist, at acetylcholine receptors.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Secretion of prolactin is inhibited by?
questions.explanation: Prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary is tonically inhibited by dopamine (also known as prolactin-inhibiting factor or PIF) released from the hypothalamus via the tuberoinfundibular pathway.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the primary hypothalamic regulator inhibiting prolactin secretion.
questions.reasoningChain: Anterior pituitary prolactin is under tonic inhibitory control -> Dopamine acts as the primary prolactin-inhibiting factor -> Dopamine suppresses prolactin release.
optionExplanations: Dopamine acts as prolactin-inhibiting factor, exerting tonic suppression on pituitary prolactin secretion.
Noradrenaline does not serve as the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter for prolactin.
Adrenaline functions primarily as a sympathomimetic hormone rather than a prolactin inhibitor.
Serotonin typically stimulates rather than inhibits prolactin release.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: What is the cause of dicrotic notch?
options: Passive filling of blood in ventricles
questions.explanation: The dicrotic notch (incisura) on the aortic pressure pulse wave is caused by the brief, sharp retrograde flow of blood against the aortic valve as it snaps shut at the end of ventricular ejection, marking the closure of the semilunar valves.
questions.educationalObjective: Relate the dicrotic notch on arterial pulse waveforms to cardiac valve closure.
questions.reasoningChain: Ventricular ejection ends -> Aortic pressure drops slightly below ventricular pressure -> Aortic semilunar valve snaps shut, creating the dicrotic notch.
optionExplanations: Passive ventricular filling occurs during diastole, long after the dicrotic notch.
Rapid ejection phase generates the peak of the arterial pressure wave, prior to closure.
Closure of semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) directly causes the dicrotic notch on the arterial pressure curve.
Isovolumic contraction occurs at the start of systole when all valves are closed prior to ejection.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is correct regarding Isovolumic relaxation?
questions.explanation: During isovolumic relaxation, the ventricles relax with all valves closed (both atrioventricular and semilunar valves are closed) so that ventricular volume remains constant while pressure drops rapidly.
questions.educationalObjective: Characterize the state of cardiac valves during isovolumic relaxation.
questions.reasoningChain: Isovolumic relaxation begins after T-wave -> Ventricles relax while pressure falls -> Both AV and semilunar valves remain closed.
optionExplanations: Atrioventricular (AV) valves are closed during isovolumic relaxation (along with semilunar valves).
QT interval corresponds to ventricular depolarization and repolarization (systole), whereas isovolumic relaxation follows T-wave.
The 'c' wave of JVP is caused by bulging of the tricuspid valve into the atrium during isovolumic contraction.
Semilunar valves close at the start of relaxation, they do not open.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Adequate O2 oxygen delivery at cellular level occurs in which type of hypoxia?
questions.explanation: In histotoxic hypoxia, arterial oxygen tension, hemoglobin concentration, and cardiac output are entirely normal, but tissues are unable to utilize oxygen due to cellular poisoning (e.g., cyanide inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase), meaning oxygen is delivered but cannot be consumed.
questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish the pathophysiology of histotoxic hypoxia from other hypoxia types.
questions.reasoningChain: Oxygen delivery to tissues is adequate -> Cellular oxidative phosphorylation is blocked by toxins -> Cells cannot utilize oxygen (histotoxic hypoxia).
optionExplanations: Hypoxic hypoxia is characterized by low arterial PO2 and inadequate oxygen delivery.
Anemic hypoxia involves reduced oxygen-carrying capacity due to low hemoglobin or anemia.
Stagnant hypoxia results from slow blood flow and inadequate circulatory delivery of oxygen.
