Congenital hyperbilirubinemia presents with prolonged unconjugated or conjugated jaundice.
Biliary atresia presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia appearing after the first week of life.
Physiological jaundice typically appears after 24 to 48 hours of life.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: MC congenital defect in Down's syndrome:
questions.explanation: Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD), also known as an endocardial cushion defect, is the most common congenital heart defect associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21), followed by ventricular septal defect (VSD) and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify atrioventricular septal defect as the most frequent congenital cardiac anomaly in Down syndrome.
questions.reasoningChain: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) -> abnormal endocardial cushion development -> Atrioventricular septal defect.
optionExplanations: Patent ductus arteriosus can occur in Down syndrome but is not the most common heart defect.
Atrial septal defect occurs in Down syndrome but less frequently than complete AVSD.
Atrioventricular septal defect is the classic and most prevalent cardiac malformation in Down syndrome.
Ventricular septal defect is common in the general population but less prevalent than AVSD in Down syndrome.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: MC malignancy in children is:
questions.explanation: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common malignancy overall in pediatric patients, accounting for approximately 30% of all childhood cancers. It typically presents with bone marrow failure symptoms, fever, bone pain, and lymphadenopathy.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify leukemia (specifically ALL) as the most common malignancy in children.
questions.reasoningChain: Childhood malignancy prevalence -> hematologic malignancies most common -> Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL).
optionExplanations: Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children, but not the overall most common.
Leukemia (specifically ALL) is the most common pediatric malignancy.
Wilms tumor is the most common renal malignancy in children.
Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor in infancy and childhood.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: A child aged 2 years presents with nonspecific symptoms suggestive of anemia. Peripheral smear shows target cells. He has microcytic hypochromia picture & Hb of 6 gm%. There is positive family history. Next investigation is:
questions.explanation: A young child with microcytic hypochromic anemia, target cells, and a positive family history strongly suggests a thalassemia syndrome (e.g., beta-thalassemia minor or major). Hb electrophoresis is the definitive diagnostic test used to quantify hemoglobin variants (HbA, HbA2, HbF) and confirm thalassemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Select hemoglobin electrophoresis as the definitive diagnostic test for suspected thalassemia.
questions.reasoningChain: Microcytic anemia + target cells + family history -> suspicion of thalassemia -> Hb electrophoresis for definitive diagnosis.
optionExplanations: NESTROFT is a screening test for beta-thalassemia trait, not the definitive diagnostic investigation.
HbA1c estimation is used for long-term glycemic control monitoring in diabetes mellitus.
Hb electrophoresis separates and quantifies hemoglobin variants to diagnose thalassemia accurately.
Osmotic fragility test evaluates red blood cell membrane stability, useful for hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Best method to diagnose HIV in infancy is:
questions.explanation: In infants born to HIV-positive mothers, maternal antibodies cross the placenta and can persist for up to 18 months, causing serological tests like ELISA and Western blot to yield false positives. Therefore, virological testing using Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is the best method to diagnose HIV infection in infancy.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify PCR as the preferred diagnostic method for HIV in infants due to transplacental maternal antibodies.
questions.reasoningChain: Infants < 18 months carry maternal antibodies -> antibody tests unreliable -> HIV DNA/RNA PCR used for direct diagnosis.
optionExplanations: Western blot detects antibodies, which persist maternally in infants and confound diagnosis.
ELISA detects antibodies, yielding false positives from maternal transfer in infants under 18 months.
PCR detects viral nucleic acid directly, making it the gold standard for diagnosing HIV in infancy.
ALL stands for acute lymphoblastic leukemia and is a distractor.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Drug of choice for paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia is:-
questions.explanation: Adenosine is the drug of choice for the acute termination of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) involving a re-entrant pathway in the AV node. It acts by transiently blocking AV nodal conduction due to hyperpolarization mediated by potassium currents.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify adenosine as the drug of choice for acute paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.
questions.reasoningChain: PSVT with AV nodal re-entry -> short half-life drug needed -> Adenosine administered for rapid AV block.
optionExplanations: Digoxin is a slower-acting inotropic and chronotropic agent, no longer first-line for acute PSVT.
Propranolol is a beta-blocker used for rate control, but not acute first-line termination like adenosine.
Adenosine is the ultra-short-acting first-line drug of choice for terminating acute PSVT.
Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker used for rate control or termination, but adenosine is preferred acutely.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Malignant neuroleptic syndrome is caused by:-
questions.explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction caused by dopamine antagonists, most notably typical and atypical antipsychotics. It is characterized by severe hyperthermia, muscular rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered mental status.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify antipsychotics as the primary causative agents of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
questions.reasoningChain: Dopamine D2 receptor blockade by antipsychotics -> central dopaminergic depletion -> Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome.
optionExplanations: Antidepressants can cause serotonin syndrome, but NMS is specifically linked to antipsychotics.
Anxiolytics like benzodiazepines are used to treat agitation, not cause NMS.
Antipsychotics block dopamine receptors and are the direct cause of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Anti-epileptics stabilize neuronal membranes and do not cause NMS.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A 56-year-old male comes to the outpatient department for a routine health check-up. The patient is obese and has smoked for 30 years. His past medical history includes hypertension for 10 years and diabetes mellitus for 8 years, for which he takes amlodipine and metformin pills regularly. On examination, his blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg, and lab findings reveal a cholesterol level of 170 mg/dL. The physician prescribes aspirin to prevent ischemic heart disease. This drug prevents ischemic heart disease by which of the following mechanism of action?
questions.explanation: Low-dose aspirin is used for primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular events by irreversibly inhibiting platelet cyclooxygenase (COX-1). This inhibition blocks the conversion of arachidonic acid to thromboxane A2 (TXA2), a potent vasoconstrictor and platelet aggregator, thereby preventing ischemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Explain that aspirin prevents ischemic heart disease by inhibiting platelet thromboxane A2 (TXA2) synthesis.
questions.reasoningChain: Aspirin acetylates COX-1 in platelets -> decreases thromboxane A2 (TXA2) production -> inhibits platelet aggregation.
optionExplanations: Inhibiting TXA2 synthesis by platelets prevents platelet aggregation and reduces ischemic events.
Inhibiting prostacyclin synthesis would promote thrombosis; aspirin spares endothelial prostacyclin at low doses.
Endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF/NO) synthesis is not inhibited by aspirin.
Endothelin synthesis is not the primary target of aspirin's cardiovascular protective mechanism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Immediate treatment of anaphylaxic shock is
questions.explanation: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is the definitive, life-saving immediate treatment for anaphylactic shock. It acts via alpha-1 receptors to cause vasoconstriction (reversing hypotension and edema) and via beta-2 receptors to cause bronchodilation, while stabilizing mast cells.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify adrenaline as the immediate, life-saving drug of choice for anaphylactic shock.
questions.reasoningChain: Anaphylaxis (vasodilation + bronchospasm) -> immediate adrenaline administration -> alpha/beta receptor stimulation reverses symptoms.
optionExplanations: Hydrocortisone is an adjunct anti-inflammatory agent with a delayed onset, not immediate treatment.
Atropine is an anticholinergic used for bradycardia, not first-line for anaphylaxis.
Adrenaline is the rapid, life-saving first-line agent for anaphylaxis.
Benzylpenicillin is an antibiotic that can precipitate allergies rather than treat anaphylaxis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A 44-year-old male was admitted to the ICU after being diagnosed with Subarachnoid hemorrhage secondary to a ruptured aneurysm. The patient is a known case of stage 2 hypertension and was taking Ramipril for the same. Which of the following calcium channel blockers can be used in this case, which might help relieve the cerebral vasospasm?
questions.explanation: Nimodipine is a lipophilic dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that crosses the blood-brain barrier effectively. It is specifically indicated for patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage to prevent and treat cerebral vasospasm and subsequent ischemic neurological deficits.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify nimodipine as the calcium channel blocker used to prevent cerebral vasospasm following subarachnoid hemorrhage.
questions.reasoningChain: Subarachnoid hemorrhage -> risk of cerebral vasospasm -> Nimodipine administered to prevent ischemia.
optionExplanations: Nimodipine is lipophilic, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and prevents cerebral vasospasm after hemorrhage.
Felodipine is used for systemic hypertension, lacking specific cerebral vasospasm indications.
Amlodipine is a long-acting calcium channel blocker for systemic hypertension and stable angina.
Nitrendipine is used for systemic hypertension, not targeted for subarachnoid hemorrhage vasospasm.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following receptors mediate stretch reflex?
questions.explanation: The muscle spindle is the primary sensory receptor that mediates the stretch reflex (myotatic reflex). It detects changes in muscle length and rate of change, sending afferent signals via group Ia and II fibers to spinal motor neurons.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the muscle spindle as the receptor responsible for the stretch reflex.
questions.reasoningChain: Muscle stretch -> activated muscle spindle -> Ia afferents -> alpha motor neuron excitation -> stretch reflex.
optionExplanations: Golgi tendon organs measure muscle tension and mediate the inverse stretch reflex.
Merkel's discs are slowly adapting mechanoreceptors in the skin detecting touch and pressure.
Muscle spindles act as stretch receptors mediating the monosynaptic stretch reflex.
Meissner's corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors for fine touch in glabrous skin.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following hormones regulates blood levels of 1,25-OH-cholecalciferol positively?
questions.explanation: Parathormone (PTH) positively regulates the renal activation of vitamin D by stimulating the 1-alpha-hydroxylase enzyme in the proximal convoluted tubules. This enzyme converts 25-hydroxycholecalciferol into the active hormone 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol), which increases calcium absorption.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that parathormone positively regulates the production of active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol.
questions.reasoningChain: Low calcium -> increased PTH release -> stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase -> increased 1,25-(OH)2-D3.
optionExplanations: Thyroxine regulates basal metabolic rate and is not a direct positive regulator of 1,25-OH-cholecalciferol.
Parathormone stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase to increase active vitamin D synthesis.
Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, not vitamin D activation.
Calcitonin inhibits bone resorption and decreases calcium levels, opposing PTH.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Do electrical impulses originate in?
questions.explanation: Electrical impulses in the normal heart originate spontaneously in the sinoatrial (SA) node, which acts as the primary physiological pacemaker due to its highest rate of spontaneous diastolic depolarization (funny current).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the SA node as the primary natural pacemaker where cardiac electrical impulses originate.
questions.reasoningChain: Highest rate of phase 4 depolarization -> Sinoatrial (SA) node -> normal pacemaker origin.
optionExplanations: SA node serves as the primary natural pacemaker initiating electrical impulses in the heart.
AV node acts as a secondary pacemaker and delays conduction to allow ventricular filling.
Endocardium is the inner lining of the heart wall, not the impulse generation site.
Epicardium is the outer protective layer of the heart wall.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: The cardiac event at the end of the isometric relaxation phase?
options: Corresponds to the peak of C wave in JVP
Corresponds to T wave in ECG
questions.explanation: During isovolumetric relaxation, all heart valves are closed as ventricular pressure drops rapidly. At the very end of this phase, ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, causing the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves to open, initiating the rapid ventricular filling phase.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify that atrioventricular valves open at the end of the isovolumetric relaxation phase.
questions.reasoningChain: Isovolumetric relaxation (all valves closed) -> ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure -> AV valves open.
optionExplanations: Atrioventricular valves open at the end of isovolumetric relaxation as ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure.
Atrioventricular valves close at the beginning of isovolumetric contraction.
Peak of C wave in JVP corresponds to tricuspid valve bulging into the atrium during isovolumetric contraction.
T wave in ECG represents ventricular repolarization occurring during ventricular systole/relaxation.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Incidence is best measure by:
questions.explanation: Incidence measures the frequency of new cases of a disease in a population over a specified time period. A cohort study is the ideal observational study design for measuring incidence because it follows disease-free individuals over time to observe who develops the outcome.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify cohort studies as the best epidemiological study design for measuring incidence.
questions.reasoningChain: Cohort study -> follows disease-free population forward in time -> directly calculates incidence.
optionExplanations: Cross-sectional studies measure prevalence by assessing exposure and outcome simultaneously.
Cohort studies follow participants forward to determine new disease events, best for incidence.
Case-control studies start with diseased and non-diseased groups, measuring odds ratios, not incidence.
Double-blind studies are experimental designs (RCTs) used to minimize bias during interventions.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: A microbiologist is preparing BCG vaccine in the laboratory. Which of the following is diluent used with BCG vaccine?
questions.explanation: The BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) vaccine is a live attenuated bacterial vaccine that is supplied as a freeze-dried powder and must be reconstituted strictly with normal saline (sterile 0.9% sodium chloride) prior to administration. Using other diluents can compromise viability.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify normal saline as the correct diluent used for reconstituting the BCG vaccine.
questions.reasoningChain: BCG freeze-dried vaccine -> requires safe reconstitution -> Normal saline is the authorized diluent.
optionExplanations: Normal saline is the standard sterile diluent used for reconstituting the BCG vaccine.
Distilled water is hypotonic and can cause hemolysis or damage live attenuated bacteria upon injection.
Dextrose solutions are not used as reconstitution diluents for BCG.
Colloids are intravascular volume expanders, completely inappropriate for vaccine reconstitution.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Cyclopropagative life cycle is defined as the disease agent which undergoes cyclical change and multiplies in the body of the arthropod. This type of life cycle is seen in which of the following disease?
questions.explanation: A cyclopropagative life cycle is defined as a parasite that undergoes both development (cyclical changes) and multiplication inside the vector's body. This exact life cycle occurs with Plasmodium species in mosquitoes, causing malaria.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify malaria as an example of a disease with a cyclopropagative vector life cycle.
questions.reasoningChain: Parasite development + multiplication in arthropod vector -> cyclopropagative -> Malaria (Plasmodium in Anopheles).
optionExplanations: Malaria exhibits a cyclopropagative life cycle where Plasmodium undergoes sexual/asexual multiplication in mosquitoes.
Plague involves multiplication in fleas without complex developmental cycle changes like protozoa.
Filarial worms undergo development without multiplication (cyclo-developmental) in mosquitoes.
Yellow fever involves propagative cycle in mosquitoes where virus multiplies without cyclical stage changes.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Sensitive parameter of combined obstetric and pediatric care in the country is:
questions.explanation: The perinatal mortality rate (combining late fetal deaths and early neonatal deaths per 1,000 total births) is considered the most sensitive indicator reflecting the quality, availability, and effectiveness of combined obstetric and pediatric care in a country.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the perinatal mortality rate as the most sensitive parameter for combined obstetric and pediatric care.
questions.reasoningChain: Obstetric care (fetal health) + pediatric care (neonatal health) -> Perinatal mortality rate captures both.
optionExplanations: Post neonatal mortality rate reflects environmental and nutritional factors rather than obstetric care.
Infant mortality rate reflects overall socioeconomic development and pediatric healthcare standards.
Neonatal mortality rate specifically reflects neonatal and delivery care quality.
Perinatal mortality rates encompass late fetal and early neonatal deaths, serving as the best combined obstetric-pediatric index.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Value of free residual chlorine in Drinking water should be:
questions.explanation: According to public health standards, the recommended concentration of free residual chlorine in safely treated drinking water at the point of delivery (or after a contact period of at least 30 minutes) is 0.5 mg/L, ensuring adequate disinfection against pathogens.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall that the standard free residual chlorine level in drinking water is 0.5 mg/L.
questions.reasoningChain: Water chlorination -> disinfection contact time -> target free residual chlorine of 0.5 mg/L.
optionExplanations: 0.2 mg/L is often considered the minimum acceptable residual, but 0.5 mg/L is the standard target.
0.3 mg/L is below the optimal standard target for effective residual disinfection.
0.4 mg/L is close but standard public health guidelines specify 0.5 mg/L.
0.5 mg/L is the standard free residual chlorine concentration required in drinking water.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Bagassosis occurs with:
questions.explanation: Bagassosis is an occupational hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by the inhalation of dust from moldy sugarcane fibers (bagasse) remaining after juice extraction. It presents with respiratory symptoms, cough, and dyspnea in sugar-mill workers.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify bagassosis as an occupational lung disease caused by exposure to sugarcane fibers.
questions.reasoningChain: Sugarcane fiber inhalation -> thermophilic actinomycetes exposure -> Bagassosis (hypersensitivity pneumonitis).
optionExplanations: Silica fibers cause silicosis, a classic nodular fibrotic lung disease.
Carbon particles cause anthracosis (coal worker's pneumoconiosis).
Sugarcane fibers (bagasse) cause bagassosis.
Cotton dust inhalation causes byssinosis in textile workers.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: The Factories Act, 1948 is a social legislation which has been enacted for occupational safety, health and welfare of workers at workplaces. What is the maximum number of work hours/ week prescribed under the Factories Act?
questions.explanation: Under the Factories Act of 1948 in India, the statutory maximum number of working hours per week for an adult worker is restricted to 48 hours, with provisions for daily limits and mandatory weekly rest intervals.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall that the maximum work hours per week prescribed under the Factories Act, 1948 is 48 hours.
questions.reasoningChain: Factories Act 1948 regulations -> maximum weekly working hours -> set at 48 hours.
optionExplanations: 42 hours/week is below the statutory limit set by the Indian Factories Act.
48 hours/week is the legally mandated maximum weekly working hours under the Factories Act, 1948.
54 hours/week exceeds the standard legal limit and violates worker welfare regulations.
60 hours/week is excessively high and legally prohibited.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: 42-year-old obese female presented to the rural PHC. Which of the following is the appropriate statistical test to find out whether obesity is a significant risk factor for breast cancer?
questions.explanation: The Chi-square test is a non-parametric statistical test used to determine whether there is a significant association between two categorical variables (e.g., presence or absence of obesity and presence or absence of breast cancer in a cohort).
questions.educationalObjective: Select the Chi-square test for analyzing associations between categorical variables.
questions.reasoningChain: Obesity (categorical) vs. breast cancer (categorical) -> testing association -> Chi-square test.
optionExplanations: Student's paired t-test is used for comparing means of two related continuous groups.
Student's unpaired t-test is used for comparing means of two independent continuous groups.
Chi-square test evaluates independence and associations between categorical/attribute data.
Wilcoxon's signed rank test is a non-parametric alternative to the paired t-test for ordinal/continuous data.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Denominator in calculation of case fatality rate is:
options: Total number of deaths due to all causes
Total number of cases due to the disease concerned
Total number of deaths due to the disease concerned
questions.answer: Total number of cases due to the disease concerned
questions.explanation: The case fatality rate represents the proportion of diagnosed cases of a specific disease who die from that disease within a given time. Its denominator is the total number of diagnosed cases of the disease concerned, whereas the numerator is the number of deaths from that disease.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the denominator in the calculation of the case fatality rate as the total number of cases of the disease.
questions.reasoningChain: Case fatality rate formula -> Deaths from disease / Total cases of that disease -> measures severity.
optionExplanations: Total number of deaths due to all causes is the denominator for proportional mortality rate.
Total number of hospital admissions is used for hospital utilization statistics, not disease fatality.
Total number of cases due to the disease concerned serves as the denominator for case fatality rate.
Total number of deaths due to the disease concerned serves as the numerator for case fatality rate.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.topic: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
questions.prompt: Not a fundamental symptom of schizophrenia:-
questions.explanation: Bleuler classified the symptoms of schizophrenia into fundamental (primary) and accessory (secondary) symptoms. Fundamental symptoms include the 4 As: Autism, Association defect (loosening of associations), Affective disturbance, and Ambivalence. Automatism is not a fundamental symptom.
questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish Bleuler's fundamental symptoms of schizophrenia from other psychiatric phenomena.
questions.reasoningChain: Bleuler's fundamental symptoms (4 As: Autism, Association, Affect, Ambivalence) -> Automatism is excluded.
optionExplanations: Autism is one of Bleuler's fundamental symptoms of schizophrenia.
Automatism refers to automatic motor behaviors without conscious intent, not a fundamental symptom.
Association defect (loosening of associations) is a fundamental symptom.
Ambivalence is a fundamental symptom involving simultaneous conflicting feelings.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: True for lithium:-
options: Can be given safely in renal dysfunction
questions.explanation: Lithium is a mood stabilizer used primarily in bipolar disorder. It has a very narrow therapeutic index (therapeutic window roughly 0.6–1.2 mEq/L), requiring regular therapeutic drug monitoring to prevent severe toxicity.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that lithium possesses a narrow therapeutic index necessitating blood level monitoring.
questions.reasoningChain: Lithium pharmacokinetics -> small margin between therapeutic and toxic blood levels -> narrow therapeutic index.
optionExplanations: Lithium is absorbed relatively rapidly, not delayed.
Narrow therapeutic index means slight increases in blood concentration lead to toxicity, requiring careful monitoring.
Lithium is not significantly protein-bound; it circulates freely as a small un-ionized cation.
Lithium is excreted entirely by the kidneys and must be used with extreme caution or avoided in renal failure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: In traumatic cases, shock is most likely due to:
questions.explanation: In severe trauma cases presenting with hypovolemic shock, the most common source of acute intra-abdominal hemorrhage leading to shock is injury to intra-abdominal solid organs (such as the spleen or liver), which are highly vascular.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify injury to intra-abdominal solid organs as the leading cause of shock in trauma cases.
questions.reasoningChain: Severe trauma -> blunt/penetrating abdominal injury -> hemorrhage from solid organs (spleen/liver) -> hypovolemic shock.
optionExplanations: Injury to intra-abdominal solid organs leads to massive hemoperitoneum and rapid hypovolemic shock.
Head injury causes intracranial bleeding but rarely causes acute hypovolemic shock unless severe brainstem failure occurs.
Septicemia is a delayed infectious complication, not immediate trauma shock.
Cardiac failure is less common than hypovolemia as an immediate cause of trauma shock.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: All of the following are features of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome except:-
options: Arise from beta cell tumors of the pancreas
questions.answer: Arise from beta cell tumors of the pancreas
questions.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma) that typically arises in the 'gastrinoma triangle' (duodenum or pancreas), not from insulin-producing beta-cell tumors of the pancreas, which cause hypoglycemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that Zollinger-Ellison gastrinomas arise from non-beta islet cells, not beta cells.
questions.reasoningChain: Gastrinoma in ZES -> hypergastrinemia -> excessive gastric acid -> arises from non-beta cells (delta cells or G cells), not beta cells.
optionExplanations: Intractable peptic ulcers are a classic feature of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome due to hyperacidity.
Severe diarrhea occurs due to inactivation of pancreatic enzymes by extreme acid load.
Arising from beta-cell tumors is incorrect; beta-cell tumors secrete insulin (insulinomas).
Very high gastric acid output is a hallmark laboratory finding in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Most common type of intussusception:-
questions.explanation: Intussusception occurs when a proximal segment of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent distal segment. The ileocolic region is by far the most common site, accounting for over 85% of cases in infants and children.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the ileocolic region as the most common anatomical site for intussusception.
questions.reasoningChain: Pediatric intussusception -> terminal ileum invaginates into cecum/colon -> Ileocolic is most common.
optionExplanations: Colocolic intussusception involves colon-to-colon telescoping and is relatively rare.
Ileoileal intussusception is confined to the small bowel and is less common than ileocolic.
Ileocolic is the most frequent anatomical type of intussusception in children.
Ileal intussusception refers to small bowel involvement without colonic entry, uncommon as primary presentation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Serum acid phosphate is raised in:-
questions.explanation: Serum acid phosphatase is an enzyme that was historically used as a tumor marker and is characteristically elevated in metastatic prostatic carcinoma, as well as in other bone or lysosomal disorders, though prostate-specific antigen (PSA) has largely replaced it.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify serum acid phosphatase elevation as a classic marker for prostatic carcinoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Prostate epithelial cells rich in acid phosphatase -> prostatic carcinoma metastasis -> elevated serum acid phosphatase.
optionExplanations: Osteosarcoma typically features elevated serum alkaline phosphatase due to osteoblastic activity.
Prostatic carcinoma classically elevates serum acid phosphatase and PSA.
Paget's disease of bone shows markedly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate.
Hyperparathyroidism elevates serum calcium and alkaline phosphatase.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Paget's disease of the nipple is:-
questions.explanation: Paget's disease of the nipple is a manifest cutaneous manifestation of an underlying intraductal breast carcinoma. It is characterized by eczematous changes of the nipple-areola complex caused by malignant intraepithelial adenocarcinoma cells (Paget cells) infiltrating the epidermis.
questions.educationalObjective: Classify Paget's disease of the nipple as an underlying intraepithelial breast malignancy.
questions.reasoningChain: Nipple eczematous lesion -> malignant glandular cells in epidermis -> Neoplasia (underlying ductal carcinoma).
optionExplanations: Infection is incorrect; Paget's disease is neoplastic, not infectious.
Dermatitis is a benign inflammatory condition, whereas Paget's disease is malignant.
Neoplasia accurately describes Paget's disease as a manifestation of underlying breast carcinoma.
Hypopigmentation refers to loss of skin color, whereas Paget's disease is a neoplastic disorder.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Commonest site of branchial cyst:-
questions.explanation: A branchial cyst is a congenital epithelial cyst arising from remnants of the pharyngeal apparatus (typically the second branchial cleft). The classic and most common anatomical location is along the upper third of the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the upper third of the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle as the most common site for a branchial cyst.
questions.reasoningChain: 2nd branchial cleft remnant -> anterior to upper sternocleidomastoid -> Branchial cyst location.
optionExplanations: Lower 1/3 anterior border is an incorrect location for branchial cleft anomalies.
Lower 1/3 posterior border is not the typical site for branchial cysts.
Upper 1/3 sternomastoid on the anterior border is the classic presentation site for branchial cysts.
Upper 1/3 posterior border is the classic site for cystic hygromas or pharyngeal pouch remnants.
questions.reviewNote: The prompt option text says 'anterior border' for upper 1/3 sternomastoid, which is correct anatomically for branchial cleft cysts.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: In the treatment of hand injuries, the greatest priority is-
questions.explanation: In acute complex hand trauma and microsurgery, restoring structural integrity to flexor and extensor tendons is given top priority to ensure functional recovery of hand movement, alongside immediate skin coverage and neurovascular repair depending on ischemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize tendon repair as a high priority in complex hand injury management to preserve movement.
questions.reasoningChain: Hand trauma -> complex tissue damage -> tendon repair prioritized for functional mobility.
optionExplanations: Repair to tendons is prioritized to restore active movement and hand function.
Repair of skin cover is essential to prevent infection, but tendon/bone stability comes alongside.
Repair of nerves is crucial for sensation, but mechanical function relies heavily on tendons.
All structures are important, but tendon repair is traditionally emphasized for functional outcome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Cock's peculiar tumor is:-
questions.explanation: Cock's peculiar tumor is a clinical term used to describe an infected, ulcerated, and fungating sebaceous cyst of the scalp. Due to chronic inflammation and secondary infection, the squamous lining proliferates and protrudes, mimicking a malignant squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify 'Cock's peculiar tumor' as an infected sebaceous cyst of the scalp.
questions.reasoningChain: Scalp sebaceous cyst + chronic infection and ulceration -> fungating mass -> Cock's peculiar tumor.
optionExplanations: Papilloma is a benign epithelial projection, not a specific infected scalp cyst.
Infected sebaceous cyst of the scalp is the exact definition of Cock's peculiar tumor.
Cylindroma is a benign adnexal tumor of the skin, classically known as 'turban tumor'.
Squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant skin cancer that can mimic or arise from chronic ulcers.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: All the following are features of polycystic disease of kidneys except:-
questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) typically presents with flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, and progressive renal failure due to cyst expansion. Unlike renal cell carcinoma, ADPKD does not cause erythrocytosis (in fact, anemia of chronic kidney disease is common due to reduced erythropoietin).
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize clinical features of polycystic kidney disease and identify erythrocytosis as an exception.
questions.reasoningChain: ADPKD -> cyst formation -> hematuria, hypertension, renal failure (anemia, not erythrocytosis).
optionExplanations: Hematuria is a frequent feature due to cyst rupture or hemorrhage.
Hypertension is very common in ADPKD due to renin-angiotensin system activation by compressed parenchyma.
Renal failure occurs progressively as cysts destroy normal functioning nephrons.
Erythrocytosis is associated with renal cell carcinoma, whereas ADPKD leads to renal anemia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Most common cause of facial nerve palsy:
questions.explanation: Bell's palsy is an acute, idiopathic, unilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve paralysis. It represents the single most common cause of facial nerve palsy, often suspected to be linked to reactivation of Herpes Simplex Virus.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify idiopathic Bell's palsy as the most common cause of facial nerve palsy.
questions.reasoningChain: Acute peripheral facial paralysis -> no identifiable secondary cause -> Idiopathic Bell's palsy is most common.
optionExplanations: Idiopathic Bell's palsy is the single most frequent etiology of lower motor neuron facial palsy.
Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) causes facial paralysis accompanied by vesicular ear rashes.
Mastoid surgery can cause iatrogenic facial nerve injury, but it is not the most common overall cause.
Chronic suppurative otitis media can erode the facial canal, but it is less common than Bell's palsy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Recruitment phenomenon is seen in:
questions.explanation: Recruitment is the phenomenon of abnormally rapid growth in the perception of loudness for tones above threshold, despite a mild hearing loss. It is classically positive in cochlear pathologies such as Meniere's disease and presbycusis, but absent in retrocochlear lesions like acoustic neuromas.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Meniere's disease as a classic condition exhibiting the recruitment phenomenon.
questions.reasoningChain: Cochlear lesion (Meniere's disease) -> outer hair cell loss -> loudness recruitment phenomenon positive.
optionExplanations: Otitis media with effusion causes a conductive hearing loss without recruitment.
Acoustic nerve schwannoma is a retrocochlear lesion characterized by absence of recruitment and tone decay.
Meniere's disease is a cochlear endolymphatic hydrops condition showing positive loudness recruitment.
Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss with absence of recruitment.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: 21 years old patient came to your clinic with complaints of recurrent pain in the neck and ear. You made an initial diagnosis of the syndrome involved in relation to the below-marked bone. Which of the following nerve is responsible for the referred pain in the ear?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario and bone marked in red (the styloid process of the temporal bone, elongated in Eagle syndrome) can cause referred otalgia. Referred pain to the ear from the throat, tonsils, or styloid process is mediated primarily by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) or vagus nerve (CN X).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the glossopharyngeal nerve as responsible for referred otalgia in conditions like Eagle syndrome.
questions.reasoningChain: Elongated styloid process (Eagle syndrome) -> irritation of glossopharyngeal nerve -> referred pain to the ear.
optionExplanations: Auriculotemporal nerve supplies primary sensory innervation to the auricle and TMJ, causing direct ear pain.
Posterior auricular nerve supplies the occipitalis and auricular muscles.
Occipital nerves supply the posterior scalp, not visceral referred otalgia from pharyngeal structures.
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) mediates referred pain from the oropharynx, tonsils, and styloid process to the ear.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies are seen in:
questions.explanation: Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous bacterial infection caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. Histopathologically, it is characterized by large foamy histiocytes containing bacteria known as Mikulicz cells, along with plasma cells containing Russell bodies (eosinophilic immunoglobulin inclusions).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies as histopathological hallmarks of rhinoscleroma.
questions.reasoningChain: Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis infection -> granulomatous response -> Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies on histology.
optionExplanations: Rhinoscleroma histopathology features Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies.
Rhinosporidiosis is caused by an aquatic protist (Rhinosporidium seeberi) showing large sporangia.
Rhinophyma is a severe cutaneous manifestation of neglected rosacea with sebaceous gland hyperplasia.
Rhinitis is an acute or chronic inflammation of the nasal mucosa without these pathognomonic cells.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: In the small intestine, cholera toxin acts by:
options: ADP ribosylation of the G regulatory protein
questions.answer: ADP ribosylation of the G regulatory protein
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin enters intestinal epithelial cells and catalyzes the ADP-ribosylation of the Gs regulatory stimulatory protein. This locks Gs in its active GTP-bound state, leading to continuous activation of adenylate cyclase, elevated cAMP, and massive watery diarrhea.
questions.educationalObjective: Describe the mechanism of cholera toxin via ADP-ribosylation of Gs regulatory proteins.
questions.reasoningChain: Cholera toxin binding -> ADP ribosylation of Gs protein -> persistent activation of adenylate cyclase -> high cAMP.
optionExplanations: ADP ribosylation of the Gs regulatory protein leads to excessive cAMP production and fluid secretion.
Inhibition of adenyl cyclase is incorrect; cholera toxin stimulates adenylate cyclase.
Activation of GTPase is incorrect; it inhibits GTPase activity, keeping Gs active.
Active absorption of NaCl is inhibited, while active secretion of chloride and water is stimulated.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Which subtype of human papilloma virus has maximum chances of causing carcinoma cervix:
questions.explanation: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) high-risk genotypes 16 and 18 are responsible for over 70% of all invasive cervical carcinomas worldwide. Their E6 and E7 viral oncoproteins inactivate tumor suppressor proteins p53 and Rb, respectively.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify HPV types 16 and 18 as the high-risk strains most commonly responsible for cervical carcinoma.
questions.reasoningChain: High-risk HPV infection -> integration of viral DNA -> E6/E7 oncoproteins -> malignant transformation to cervical cancer.
optionExplanations: HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk strains primarily responsible for cervical and anogenital carcinomas.
HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk types responsible for benign genital warts (condyloma acuminata).
HPV 31 and 32 are intermediate/low-risk types associated with mucosal lesions.
HPV 1 and 2 cause benign cutaneous plantar and common warts.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Progesterone of choice in emergency contraception:
questions.explanation: Levonorgestrel is a progestin used as the progestin-only emergency contraceptive pill (taken within 72 to 120 hours of unprotected intercourse) to delay ovulation and prevent fertilization.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify levonorgestrel as the progestin of choice for emergency contraception.
questions.reasoningChain: Unprotected intercourse -> urgent need to prevent ovulation -> Levonorgestrel emergency contraceptive pill.
optionExplanations: Micronized progesterone is used for luteal phase support and hormone replacement, not emergency contraception.
Norgesterone is not the standard active progestin used for emergency contraception regimens.
Levonorgestrel is the standard progestin of choice for emergency contraception.
DMPA is an injectable progestin contraceptive providing long-acting depot protection, not emergency post-coital use.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old woman presents to the doctor with complaints of irregular cycles for a few months. Her cycles are 35-45 days long, lasting for 3 to 4 days with mild to moderate blood flow. There is, however, no passage of clots and no dysmenorrhea. Which of the following accurately describes this condition?
questions.explanation: Oligomenorrhea is defined as menstrual cycles that occur at intervals greater than 35 days (infrequent menstruation), with typical cycle lengths ranging from 35 to 45 days or more, maintaining normal menstrual flow characteristics.
questions.educationalObjective: Define oligomenorrhea as menstrual cycles with intervals exceeding 35 days.
questions.reasoningChain: Menstrual cycles 35-45 days long -> prolonged interval between cycles -> Oligomenorrhea.
optionExplanations: Amenorrhoea is the complete absence of menstruation for 3 or more cycles or 6 months.
Oligomenorrhea describes infrequent menstrual cycles occurring at intervals longer than 35 days.
Polymenorrhea refers to frequent menstrual cycles occurring at intervals shorter than 21 days.
Menorrhagia is heavy menstrual bleeding occurring at regular intervals.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the treatment of choice for Trichomonas vaginalis?
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is the established first-line antimicrobial treatment of choice for infections caused by the flagellated protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis, administered orally to both the patient and sexual partners.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify metronidazole as the treatment of choice for Trichomonas vaginalis infection.
questions.reasoningChain: Trichomonas vaginalis protozoal infection -> systemic antimicrobial coverage -> Metronidazole.
optionExplanations: Amikacin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used for severe Gram-negative bacterial infections.
Metronidazole is the drug of choice for treating Trichomonas vaginalis infections.
Chloramphenicol is a broad-spectrum antibiotic reserved for specific serious infections due to toxicity.
Ampicillin is a beta-lactam antibiotic used for susceptible bacterial infections.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Low osmolarity ORS has (as compared to WHO-ORS):
questions.explanation: Low-osmolarity Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) recommended by the WHO feature reduced concentrations of both sodium chloride (low sodium) and anhydrous glucose compared to the original standard WHO-ORS formula, which reduces stool output and the need for intravenous infusions.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall the composition of low-osmolarity ORS featuring reduced levels of glucose and sodium.
questions.reasoningChain: Low-osmolarity ORS -> reduced sodium and glucose -> decreases osmotic diarrhea and stool output.
optionExplanations: Low glucose and low sodium define the composition of WHO low-osmolarity ORS.
Low glucose and high sodium is incorrect; both glucose and sodium are reduced.
Low glucose and low potassium is incorrect; potassium content remains standard.
Low glucose and high potassium is incorrect; sodium is reduced alongside glucose.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A pediatric patient was prescribed erythromycin for the prevention of recurrent rheumatic fever in a rural health center. If the patient complained of a history of constipation, which medication should be avoided to prevent the development of any arrhythmia?
questions.explanation: Cisapride is a prokinetic agent that prolongs the QT interval and can induce fatal cardiac arrhythmias (such as torsades de pointes) when co-administered with CYP3A4 inhibitors like erythromycin, which inhibit its metabolism. Therefore, cisapride must be strictly avoided.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmias when cisapride is combined with CYP3A4 inhibitors like erythromycin.
questions.reasoningChain: Erythromycin (CYP3A4 inhibitor) + Cisapride (QT prolongation risk) -> impaired metabolism -> dangerous arrhythmias.
optionExplanations: Lubiprostone is a chloride channel activator used for constipation without significant cardiac arrhythmia risk.
Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used for tuberculosis, not linked to this specific interaction.
Ebastine is a non-sedating antihistamine.
Cisapride causes QT prolongation and fatal arrhythmias when combined with macrolide inhibitors like erythromycin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: A hypertensive patient was started on some anti-hypertensive drug but he developed a dry cough. Which of the following drug can be responsible for this effect?
questions.explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors (such as enalapril or ramipril) frequently cause a persistent, dry, hacking cough as a side effect. This occurs due to the accumulation of bradykinin and substance P in the lungs, which are normally degraded by ACE.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify ACE inhibitors as the antihypertensive drug class responsible for causing a persistent dry cough.
questions.reasoningChain: ACE inhibitor therapy -> reduced bradykinin breakdown -> bradykinin accumulation in lungs -> dry cough.
optionExplanations: Calcium channel blockers cause peripheral edema and flushing, not a dry cough.
Beta-blockers can cause bronchospasm in susceptible patients, but not a classic isolated dry cough.
ACE inhibitors inhibit bradykinin degradation, leading to the classic side effect of dry cough.
Diuretics cause electrolyte imbalances and volume depletion without inducing a dry cough.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.prompt: Antidote for alprazolam is:-
questions.explanation: Flumazenil is a competitive GABA-A receptor antagonist that serves as the specific pharmacological antidote for benzodiazepine overdose (such as alprazolam, diazepam, or midazolam).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify flumazenil as the specific antidote for benzodiazepine overdose.
questions.reasoningChain: Benzodiazepine (alprazolam) overdose -> competitive receptor antagonism -> Flumazenil reverses sedation.
optionExplanations: Protamine sulphate is the reversal agent and antidote for heparin overdose.
Flumazenil is the specific competitive antagonist and antidote for benzodiazepines.
EDTA is a chelating agent used for heavy metal poisonings such as lead.
BAL (British Anti-Lewisite) is a chelating agent used for arsenic, mercury, and lead poisoning.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: The resting membrane potential of nerve fibre is close to the isoelectric potential of:
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential of a typical nerve fiber is primarily determined by the potassium equilibrium potential. Because the resting neuronal membrane is highly permeable to potassium via leak channels, the resting potential is very close to the Nernst equilibrium potential for potassium ions.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that the resting membrane potential of nerve fibers is close to the potassium equilibrium potential.
questions.reasoningChain: High resting potassium permeability -> K+ efflux -> resting membrane potential approaches potassium equilibrium potential.
optionExplanations: Potassium ions have high resting membrane permeability, setting the resting potential near its Nernst potential.
Sodium ions have very low resting permeability, contributing only during the action potential upstroke.
Chloride ions are distributed passively in most nerve cells, close to resting potential but secondary to potassium.
Magnesium ions play intracellular cofactor roles and do not dictate resting membrane potential.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: Inhibin is secreted by?
questions.explanation: Inhibin is a peptide hormone secreted by the Sertoli cells of the testes (in males) and granulosa cells of the ovaries (in females). It acts on the anterior pituitary to selectively inhibit the synthesis and secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Sertoli cells as the site of inhibin secretion in the testes.
questions.reasoningChain: Sertoli cells in seminiferous tubules -> secrete inhibin -> negative feedback inhibition of pituitary FSH.
optionExplanations: Leydig cells reside in the interstitial space and secrete testosterone.
Sertoli cells provide nutritional support to sperm and secrete inhibin and anti-Müllerian hormone.
Interstitial cells (Leydig cells) produce androgens.
Peg cells are secretory epithelial cells located in the fallopian tubes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.prompt: The adrenal medulla is derived from neural crest cells. These neural crest cells originate from the dorsal aorta. Clusters of chromaffin cells become the distinct medulla after birth. The adrenal gland first appears 28-30 days post-conception. Does the adrenal medulla secrete the following hormones?
questions.explanation: The adrenal medulla is embryologically derived from neural crest cells and functions as a modified sympathetic ganglion. It synthesizes and secretes catecholamines, predominantly epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine, in response to sympathetic stimulation.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify epinephrine as a primary hormone secreted by the adrenal medulla.
questions.reasoningChain: Adrenal medulla chromaffin cells -> neural crest origin -> synthesis and secretion of epinephrine and norepinephrine.
optionExplanations: Sex hormones (androgens and estrogens) are produced by the adrenal cortex (zona reticularis).
Thyroid stimulating hormone is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland, not the adrenal gland.
Epinephrine is synthesized and secreted by the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.
Glucocorticoids (cortisol) are secreted by the adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Which of the following Ions is involved in cell injury
questions.explanation: Intracellular calcium overload plays a pivotal and final common pathway in irreversible cell injury. Ischemia or toxins cause failure of ATP-dependent calcium pumps, leading to a massive influx of cytosolic calcium, which activates destructive intracellular enzymes like phospholipases, proteases, and endonucleases.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize intracellular calcium influx as a key mediator of cell injury and necrosis.
questions.reasoningChain: ATP depletion -> failure of Ca2+ extrusion pumps -> cytosolic calcium overload -> activation of degradative enzymes -> cell injury.
optionExplanations: Calcium influx and intracellular accumulation are critical mediators activating degradative enzymes in cell injury.
Copper overload is seen in Wilson's disease, not a universal mediator of general acute cell injury.
Selenium is an essential trace element acting as an antioxidant cofactor, not a mediator of injury.
All above is incorrect since only calcium is the universal mediator of cell injury among the choices.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: Delusion is a disorder of which of the following?
questions.explanation: A delusion is defined as a false, fixed belief that is not amenable to change in light of conflicting evidence and is not culturally sanctioned. It is classified as a fundamental disorder of thought content.
questions.educationalObjective: Classify delusions as a disorder of thought content.
questions.reasoningChain: False fixed belief -> abnormality in thinking process/content -> Disorder of thought.
optionExplanations: Thought is the psychological domain where delusions (content disorders) and formal thought disorders occur.
Affect refers to the external expression of emotion, disorders of which include blunting or lability.
Perception involves sensory processing, disorders of which include hallucinations and illusions.
Memory involves recall and retention, disorders of which include amnesia and confabulation.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Which of the following has Autosomal Recessive inheritance?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anemia is a classic monogenic hemoglobinopathy inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. It results from a point mutation in the beta-globin gene substituting valine for glutamic acid.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify sickle cell anemia as an autosomal recessive disorder.
questions.reasoningChain: Mutated beta-globin gene -> requires two defective alleles for disease expression -> Autosomal recessive inheritance.
optionExplanations: Hereditary spherocytosis is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive genetic hematological disorder.
Osteogenesis imperfecta is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder of type I collagen.
Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, usually inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Liquefactive necrosis is seen in
questions.explanation: Liquefactive necrosis occurs when tissue transforms into a liquid viscous mass due to enzymatic dissolution of dead cells. It is classically seen in the brain (infarction of neural tissue) due to high lipid and hydrolytic enzyme content, as well as in abscesses.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the brain as the classic site where liquefactive necrosis occurs.
questions.reasoningChain: Brain tissue ischemia -> high lipid content and abundant hydrolytic enzymes -> Liquefactive necrosis.
optionExplanations: Heart tissue undergoes coagulative necrosis following myocardial infarction.
Brain tissue undergoes liquefactive necrosis due to rich enzymatic digestion and minimal structural protein matrix.
Lungs can undergo caseous necrosis in tuberculosis or coagulative/gangrenous patterns depending on etiology.
Kidneys undergo classic coagulative necrosis following renal infarction.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old male had a road traffic accident, after which he is fearful of driving a vehicle and going to that place for 6 weeks. He is having flashes of that incident and difficulty going to work. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is diagnosed when psychological symptoms following a traumatic event (intrusive thoughts, flashbacks, avoidance, hyperarousal) persist for more than 1 month. If symptoms last less than 1 month, acute stress disorder is diagnosed.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose post-traumatic stress disorder when trauma-related symptoms persist beyond one month.
questions.reasoningChain: Trauma exposure -> symptoms of intrusion, avoidance, hyperarousal lasting 6 weeks (>1 month) -> PTSD.
optionExplanations: Acute stress disorder presents with similar symptoms but lasts from 3 days up to 1 month post-trauma.
Post-traumatic stress disorder is diagnosed when symptoms persist beyond 1 month (here 6 weeks).
Panic disorder involves recurrent unexpected panic attacks without necessarily being tied to trauma.
Major depressive disorder involves pervasive low mood and anhedonia, though it can co-occur with trauma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: The cause of edema in nephrotic syndrome is
questions.explanation: The primary mechanism of generalized edema in nephrotic syndrome is severe proteinuria leading to hypoalbuminemia. Reduced serum albumin levels decrease plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure, causing fluid to shift from the intravascular space into the interstitial tissues.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify decreased colloid osmotic pressure as the primary cause of edema in nephrotic syndrome.
questions.reasoningChain: Massive proteinuria -> hypoalbuminemia -> decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure -> fluid extravasation into interstitium (edema).
optionExplanations: Increase colloid osmotic pressure would draw fluid into vessels, which is the opposite of nephrotic edema.
Increase hydrostatic pressure is the primary mechanism of edema in congestive heart failure.
Decreased colloid osmotic pressure caused by hypoalbuminemia is the hallmark mechanism of nephrotic edema.
Decreased hydrostatic pressure would reduce fluid filtration, not cause generalized edema.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Which of the following is an Autosomal Dominant disease?
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance, caused by quantitative or qualitative defects in von Willebrand factor.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Von Willebrand disease as an autosomal dominant disorder.
questions.reasoningChain: Defect in von Willebrand factor gene -> transmitted across generations in dominant fashion -> Autosomal dominant.
optionExplanations: Von Willebrand disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.
Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive copper metabolism disorder caused by ATP7B mutations.
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive chloride channel (CFTR) disorder.
Friedreich's ataxia is an autosomal recessive trinucleotide repeat (frataxin) neurodegenerative disorder.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.prompt: Which of the following mineral deficiencies can lead to the condition shown in the image below:
questions.explanation: Zinc deficiency classically presents with acrodermatitis enteropathica, characterized by periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea. Treatment involves oral supplementation with elemental zinc (30-50 mg daily).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify zinc deficiency as the cause of periorificial/acral dermatitis and treat with zinc supplementation.
questions.reasoningChain: Periorificial and facial skin lesions + acral dermatitis -> zinc deficiency -> treated with elemental zinc.
optionExplanations: Zinc deficiency presents with characteristic periorificial dermatitis, treated with elemental zinc supplementation.
Iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia, koilonychia, and glossitis.
Calcium deficiency causes tetany, neuromuscular irritability, and bone mineralization defects.
Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, xerophthalmia, and Bitot spots.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Which of the following can be given in celiac disease patient:
questions.explanation: Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by the ingestion of gluten, a protein composite found in wheat, barley, and rye. Quinoa is a pseudo-cereal that is naturally gluten-free and safe for consumption by patients with celiac disease.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify quinoa as a safe, gluten-free grain alternative for patients with celiac disease.
questions.reasoningChain: Celiac disease -> gluten-induced enteropathy -> wheat, barley, rye contain gluten -> Quinoa is gluten-free.
optionExplanations: Rye contains gluten proteins that trigger celiac enteropathy and must be avoided.
Wheat contains gluten (gliadin), the primary trigger for celiac disease.
Quinoa is a gluten-free seed/pseudo-cereal and can be safely consumed in celiac disease.
Barley contains hordein (gluten protein) and is harmful to celiac patients.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: A 16-year-old girl presents with short height, primary amenorrhea, with widely spaced nipples. Her probable karyotype is?
questions.explanation: A phenotypic female presenting with short stature, primary amenorrhea, and widely spaced nipples (shield chest) has classic features of Turner syndrome, which is caused by complete or partial absence of one X chromosome, resulting in a 45,XO karyotype.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify 45,XO karyotype as the genetic basis of Turner syndrome.
questions.reasoningChain: Short stature + primary amenorrhea + shield chest -> Turner syndrome -> 45,XO karyotype.
optionExplanations: 45,XO represents Turner syndrome, matching the clinical presentation of short stature and primary amenorrhea.
46,XO is non-viable or mosaic, but standard classical monosomy X is written as 45,XO.
47,XXX represents Triple X syndrome, which typically presents with tall stature and normal fertility.
46,XY karyotype in a phenotypic female with primary amenorrhea would suggest Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Which of the following antibody is present in Celiac disease
questions.explanation: Celiac disease diagnosis is confirmed by serological testing detecting IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA), endomysium (EMA-IgA), and reticulin. Therefore, all these antibodies are associated with celiac disease.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that tTG-IgA, endomysial IgA, and reticulin IgA are all associated autoantibodies in celiac disease.
questions.reasoningChain: Celiac disease -> autoimmune reaction to gluten -> production of tTG-IgA, endomysial IgA, and reticulin IgA.
optionExplanations: Tissue transglutaminase IgA is the primary screening antibody test for celiac disease.
Endomysial IgA antibodies are highly specific for celiac disease diagnosis.
Reticulin IgA antibodies are also historically associated with celiac enteropathy.
All above is correct as all listed antibodies are tested and present in celiac disease.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Koplik spots are seen in?
questions.explanation: Koplik spots are pathognomonic enanthems characterized by tiny white or bluish-white papules on an erythematous base appearing on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars 1-2 days before the maculopapular rash of measles (rubeola).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Koplik spots as the pathognomonic enanthem of measles.
questions.reasoningChain: Measles prodrome -> buccal mucosa enanthem -> Koplik spots pathognomonic for measles.
optionExplanations: Mumps causes parotid gland swelling and orchitis, not Koplik spots.
Measles characteristically presents with Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa.
Rubella presents with discrete maculopapular rash and forchheimer spots, not Koplik spots.
Varicella causes pruritic vesicular skin lesions in successive crops.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.topic: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
questions.prompt: A person finds a decrease in pleasure in activities that he would enjoy previously. What is it called?
questions.explanation: Anhedonia is defined as the inability to feel pleasure or a marked decrease in interest or enjoyment in activities that were previously found pleasurable. It is a core negative symptom of schizophrenia and a major diagnostic criterion for major depressive disorder.
questions.educationalObjective: Define anhedonia as the loss of capacity to experience pleasure from previously enjoyable activities.
questions.reasoningChain: Loss of enjoyment in previously liked activities -> inability to experience pleasure -> Anhedonia.
optionExplanations: Tangentiality is a formal thought disorder where a patient replies to a question in an oblique or irrelevant manner.
Anhedonia is the clinical term for decreased or absent pleasure in previously enjoyed activities.
Alexithymia is the inability to recognize and describe one's own emotions.
Asociality is the lack of motivation to engage in social interaction or maintain relationships.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Most specific antibodies in systemic sclerosis
questions.explanation: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is associated with specific autoantibodies. Anti-topoisomerase I (also known as Scl-70) is highly specific for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and correlates with internal organ involvement and pulmonary fibrosis.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) as a highly specific antibody in systemic sclerosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Systemic sclerosis -> autoimmune fibrotic process -> Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) antibodies.
optionExplanations: Anti-DNA antibodies (like anti-dsDNA) are diagnostic and specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) is highly specific for diffuse systemic sclerosis.
ANA (Antinuclear antibodies) are sensitive screening markers for autoimmune connective tissue diseases, but non-specific.
Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies are associated with Sjögren syndrome and neonatal lupus.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis is a rare and dangerous complication of?
questions.explanation: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare, fatal, slow-virus degenerative disease of the central nervous system caused by a defective measles virus persisting in neural tissue years after primary measles infection.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify measles as the causative viral infection leading to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.
questions.reasoningChain: Primary measles infection -> viral latency -> years later develops progressive encephalitis -> SSPE.
optionExplanations: Measles virus persistent infection leads to delayed progressive SSPE.
Mumps virus causes parotitis and aseptic meningitis, not SSPE.
Rubella causes congenital syndrome, not SSPE.
Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox and shingles, with potential post-herpetic neuralgia rather than SSPE.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A female was brought to the psychiatrist 5 weeks after her delivery. She is appearing fearful, irritable and having suicidal thoughts. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-partum depression typically begins within 4 weeks to a few months after delivery, presenting with depressive symptoms, severe irritability, anxiety, and suicidal ideation, distinguishing it from transient postpartum blues or severe psychotic episodes.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose post-partum depression based on timing (weeks after delivery) and psychiatric symptoms including suicidal ideation.
questions.reasoningChain: Delivery 5 weeks ago -> depressed mood, fear, suicidal thoughts -> Post-partum depression.
optionExplanations: Post-partum blues is a transient, mild mood disturbance occurring within the first 10 days post-delivery and resolving spontaneously.
Post-partum psychosis features severe delusions, hallucinations, and loss of touch with reality, requiring emergency care.
Post-partum depression manifests weeks to months postpartum with depressive features and suicidal ideation.
Panic disorder involves recurrent acute panic attacks, not primarily post-partum depressive features.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Most common brain tumors seen in children
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children, typically arising in the cerebellum (posterior fossa) and often causing obstructive hydrocephalus and cerebellar ataxia.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify medulloblastoma as the most common malignant brain tumor in pediatric patients.
questions.reasoningChain: Pediatric central nervous system malignancy -> posterior fossa tumor -> Medulloblastoma is most common.
optionExplanations: Medulloblastoma is the most frequent malignant pediatric brain tumor.
Pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common benign pediatric brain tumor overall.
Meningioma is a common benign extra-axial tumor occurring predominantly in adults.
Glioma is a broad category, but medulloblastoma holds the highest frequency for malignant pediatric brain tumors.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Protection given by Yellow vaccine is valid for?
questions.explanation: According to the WHO International Health Regulations (IHR) updated guidelines, the certificate of vaccination against Yellow Fever is valid for the lifetime of the person vaccinated, eliminating the previous 10-year booster requirement.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall that international yellow fever vaccination protection is now valid for life.
questions.reasoningChain: Yellow fever vaccine administration -> lifetime immunity conferred -> certificate valid for life.
optionExplanations: Life long is the current valid duration for yellow fever vaccine protection per WHO regulations.
10 years was the historical validity period before WHO regulations were updated in 2016.
5 years is incorrect for yellow fever vaccination validity.
20 years exceeds historical guidelines and is not the standard rule.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 21 year old female is afraid to use an elevator and she always uses the stairs instead. What is the diagnosis ?
questions.explanation: A specific phobia is an excessive, unreasonable, and persistent fear triggered by a specific object or situation (such as elevators, heights, or animals), leading to active avoidance. Avoiding elevators by always taking stairs exemplifies a situational specific phobia.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose specific phobia based on marked, irrational fear and avoidance of a circumscribed object or situation.
questions.reasoningChain: Fear of using an elevator -> persistent avoidance -> Specific phobia.
optionExplanations: Social phobia involves intense fear of social scrutiny or performance situations.
Agoraphobia involves anxiety about being in places where escape might be difficult, such as open spaces or crowds.
Specific phobia involves distinct, irrational fear and avoidance of a particular stimulus like elevators.
Panic disorder involves recurrent unexpected panic attacks without specific triggers.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Breastfeeding should be continued for a minimum of how many months?
questions.explanation: According to WHO and UNICEF infant nutrition guidelines, exclusive breastfeeding should be continued for the first 6 months of life, after which appropriate complementary foods should be introduced alongside continued breastfeeding.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall that exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first 6 months of life.
questions.reasoningChain: Infant nutrition policy -> exclusive breastfeeding recommended duration -> minimum of 6 months.
optionExplanations: 6 months is the internationally recommended duration for exclusive breastfeeding.
2 months is far too short and lacks adequate nutritional and immunological protection.
12 months marks a milestone, but exclusive breastfeeding is specifically targeted for the first 6 months.
5 months is close but falls short of the full 6-month recommendation.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: Football player with knee injury diagnosed as medial collateral ligament injury. Which structure is most commonly associated with this type of injury
questions.explanation: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) tears of the knee frequently occur in conjunction with injuries to the medial meniscus due to their anatomical attachments and combined valgus stress mechanisms during sports trauma.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the association between medial collateral ligament knee injuries and medial meniscus damage.
questions.reasoningChain: Valgus stress injury to knee -> medial collateral ligament tear -> concurrent injury to attached medial meniscus.
optionExplanations: Anterior cruciate ligament is commonly injured with valgus-rotation forces, but MCL tears classically co-occur with the medial meniscus.
Medial meniscus is firmly attached to the MCL, making it the most commonly associated internal derangement.
Posterior cruciate ligament is injured by dashboard trauma or severe hyperextension, less commonly tied to isolated MCL tears.
Lateral lemniscus is a neural auditory pathway in the brainstem, entirely unrelated to knee anatomy.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A Clinician asks a patient “how is your mood”. Patient replies by saying “ It is going up & down”. What is the phenomenon seen here?
questions.explanation: Tangentiality is a formal thought disorder where a patient responds to a question with an answer that drifts off topic and never reaches the original point or answers the question, as seen when a query about mood is answered vaguely by 'going up and down' without clear elaboration.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify tangentiality as a formal thought disorder characterized by wandering off-topic without returning.
questions.reasoningChain: Patient questioned about mood -> gives drifting, oblique response -> Tangentiality.
optionExplanations: Derailment involves sudden, complete shifts from one unrelated topic to another mid-thought.
Tangentiality involves straying from the topic without returning to answer the initial question.
Clang association involves grouping words based on rhyming sounds rather than meaning.
Neologism involves inventing entirely new words or condensing words with private meaning.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: Avascular necrosis of the femur head is due to which of the following artery
questions.explanation: Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head typically results from disruption of its primary blood supply, which is delivered by the medial circumflex femoral artery (via ascending cervical branches forming the retinacular vessels).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the medial circumflex femoral artery as the primary blood supply vulnerable in femoral head AVN.
questions.reasoningChain: Femoral head blood supply -> predominantly from medial circumflex femoral artery -> disruption leads to AVN.
optionExplanations: Medial circumflex femoral artery provides the primary blood supply to the femoral head and neck.
Lateral circumflex femoral artery primarily supplies the anterior and lateral muscles and vastus lateralis.
Obturator artery supplies the ligamentum teres, providing minimal blood to the adult femoral head.
Profunda femoris artery is the deep artery of the thigh giving rise to the circumflex femoral branches.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: A primigravida patient came to the hospital without any antenatal check-up at 37 weeks of gestation and presented with an onset of labor. On investigation, the mother is Hep B positive. What management should be given to the neonate?
options: First immunoglobulin, then Hep B vaccine after 1 month
questions.explanation: When an infant is born to a mother who is hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) positive, the neonate must receive immunoprophylaxis consisting of both Hepatitis B vaccine and Hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) administered at separate sites within 12 hours of birth to prevent vertical transmission.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that neonates born to HBsAg-positive mothers require both Hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG at birth.
questions.reasoningChain: Maternal Hepatitis B positivity -> high risk of neonatal infection -> Administer Hep B vaccine + HBIG immediately at birth.
optionExplanations: Hep B vaccine only is insufficient for infants of HBsAg-positive mothers without HBIG.
Hep B vaccine + immunoglobulin administered simultaneously at birth is the correct standard protocol.
Delaying immunoglobulin for 1 month is incorrect; HBIG must be given immediately at birth.
Only immunoglobulin provides short-term protection and fails to induce active immunity without the vaccine.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: Which of the following is related to Mc Naughten’s rule?
questions.explanation: M'Naghten's rules are the foundational legal test for criminal insanity in many jurisdictions, asserting that a defendant is not criminally responsible if a mental disease caused a defect of reason such that they did not know the nature and quality of the act, or did not know it was wrong. In Indian Penal Code (IPC), this is codified under Section 84.
