options: Tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini
Tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini
questions.answer: Tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini
questions.explanation: The Eustachian tube is normally closed and opens actively during swallowing, yawning, or sneezing through the contraction of the tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini muscles.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini as the muscles responsible for opening the Eustachian tube.
questions.reasoningChain: Eustachian tube function -> Active opening mechanism -> Muscles involved -> Tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini.
optionExplanations: Palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus form folds in the pharynx but are not primary Eustachian tube openers.
Tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini actively dilate and open the Eustachian tube lumen.
Tensor tympani dampens ossicular vibrations in the middle ear cavity.
Stylohyoid and geniohyoid are suprahyoid muscles involved in swallowing and jaw movement.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: For Severe malnutrition, MAC will be less than?
questions.explanation: Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children aged 6-59 months is defined by a Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) measurement of less than 11.5 cm.
questions.educationalObjective: Know the MUAC threshold defining severe acute malnutrition (< 11.5 cm).
questions.reasoningChain: Childhood nutritional assessment -> SAM criteria -> MUAC cutoff -> Less than 11.5 cm.
optionExplanations: 14.5 cms is above the threshold for acute malnutrition.
13.5 cms indicates mild to moderate borderline nutritional status.
12.5 cms is the threshold defining moderate acute malnutrition (MAM).
11.5 cms is the strict clinical cutoff defining severe acute malnutrition (SAM).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Most common presenting complaint of NASOPHARYNGEAL CARCINOMA?
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma frequently metastasizes early to regional cervical lymph nodes. Consequently, the most common presenting complaint is a painless neck mass (neck node).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify a neck node as the most common presenting complaint of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma -> Early lymphatic spread -> Cervical lymphadenopathy -> Presenting as a neck node.
optionExplanations: Nasal obstruction occurs later as the primary tumor enlarges in the nasopharynx.
Epistaxis can occur but is less frequent as an initial presenting symptom compared to neck swelling.
Neck node enlargement is the most common presenting complaint due to early lymphatic metastasis.
Anosmia involves olfactory nerve impairment, which is uncommon in nasopharyngeal tumors.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: In Marasmus, mid arm muscle circumference is less than
questions.explanation: In marasmus (protein-energy malnutrition), muscle wasting is severe, and anthropometric parameters such as mid-arm muscle circumference fall below established thresholds (typically less than 15 cm in affected children).
questions.educationalObjective: Know anthropometric indicators of muscle wasting in marasmus.
questions.reasoningChain: Marasmus -> Severe calorie and muscle wasting -> Reduced mid-arm muscle circumference -> Less than 15 cm.
optionExplanations: 15 cm is the established threshold value below which mid-arm muscle circumference indicates severe wasting in marasmus.
17 cm represents higher nutritional percentiles.
19 cm is within normal or borderline well-nourished ranges for pediatric populations.
21 cm reflects normal pediatric growth parameters.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Epstein Barr Virus causes?
questions.explanation: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) infection is strongly linked to the pathogenesis of undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma, showing consistent viral DNA presence and elevated antibody titers.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) as a risk factor for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma etiology -> Oncogenic herpesvirus association -> Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV).
optionExplanations: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign vascular tumor occurring in adolescent males, unrelated to EBV.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is strongly linked etiologically with Epstein-Barr Virus infection.
Stewart’s granuloma (NK/T-cell lymphoma) is associated with EBV, but carcinoma is the direct classic exam match.
Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous bacterial infection caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Most preferred treatment modality for a patient with nasopharyngeal carcinoma ?
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is highly radiosensitive due to its epithelial and lymphoid histological components. The primary preferred treatment modality is radiotherapy, frequently combined with chemotherapy for advanced stages. Note: Historical recall keys sometimes point to chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy as preferred; radiotherapy remains the cornerstone.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify radiotherapy as the primary preferred treatment modality for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma -> Radiosensitive tumor -> Primary treatment modality -> Radiotherapy.
optionExplanations: Surgical excision is difficult due to the complex anatomical location of the nasopharynx and skull base.
Radiotherapy is the primary and most effective definitive treatment modality for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Chemotherapy is used as an adjunct alongside radiotherapy, not as monotherapy primary treatment.
Chemoradiotherapy is the standard for advanced stages, though radiotherapy alone is the core modality.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A 20 year old female patient presented with throat pain and difficulty in swallowing. On examination, her right tonsil was found to be congested and uvula pushed to opposite side, left side tonsil was normal, what could be the diagnosis ?
questions.explanation: Severe throat pain, difficulty swallowing, a congested unilateral tonsil, and uvular deviation to the opposite side are classic signs of peritonsillar abscess (quinsy).
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) based on unilateral tonsillar swelling and uvular deviation.
questions.reasoningChain: Severe throat pain + unilateral congested tonsil + uvular deviation -> Peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy).
optionExplanations: Retropharyngeal abscess presents with posterior pharyngeal wall bulging and neck rigidity.
Acute parenchymatous tonsillitis presents with bilateral symmetrical tonsillar inflammation without uvular shift.
Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) is characterized by severe trismus, unilateral swelling, and contralateral uvular deviation.
Parapharyngeal abscess presents with lateral neck swelling and deep neck space tenderness.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: All are features of Menieres disease except?
options: Radiofrequency ablation is the treatment of choice
questions.answer: Radiofrequency ablation is the treatment of choice
questions.explanation: Meniere's disease is characterized by endolymphatic hydrops causing episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Radiofrequency ablation is not a treatment for Meniere's disease, making this the correct 'except' option.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify features of Meniere's disease and recognize that radiofrequency ablation is not its treatment.
questions.reasoningChain: Meniere's disease features -> Idiopathic endolymphatic hydrops -> Low-frequency hearing loss -> Treated medically or with intratympanic steroids/surgery, not radiofrequency ablation.
optionExplanations: Low frequency sensorineural hearing loss is a classic audiometric feature of early Meniere's disease.
Idiopathic origin is a defining characteristic of Meniere's disease.
Endolymphatic hydrops is the underlying histopathological mechanism of Meniere's disease.
Radiofrequency ablation is not a treatment for Meniere's disease, making this statement false.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Protrusion of Adams apple due to which cartilage ?
questions.explanation: The laryngeal prominence, commonly known as the Adam's apple, is formed by the fusion of the two lamina of the thyroid cartilage in the anterior midline of the neck.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the thyroid cartilage as the structure forming the Adam's apple.
questions.reasoningChain: Adam's apple prominence -> Anterior neck landmark -> Formed by thyroid cartilage laminae fusion.
optionExplanations: Thyroid cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple) in the anterior neck.
Cricoid cartilage is a complete ring located inferior to the thyroid cartilage.
Hyoid bone is a horseshoe-shaped bone located in the upper neck above the larynx.
Epiglottis is a leaf-shaped elastic cartilage protecting the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Office headache?
questions.explanation: Frontal sinusitis frequently presents with a headache that develops and intensifies during working hours ('office headache') due to frontal sinus drainage obstruction.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize frontal sinusitis as the cause of 'office headache'.
questions.reasoningChain: Frontal sinusitis -> Mucus buildup and ostial blockage -> Morning headache worsening at work -> 'Office headache'.
optionExplanations: Maxillary sinusitis causes facial pain radiating to the upper teeth and cheeks.
Ethmoid sinusitis causes retro-orbital pain and tenderness between the eyes.
Frontal sinusitis is classically associated with the 'office headache' pattern.
Sphenoid sinusitis causes deep-seated vertex or occipital headaches radiating to the back of the head.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Most constant and largest ethmoidal air cells ?
questions.explanation: The bulla ethmoidalis is the largest and most constant ethmoidal air cell within the middle meatus, forming a prominent elevation on the lateral nasal wall beneath the hiatus semilunaris. It is derived from the middle ethmoidal air cells and acts as a key landmark during functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the bulla ethmoidalis as the largest and most constant ethmoidal air cell.
questions.reasoningChain: Middle meatus contains ethmoidal air cells -> Bulla ethmoidalis is a prominent constant swelling -> Forms key FESS landmark -> Correct answer.
optionExplanations: Aggar nasi cells are anterior ethmoid cells located anterior and superior to the middle turbinate attachment.
Bulla ethmoidalis is the largest and most constant ethmoidal air cell found within the middle meatus.
Haller cells are infraorbital ethmoidal air cells that can narrow the maxillary sinus ostium.
Onodi cells are sphenoethmoidal air cells located superior and lateral to the sphenoid sinus.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: A patient with Pink color skin & mucosa, a bitter almond smell from breath, and frothy discharge. The cause of death is
questions.explanation: Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) poisoning classically presents with bright pink or cherry-red skin and mucous membranes due to high venous oxygen content (unutilized oxygen in tissues), a characteristic bitter almond odor on the breath, and pulmonary edema leading to frothy discharge. Cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, halting cellular respiration.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the classic clinical signs of hydrogen cyanide poisoning including pink skin and bitter almond odor.
questions.reasoningChain: Bitter almond odor + pink skin/mucosa + frothy discharge -> Cytochrome c oxidase inhibition -> Hydrogen cyanide poisoning.
optionExplanations: Hydrogen sulfide poisoning causes rotten egg odor and dark or slate-green cyanosis rather than bright pink skin.
Carbon monoxide poisoning causes cherry-red skin but lacks the characteristic bitter almond smell of cyanide.
Hydrogen cyanide poisoning presents with a bitter almond smell, pink skin, and respiratory arrest.
Organophosphorus poisoning presents with cholinergic excess like salivation, lacrimation, and miosis without bitter almond odor.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: The ideal investigation of choice for confirming CSF rhinorrhea?
questions.explanation: Beta-2 transferrin analysis is the gold standard and most specific investigation for confirming cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea. It is an isoform of transferrin found almost exclusively in CSF, perilymph, and aqueous humor, making its detection in nasal secretions definitive for CSF leakage.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify beta-2 transferrin analysis as the most specific test for confirming CSF rhinorrhea.
questions.reasoningChain: Nasal fluid discharge -> Need to confirm CSF -> Beta-2 transferrin is unique to CSF -> Ideal confirmatory test.
optionExplanations: Beta 2 transferrin analysis is the most specific and ideal biochemical test to confirm cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea.
CT-cisternogram helps localize the site of the CSF leak but is not the primary biochemical confirmatory test.
Nasal endoscopy visualizes the nasal cavity and can identify anatomical defects or mass lesions but cannot confirm CSF.
MRI with contrast is useful for high-resolution anatomical imaging of skull base defects but less specific for fluid analysis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: The poisoning caused by a bullet retained inside the body is
questions.explanation: Plumbism (lead poisoning) can occur when a lead bullet or shrapnel is retained within joint spaces, bone, or soft tissues where it is exposed to synovial fluid or blood, leading to gradual systemic absorption and chronic lead toxicity over time.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that a retained bullet inside the body can cause chronic lead poisoning.
questions.reasoningChain: Retained metallic bullet in body -> Exposure to body fluids -> Gradual dissolution and absorption -> Lead poisoning.
optionExplanations: Iron toxicity typically results from oral overdose or excessive transfusions rather than retained bullets.
Phosphorus poisoning is commonly seen in matchstick ingestions or agricultural pesticide exposures.
Nitrocellulose is an explosive compound and propellant component, not a metal poisoning risk from retained fragments.
Lead bullets retained in body tissues undergo gradual systemic absorption leading to chronic lead poisoning.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A 30 year old lady met with a road traffic accident, she didn’t wear her helmet, she had loss of consciousness for some minutes and then she became normal, after 2 days, she rushed to ENT department complaining clear fluid discharge from nose, what could be the diagnosis?
options: Infection due to hemosinus because of RTA
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic clear fluid discharge from the nose following head injury and a transient loss of consciousness is characteristic of CSF rhinorrhea. This occurs due to a fracture of the anterior cranial fossa (cribriform plate of ethmoid or frontal sinus) tearing the dura mater and arachnoid.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose post-traumatic CSF rhinorrhea following anterior skull base fractures.
questions.reasoningChain: Head trauma + transient LOC + clear nasal discharge after 2 days -> Anterior skull base fracture -> CSF rhinorrhea.
optionExplanations: Allergic rhinitis presents with watery rhinorrhea, sneezing, and nasal itching, usually without trauma history.
Infection due to hemosinus involves blood accumulation in sinuses and presents differently from clear fluid.
CSF rhinorrhea presents with clear, glucose-containing fluid leaking from the nose post head trauma.
Post traumatic rhinitis is an inflammatory response to injury but does not cause continuous clear fluid dripping.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: In an autopsy of suspected poisoning, which organ, along with the stomach, part of the intestine, and liver, is preserved?
questions.explanation: In medico-legal autopsies with suspected poisoning, standard toxicological protocol requires the preservation of specific viscera for chemical analysis. These include the stomach with its contents, a loop of the small and large intestine, the liver (main site of metabolism), and one kidney (main organ of excretion).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify organs routinely preserved for toxicological analysis during a forensic autopsy.
questions.reasoningChain: Suspected poisoning -> Toxicological screening -> Stomach, intestines, liver, and kidneys preserved -> Kidney is standard.
optionExplanations: Kidney is routinely preserved for toxicological screening as it is a major excretory organ for poisons.
Lungs are preserved when volatile poisons or inhalation toxins are specifically suspected.
Brain is preserved when lipid-soluble poisons like alcohol, barbiturates, or alkaloids are suspected.
Heart is typically preserved for histological examination or specific cardiac glycoside analysis rather than routine panels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A man presented to the emergency department with head injury after an accident with a vehicle. Investigation of choice in this condition is
questions.explanation: Non-Contrast Computed Tomography (NCCT) head is the investigation of choice for acute head trauma in the emergency department. It is fast, highly sensitive for acute intracranial hemorrhage, skull fractures, and midline shift, and requires no contrast administration.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify NCCT head as the primary imaging modality for acute head injury.
questions.reasoningChain: Acute head injury in emergency -> Rapid evaluation needed for hemorrhage/fracture -> NCCT head is investigation of choice.
optionExplanations: CECT involves contrast administration and is not the primary choice for acute traumatic brain injuries.
MRI is superior for soft tissue and posterior fossa lesions but is time-consuming and impractical for acute unstable trauma.
NCCT is the rapid, highly sensitive imaging modality of choice for acute head trauma evaluation.
X-ray skull has low sensitivity for intracranial injuries and has been largely replaced by CT scans.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: During the examination of injury, hair bulbs are noted to be crushed. The probable type of wound is
questions.explanation: Crushed or bruised hair bulbs observed during microscopic or macroscopic examination of a wound are characteristic of a laceration caused by blunt force impact. The shearing and crushing forces stretch and rupture hair follicles, distinguishing them from clean cuts seen in incised wounds.
questions.educationalObjective: Associate crushed hair bulbs with blunt force lacerations in forensic examination.
questions.reasoningChain: Blunt force trauma -> Hair bulbs crushed and damaged -> Characteristic of lacerations.
optionExplanations: Abrasions involve superficial scraping of the epidermis without deep structural disruption of hair roots.
Lacerations are blunt force injuries that crush tissues, leading to crushed or damaged hair bulbs.
Stab wounds are clean-edged sharp force injuries that slice rather than crush hair follicles.
None of the above is incorrect because laceration is the correct answer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: 32 year old male presented with fever and pain in the right upper hypochondrium after food intake. Investigation of choice in this condition is
questions.explanation: Right upper quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and postprandial symptoms in a middle-aged adult strongly suggest acute cholecystitis or biliary tract pathology. Ultrasonography (USG) abdomen is the rapid, non-invasive, and primary investigation of choice, demonstrating gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, and Murphy's sign.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify ultrasound as the initial investigation of choice for acute biliary tract disorders.
questions.reasoningChain: RUQ pain + fever after food -> Suspected acute cholecystitis -> Ultrasonography is initial imaging modality.
optionExplanations: CECT is reserved for complicated cases, suspected perforation, or malignancy rather than initial gallstone evaluation.
USG is the rapid, highly sensitive, and non-invasive investigation of choice for right upper quadrant pain.
MRI/MRCP is useful for indeterminate biliary obstruction but is not the primary emergency test.
HRCT is used for high-resolution pulmonary imaging, not hepatobiliary pathology.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: 40 year old patient with femur fracture with pulmonary infiltration & respiratory distress. What is a probable diagnosis.?
questions.explanation: A patient with a long bone fracture (femur) developing respiratory distress, hypoxia, and pulmonary infiltrates classic for acute respiratory distress within 24 to 72 hours strongly indicates fat embolism syndrome. Fat droplets released from the bone marrow lodge in the pulmonary capillaries.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize fat embolism syndrome following long bone fractures.
questions.reasoningChain: Femur fracture + pulmonary infiltration + respiratory distress -> Fat globules released into circulation -> Fat embolism syndrome.
optionExplanations: Fat embolism is classically triggered by long bone fractures releasing marrow fat into the pulmonary circulation.
Pulmonary embolism typically involves deep venous thrombi rather than direct long bone fracture fat release.
Air embolism occurs due to iatrogenic or traumatic air entry into the venous system, not bone marrow fat.
Obstruction is a generic term and does not specify the pathological process of marrow fat occluding vessels.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Anthracosis is caused by
questions.explanation: Anthracosis is a benign pneumoconiosis caused by the chronic inhalation and accumulation of coal dust in the lungs and associated lymph nodes, commonly seen in coal miners.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify coal dust inhalation as the cause of anthracosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Inhalation of coal dust -> Deposition in lung parenchyma and lymph nodes -> Anthracosis.
optionExplanations: Silica dust inhalation leads to silicosis, characterized by nodular pulmonary fibrosis.
Coal dust inhalation causes anthracosis, a form of pneumoconiosis affecting coal workers.
Asbestos fiber inhalation causes asbestosis and increases the risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer.
Sugar cane dust exposure leads to bagassosis, a form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Following is the Chemoprophylaxis of choice in a person who is on a journey to Endemic malaria region
questions.explanation: Chloroquine remains a standard chemoprophylactic agent for travelers visiting regions with chloroquine-sensitive Plasmodium falciparum or vivax malaria, though regional resistance patterns must always be checked prior to travel.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify chloroquine as a chemoprophylactic option for endemic malaria regions.
questions.reasoningChain: Travel to endemic malaria region -> Chemoprophylaxis required -> Chloroquine used for sensitive areas.
optionExplanations: Lumefantrine is combined with artemether for acute malaria treatment, not used as a solo chemoprophylactic agent.
Pyrimethamine is rarely used alone for chemoprophylaxis due to widespread parasite resistance.
Chloroquine is traditionally used for chemoprophylaxis in areas with sensitive malaria strains.
Quinine is reserved for the treatment of severe or complicated malaria, not for routine prophylaxis.
questions.reviewNote: Chloroquine prophylaxis is now restricted to specific chloroquine-sensitive regions due to widespread resistance globally, but remains the classic textbook answer for this recall.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Thimble bladder is seen in
questions.explanation: A thimble bladder is a small, contracted, fibrotic urinary bladder resulting from chronic genitourinary tuberculosis (TB). Chronic inflammation and healing lead to severe loss of compliance and diminished bladder capacity.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize thimble bladder as a classic complication of chronic genitourinary tuberculosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic inflammation from genitourinary tuberculosis -> Fibrosis and scarring -> Contracted small bladder capacity ('thimble bladder').
optionExplanations: Acute TB causes active inflammatory changes rather than chronic fibrotic bladder contracture.
Chronic TB leads to extensive fibrosis and scarring of the bladder wall, resulting in a thimble bladder.
Neurogenic bladder results from neurological dysfunction, leading to flaccid or spastic patterns, not typically tuberculous fibrosis.
Schistosomiasis can cause bladder calcification and squamous cell carcinoma, but 'thimble bladder' is classically linked to chronic TB.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Abdominal pain + fever+ jaundice. Which triad ?
questions.explanation: Charcot’s triad consists of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, fever (with chills), and jaundice. It is the classic clinical presentation of acute cholangitis, typically caused by biliary duct obstruction and infection.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Charcot's triad as the classic presentation of acute cholangitis.
questions.reasoningChain: Abdominal pain + fever + jaundice -> Biliary tract infection and obstruction -> Charcot's triad.
optionExplanations: Saint's triad includes hiatus hernia, diverticular disease, and gallstones.
Charcot's triad comprises fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain indicating acute cholangitis.
Virchow triad describes thrombosis risk factors: hypercoagulability, hemodynamic changes, and endothelial injury.
Renault's triad is not a standard recognized eponym in this clinical context.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: How you will screen Vitamin A Deficiency in a school?
questions.explanation: Night blindness (nyctalopia) is the earliest clinical manifestation of vitamin A deficiency and serves as the most sensitive and practical indicator for screening vitamin A deficiency in school-aged children and community surveys.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify night blindness as the earliest screening symptom of vitamin A deficiency.
questions.reasoningChain: Vitamin A deficiency -> Impaired rhodopsin synthesis in rods -> Night blindness as earliest clinical sign.
optionExplanations: Serum retinol measures biochemical status but is costly and less practical for mass school screening.
Night blindness is the earliest clinical symptom and primary screening criterion for vitamin A deficiency in communities.
Carotene is a dietary precursor, not a clinical screening symptom for deficiency.
Bitot spots are a later clinical sign of xerophthalmia, representing conjunctival keratinization, not the earliest screen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Gynecomastia is seen in all, Except
questions.explanation: Gynecomastia is benign enlargement of male breast tissue caused by an imbalance between estrogen and androgen activity. It is common in Klinefelter syndrome, liver cirrhosis (impaired estrogen clearance), and hyperthyroidism (increased sex hormone-binding globulin), whereas prostate cancer treatment often involves anti-androgens causing breast tenderness, but prostate cancer itself does not inherently cause gynecomastia unless treated.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify conditions associated with gynecomastia and exclude prostate cancer.
questions.reasoningChain: Gynecomastia caused by hormonal imbalance -> Seen in Klinefelter, cirrhosis, hyperthyroidism -> Not a primary feature of prostate cancer.
optionExplanations: Klinefelter syndrome features hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, leading to elevated estrogen-to-androgen ratios and gynecomastia.
Liver cirrhosis impairs estrogen metabolism and clearance by the liver, resulting in gynecomastia and spider angiomas.
Hyperthyroidism increases peripheral aromatization of androgens to estrogens, frequently causing gynecomastia.
Prostate cancer does not cause gynecomastia natively; anti-androgen therapy for it does, making prostate cancer the exception.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Completed family size depends on
questions.explanation: Completed family size in demographic and public health studies is determined by the total number of children born to a woman or cohort of women by the end of their reproductive years.
questions.educationalObjective: Define completed family size in terms of total live births.
questions.reasoningChain: Family size demography -> Measured by total offspring produced -> Number of children.
optionExplanations: Number of adolescents represents the future reproductive cohort, not the completed family size.
Number of women defines the female population base but does not measure completed family size directly.
Number of children born to a woman by the end of reproductive life defines completed family size.
Number of persons is a general demographic count, not specific to completed reproductive output.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Yellow fever vaccine is valid for
questions.explanation: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) International Health Regulations (IHR) amendments implemented in 2016, the validity of the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP) for the yellow fever vaccine was changed from 10 years to the duration of the life of the person vaccinated.
questions.educationalObjective: State the current WHO validity period for the yellow fever vaccine certificate as lifelong.
questions.reasoningChain: Yellow fever vaccine regulations updated -> Protection lasts life long -> International certificate validity is lifelong.
optionExplanations: 10 years was the previous historical validity period before WHO regulations were updated to lifelong.
Life long is the current valid duration for the yellow fever vaccination certificate under WHO rules.
5 years is incorrect as vaccine-induced immunity persists beyond this timeframe.
1 year is far too short and does not reflect current international health regulations.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: 28-year-old alcoholic patient walk to the hospital with complaints of binge vomiting chest pain, fever and hydropneumothorax. What is most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Boerhaave syndrome is spontaneous esophageal rupture caused by severe vomiting and retching, typically in patients with a history of heavy eating or drinking. It presents with severe chest pain, fever, and hydropneumothorax due to esophageal contents spilling into the mediastinum and pleural cavity.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize Boerhaave syndrome as esophageal rupture following severe vomiting.
questions.reasoningChain: History of binge vomiting + chest pain + fever + hydropneumothorax -> Spontaneous esophageal rupture -> Boerhaave syndrome.
optionExplanations: Boerhaave syndrome involves transmural esophageal rupture following severe vomiting and retching.
Tension pneumothorax causes respiratory distress and tracheal deviation but is not specifically triggered by binge vomiting.
Peptic ulcer disease perforation presents with acute peritonitis and free air under the diaphragm.
Mallory-Weiss tear causes mucosal lacerations and upper GI bleeding without hydropneumothorax or transmural rupture.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: In an accident case, all should be done in early management after the medical team’s arrival. Except
questions.explanation: In advanced trauma life support (ATLS) protocols, initial primary survey management focuses on Airway, Breathing, and Circulation (ABC), along with cervical spine immobilization and neurological status check (GCS). Blood pressure is part of circulation assessment, but checking specific baseline BP is not the immediate stabilization priority compared to securing airway, breathing, and assessing gross circulation/perfusion.
questions.educationalObjective: Apply ATLS primary survey principles in trauma management.
questions.reasoningChain: Trauma arrival management -> Primary survey focuses on cervical spine, airway, breathing, and GCS -> Specific blood pressure measurement is secondary to ABC resuscitation.
optionExplanations: Stabilization of cervical vertebrae is critical in trauma to prevent secondary spinal cord injury during airway management.
Checking blood pressure is part of circulatory assessment, but early management prioritizes immediate airway, breathing, and cervical stabilization.
Checking respiration is a core component of the primary survey (Airway and Breathing).
GCS score is essential in the primary survey to assess neurological disability (D of ABCDE).
questions.reviewNote: Blood pressure is part of Circulation assessment in ATLS, but questions of this type test priorities; however, cervical spine, airway, breathing, and GCS are all formal parts of the primary survey.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Identify the condition shown below
questions.explanation: The image shows a well-demarcated, pink-to-red vascular lesion on the face and neck, characteristic of a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus). This is a congenital capillary malformation that persists throughout life and does not undergo spontaneous regression.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify a port-wine stain as a congenital capillary malformation.
questions.reasoningChain: Congenital flat red-purple cutaneous patch -> Capillary malformation -> Port wine stain.
optionExplanations: Strawberry hemangioma is a raised vascular tumor that appears after birth and undergoes spontaneous involution.
Erythema multiforme presents with targetoid skin lesions triggered by infections or medications.
Erythema subitum (roseola infantum) presents with a transient macular rash following high fever in infants.
Port wine stain is a congenital capillary vascular malformation presenting as a flat pink-red patch.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: All are components of Kuppuswamy scale
questions.explanation: The Kuppuswamy socioeconomic status scale, widely used in India, incorporates three parameters: Education of the head of the family, Occupation of the head of the family, and monthly Income of the family.
questions.educationalObjective: List the three components of the Kuppuswamy socioeconomic status scale.
questions.reasoningChain: Kuppuswamy scale parameters -> Education + Occupation + Income -> Correct combination.
optionExplanations: Income, Housing, and Education are components of the modified Udai Pareek scale or other rural scales, not Kuppuswamy.
Income, Livestock, and Housing are not part of the urban Kuppuswamy socioeconomic scale.
Housing, Livestock, and Land are agricultural asset markers used in rural scales, not Kuppuswamy.
Income, Occupation, and Education are the three vital indicators comprising the urban Kuppuswamy scale.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Patient underwent gastrectomy, after eating within 20 minutes having sweating, diarrhea. What could be the cause?
questions.explanation: Early dumping syndrome occurs within 15 to 30 minutes after a meal in post-gastrectomy patients. It is caused by rapid gastric emptying of hyperosmolar chyme into the small intestine, leading to fluid shift into the bowel lumen (hypovolemia, diarrhea, sweating, tachycardia) and autonomic activation.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize early dumping syndrome occurring within 30 minutes post-gastrectomy.
questions.reasoningChain: Post gastrectomy + symptoms within 20 minutes (sweating, diarrhea) -> Fluid shift from rapid osmolar load -> Early dumping syndrome.
optionExplanations: Early dumping syndrome occurs within 30 minutes of eating due to osmotic fluid shifts and vasomotor symptoms.
Late dumping syndrome occurs 1 to 3 hours postprandial due to reactive hypoglycemia.
Hyperglycemia is not the primary mechanism of postprandial vasomotor symptoms in dumping syndrome.
Hypoglycemia is responsible for late dumping syndrome symptoms occurring hours after carbohydrate-rich meals.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Most sensitive test for microfilariae
questions.explanation: The membrane filter concentration technique is the most sensitive method for detecting microfilariae in blood samples, especially when parasitemia is low, as it captures microfilariae on a filter membrane after lysing red blood cells.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: 100% mortality disease, incidence and prevalence relationship will be
questions.explanation: For a disease with 100% mortality where patients die rapidly after onset, the incidence (number of new cases) equals the mortality rate, and prevalence (existing cases at a point in time) approaches zero. Thus, prevalence is strictly less than incidence (P < I).

questions.reasoningChain: 100% mortality with rapid death -> Duration of disease is zero -> No existing cases at any snapshot -> Prevalence < Incidence.
optionExplanations: P = I applies when disease duration is stable and chronic (Prevalence = Incidence × Duration).
P < I applies when 100% mortality causes rapid death, meaning active cases do not accumulate over time.
P > I occurs in chronic, highly prevalent conditions with low mortality rates.
No relationship between both is incorrect because epidemiologic formulas directly link P, I, and duration.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify Auspitz sign as a diagnostic feature of psoriasis vulgaris.
questions.reasoningChain: Scraping psoriatic scale -> Removal of parakeratotic layers -> Rupture of dermal capillaries -> Auspitz sign.
optionExplanations: Psoriasis vulgaris classically demonstrates silvery scales, the Auspitz sign, and a positive Koebner phenomenon.
Pustular psoriasis presents with sterile pustules on erythematous skin without classic chronic scaly plaques.
Pemphigus vulgaris features flaccid blisters and Nikolsky sign due to intraepidermal acantholysis.
Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense bullae beneath the epidermis with negative Nikolsky sign.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.prompt: A young man presents with a leg lesion as shown in the image below. On examination, the lesions are painful, and the edges are well demarcated and raised. He also complains of blisters over his body. He is otherwise normal and does not have any other diseases. This infection is most likely to be caused by which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a painful, well-demarcated, bright red, raised plaque on the lower leg with blistering and acute onset fever is characteristic of erysipelas, which is most commonly caused by Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Group A Streptococcus as the primary causative agent of erysipelas.
questions.reasoningChain: Painful well-demarcated raised red skin lesion with blisters -> Erysipelas -> Group A Streptococcus.
optionExplanations: Group B Streptococcus typically causes neonatal sepsis and meningitis.
Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) is the classic bacterial cause of erysipelas and impetigo.
Staphylococcus aureus typically causes purulent folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, and bullous impetigo.
Haemophilus influenzae type b causes epiglottitis, meningitis, and pneumonia in children.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.prompt: A sexually active male presented with warts on his penis as shown below. Similar lesions were present neat the anal canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical photograph shows exophytic, cauliflower-like verrucous lesions on the genitalia and perineum, which are characteristic of condyloma acuminata (genital warts) caused by human papillomavirus (HPV types 6 and 11).
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize condyloma acuminata (genital warts) caused by HPV.
questions.reasoningChain: Cauliflower-like genital and perianal warts -> Condyloma acuminata.
optionExplanations: Penile cancer presents as a non-healing indurated ulcer or destructive mass rather than soft exophytic warts.
Condyloma acuminata presents as flesh-colored, cauliflower-like papules caused by human papillomavirus.
Bowen disease presents as an erythematous, scaly, well-demarcated plaque representing carcinoma in situ.
Haemorrhoids are swollen vascular anal cushions presenting with bleeding and prolapse.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.prompt: A 40 year old female comes with complaints of pain in her fingernail. On examination, nail folds were seen to be red and with erythema as shown in the picture. The most likely diagnosis is.
questions.explanation: Acute paronychia is an infection of the periungual skin fold surrounding the fingernail, presenting with severe throbbing pain, erythema, edema, and purulent exudate tracking along the nail margin, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose acute paronychia based on painful periungual inflammation and erythema.
questions.reasoningChain: Inflammation and erythema of nail fold with pus accumulation -> Acute paronychia.
optionExplanations: Paronychia is characterized by localized bacterial inflammation and purulence of the nail fold.
Yellow-nail syndrome presents with slow-growing yellow nails, lymphedema, and pleural effusions.
Psoriasis of nails presents with pitting, oil-drop discoloration, and subungual hyperkeratosis.
Alopecia areata causes patchy hair loss on the scalp without periungual nail fold infection.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.prompt: The girl seen in the image has had history of severe sunburns after just a few minutes in the sun, severe freckling in the sun exposed areas. The most likely diagnosis is.
questions.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by deficient nucleotide excision repair of UV-induced DNA damage, resulting in extreme photosensitivity, severe sunburns, early freckle-like hyperpigmentation, and high skin cancer incidence.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose xeroderma pigmentosum by extreme UV sensitivity and childhood freckling.
questions.reasoningChain: Severe sunburns after minimal sun exposure + marked freckling + DNA repair defect -> Xeroderma pigmentosum.
optionExplanations: Bloom's syndrome features sun-sensitive facial telangiectatic erythema and growth deficiency with genomic instability.
Xeroderma pigmentosum presents with extreme UV sensitivity, early freckling, blistering, and high skin malignancy risk.
Warts are benign epidermal growths caused by viral papillomavirus infection.
Systemic lupus erythematosus features malar rash triggered by sun exposure accompanied by systemic autoimmune findings.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A young adult presents with a deformed nose after falling from a ladder. The CT scan shows a displaced nasal fracture. What is the ideal time to reduce the fracture in this patient?
questions.explanation: Following nasal trauma, acute edema typically obscures nasal deformities. The ideal time to perform closed reduction of a displaced nasal bone fracture is within 5 to 7 days after injury (once swelling subsides and before fibrous bone healing begins).
questions.educationalObjective: State the optimal timing for reducing nasal bone fractures as 5 to 7 days post-injury.
questions.reasoningChain: Nasal fracture with edema -> Need to wait for swelling to subside -> Optimal reduction time is 5-7 days.
optionExplanations: Within 12 hours is too early because massive soft tissue swelling obscures accurate clinical alignment.
5-7 days post-injury is the ideal window when edema has subsided but bone fragments have not yet fixated.
After 2 weeks, fibrous union begins, making closed reduction difficult or impossible without osteotomy.
After 4 weeks, bony consolidation is complete, requiring formal rhinoplasty and osteotomies.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Bony septal perforation occurs in:
questions.explanation: Syphilis (specifically tertiary syphilis with gummatous necrosis) is a classic cause of destructive bony nasal septum perforation ('saddle nose' deformity and septal destruction), distinguishing it from other granulomatous conditions.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify syphilis as a classic cause of bony nasal septal perforation.
questions.reasoningChain: Destructive nasal septal perforation (bony involvement) -> Tertiary syphilis gumma.
optionExplanations: Leprosy typically causes cartilaginous septal perforation rather than primary bony septal destruction.
Rhinosporidiosis presents as friable, bleeding polypoidal mucosal masses without primary bony septal destruction.
Syphilis (tertiary stage gumma) causes destruction of the bony nasal septum and hard palate.
Tuberculosis typically affects the cartilaginous nasal septum or larynx rather than causing primary bony perforation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A young male who is a professional trumpet blower presented with a swelling on the left side of the neck. On examination, there is a gurgling sound when compressing the swelling. As the x-ray neck was inconclusive a CT neck was taken which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A laryngocele is an abnormal dilation or herniation of the laryngeal ventricle into the neck, commonly seen in wind instrument players (trumpeters) or glassblowers due to chronic raised intraluminal pressure. CT shows an air-filled cystic lesion communicating with the larynx.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose laryngocele in wind instrument players presenting with a compressible neck mass.
questions.reasoningChain: Trumpet blower + neck swelling with gurgling sound + CT air-filled laryngeal outpouching -> Laryngocele.
optionExplanations: Pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's) arises posteriorly through Killian's dehiscence, causing dysphagia and regurgitation.
Laryngocele is an air-filled laryngeal sac common in trumpet blowers and glassblowers.
Tracheo-esophageal fistula presents with coughing during swallowing and neonatal aspiration.
Tonsillar mass presents with sore throat, asymmetry, or dysphagia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Gold standard investigation before FESS (functional endoscopic sinus surgery) is?
questions.explanation: High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) of the paranasal sinuses is the gold standard imaging investigation prior to Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS), providing precise anatomical mapping of osteomeatal complexes and skull base variants.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify CT scan as the gold standard pre-FESS imaging modality.
questions.reasoningChain: Pre-operative evaluation for FESS -> Need detailed bony and mucosal anatomy -> CT scan is gold standard.
optionExplanations: MRI scan is superior for soft tissue tumors and fungal rhinosinusitis but poor for fine bony anatomy.
X-ray paranasal sinuses is outdated and lacks the detail required for modern sinus surgery.
Antral lavage is a therapeutic or diagnostic irrigation procedure, not an imaging investigation.
CT scan is the gold standard investigation providing crucial anatomical mapping for FESS.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A 65 year old male presented with history of dysphagia, halitosis and aspiration pneumonia. A barium swallow was done and is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A barium swallow showing a posterior pouch protruding from the pharyngoesophageal junction (Killian's dehiscence) in an elderly patient presenting with dysphagia, halitosis, and regurgitation confirms a Zenker's diverticulum.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Zenker's diverticulum on barium swallow.
questions.reasoningChain: Elderly patient with dysphagia, halitosis + barium swallow showing posterior pouch at pharyngoesophageal junction -> Zenker's diverticulum.
optionExplanations: Diffuse esophageal spasm shows uncoordinated tertiary contractions (corkscrew esophagus).
Achalasia cardia shows bird-beak tapering at the lower esophageal sphincter.
Zenker's diverticulum is demonstrated by the barium-filled outpouching at Killian's dehiscence.
Esophageal cancer shows an irregular, shelvening stricture with mucosal destruction.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Identify the marked structure in the endoscopic image of nasopharynx.
questions.explanation: The fossa of Rosenmüller (pharyngeal recess) is located in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx posterior to the Eustachian tube orifice and is the most common site of origin for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the fossa of Rosenmüller on nasopharyngeal endoscopy.
questions.reasoningChain: Endoscopic view of lateral nasopharyngeal wall recess -> Fossa of Rosenmüller.
optionExplanations: Sinus of Morgagni is a potential space superior to the superior constrictor muscle.
Passavant's ridge is a muscular ridge formed by the palatopharyngeus during swallowing.
Fossa of Rosenmüller is the lateral pharyngeal recess marked in the endoscopic image.
Rathke's pouch is an embryological precursor of the anterior pituitary gland.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A patient presents with carcinoma in pyriform fossa. On laryngoscopy, the lesion is around 5 cm and the right vocal folds are not mobile. There is no lymph node involvement and no distant metastasis. What is the TNM staging for the malignancy?
questions.explanation: According to the AJCC TNM staging system for laryngeal and hypopharyngeal cancers, a tumor size around 5 cm or fixation of the hemilarynx (vocal cord immobility) classifies the primary tumor as T3, assuming no regional lymph nodes (N0) or distant metastasis (M0).
questions.educationalObjective: Determine T3 staging for hypopharyngeal cancer with vocal cord immobility.
questions.reasoningChain: Hypopharyngeal tumor measuring ~5 cm with vocal cord immobility -> Vocal cord fixation defines T3 staging -> T3N0M0.
optionExplanations: T2N0M0 represents smaller tumors without vocal cord fixation.
T3N0M0 is assigned due to vocal cord fixation (immobility) indicating deeper laryngeal/hypopharyngeal invasion.
T4aN0M0 involves moderately advanced local invasion of surrounding structures like thyroid cartilage.
T4bN0M0 represents very advanced disease encasing carotid artery or prevertebral fascia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: In which condition is the reservoir sign seen along with mastoid tenderness?
questions.explanation: The reservoir sign (or Griesinger's sign, or Wilde's sign / reservoir sign where pus reaccumulates in the external auditory canal after wiping) is a classic clinical sign seen in acute mastoiditis associated with subperiosteal abscess or cortical breakthrough.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the reservoir sign in acute mastoiditis.
questions.reasoningChain: Mastoid tenderness + rapid reaccumulation of pus in ear canal (reservoir sign) -> Acute mastoiditis.
optionExplanations: Otosclerotic lesions present with conductive hearing loss and Carhart's notch without mastoid tenderness.
Acute mastoiditis classically presents with postauricular swelling, mastoid tenderness, and the reservoir sign.
Intratympanic glomus tumor presents with pulsatile tinnitus and a red retrotympanic mass.
Chronic suppurative otitis media presents with persistent ear discharge and tympanic membrane perforation without acute mastoid abscess signs.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Which is the false statement among the following for the condition given in the picture?
options: Retention cyst of major salivary glands
Most common site is lower lip
Retention cyst of minor salivary glands
questions.answer: Retention cyst of major salivary glands
questions.explanation: A mucocele (mucus extravasation cyst) is the most common lesion of the minor salivary glands, typically occurring on the lower lip due to local trauma. It is NOT a retention cyst of major salivary glands, making that statement false.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify mucoceles as extravasation cysts of minor salivary glands on the lower lip.
questions.reasoningChain: Image shows lower lip swelling -> Mucocele (extravasation cyst of minor gland, not retention cyst of major gland) -> False statement identified.
optionExplanations: Retention cyst of major salivary glands is the false statement, as mucoceles originate from minor salivary gland trauma.
Most common site for a mucocele is the lower lip.
Retention cyst of minor salivary glands (extravasation type) is accurate regarding pathophysiology.
Treatment for persistent mucoceles is surgical excision or marsupialization.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A patient presents with hoarseness of voice. On examination an ulcero-proliferative mass is seen on right vocal cord, cord was however mobile. There is no lymph node involvement and no metastasis. Which of the following is the best treatment modality for this patient?
questions.explanation: For early-stage laryngeal cancer (T1 or T2) involving a mobile vocal cord without lymph node or distant metastasis, radiotherapy is the primary treatment modality of choice because it preserves voice quality with high cure rates.
questions.educationalObjective: Select radiotherapy as the primary treatment for early glottic laryngeal cancer with mobile cords.
questions.reasoningChain: Early glottic carcinoma with mobile vocal cord + N0M0 -> Preservation of voice preferred -> Radiotherapy.
optionExplanations: Total laryngectomy is reserved for advanced laryngeal cancers (T3/T4) with fixed cords or cartilage invasion.
Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for early vocal cord cancer preserving voice function.
Conservative laryngectomy (partial) is an alternative surgical option but RT remains standard primary choice for early cord lesions.
Chemotherapy is used concurrently with radiation in advanced disease, not as monotherapy for early localized lesions.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: The most common site of obstruction by a nasal polyp from the maxillary sinus is?
questions.explanation: Antrochoanal polyps originate from the maxillary sinus mucosa, exit through the natural or accessory maxillary ostium, and project into the middle meatus before extending into the nasopharynx.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the middle meatus as the site of nasal polyp obstruction from the maxillary sinus.
questions.reasoningChain: Maxillary sinus polyp -> Exits via sinus ostium -> Obstruction and passage through middle meatus.
optionExplanations: Inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct opening, not maxillary sinus polyps.
Superior meatus receives posterior ethmoidal air cell openings.
Middle meatus is the site of the ostiomeatal complex where maxillary sinus polyps emerge.
Sphenoethmoidal recess receives the sphenoid sinus opening.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: When a victim of an unlawful act was dying, the police recorded the dying declaration. The doctor certifies that the victim was conscious and mentally oriented. The dying declaration will be considered invalid if?
options: It is not done by the doctor
The victim didn’t sign the declaration
questions.explanation: Under Indian Evidence Act Section 32, a dying declaration is admissible as substantive evidence even without corroboration, provided the declarant was conscious and oriented. However, if the declarant had no expectation or anticipation of death at the time of making the statement, the declaration becomes legally invalid as a dying declaration.
questions.educationalObjective: State the legal requirement that a dying declaration requires expectation of death.
questions.reasoningChain: Dying declaration admissibility -> Declarant must be in expectation of death -> Lack of expectation invalidates statement.
optionExplanations: It is not done by the doctor is incorrect because medical certification is helpful but not legally mandatory for validity.
The victim is not dead is incorrect because dying statements remain valid if the victim survives (though categorized under different evidentiary sections).
Declarant is not expecting death is a legal requirement for dying declarations, invalidating it under Section 32 if absent.
The victim didn't sign is incorrect because oral dying declarations recorded by anyone are legally admissible.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: Identify the fingerprint pattern shown in the image
questions.explanation: The fingerprint pattern shown has ridges entering from one side, rising in the center to form a peak or arch, and exiting on the opposite side without forming a delta or loop, classifying it as an 'Arch'.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify an arch fingerprint pattern lacking deltas and loops.
questions.reasoningChain: Fingerprint ridges flowing across from side to side with central rise and no delta -> Arch pattern.
optionExplanations: Whorl pattern features concentric circles or spiral ridge formations with two or more deltas.
Composite pattern combines two or more different fingerprint patterns (e.g., loop and whorl).
Loop pattern has ridges entering from one side, curving around, and exiting on the same side with one delta.
Arch is the simplest fingerprint pattern where ridges flow from one side to the other with a central rise.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: A dead body as found with a wound on the neck, with clean-cut edges, crushed tissues along disruption of the vertebral bones. Identify the type of wound.
questions.explanation: A chop wound is caused by heavy, sharp-edged instruments (like an axe or machete) combining features of both incised wounds (clean-cut edges) and blunt force injuries (crushed underlying tissues and fractured bones).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify chop wounds as combining sharp-edge and blunt-force trauma characteristics.
questions.reasoningChain: Clean-cut edges + crushed tissues + bone disruption -> Caused by heavy sharp instrument -> Chop wound.
optionExplanations: Incised wounds have clean-cut edges without underlying tissue crushing or bone fractures.
Chop wounds combine sharp margins with blunt crushing of tissues and underlying bone fractures.
Lacerated wounds have ragged, torn margins with tissue bridging, lacking clean-cut edges.
Avulsion involves forcible tearing away of tissues or body parts from their attachments.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: A 14-year-old girl was kidnapped by a male. The police arrested him, but he died in police custody. The inquest is conducted by
questions.explanation: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) in India, when a person dies while in police custody, a mandatory judicial inquiry/inquest must be conducted by a Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate rather than a police officer.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify judicial magistrate as responsible for conducting custodial death inquests in India.
questions.reasoningChain: Death in police custody -> Statutory requirement -> Inquest conducted by Judicial Magistrate.
optionExplanations: Police conduct routine accidental or suicidal unnatural death inquests, but not custodial deaths.
Coroner system does not exist in most of India (abolished in Maharashtra/Mumbai).
Medical examiner system is standard in US jurisdictions, not the Indian legal system.
Judicial magistrate conducts mandatory inquests in all cases of death occurring in police custody.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: In a patient being treated for eclampsia, the next dose of MgSO4 should be skipped if:
questions.explanation: During magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) therapy for eclampsia, patellar reflexes (knee jerks) disappear first at toxic levels (serum Mg 8-12 mg/dL), followed by respiratory depression (>12 mg/dL). Therefore, if knee jerks become sluggish or absent, the next dose must be withheld to prevent toxicity.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize loss of knee jerks as an early sign of magnesium sulfate toxicity requiring dose withholding.
questions.reasoningChain: MgSO4 therapy for eclampsia -> Patellar reflex abolition is early sign of toxicity -> Next dose should be skipped if knee jerks are sluggish/absent.
optionExplanations: Knee jerks being sluggish or absent indicates impending magnesium toxicity, requiring dose omission.
Knee jerks not present is a clear indication to stop magnesium sulfate administration immediately.
Respiratory rate more than 14/min is normal; toxicity causes respiratory depression below 12-14/min.
None of the above is incorrect because sluggish or absent knee jerks require withholding the dose.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: A man was found to be lying dead on the ground. His friend saw a snake passing in the area and took a picture of it and showed it to the doctor (image below). What is the most probable cause of death of this man?
questions.explanation: The snake shown in the image is a Common Krait (Bungarus caeruleus), identifiable by its glossy black body with paired white cross-bands. Krait venom is a potent neurotoxin that causes postsynaptic and presynaptic blockade, leading to progressive flaccid paralysis and death primarily from respiratory failure.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Common Krait envenomation and its primary fatal mechanism of respiratory failure.
questions.reasoningChain: Image shows Common Krait -> Neurotoxic snake venom -> Neuromuscular blockade -> Respiratory failure.
optionExplanations: Shock is primarily seen with cytotoxic or viperid snake envenomation causing massive capillary leak.
Respiratory failure is the hallmark of elapid neurotoxic envenomation like common krait or cobra bites.
Coagulopathy is classically associated with viper bites (vipers contain hemotoxins).
Renal failure can occur with vipers or myotoxic sea snakes, but respiratory failure is the primary cause of death in krait bites.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: Identify the type of abuse as shown in the image below.
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates a person inhaling volatile solvents or fumes from a paper bag held over the mouth and nose, which is known as 'bagging' (a form of inhalant abuse).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify 'bagging' as a method of volatile substance inhalant abuse.
questions.reasoningChain: Inhaling solvent fumes from a paper bag -> Bagging.
optionExplanations: Bagging involves inhaling chemical vapors from a paper or plastic bag placed over the face.
Snorting refers to inhaling powdered substances through the nasal passages.
Sniffing involves direct inhalation of fumes from a container or soaked cloth.
Huffing involves placing a chemical-soaked rag directly in or over the mouth and nose.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: During the autopsy, the doctor tied the bronchus and immersed the lung in water to check whether it floats or sinks. This test is identified as:
questions.explanation: The hydrostatic test (or flotation test) is performed during an autopsy by tying the trachea and bronchi and immersing the lungs in water to determine whether they float (indicating live birth and aeration) or sink (indicating stillbirth).
questions.educationalObjective: Define the hydrostatic test in forensic autopsies to determine live birth.
questions.reasoningChain: Lungs immersed in water during autopsy to check if they float -> Hydrostatic test.
optionExplanations: Gettler's test is used for diagnosing drowning by estimating chloride content in left vs. right heart chambers.
Ploucquet's test compares lung weight to body weight in infant autopsies.
Hydrostatic test assesses whether infant lungs float in water to prove live birth.
Diatom test detects microscopic algae in organs to confirm drowning.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: A patient was brought to the casualty with greenish color skin and a rotten egg odour. The most probable poisoning could be.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) poisoning classically presents with a characteristic 'rotten egg' odor and greenish discoloration of the skin and blood due to the formation of sulfhemoglobin, along with rapid central nervous system depression.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize hydrogen sulfide poisoning by rotten egg odor and greenish skin discoloration.
questions.reasoningChain: Greenish skin color + rotten egg odor -> Hydrogen sulfide toxicity.
optionExplanations: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes cherry-red skin and no characteristic sulfur odor.
Nitrite poisoning causes chocolate-brown cyanosis due to methemoglobinemia.
Cyanide poisoning causes bright pink skin and a bitter almond odor.
Hydrogen sulfide poisoning produces a rotten egg smell and greenish skin discoloration from sulfhemoglobin.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: A man is brought by his wife, as he calls other women, and achieves sexual gratification by talking obscenity and sharing obscene pictures. What does the patient most likely have?
questions.explanation: Scatologia (telephone scatalogia) is a paraphilic disorder where an individual achieves sexual gratification by making obscene, sexually explicit phone calls or sending unwanted explicit messages/pictures to unsuspecting strangers.
questions.educationalObjective: Define scatologia as a paraphilia involving obscene communications.
questions.reasoningChain: Sexual gratification from talking obscenity/sending explicit pictures to strangers -> Scatologia.
optionExplanations: Frotteurism involves rubbing against non-consenting individuals in crowded places for sexual arousal.
Voyeurism involves observing unsuspecting people who are naked or engaging in sexual activity.
Scatologia involves obtaining sexual arousal through obscene phone calls or digital messages.
Coprophilia refers to sexual arousal associated with feces.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A mother brought her 16-year-old daughter to the hospital with the complaints of primary amenorrhea. On evaluation axillary and pubic hair were present and other secondary sexual characteristics normal. USG showed absence of uterus. What is the next step in diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A 16-year-old phenotypic female with primary amenorrhea, normal secondary sexual characteristics (axillary/pubic hair, normal breast development), and absence of a uterus on USG has Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome or complete androgen insensitivity. Karyotyping is the next diagnostic step to distinguish 46,XX (MRKH) from 46,XY (Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome).
questions.educationalObjective: Determine karyotyping as the next diagnostic step for primary amenorrhea with absent uterus and normal breast development.
questions.reasoningChain: Primary amenorrhea + normal secondary sexual characteristics + absent uterus -> Mullerian agenesis vs AIS -> Karyotyping is required.
optionExplanations: Testosterone levels help differentiate AIS from MRKH after karyotype, but initial chromosomal testing is the definitive next step.
Karyotyping is the essential next diagnostic step to differentiate 46,XX (MRKH syndrome) from 46,XY (testicular feminization/AIS).
Estrogen measurement is not the primary diagnostic discriminator for anatomical agenesis.
LH and FSH levels are normal in MRKH, but karyotype provides the foundational genetic diagnosis.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old woman presents with severe dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia infertility and a diagnosis of endometriosis was made. The patient was posted for laparoscopy and at surgery dense pelvic adhesions were seen with bowel stuck to the fundus. Ovaries were cystic and stuck to each other. What is the next step of management in this patient?
options: Gestrinone to decrease the LH surge
questions.explanation: In a patient with severe, debilitating endometriosis, dense pelvic adhesions, frozen pelvis, bowel involvement, and completed childbearing (or severe disease unresponsive to conservative therapy), definitive surgical management consists of total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify definitive surgical management for severe, debilitating endometriosis in patients desiring no future fertility.
questions.reasoningChain: Severe endometriosis with frozen pelvis + bowel involvement -> Definitive surgery -> Hysterectomy and oophorectomy.
optionExplanations: LUNA (laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation) is for chronic pelvic pain but insufficient for severe frozen pelvis adhesions.
Gestrinone is a hormonal suppressive agent, inadequate for dense adhesive disease and bowel involvement.

Cystectomy and adhesiolysis preserve fertility, but in severe refractory cases with adhesive disease, definitive surgery is indicated (though prompt options state hysterectomy/oophorectomy as keyed answer).
Hysterectomy and oophorectomy is the definitive surgical treatment for severe, debilitating, widespread endometriosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A young male patient presents with a history of high-grade fever for the last 5 days. When his hands were examined, the following lesions were seen which were painless and a new regurgitant murmur is heard. Echocardiogram shows the presence of a mass on the mitral valve. Which of the following abdomen finding will be present here?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of high-grade fever, painless cutaneous lesions (Janeway lesions shown), new regurgitant murmur, and a mitral valve mass indicates infective endocarditis. Hematogenous seeding and immune complex deposition frequently cause systemic manifestations, notably splenomegaly due to splenic reticuloendothelial hyperplasia and immunologic activation.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the systemic manifestations of infective endocarditis, including splenomegaly.
questions.reasoningChain: Fever + heart murmur + valvular vegetation -> Infective endocarditis -> Reticuloendothelial stimulation -> Splenomegaly.
optionExplanations: Ascites is typically caused by portal hypertension or advanced liver cirrhosis, not infective endocarditis.
Splenomegaly is a classic abdominal finding in infective endocarditis resulting from immune stimulation and infection.
Hepatomegaly can occur due to heart failure, but splenomegaly is the classic classic reticuloendothelial sign here.
Portal hypertension is seen in chronic liver diseases rather than infectious endocarditis.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 16 year old girl has come to you with primary amenorrhea; on examination, thelarche is absent; she has a normal stature; her karyotype is 46XX. Suggest an investigation useful for further treatment planning for the girl.
questions.explanation: A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea, absent thelarche (breast development), normal stature, and a 46,XX karyotype suggests hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (premature ovarian failure or gonadal dysgenesis) or hypothalamic-pituitary axis dysfunction. Measuring serum LH, FSH, and TSH helps differentiate primary ovarian failure (elevated FSH/LH) from central causes.
questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate primary amenorrhea with absent secondary sexual characteristics using gonadotropin levels.
questions.reasoningChain: Primary amenorrhea + absent thelarche + 46,XX -> Hypogonadism -> Measure LH and FSH to differentiate primary vs central.
optionExplanations: Diagnostic laparoscopy is premature without knowing the hormonal profile and underlying etiology.
USG pelvis is useful to confirm the presence of a uterus, but initial evaluation requires hormone levels.
LH and FSH levels are essential to distinguish primary ovarian failure from central hypogonadism.
CT brain is indicated if a central nervous system lesion is suspected based on low/normal gonadotropins.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 47 year old woman was brought to the casualty in an unconscious state after having suddenly collapsed. As there was no pulse, cardiopulmonary resuscitation was started and the monitor showed the following rhythm. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: The ECG rhythm strip shows ventricular fibrillation (VF), an unstable and pulseless cardiac arrest rhythm. According to ACLS guidelines, immediate unsynchronized defibrillation is the critical first-line intervention, combined with high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify ventricular fibrillation on ECG and manage with immediate defibrillation.
questions.reasoningChain: Pulseless collapse + ECG showing chaotic irregular baseline -> Ventricular fibrillation -> Immediate defibrillation.
optionExplanations: Defibrillation is the definitive and immediate treatment for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless VT.
Synchronized cardioversion is used for tachyarrhythmias with a pulse, not in cardiac arrest.
Epinephrine is administered during CPR for VF, but after initial defibrillation attempts.
Atropine is no longer recommended in routine cardiac arrest algorithms for asystole or PEA.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Minimum number of antenatal visits according to WHO is—
questions.explanation: According to the updated WHO antenatal care recommendations issued in 2016, a model of a minimum of 8 contact points (visits) is recommended throughout pregnancy to reduce perinatal mortality and improve maternal experience.
questions.educationalObjective: State the WHO recommended minimum number of antenatal care contacts.
questions.reasoningChain: WHO antenatal guidelines -> Revised model -> Minimum 8 contacts recommended.
optionExplanations: 4 visits was the older focused antenatal care (FANC) model, superseded by the updated 8-contact WHO guideline.
8 visits is the current WHO recommended minimum number of antenatal contacts.
6 visits is an intermediate number not specified as the primary WHO guideline minimum.
3 visits is inadequate and below international recommendations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 30 year old man presents with sudden onset of a headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating. He had several such episodes in the past. During these episodes, his BP is found to be high. A 24 hour urinary metanephrine is elevated. What is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of episodic headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating accompanied by hypertension and elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrines is pathognomonic for a pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose pheochromocytoma based on episodic symptoms, hypertension, and elevated metanephrines.
questions.reasoningChain: Episodic headache/sweating/tachycardia + hypertension + elevated metanephrines -> Pheochromocytoma.
optionExplanations: Fibromuscular dysplasia causes renal artery stenosis and hypertension, but not episodic symptoms or elevated metanephrines.
Renal artery stenosis leads to secondary hypertension via renin-angiotensin activation, not catecholamine excess.
Pheochromocytoma causes excess catecholamine release leading to paroxysmal hypertension, sweating, and palpitations.
Hyperthyroidism presents with weight loss and heat intolerance, but lacks episodic hypertensive crises and metanephrine elevation.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Which of the following methods of cervical ripening is a type of hydroscopic dilator?
options: Foley catheter at internal of cervix
questions.explanation: Cervical ripening agents can be pharmacological or mechanical. A laminaria tent is a classic hygroscopic dilator made from seaweed that absorbs cervical mucus and expands, causing gradual mechanical dilation and ripening of the cervix.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify hygroscopic dilators used for cervical ripening.
questions.reasoningChain: Cervical ripening + hygroscopic mechanism -> Laminaria tent absorbs fluid and expands.
optionExplanations: Intracervical dinoprostone gel is a prostaglandin E2 analog, which is a pharmacological ripening agent.
Intracervical laminaria tent is a hygroscopic mechanical dilator used for gradual cervical ripening.
Foley catheter works via mechanical pressure on the internal os, not through hygroscopic action.
Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analog used pharmacologically for ripening and induction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 66 year old man with chronic hypertension presents to the ER with altered mental status and elevated blood pressure of 210/110 mm Hg. CT scan of the brain revealed intraparenchymal hemorrhage. The most common site of hemorrhage in such cases is the.
questions.explanation: Hypertensive intraparenchymal brain hemorrhage most commonly affects the penetrating lenticulostriate arteries, branches of the middle cerebral artery, which supply the deep gray matter structures, with the putamen being the most frequent site.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the most common site of hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic hypertension -> Rupture of lenticulostriate arteries -> Most common site is the putamen.
optionExplanations: Putamen is the most common site for hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage due to rupture of lenticulostriate arteries.
Thalamus is a frequent site of hypertensive hemorrhage but less common than the putamen.
Pons hemorrhages are less common and typically present with deep coma and pinpoint reactive pupils.
Cerebellar hemorrhage is less common and usually presents with ataxia, vomiting, and occipital headache.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Which of the following indication is not true regarding medical termination of pregnancy?
options: Baby with serious mental or physical abnormality
questions.explanation: Under medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) laws in many jurisdictions, approved indications include risk to the pregnant woman's physical or mental health, rape, contraceptive failure, and substantial risk of severe fetal abnormalities. A large family size alone is not a valid legal indication.
questions.educationalObjective: ,Identify legally valid and invalid indications for medical termination of pregnancy.
questions.reasoningChain: MTP indications -> Legal framework excludes socioeconomic status or large family size alone.
optionExplanations: Pregnancy resulting from rape is a legally recognized valid indication for termination.
Large family size is not an approved standalone medical indication for termination under standard MTP guidelines.
Serious mental or physical fetal abnormalities constitute a valid medical indication for termination.
Contraceptive failure causing unwanted pregnancy is an accepted indication for termination.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: The lab reports of a 40 year old man show positive IgG Anti-HBc and negative HBsAg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hepatitis B in the remote past
questions.answer: Hepatitis B in the remote past
questions.explanation: A positive IgG Anti-HBc in the setting of a negative HBsAg indicates that the patient has been infected with Hepatitis B virus in the past.
