Since HBsAg is negative, active infection is absent, and positive total/IgG anti-HBc points toward past resolved infection rather than isolated immunization.
questions.educationalObjective: Interpret hepatitis B serology with positive IgG anti-HBc and negative HBsAg.
questions.reasoningChain: HBsAg negative + IgG anti-HBc positive -> Past resolved Hepatitis B infection.
optionExplanations: Recovering from acute hepatitis B typically shows both IgM anti-HBc and disappearing HBsAg.
Hepatitis B in the remote past is characterized by negative HBsAg, positive IgG anti-HBc, and positive anti-HBs.
Immunization with HBsAg results in isolated positive anti-HBs with negative anti-HBc.
Both B & C is incorrect because vaccination does not produce anti-HBc antibodies.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 23 year old G3 P1L1 A1 at 37 weeks of gestation with a previous history of emergency caesarean section and a dilatation and curettage presents to the ER with labor pains. During abdominal examination it was difficult to palpate fetal parts. Per vaginal examination revealed a 5 cm dilated cervix and her vitals were: BP-80/60 mm of Hg, RR – 20/min, Hr-106/min, SpO2 – 97% under room air. CTG showed a non-reassuring variable fetal heart rate pattern. The most likely diagnosis is—
questions.explanation: A patient with previous cesarean section presenting with labor pains, difficult-to-palpate fetal parts, vaginal bleeding, and maternal shock (hypotension, tachycardia) suggests uterine rupture. However, the exact prompt details align closely with classic signs of uterine rupture or placental abruption; review note highlights classic overlap, but historical key points to placental abruption or rupture.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation and risk factors of uterine rupture in scarred uteri.
questions.reasoningChain: Prior scar + sudden labor pain + hemodynamic instability + non-reassuring FHR -> Uterine rupture.
optionExplanations: Amniotic fluid embolization presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse and coagulopathy, less localized to prior scars.
Placental abruption presents with painful vaginal bleeding and uterine hypertonus.
Uterine rupture is strongly suspected given prior cesarean section, shock, and difficult fetal palpation.
Placenta praevia typically presents with painless bleeding, unlike this painful presentation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 52 year old woman presented with deformity of the hand as shown below. There is decreased motion in the small joints and loss of wrinkle lines on the facial skin. Her chest radiograph showed prominent bilateral lower lobe infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates sclerodactyly with skin tightening and flexion contractures of the hands. Combined with facial skin changes (loss of wrinkles) and pulmonary involvement (lower lobe infiltrates/fibrosis), this represents systemic sclerosis (scleroderma).
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose systemic sclerosis based on sclerodactyly, skin tightening, and pulmonary fibrosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Hand deformity + skin tightening + pulmonary infiltrates -> Scleroderma.
optionExplanations: Rheumatoid arthritis causes symmetrical joint deformities like ulnar deviation, not sclerodactyly and lung fibrosis.
Scleroderma presents with skin thickening, sclerodactyly, and interstitial lung disease.
Systemic lupus erythematosus features malar rash and arthritis, lacking prominent sclerodactyly.
Pneumonia is an acute infection, not a chronic multisystem autoimmune connective tissue disease.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: True regarding UTI in pregnancy
options: It is lower in people with sickle cell trait
The preferred antibiotic in pregnancy is amoxicillin
If ASB is not treated 75% of them will develop symptomatic infection
questions.answer: If ASB is not treated 75% of them will develop symptomatic infection
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy, if left untreated, carries a high risk (approximately 25-40% up to 40-75% historically cited) of progressing to acute pyelonephritis due to pregnancy-induced urinary stasis and ureteral dilation.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the complications of untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy.
questions.reasoningChain: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy -> Untreated -> High progression rate to symptomatic pyelonephritis.
optionExplanations: The prevalence of ASB in pregnancy is typically 2-10%, not 50%.
UTI prevalence is not lower in people with sickle cell trait.
Amoxicillin is not the preferred first-line antibiotic due to high resistance; nitrofurantoin or cephalexin are preferred.
Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria frequently progresses to symptomatic urinary tract infection/pyelonephritis.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Arjun (32/M) comes to your clinic for a regular health check-up with his wife (28/F). he weighs 65 kgs and his lifestyle is predominantly sedentary. His wife weighs 55kg, is pregnant and is in her second trimester. Her lifestyle is secondary too. According to the latest NIN RDA guideline, how many calories should Arjun and his wife respectively consume?
questions.explanation: According to the National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) RDA guidelines for Indians, a sedentary adult male requires approximately 2180 kcal/day, and a pregnant woman in her second trimester requires her baseline plus an additional 350 kcal/day, totaling around 2110 kcal/day.
questions.educationalObjective: Apply NIN RDA calorie guidelines for a sedentary man and a pregnant woman.
questions.reasoningChain: Sedentary adult male energy requirement (2180 kcal) and pregnant woman second trimester (2110 kcal).
optionExplanations: Incorrect calorie estimates not matching NIN RDA values.
Incorrect matching of male and pregnant female caloric requirements.
2180 kcal for adult sedentary male and 2110 kcal for second-trimester pregnant female according to NIN guidelines.
Overestimated caloric requirements for standard sedentary Indian reference weights.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 60 year old woman presents weakness in right arm for 6 hours duration. The weakness gradually became lesser and resolves. She is a known case of diabetes and hypertension and is obese. Which of the following is the probable diagnosis of this case?
questions.explanation: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is defined as a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute infarction, with symptoms typically resolving completely within 24 hours.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize transient ischemic attack by temporary neurological deficits resolving fully.
questions.reasoningChain: Arm weakness for 6 hours followed by complete resolution -> Transient ischemic attack.
optionExplanations: Compressive neuropathy causes persistent localized nerve dysfunction rather than sudden transient central deficits.
Transient ischaemic attack presents with temporary neurological deficits resolving within 24 hours.
Ischaemic stroke causes permanent neurological deficits seen on neuroimaging.
Diabetic neuropathy presents as chronic symmetrical distal sensory loss or pain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which clinical examination is being done in the picture?
questions.explanation: The clinical examination maneuver shown demonstrates the elicitation of a fluid thrill (or fluid wave test), used to detect moderate to large volumes of ascites by feeling propagated fluid waves across the abdomen.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the fluid thrill examination maneuver for ascites.
questions.reasoningChain: Tapping flank while stabilizing midline -> Fluid wave propagation -> Fluid thrill test for ascites.
optionExplanations: Shifting dullness involves percussing changes in resonance across the abdomen in different positions.
Ascites is the clinical sign being tested for, whereas the specific maneuver is the fluid thrill.
Puddle sign is used for detecting minimal quantities of ascites with the patient on hands and knees.
Fluid thrill is the correct physical examination technique depicted for detecting peritoneal fluid.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old woman comes with chronic vulval itching and pain. On examination, there is a vulval lesion suspicious of vulval cancer. Which of the following lymph node/s should be considered for sentinel node biopsy to look for the metastatic spread?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage of the vulva primarily flows to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, which serve as the primary sentinel lymph nodes for staging and assessing metastasis in vulvar malignancies.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the primary lymph node drainage site for vulvar cancer.
questions.reasoningChain: Vulvar lesion suspicious for cancer -> Lymphatic drainage -> Superficial inguinal lymph nodes.
optionExplanations: Pelvic lymph nodes are secondary drainage sites involved later in advanced disease.
Cloquet node (node of Cloquet) is a deep inguinal/femoral node, not the primary sentinel site.
Superficial inguinal lymph nodes are the primary sentinel nodes for metastatic spread of vulvar cancer.
Deep inguinal lymph nodes receive drainage secondarily from superficial nodes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 65 year old male patient presented with chest pain, exertional dyspnea and syncope. He was diagnosed as a case of aortic stenosis and his chest x-ray was taken which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In aortic stenosis, the high-velocity jetting of blood through the narrowed aortic valve causes turbulent flow that impinges on the wall of the ascending aorta, resulting in localized post-stenotic dilatation of the aorta visible on chest radiographs.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize post-stenotic dilatation of the aorta in aortic stenosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Aortic stenosis -> High-velocity jet -> Vessel wall stress -> Post-stenotic dilatation of aorta.
optionExplanations: Dilated aortic root refers to generalized aortic root enlargement, often seen in connective tissue disorders.
Widening of aortic knob is typically seen in systemic hypertension or aortic aneurysm.
Widening of vascular pedicle is seen in superior vena cava obstruction or mediastinal hemorrhage.
Post-stenotic dilatation of aorta is the classic radiographic finding associated with valvular aortic stenosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 53 year old patient as brought to the emergency room with altered sensorium and rapid shallow breathing. His abdomen is distended with palpable hepatomegaly and splenomegaly and sclerae are icteric. The other examination findings are given below. Laboratory tests show that the AST: ALT ratio is 3:1. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s presentation?
questions.explanation: An AST to ALT ratio greater than 2:1 (often 3:1 in classic severe cases) combined with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and alcoholic history strongly points toward alcoholic liver disease as the etiology of hepatic decompensation.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose alcoholic liver disease based on AST:ALT ratio > 2:1 and clinical findings.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic alcohol use + AST:ALT > 2:1 + jaundice + hepatosplenomegaly -> Alcoholic liver disease.
optionExplanations: Alcoholic liver disease classically presents with an AST to ALT ratio greater than 2:1.
Acute viral hepatitis typically features an ALT higher than AST or an AST:ALT ratio less than 1.
Autoimmune hepatitis usually has an ALT predominance rather than elevated AST:ALT > 2:1.
Acetaminophen poisoning causes severe acute centrilobular hepatic necrosis with massive transaminase elevations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 30 year old woman presents to the OPD with palpitation, weight loss. On examination of her legs the following lesion was found which on applying pressure, the indentation does not persist on release. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. What is the probable cause for the edema?
questions.explanation: Pitting edema (indentation that persists temporarily) accompanied by hypoalbuminemia, heavy proteinuria, and hyperlipidemia in a patient with glomerulopathy suggests nephrotic syndrome as the underlying cause.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify nephrotic syndrome as a cause of pitting pedal edema.
questions.reasoningChain: Heavy proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia -> Decreased oncotic pressure -> Pitting edema in nephrotic syndrome.
optionExplanations: Myxedema causes non-pitting edema due to accumulation of mucopolysaccharides in the dermis.
Nephrotic syndrome leads to hypoalbuminemia and generalized pitting edema.
Chronic lymphangitis causes non-pitting lymphedema, unlike nephrotic pitting edema.
Heart failure causes pitting edema due to increased hydrostatic pressure, but nephrotic syndrome is specified by massive proteinuria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 50 year old man presents with recurrent episodes of chest pain which is seen only on exertion or exercise and lasts 2-5 minutes. He was assessed and was diagnosed with a case of stable angina however his BP was consistently elevated. What is the most appropriate antihypertensive for this patient?
questions.explanation: In stable angina accompanied by hypertension, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers like amlodipine are excellent antihypertensive agents because they reduce peripheral vascular resistance and myocardial oxygen demand without worsening coronary perfusion.
questions.educationalObjective: Select appropriate antihypertensive medication for stable angina.
questions.reasoningChain: Stable angina + hypertension -> Dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine) lowers BP and myocardial work.
optionExplanations: Atenolol is a beta-blocker; while useful for angina, amlodipine is a direct vasodilator frequently chosen for blood pressure control.
Thiazides are standard antihypertensives but do not treat coronary vasospasm or angina directly as effectively as CCBs.
Enalapril (ACE inhibitor) is protective in vascular disease, but calcium channel blockers are potent antianginals.
Amlodipine effectively lowers blood pressure and relieves angina by inducing smooth muscle relaxation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 46 year old chronic alcoholic male presents to the OPD with fever, headache, shortness of breath, chest pain, and productive cough for the last two days. On examination, there was bronchial breathing on the right side, increased vocal fremitus, increased vocal resonance, and a dull note on percussion. The patient’s plain radiograph is shown below. Which is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: The chest radiograph shows lobar consolidation with bulging fissures, a classic appearance known as the 'bulge sign' associated with Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia, especially common in chronic alcoholics and debilitated patients.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Klebsiella pneumoniae lobar pneumonia with bulging fissures on chest X-ray.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic alcoholic + upper lobe consolidation with bulging fissure -> Klebsiella pneumoniae.
optionExplanations: Streptococcus pneumoniae typically causes lobar pneumonia without bulging fissures.
Klebsiella pneumoniae classically causes severe lobar pneumonia with bulging fissures in alcoholics.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa typically causes nosocomial bronchopneumonia in immunocompromised patients.
Haemophilus influenzae causes bronchopneumonia, frequently in patients with underlying chronic lung disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: The device seen in the following image is?
questions.explanation: The chest radiograph clearly demonstrates a radiopaque pulse generator device in the right pectoral region with transvenous leads extending into the right-sided cardiac chambers, identifying it as a cardiac pacemaker.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify a cardiac pacemaker on a chest radiograph.
questions.reasoningChain: Pectoral radiopaque device + leads in cardiac silhouette -> Cardiac pacemaker.
optionExplanations: Cardiac pacemaker is correctly identified by the subcutaneous generator and leads in the heart.
Chemo port device has a small circular septum and catheter terminating in the superior vena cava.
Travel tract for accessory is an incorrect distractor term.
Chest x-ray artefact is incorrect as the device has distinct anatomical pacing leads and housing.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 19 year old woman with no comorbidities presented with numbness and paraesthesia of the fingers along with the characteristic finding as shown in the image below. She has no other illnesses and she says these episodes occur when she is under excess stress or during cold climates. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Episodic pallor, cyanosis, and erythema of the fingers triggered by cold exposure or emotional stress in a young patient without underlying connective tissue disease defines primary Raynaud's phenomenon.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose primary Raynaud's phenomenon based on episodic vasospasm triggers.
questions.reasoningChain: Young female + cold/stress triggers + digital color changes + no comorbidities -> Primary Raynaud's.
optionExplanations: Primary Raynaud’s phenomenon presents with episodic digital vasospasm without an underlying autoimmune disease.
Secondary Raynaud’s phenomenon occurs secondary to connective tissue disorders like scleroderma or lupus.
Cold sores are herpes labialis viral lesions, unrelated to digital vasospasm.
Scleredema causes indurated skin swelling, not episodic digital vasospastic color changes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: The flow – volume curve of a patient after spirometry is given below. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is--.
questions.explanation: The flow-volume loop demonstrates expiratory air trapping, scooped-out expiratory limb, and decreased peak expiratory flow, which are the hallmark spirometric features of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize COPD on a flow-volume loop.
questions.reasoningChain: Scooped-out expiratory curve + air trapping -> Obstructive ventilatory defect (COPD).
optionExplanations: Asbestosis causes a restrictive ventilatory defect with normal or increased expiratory flows.
COPD characteristically shows an obstructive flow-volume loop with scooped-out expiration.
Myasthenia gravis causes a neuromuscular weakness pattern, not typical fixed airway obstruction.
Vocal cord paralysis typically shows variable upper airway obstruction with blunting of inspiratory or expiratory loops.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: An AIDS-positive patient came with a history of fever, vomiting, and meningismus. Which of the following tests help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis?
options: Blood lateral flow assay for cryptococcal antigen
questions.answer: Blood lateral flow assay for cryptococcal antigen
questions.explanation: In HIV-positive patients presenting with meningitis symptoms, a lateral flow assay (LFA) for cryptococcal antigen in blood or CSF provides a rapid, highly sensitive, and specific point-of-care diagnosis for cryptococcal infection.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the rapid diagnostic test for cryptococcal meningitis.
questions.reasoningChain: AIDS patient with meningitis symptoms -> Rapid diagnosis -> Cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay.
optionExplanations: India ink preparation of CSF is useful for visualization but less sensitive than antigen tests.
Blood culture takes days to grow organisms and is not a rapid diagnostic test.
CSF analysis is necessary, but the specific rapid test is the cryptococcal antigen assay.
Blood lateral flow assay for cryptococcal antigen provides rapid and accurate detection of cryptococcal infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A postoperative cardiac surgical patient developed sudden hypotension, raised central venous pressure, pulsus paradoxus at the 4th post operative hour. The most probable diagnosis is.
questions.explanation: Postoperative cardiac surgical patients presenting with Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) and pulsus paradoxus are experiencing acute cardiac tamponade due to pericardial blood accumulation.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cardiac tamponade following cardiac surgery.
questions.reasoningChain: Post-cardiac surgery + hypotension + raised JVP + pulsus paradoxus -> Cardiac tamponade.
optionExplanations: Ventricular dysfunction causes heart failure signs without classical pulsus paradoxus and tamponade physiology.
Cardiac tamponade is characterized by Beck's triad and pulsus paradoxus following cardiac surgery.
CHF presents with gradual fluid overload, not acute postoperative hemodynamic collapse.
Excessive mediastinal effusion does not typically cause acute tamponade unless compressing the heart chambers.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: The egg shown below belongs to
questions.explanation: The microscopic image displays a barrel-shaped or football-shaped egg with characteristic bipolar mucous plugs at both ends, which is pathognomonic for Trichuris trichiura (whipworm).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the egg of Trichuris trichiura (whipworm).
questions.reasoningChain: Barrel-shaped egg + bipolar plugs -> Trichuris trichiura (whipworm).
optionExplanations: Hookworm eggs are oval with a clear shell containing a segmented embryo, lacking bipolar plugs.
Whipworm eggs are barrel-shaped with characteristic clear polar plugs at both ends.
Pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis) eggs are asymmetrical and flattened on one side.
Roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides) eggs are round to oval with a thick mammillated albuminous coat.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A patient with breast carcinoma presents with swelling of ankle for the past 3 monts. Urine examination shows heavy proteinuria and haematuria. Renal biopsy is likely to reveal.
questions.explanation: Malignancies, particularly solid tumors such as breast and lung carcinoma, are frequently associated with secondary membranous glomerulonephritis presenting with nephrotic syndrome.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify membranous glomerulonephritis as a paraneoplastic manifestation of solid tumors.
questions.reasoningChain: Breast carcinoma + heavy proteinuria -> Paraneoplastic glomerulopathy -> Membranous glomerulonephritis.
optionExplanations: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis can be secondary to hyperfiltration or HIV, but solid tumors classically link to membranous.
Membranous glomerulonephritis is the classic glomerulopathy associated with underlying solid tumors like breast cancer.
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is more commonly associated with chronic infections like hepatitis C.
Minimal change disease is classically associated with Hodgkin lymphoma, not solid breast carcinoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 28 year old male was brought to the emergency room with a history of RTA. GCS progressively declines over hours and axial T2 MRI below shows multiple small hypointense lesion at corticomedullary junction and basal ganglia, what is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Axial T2-weighted or GRE/SWI MRI showing multiple small hypointense hemorrhagic lesions at the grey-white matter junction and corpus callosum following road traffic accidents is diagnostic of diffuse axonal injury (DAI).
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose diffuse axonal injury based on characteristic MRI findings after trauma.
questions.reasoningChain: Road traffic accident + declining GCS + microhemorrhages at corticomedullary junction -> Diffuse axonal injury.
optionExplanations: Diffuse axonal injury presents with characteristic microhemorrhages at the gray-white matter junction on MRI.
Subarachnoid hemorrhage shows blood within the subarachnoid spaces and sulci, not isolated junctional microhemorrhages.
Hypoxic cerebral injury typically causes diffuse bilateral cortical and basal ganglia edema/infarction.
Multiple hemorrhagic contusions are larger lesions typically located in the frontal and temporal poles.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Visual field testing of a patient revealed the following type of loss. Where is the likely site of lesion in optic pathway?
questions.explanation: The visual field defect shown is a complete homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, which is classically caused by a lesion involving the occipital cortex (visual cortex), often due to posterior cerebral artery ischemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Localize homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing to the occipital lobe.
questions.reasoningChain: Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing -> Retrochiasmal lesion -> Occipital lobe.
optionExplanations: Frontal visual field lesions do not cause congruous homonymous hemianopias.
Occipital lobe lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia often characterized by macular sparing.
Optic radiation lesions typically cause incomplete or incongruous homonymous hemianopias.
Optic chiasma lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia due to crossing nasal retinal fibers.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: A 33 year old male comes with complaints of dry cough, fever and shortness of breath for 2 days along with a loss of taste and smell. He is a social worker who has been travelling a lot. What would be the investigation of choice for this patient to confirm the diagnosis of COVID-19?
questions.explanation: Real-time Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) from nasopharyngeal swabs is the gold standard and investigation of choice for confirming the diagnosis of acute SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) infection.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify RT-PCR as the diagnostic test of choice for COVID-19.
questions.reasoningChain: Suspected COVID-19 infection -> Viral RNA detection -> RT-PCR.
optionExplanations: PCR is a general term, but RT-PCR is specifically required for RNA viruses like SARS-CoV-2.
ELISA detects antibodies or antigens, used for seroprevalence rather than acute molecular diagnosis.
Serology assesses past infection or immune response, not acute viral replication.
RT-PCR is the specific gold standard molecular investigation of choice for acute COVID-19 diagnosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: An unknown disease of suspected infectious origin has come up in your town. As a microbiologist, you collect the relevant samples and detect the etiological cause. Which of the following types of PCR would you do?
questions.explanation: Real-time PCR (quantitative PCR) allows for rapid, sensitive detection and quantification of nucleic acids in clinical microbiology, making it ideal for identifying unknown pathogens quickly during outbreaks.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify real-time PCR for rapid pathogen detection.
questions.reasoningChain: Suspected infectious disease outbreak -> Rapid detection and quantification -> Real-time PCR.
optionExplanations: Real-time PCR provides rapid, sensitive detection and quantification of microbial DNA/RNA.
Nested PCR is used to improve sensitivity and specificity but is time-consuming and prone to contamination.
Reverse transcriptase PCR is specifically for RNA targets, whereas real-time PCR is the general methodology for rapid quantification.
Multiplex PCR detects multiple targets simultaneously, but real-time PCR is preferred for rapid clinical diagnosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 55 year old patient presented with chronic projectile vomiting and eight loss. What is the expected metabolic abnormality to be seen here?
options: Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia
Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypernatremia
Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypercalcemia
Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic acidosis with hyponatremia
questions.answer: Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia
questions.explanation: Chronic vomiting leads to the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) and potassium, resulting in hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Volume depletion concurrently activates aldosterone, causing renal sodium retention and hyponatremia.
questions.educationalObjective: Predict metabolic abnormalities associated with chronic vomiting and gastric fluid loss.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic vomiting -> Loss of HCl and K+ -> Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis + volume depletion/hyponatremia.
optionExplanations: Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia is the classic biochemical profile of chronic gastric outlet obstruction with vomiting.
Hypernatremia would indicate free water deficit, whereas vomiting typically leads to volume depletion and hyponatremia/normonatremia.
Hypercalcemia is not a direct metabolic consequence of chronic vomiting.
Metabolic acidosis occurs with lower gastrointestinal fluid losses (diarrhea), whereas upper GI losses cause alkalosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: A 55 year old man comes with complaints of fever and increasing fatigue for the past week. On examination, he is febrile at 40 degree C, hypotensive, and has tachycardia. The blood smear of this patient is given below. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation: The peripheral blood smear shows multiple ring forms (trophozoites), 'banana-shaped' or crescentic gametocytes, and multiple infections per red blood cell, which are characteristic features of Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Plasmodium falciparum trophozoites and gametocytes on a blood smear.
questions.reasoningChain: Fever + severe fatigue + ring forms and crescentic gametocytes on blood smear -> Plasmodium falciparum.
optionExplanations: Plasmodium vivax shows enlarged RBCs with Schuffner's dots and amoeboid trophozoites.
Plasmodium falciparum is identified by multiple ring forms, applique forms, and crescentic gametocytes.
Plasmodium ovale shows oval RBCs with fimbriated edges.
Plasmodium malariae shows band-form trophozoites and 'rosette' schizonts.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A patient with inflammatory bowel disease presents with the following lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum is an inflammatory neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by painful, rapidly progressing ulcers with undermined violaceous borders, commonly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis).
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize pyoderma gangrenosum associated with inflammatory bowel disease.
questions.reasoningChain: Inflammatory bowel disease + painful ulcer with undermined violaceous border -> Pyoderma gangrenosum.
optionExplanations: Erythema nodosum presents as tender red nodules on shins, not deep necrotizing ulcers.
Pyoderma gangrenosum presents with painful purulent ulcers with violaceous borders, common in IBD.
Diabetic ulcers are typically painless neuropathic ulcers over pressure points, unlike inflammatory lesions.
Venous ulcers are shallow and painless ulcers located over the medial malleolus associated with venous insufficiency.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: What is the average incubation period of plasmodium falciparum?
questions.explanation: The average incubation period for Plasmodium falciparum malaria is approximately 9 to 14 days (commonly cited as 12 days), which is the shortest among the human malaria species.
questions.educationalObjective: State the average incubation period of Plasmodium falciparum.
questions.reasoningChain: Plasmodium falciparum infection -> Pre-erythrocytic cycle duration -> Average incubation period of 12 days.
optionExplanations: 12 days is the standard average incubation period for Plasmodium falciparum.
16 days is longer and closer to the incubation period of Plasmodium vivax.
30 days or longer is typical for Plasmodium malariae.
28 days is typical for certain strains of Plasmodium malariae.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: A 4 year old boy presents with complaints of fever and sore throat. On examination, he has extensive cervical swelling and a well-demarcated white-gray exudative substance adherent to his oropharynx and attempts to remove this pseudomembranous result in bleeding. The parents report that all his childhood vaccines were skipped due to religious beliefs. A throat swab under Albert’s staining is as below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a pseudomembranous pharyngitis that bleeds upon removal, combined with Albert's staining demonstrating metachromatic granules in Corynebacterium diphtheriae, confirms the diagnosis of diphtheria.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose diphtheria based on pseudomembrane and Albert's staining.
questions.reasoningChain: Unvaccinated child + bleeding oropharyngeal pseudomembrane + metachromatic granules on Albert's stain -> Diphtheria.
optionExplanations: Streptococcal pharyngitis features exudative tonsillitis without an adherent, bleeding grey pseudomembrane.
Diphtheria is confirmed by pseudomembrane formation and Corynebacterium diphtheriae identified via Albert's staining.
Tetanus presents with muscle rigidity and spasms, not oropharyngeal pseudomembranes.
Pertussis presents with paroxysmal cough and whoop, lacking pseudomembranous pharyngitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A patient who is a tour guide of Mount Everest presented with blisters on her hand as shown in the figure below. She has severe pain and on examination is erythematous and tender. Which of the following is not used in the management of this patient?
options: Apply heat to the area and case it as soon as possible
questions.answer: Apply heat to the area and case it as soon as possible
questions.explanation: In cold-induced injuries like chilblains or frostbite, rapid rewarming in warm water is essential. Applying direct high heat or massaging/casting frostbitten tissue is contraindicated because it increases tissue damage and necrosis.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify correct management principles for cold injuries and avoid harmful practices.
questions.reasoningChain: Cold injury with blisters -> Management includes supportive care/vasodilators -> Applying direct heat/casting is harmful.
optionExplanations: Oxygen therapy is used as supportive care in tissue hypoxia.
Applying direct high heat or casting frozen tissue is contraindicated as it worsens necrosis.
Pentoxifylline is a hemorrheologic agent used to improve microvascular blood flow in chilblains/frostbite.
NSAIDs are used for pain and inflammation management.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of cholera toxin?
options: Toxin causes increased guanyl cyclase activity
The toxin causes continued activation of adenylate cyclase
questions.answer: The toxin causes continued activation of adenylate cyclase
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin acts via an A-B subunit structure where the A subunit activates Gs protein, leading to the continuous and persistent activation of adenylate cyclase, resulting in high cAMP levels and massive watery diarrhea.
questions.educationalObjective: Explain the mechanism of action of cholera toxin.
questions.reasoningChain: Cholera toxin enters enterocyte -> Activates Gs protein -> Continued activation of adenylate cyclase -> Increased cAMP.
optionExplanations: Inhibiting elongation factor-2 is the mechanism of action of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.
Increased guanylyl cyclase activity is the mechanism of action of heat-stable enterotoxin of E. coli.
Continued activation of adenylate cyclase is the classic mechanism of cholera toxin.
Inhibiting the 60S ribosomal subunit is the mechanism of Shiga toxin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 68 year old male came to the physician with complaints of chronic back pain and easy fatigability and past history of multiple urinary tract infections in the last 3 months. His ESR is elevated, and x-ray of his skull is shown below. Which of the following investigations is useful for diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A patient with chronic back pain, recurrent infections, and 'punched-out' lytic bone lesions on skull radiography has multiple myeloma. Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) demonstrating an M-spike (monoclonal IgG) is the key diagnostic investigation.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose multiple myeloma using serum protein electrophoresis and skull radiography.
questions.reasoningChain: Lytic skull lesions + back pain + recurrent infections -> Multiple myeloma -> Confirmed by serum electrophoresis.
optionExplanations: MRI brain is not the primary test for multiple myeloma presenting with lytic bone lesions.
PET scan can assess bone disease but SPEP is the definitive diagnostic screening test for monoclonal proteins.
Head CT scan is inferior to serum electrophoresis and skeletal surveys for multiple myeloma diagnosis.
Serum electrophoresis demonstrates the monoclonal paraprotein (M-spike) characteristic of multiple myeloma.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: A 34 year old HIV-positive male presented with low-grade fever, cough, night sweats, and weight loss for the past 3 weeks. In view of TB investigations, the Mantoux test was negative, chest X-ray showed non-specific findings and an adequate amount of sputum could not be collected for slide examination. Which of the following is used to diagnose latent TB infection in this patient?
questions.explanation: In immunocompromised patients like those with HIV where tuberculin skin tests (Mantoux) can yield false negatives, Interferon-Gamma Release Assays (IGRAs) are the preferred test for diagnosing latent tuberculosis infection.
questions.educationalObjective: Select the appropriate test for latent tuberculosis in immunocompromised patients.
questions.reasoningChain: HIV-positive patient requiring latent TB screening -> T-cell mediated response test -> Interferon gamma release assay.
optionExplanations: T-SPOT-TB is a specific IGRA brand, but Interferon gamma release assay is the general diagnostic category.
TrueNat is a molecular test used for active TB detection, not latent TB infection.
Interferon gamma release assay is the preferred blood test for diagnosing latent tuberculosis infection.
Lymph node biopsy is invasive and used for active extrapulmonary TB diagnosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: While collecting a blood sample for investigations, you accidentally drop and spill a 5 ml tube of blood. Which among the following is the best solution to clean it?
questions.explanation: According to standard laboratory biosafety guidelines, blood spills and infectious biological fluid spills require disinfection with a 1:10 dilution of sodium hypochlorite (bleach) for effective decontamination.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the correct disinfectant dilution for blood spills in the laboratory.
questions.reasoningChain: Blood spill in laboratory -> Decontamination protocol -> 1:10 sodium hypochlorite solution.
optionExplanations: 1:10 sodium hypochlorite is the recommended concentration for decontaminating blood and body fluid spills.
Isopropyl alcohol is inadequate as a primary disinfectant for large proteinaceous blood spills.
Hydrogen peroxide is not the standard primary disinfectant recommended for blood spill cleanup.
1:100 sodium hypochlorite is too dilute for effective blood spill disinfection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following pneumoconiosis is associated with an increased incidence of tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Silicosis is a classic fibronodular pneumoconiosis caused by silica dust inhalation that significantly impairs macrophage function, thereby markedly increasing the patient's susceptibility to pulmonary tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis).
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the association between silicosis and increased incidence of tuberculosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Silica dust inhalation -> Macrophage impairment -> High susceptibility to tuberculosis.
optionExplanations: Asbestosis increases the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma, not tuberculosis.
Silicosis impairs alveolar macrophage function, predisposing patients to tuberculosis infection.
Coal worker’s pneumoconiosis causes progressive massive fibrosis but lacks the specific high TB association of silicosis.
Berylliosis causes chronic non-caseating granulomatous lung disease resembling sarcoidosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Identify the dermatophyte based on the macroconidia shown in the image below
questions.explanation: Epidermophyton species produce characteristic smooth, club-shaped, multiseptate macroconidia that are borne singly or in clusters directly on the hyphae, distinguishing them from Microsporum and Trichophyton.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Epidermophyton dermatophytes by their characteristic macroconidia.
questions.reasoningChain: Dermatophyte macroconidia morphology -> Club-shaped and smooth -> Epidermophyton.
optionExplanations: Trichophyton species typically have numerous microconidia and rare, smooth, thin-walled macroconidia.
Microsporum species produce rough, thick-walled echinulate macroconidia.
Epidermophyton produces smooth, club-shaped, multiseptate macroconidia in clusters.
None of the above is incorrect because Epidermophyton is clearly identified.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: A chronic asthmatic patient who is on inhaled steroids present with a history of burning sensation on eating hot or spicy food and the following findings are seen. What is the most possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of white pseudomembranous patches on the tongue that can be scraped off, occurring in a patient on inhaled corticosteroids, is characteristic of oral candidiasis (oral thrush).
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose oral candidiasis in patients using inhaled steroids.
questions.reasoningChain: Inhaled steroid use + white plaques on tongue -> Immunosuppression in oral cavity -> Candida infection.
optionExplanations: Candida infection presents with removable white plaques on an erythematous base, often triggered by inhaled steroids.
Burning mouth syndrome presents with oral pain without visible mucosal lesions.
Geographical tongue features smooth, red patches with depapillation surrounded by white borders.
Oral lichen planus shows lacy white striae (Wickham striae) on the buccal mucosa.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.prompt: Oral hairy leukoplakia is associated with which of the following infections?
questions.explanation: Oral hairy leukoplakia is a non-malignant white lesion on the lateral border of the tongue caused by reactivation of the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), typically occurring in immunocompromised individuals such as those with HIV.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the viral etiology of oral hairy leukoplakia.
questions.reasoningChain: Immunocompromised state + white lesion on tongue border -> Epstein-Barr virus reactivation -> Oral hairy leukoplakia.
optionExplanations: Cytomegalovirus causes retinitis and colitis in immunocompromised patients, not hairy leukoplakia.
Human papillomavirus causes oral papillomas and verruca vulgaris.
Herpes simplex 1 causes painful vesicular labial cold sores.
Epstein Barr virus is the etiologic agent responsible for oral hairy leukoplakia.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: A young male patient sustained a right tibial shaft fracture following a road traffic accident. The patient’s right leg was immobilized with a plaster cast. This patient now presents to the emergency with severe pain in the leg. On examination, the distal pulses are absent, on passive stretching the pain increases, and on opening the plaster, the right leg appears edematous and numerous blisters are seen. Considering the suspected diagnosis, what would be the most appropriate management in this case?
options: Opening of the plaster is sufficient
questions.explanation: Severe pain, absent distal pulses, pain on passive stretch, and tense swelling following fracture and cast immobilization indicate acute compartment syndrome, which is an orthopedic surgical emergency requiring immediate fasciotomy.
questions.educationalObjective: Manage acute compartment syndrome with emergency fasciotomy.
questions.reasoningChain: Fracture + severe pain out of proportion + pain on passive stretch -> Acute compartment syndrome -> Emergency fasciotomy.
optionExplanations: Fasciotomy is the definitive emergency surgical treatment required for acute compartment syndrome.
Elevation of the limb can worsen tissue perfusion in compartment syndrome and is contraindicated.
Opening the plaster is an initial step, but definitive treatment for established compartment syndrome is surgical fasciotomy.
Closed reduction addresses bone alignment, not elevated intracompartmental tissue pressure.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: A young girl had thigh swelling with discharging sinus from which a bony fragment came out. The parents were concerned about what it was and asked the doctor. What is the term used for it?
questions.explanation: In chronic osteomyelitis, necrotic, devitalized bone that gets separated from living bone is termed a sequestrum. The surrounding new bone formed by the periosteum is called the involucrum.
questions.educationalObjective: Define sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic bone infection -> Dead devitalized bone fragment -> Sequestrum.
optionExplanations: Sequestrum refers to the piece of dead, devitalized bone found in chronic osteomyelitis.
Involucrum is the layer of new bone formed surrounding the necrotic sequestrum.
Cloacae are openings in the involucrum through which pus and sequestra discharge.
Sinus tract is the epithelialized channel connecting the bone infection to the skin surface.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: With respect to tuberculosis of hip, which of the marked areas are affected commonly?
options: May be treated initially by antibiotics
questions.explanation: In tuberculosis of the hip joint, the disease frequently begins in the weight-bearing areas or the superior/superolateral articular surface of the femoral head or acetabulum (commonly marked as area 1 or weight-bearing zone).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the common anatomical site affected in hip tuberculosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Tuberculosis of the hip -> Joint involvement -> Most common initial site is the weight-bearing articular surface (1).
optionExplanations: Area 1 represents the weight-bearing superior acetabular/femoral articular surface, most commonly involved.
Area 2 corresponds to the femoral neck region, less common for primary joint TB.
Area 3 represents the lesser trochanter area, an uncommon primary site.
Antibiotic treatment alone is inadequate for established joint destruction; surgical debridement and ATT are required.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: A 30 year old female developed a tumor at the knee joint. Biopsy-image is given below and shows multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells. What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation: Histopathological examination showing numerous multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells uniformly distributed among mononuclear stromal cells is diagnostic of a giant cell tumor (GCT) of bone, typically occurring around the knee joint.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose giant cell tumor of bone based on multinucleated giant cells on histology.
questions.reasoningChain: Tumor near knee joint + multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells on histology -> Giant cell tumor.
optionExplanations: Osteosarcoma shows malignant osteoid production by atypical spindle cells, not benign giant cells.
Ewing’s sarcoma exhibits sheets of uniform small round blue cells.
Giant cell tumor is characterized histologically by abundant multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells.
Osteoblastoma shows woven bone trabeculae rimmed by osteoblasts within fibrovascular stroma.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: A patient who had a history of fracture of his right leg came for a follow-up appointment where his cast was removed for assessment. The doctor found that the area was deformable but not displaceable and thus he re-applied the cast. What stage of fracture healing is the patient likely to be in?
questions.explanation: During fracture healing, when the fracture site is deformable (springy stability) but not yet rigidly displaced or fully calcified, the patient is in the soft callus (cartilaginous callus) stage of bone repair.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the clinical characteristics of the soft callus stage in fracture healing.
questions.reasoningChain: Fracture healing stage -> Deformable but not displaceable -> Soft callus stage.
optionExplanations: Inflammation stage is characterized by acute pain, swelling, and hematoma formation without bridging stability.
Soft callus stage provides stability that is deformable and non-displaceable.
Hard callus stage provides rigid bony bridging and stability.
Remodeling stage restores the original bone architecture and medullary canal over months to years.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old pregnant woman develops back pain radiating to the posterolateral aspect of the leg after lifting a heavy suitcase from the ground. There is sensory loss over the anterolateral aspect of the leg, dorsum of the foot, and great toe. Medial Hamstring reflex is diminished. Other deep tendon reflexes are normal. MRI picture is shown below. The most probable diagnosis is—
questions.explanation: Lumbar disc herniation at the L4-L5 level typically compresses the exiting L5 nerve root, leading to pain radiating to the posterolateral leg, sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and great toe, and often foot drop.
questions.educationalObjective: Localize nerve root compression in L4-L5 disc prolapse.
questions.reasoningChain: Lifting heavy object + L5 dermatome sensory loss + foot drop/weakness -> L4-L5 disc prolapse.
optionExplanations: L5 fracture causes localized bone pain rather than classic radicular disc compression patterns.
L5-S1 disc prolapse compresses the S1 root, affecting the Achilles reflex and posterior calf/lateral foot.
L3-L4 disc prolapse affects the L4 root, causing anterior thigh pain and diminished knee jerk reflex.
L4-L5 disc prolapse compresses the L5 nerve root, causing anterolateral leg and great toe sensory/motor deficits.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: What is the x-ray finding seen in a patient with fluorosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic fluoride toxicity (fluorosis) leads to increased bone density and abnormal bone formation due to osteoblast stimulation, classically resulting in generalized osteosclerosis (marble bone appearance) on radiography.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify radiographic bone findings in fluorosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Excess fluoride exposure -> Increased bone matrix mineralization -> Osteosclerosis.
optionExplanations: Osteomalacia involves defective bone mineralization, opposite to the sclerotic changes of fluorosis.
Osteoporosis features decreased bone mass, whereas fluorosis increases bone density.
Osteosclerosis is the characteristic radiological finding in chronic skeletal fluorosis.
Osteopetrosis is a congenital genetic bone disorder, not caused by acquired fluoride toxicity.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: A mother with history of breech during her pregnancy brings her newborn baby to the OPD. On examination, the doctor notices asymmetric thigh folds in her child, with limited abduction of thigh and gets a click sound on doing so. A brace as shown in the picture is prescribed by the doctor. What can be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Asymmetric thigh folds, limited hip abduction, and a positive click (Ortolani/Barlow sign) in a newborn with breech history indicate developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), managed with a Pavlik harness brace.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose developmental dysplasia of the hip based on clinical exam and Pavlik harness usage.
questions.reasoningChain: Breech presentation + limited abduction + positive click + Pavlik harness -> Developmental dysplasia of hip.
optionExplanations: Congenital coxa vara features a decreased neck-shaft angle of the femur, causing a limp.
Congenital dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is characterized by asymmetric thigh folds, limited abduction, and click signs.
Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head seen in older children (4-8 years).
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis occurs in adolescent adolescents, presenting with a painful limp.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.prompt: A child is unable to carry supination and pronation movements but is able to flex his elbow, since his childhood. His x-ray was taken and is as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Congenital failure of segmentation of the proximal radius and ulna leads to proximal radioulnar synostosis, resulting in fixed pronation of the forearm and inability to perform supination since childhood.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose proximal radioulnar synostosis based on fixed forearm pronation.
questions.reasoningChain: Inability to supinate/pronate since childhood + fused proximal radius and ulna on X-ray -> Proximal radioulnar synostosis.
optionExplanations: Distal radioulnar synostosis affects the wrist joint area, which is less common and presents distally.
Supinator muscle defect is a muscular issue, whereas this is a congenital bony fusion.
Proximal radioulnar synostosis is characterized by congenital bony fusion of the upper radius and ulna.
Humero-radio-ulnar synostosis involves congenital fusion across the entire elbow joint.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 37 year old male who is chronic alcoholic abstained from alcohol. 3 days later, he as brought to the emergency with complaints of disorientation, tremors hallucinations, an hypertension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Delirium tremens is a severe form of alcohol withdrawal occurring typically 48 to 72 hours after cessation, characterized by profound autonomic hyperactivity (hypertension, tachycardia), disorientation, tremors, and visual hallucinations.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize delirium tremens in chronic alcohol withdrawal.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic alcoholic + cessation + symptoms after 3 days (disorientation, tremors, hypertension) -> Delirium tremens.
optionExplanations: Alcoholic hallucinosis presents with auditory hallucinations while maintaining a clear sensorium.
Korsakoff’s psychosis features chronic amnestic syndrome and confabulation due to thiamine deficiency.
Delirium tremens is the severe alcohol withdrawal syndrome characterized by autonomic instability and confusion.
Marchiafava-Bignami disease involves demyelination of the corpus callosum in chronic alcoholism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A patient is having loose stools around 20 per day and his urine frequency is reduced now. Which of the following laboratory values is seen in patient?
options: BUN: Cr >40:1, urine Na <40, FENa <1% urine osmolality >500
BUN: Cr >20:1, urine Na <20, FENa <1% urine osmolality >500
BUN: Cr >20:1, urine Na <20, FENa <1% urine osmolality >250
BUN: Cr >40:1, urine Na <20, FENa <1% urine osmolality >250
questions.answer: BUN: Cr >20:1, urine Na <20, FENa <1% urine osmolality >500
questions.explanation: Prerenal azotemia resulting from severe volume depletion (such as severe diarrhea) causes avid renal sodium and water reabsorption, reflected by a BUN to creatinine ratio > 20:1, low urine sodium (< 20 mEq/L), fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) < 1%, and concentrated urine osmolality > 500 mOsm/kg.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify laboratory findings of prerenal azotemia due to volume depletion.
questions.reasoningChain: Severe diarrhea and volume depletion -> Prerenal azotemia -> BUN:Cr > 20:1, Urine Na < 20, FENa < 1%, Osm > 500.
optionExplanations: Urine sodium < 40 is less specific than the classic < 20 cutoff for acute prerenal azotemia.
BUN:Cr > 20:1, urine Na < 20 mEq/L, FENa < 1%, and urine osmolality > 500 mOsm/kg are classic for prerenal azotemia.
Urine osmolality > 250 is too low; maximally concentrated prerenal urine typically exceeds 500 mOsm/kg.
Urine sodium < 20 with osmolality > 250 is incomplete compared to the maximally concentrated specific option.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 50 year old lady with hypertension is brought with shortness of breath and dyspnea on exertion for the past week. Physical examination reveals the presence of elevated jugular venous pressure and crepitations in the lungs along with palpable liver 3 cm below the costal margin. The image of her legs is given below what is the finding called?
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates firm digital pressure applied to the shin resulting in a persistent indentation, which defines pitting pedal edema, a classic clinical sign of elevated interstitial fluid pressure associated with congestive heart failure.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify pitting pedal edema on clinical examination.
questions.reasoningChain: Finger indentation on shin -> Pitting edema -> Sign of fluid overload in heart failure.
optionExplanations: Superficial venous thrombosis presents with a tender, palpable cord-like superficial vein.
Deep vein thrombosis causes unilateral swelling, pain, and erythema, not bilateral symmetric pitting edema.
Congestive cardiac failure is the underlying etiology causing the peripheral pitting edema shown.
Pitting pedal edema is the exact physical finding demonstrated by the finger indentation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 3 year old boy has presented with multiple episodes of hematemesis. On admission his vitals are stable, and splenomegaly is noted. The mother tells that at birth the boy had developed jaundice and an exchange transfusion procedure had been performed through the umbilicus after birth. The most likely cause of hematemesis is?
questions.explanation: A history of neonatal umbilical vein catheterization or exchange transfusion is a major risk factor for umbilical vein thrombophlebitis, leading subsequently to extrahepatic portal vein obstruction (portal vein thrombosis) and variceal bleeding in childhood.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify neonatal umbilical vein catheterization as a cause of portal vein thrombosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Neonatal umbilical line/exchange transfusion -> Endothelial injury -> Portal vein thrombosis -> Variceal bleeding.
optionExplanations: Portal vein thrombosis is classically linked to neonatal umbilical catheterization and presents with hematemesis.
Sinusoidal fibrosis is typically seen in chronic liver cirrhosis from viral or metabolic causes.
Hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome occurs due to toxic injury to sinusoidal endothelial cells.
Budd-Chiari syndrome involves hepatic venous outflow obstruction, not extrahepatic portal vein thrombosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: An 8 year old girl presents with abrupt onset of fever, oliguria, nausea, smoky urine, and puffy eyes. The parents say that she had lesions on her face similar to the ones shown in the image below, 2 weeks ago which are now resolving. Which of the following findings will be present in this patient?
questions.explanation: The facial lesions shown are impetigo (honey-colored crusts), caused by streptococcal or staphylococcal skin infection. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) follows 1-3 weeks later, presenting with hematuria, smoky urine, hypertension, and periorbital edema.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis following impetigo.
questions.reasoningChain: Impetigo skin infection -> Group A strep -> Immune-complex glomerulonephritis -> Hematuria and smoky urine.
optionExplanations: Nephrotic range proteinuria is characteristic of minimal change disease or membranous nephropathy, not PSGN.
RBCs in urine (hematuria) and red cell casts are hallmark urinary findings in acute glomerulonephritis.
Derangement of liver enzymes is seen in hepatic pathologies, not post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Neurological symptoms are absent unless severe hypertensive encephalopathy develops as a complication.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A patient presented with symptoms of fatigue and a blood smear showed macrocytic anemia. Her methyl malonate levels were normal, however, homocystinuria was seen. Serum B12 values are normal. What is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Macrocytic anemia with elevated homocysteine levels but normal methylmalonic acid and normal vitamin B12 levels points directly to folate deficiency, as vitamin B12 is required for normal homocysteine metabolism via a separate pathway involving methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate folate deficiency from B12 deficiency using homocysteine and methylmalonate levels.
questions.reasoningChain: Macrocytic anemia + normal methylmalonate + elevated homocysteine + normal B12 -> Isolated folate deficiency -> Folate therapy.
optionExplanations: Iron supplements treat microcytic hypochromic anemia, not macrocytic anemia.
Treatment with both folate and B12 is unnecessary since serum B12 is normal.
Folate and vitamin B1 is incorrect because thiamine treats Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
Folate therapy is the appropriate management for isolated folate deficiency causing macrocytic anemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 25 year old male developed progressive loss of vision in both the eyes who has been on low dose oral steroid therapy for last 10 years. What is the most likely reason or his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy is a well-established and potent risk factor for the development of posterior subcapsular cataracts, leading to progressive bilateral loss of vision.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify posterior subcapsular cataract as a complication of long-term steroid use.
questions.reasoningChain: Long-term oral steroid therapy -> Lens epithelial changes -> Posterior subcapsular cataract -> Progressive vision loss.
optionExplanations: Cataract, specifically posterior subcapsular, is strongly associated with chronic corticosteroid therapy.
Glaucoma can be induced by steroids (steroid-responder), but cataracts are more common with systemic use.
Cystoid macular edema occurs after ocular surgery or retinal vascular occlusions.
Retinal detachment presents with sudden flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like visual loss.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Prophylactic cranial radiation is given for which of the following cancers?
questions.explanation: Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) is standardly indicated and administered in patients with limited-stage or extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (SCLC) who have achieved a complete response to initial chemotherapy and radiation, to reduce brain metastases.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the indication for prophylactic cranial irradiation in oncology.
questions.reasoningChain: Small cell lung cancer responding to therapy -> High risk of brain metastasis -> Prophylactic cranial irradiation.
optionExplanations: Lung cancer, specifically small cell lung cancer, is the classic indication for prophylactic cranial irradiation.
Liver cancer management does not involve prophylactic cranial irradiation.
Prostate cancer treatment involves hormonal therapy and radiation to the prostate bed.
Breast cancer treatment involves local surgery, radiation, and systemic therapy, not routine PCI.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most common delayed symptom of head and neck radiation therapy?
questions.explanation: Radiation therapy to the head and neck inevitably includes salivary glands within the radiation field, leading to radiation-induced salivary gland damage and permanent, chronic xerostomia (dry mouth) as the most common delayed symptom.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify xerostomia as the most common delayed side effect of head and neck radiation.
questions.reasoningChain: Head and neck radiation -> Salivary gland acinar destruction -> Chronic xerostomia.
optionExplanations: Dysphagia can occur due to strictures, but xerostomia is the most universal and prominent delayed complication.
Xerostomia is the most common and debilitating long-term delayed complication of head and neck radiation therapy.
Myelopathy is a rare and severe radiation complication involving the spinal cord.
Dysgeusia occurs early during treatment due to taste bud damage, whereas xerostomia persists long-term.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old woman comes for her regular antenatal check-up. Her arterial blood gas showed an arterial gas abnormality characterized by a higher pH and lower levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the blood. Which arterial gas abnormality is expected to be seen in this woman?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy induces hyperventilation driven by progesterone stimulation of the respiratory center, leading to a chronic respiratory alkalosis characterized by low partial pressure of CO2 and elevated or compensated pH.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize chronic respiratory alkalosis as the physiological acid-base change in pregnancy.
questions.reasoningChain: Pregnancy + progesterone stimulation -> Hyperventilation -> Lower CO2 and higher pH -> Chronic respiratory alkalosis.
optionExplanations: Acute metabolic acidosis features low pH and low bicarbonate, opposite to normal pregnancy physiology.
Acute metabolic alkalosis involves primary bicarbonate retention, not hyperventilation-induced hypocapnia.
Chronic respiratory alkalosis is the characteristic physiological arterial blood gas finding in normal pregnancy.
None of the above is incorrect because chronic respiratory alkalosis is accurate.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A mother of a 5 day year old baby presents with the complaint that her baby is “unable to latch on” for breastfeeding. She also says there is some leakage of milk at times and on examination, there is bilateral tenderness and swelling. What is the most likely cause of this?
questions.explanation: Breast engorgement typically occurs on postpartum days 3 to 5 due to lymphatic and vascular congestion preceding copious milk production, causing bilateral breast swelling, tenderness, and latch difficulties.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose postpartum breast engorgement based on timing and symptoms.
questions.reasoningChain: Postpartum day 5 + bilateral breast swelling and tenderness + poor latch -> Breast engorgement.
optionExplanations: Bacterial mastitis usually presents later with unilateral localized erythema, fever, and pain.
Breast abscess represents walled-off purulent infection requiring drainage, usually unilateral.
Lactational mastitis is characterized by focal inflammation, fever, and chills, unlike generalized engorgement.
Breast engorgement is the physiological swelling and vascular congestion causing early postpartum latch issues.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A woman presented in her 8th week oof pregnancy seeking MTP. The appropriate dosage of Misoprostol (administered by mucosal route) would be
questions.explanation: According to standard gynecological guidelines for medical abortion up to 9 weeks of gestation, the recommended mucosal (buccal or sublingual) dose of misoprostol following mifepristone is 800 mcg.
questions.educationalObjective: State the standard dosage of misoprostol for medical abortion.
questions.reasoningChain: Medical termination of pregnancy at 8 weeks -> Mifepristone followed by misoprostol -> 800 mcg mucosal route.
optionExplanations: 200 mcg is subtherapeutic for medical abortion regimens.
600 mcg is suboptimal compared to the standard 800 mcg recommendation.
400 mcg is sometimes used in specific second-trimester protocols, not early first-trimester MTP.
800 mcg is the standard recommended mucosal dose of misoprostol for medical abortion up to 9 weeks.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A woman 3 months postpartum who regularly breastfeeds presented with amenorrhea for 3 months and is concerned about this problem and is requesting surgery. Before considering surgery what can be done to manage this patient?
questions.explanation: Amenorrhea during exclusive breastfeeding is due to physiological lactational amenorrhea (prolactin-mediated suppression of GnRH). In a postpartum breastfeeding woman, this is normal and requires reassurance rather than surgical or medical intervention.
questions.educationalObjective: Manage physiological lactational amenorrhea with reassurance.
questions.reasoningChain: Postpartum + breastfeeding + amenorrhea -> Physiological hyperprolactinemia -> Reassure patient.
optionExplanations: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling is used for polycystic ovary syndrome resistant to clomiphene, not physiological amenorrhea.
Contraceptives can be prescribed if requested for family planning, but reassurance is the primary initial step.
Pulsatile GnRH is indicated for hypothalamic amenorrhea, not normal lactational amenorrhea.
Reassurance is the appropriate management for normal physiological amenorrhea during lactation.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 14-year-old girl brought by her mother with complaints that the child has not even menstruated once. On examination secondary sexual characters are seen and uterus and ovaries were seen to be normal on USG. What is the next step of management?
questions.explanation: A 14-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea, normal secondary sexual characteristics, and normal pelvic anatomy on ultrasound likely has constitutional delay of growth and puberty. Initial hormonal evaluation includes serum LH, FSH, and TSH levels.
questions.educationalObjective: Outline the investigation steps for primary amenorrhea with normal anatomy.
questions.reasoningChain: Primary amenorrhea + secondary sexual characteristics + normal pelvic USG -> Endocrine evaluation -> LH, FSH, and TSH levels.
optionExplanations: Combined oral contraceptives are unnecessary without a definitive diagnosis or hormone imbalance.
Karyotyping is reserved for patients with suspected Turner syndrome or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
Reassurance is premature before confirming normal baseline endocrine function.
LH, FSH level and TSH are the appropriate initial endocrine investigations for primary amenorrhea.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 19-year-old female comes to the OPD with complaints of weakness, amenorrhea, and fatigue. Upon eliciting history, she reveals that she is always worried gaining weight. Her mother complains that she doesn’t eat well. Her BMI is 15.8 laboratory findings in this patient will show which of the following?
questions.explanation: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by severe weight loss, low BMI, and functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, accompanied by hypersecretion of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) reflecting chronic physiological and psychological stress.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify endocrine alterations in anorexia nervosa.
questions.reasoningChain: Severe low BMI + amenorrhea + fear of weight gain (anorexia nervosa) -> Chronic stress response -> Hypersecretion of CRH.
optionExplanations: Hypocholesterolaemia is incorrect; hypercholesterolemia is frequently seen in anorexia nervosa.
Hyperthyroidism features increased metabolic rate and weight loss, whereas anorexia mimics a hypometabolic state.
Hypersecretion of corticotropin-releasing hormone is a classic neuroendocrine finding in patients with anorexia nervosa.
Hyperglycaemia is not characteristic; hypoglycemia or normal glucose regulation is typical due to starvation.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 25 year old female presented previous history of chlamydia infection now presents with low-grade fever and non-specific lower abdominal pain. Examination reveals mild diffuse lower abdominal tenderness on deep palpation, cervical motion tenderness, and a mucopurulent vaginal discharge. What are the long-term sequelae of this condition?
questions.explanation: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) resulting from sexually transmitted infections like Chlamydia trachomatis causes chronic fallopian tube inflammation, leading to tubal scarring, adhesion formation, and a significantly increased risk of tubal factor infertility.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify infertility as a major long-term sequela of pelvic inflammatory disease.
questions.reasoningChain: Chlamydia infection / PID -> Tubal inflammation and scarring -> Increased risk of tubal factor infertility.
optionExplanations: Infertility is a well-known long-term sequela of pelvic inflammatory disease due to tubal scarring.
Uterine cancer is linked to estrogen exposure and genetic factors, not Chlamydia PID.
Pelvic organ prolapse is caused by pelvic floor laxity during childbirth, not upper genital tract infections.
Cervical cancer is caused by persistent high-risk HPV infection, distinct from chlamydial PID.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 26-year-old unmarried woman complained of missed periods. She always had regular menstrual cycles. The pelvic examination is normal. What is the next step of management for this patient?
options: Reassure her that it’s normal to have delayed period
questions.explanation: In a sexually active or potentially reproductive-aged woman presenting with sudden secondary amenorrhea and previously regular cycles, pregnancy must be ruled out first by estimating serum or urine beta-hCG.
questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize pregnancy testing in secondary amenorrhea.
questions.reasoningChain: Missed periods in reproductive-aged woman -> Rule out pregnancy -> Beta HCG estimation.
optionExplanations: Transvaginal ultrasound is performed after pregnancy is ruled out or if pelvic pathology is suspected.
Reassurance without ruling out pregnancy is clinically unsafe.
Beta HCG estimation is the essential first investigation to rule out pregnancy in secondary amenorrhea.
Serum FSH and LH are evaluated later if pregnancy is negative and secondary amenorrhea persists.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A patient is seen in the OPD after her delivery which was 5 days ago. She presents with smelly greenish vaginal discharge. What is the initial step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: A postpartum patient presenting with smelly greenish vaginal discharge suggests postpartum endometritis or infection. The essential initial clinical step in evaluating gynecological symptoms is direct inspection via per vaginal (speculum/bimanual) examination.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify per vaginal examination as the initial clinical evaluation step for postpartum discharge.
questions.reasoningChain: Postpartum vaginal discharge -> Clinical assessment -> Per vagina examination to evaluate source and lochia.
optionExplanations: Antibiotics are required for infection, but physical examination must precede empirical therapy.
USG is useful for retained products of conception, but physical examination is the immediate initial step.
Urine analysis evaluates urinary tract infections, not primary puerperal vaginal discharge.
Per vagina examination is the necessary initial clinical step to assess the cervix, uterus, and lochia.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: As a senior resident in the OBG department, you would consider uterine artery embolization as a treatment option in all of the following cases except
options: Prior to the removal of placenta accreta in Multiparous woman
Patient diagnosed with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids
questions.answer: Patient diagnosed with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids
questions.explanation: Uterine artery embolization (UAE) is contraindicated in calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids because calcified fibroids do not respond well to ischemic necrosis, and pedunculated submucous myomas carry a high risk of sloughing into the uterine cavity and causing infection.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify contraindications for uterine artery embolization in fibroids.
questions.reasoningChain: Pedunculated/calcified submucous fibroids -> Risk of necrosis and expulsion/infection -> Contraindication for UAE.
optionExplanations: Uterine artery embolization is used in PPH to control hemorrhage when conservative measures fail.
UAE can be used temporarily in placenta accreta management to reduce bleeding before surgical removal.
Calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids are contraindicated for UAE due to expulsion and infection risks.
Multiparous woman with symptomatic menorrhagia from appropriate fibroid types is an ideal candidate for UAE.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 45-year P3L3 woman presented with a lower abdominal mass and lower abdominal discomfort. On examination, the uterus appears uniformly enlarged and adnexa is free. MRI shows the presence of a myometrial cyst. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adenomyosis is characterized by the presence of ectopic endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, leading to a diffusely enlarged uterus and MRI findings showing myometrial cysts or widening of the junctional zone.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose adenomyosis based on uterine enlargement and myometrial cysts on MRI.
questions.reasoningChain: Uniformly enlarged uterus + myometrial cyst on MRI -> Adenomyosis.
optionExplanations: Endometriosis involves ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus, typically in the pelvis or ovaries.
Adenomyosis is characterized by myometrial invasion of endometrial tissue, showing myometrial cysts on MRI.
Leiomyomas are well-circumscribed benign monoclonal smooth muscle tumors, presenting as focal masses.
Endometrial hyperplasia involves thickening of the endometrial lining inside the uterine cavity.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A 34-year-old G2P1L1 presents with abdominal pain, bleeding per vaginum in labour and loss of fetal movements. She occasionally smokes but does not consume alcohol or recreational drugs. On examination, her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP is 150/90 mm of Hg and a tense abdomen on palpation. What is the probable diagnosis?
