Diphtheria is characterized by a tightly adherent gray pseudomembrane and marked cervical edema (bull-neck).
Candidiasis presents with removable white curd-like plaques on oral mucosa.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old woman presents with chronic mucopurulent discharge from her left eye and swelling near the medial canthus. Which of the following is the treatment of choice in this patient?
questions.explanation: Chronic mucopurulent discharge and swelling near the medial canthus due to nasolacrimal duct obstruction (chronic dacryocystitis) is definitively treated with dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) to create a bypass into the nasal cavity.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the treatment of choice for chronic dacryocystitis.
questions.reasoningChain: Chronic dacryocystitis / nasolacrimal duct obstruction -> Surgical bypass -> Dacryocystorhinostomy.
optionExplanations: Dacryocystorhinostomy establishes a new drainage pathway between the lacrimal sac and nasal cavity.
Dacryocystectomy removes the lacrimal sac entirely and is reserved for elderly or infirm patients.
Conjunctivo-cystorhinostomy involves placing a Jones tube for canalicular obstruction.
Balloon catheter dilation is used for simple congenital nasolacrimal duct obstructions in infants.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: The fallopian tube is lined by.
questions.explanation: The epithelial lining of the fallopian tube consists of a simple columnar epithelium containing both ciliated cells (which help transport the ovum) and secretory (peg) cells.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the histological lining of the fallopian tube.
questions.reasoningChain: Fallopian tube histology -> Simple columnar epithelium with ciliated and secretory cells.
optionExplanations: Simple columnar epithelium lines the fallopian tube, featuring ciliated cells.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines the respiratory tract.
Ciliated columnar epithelium correctly specifies the functional cell type lining the oviduct.
Cuboidal epithelium lines renal tubules and small ducts.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A 6-year-old boy fell from the bed and developed nose swelling and difficulty breathing. Examination revealed smooth rounded swellings on either side of the septum through both nares. On palpation, it was soft and fluctuant. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: Nasal trauma resulting in a soft, fluctuant, bilateral swelling of the nasal septum indicates a nasal septal hematoma, which requires urgent incision and drainage to prevent septal cartilage necrosis and saddle nose deformity.
questions.educationalObjective: Manage nasal septal hematoma emergently.
questions.reasoningChain: Nasal trauma + soft fluctuant bilateral septal swelling -> Septal hematoma -> Urgent incision and drainage.
optionExplanations: Systemic antibiotics alone cannot resolve collected blood in a hematoma.
Incision and drainage is mandatory to evacuate the hematoma and prevent cartilage necrosis.
High-resolution CT is unnecessary when physical examination clearly confirms septal hematoma.
Submucosal resection is performed for deviated nasal septum, not acute hematoma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: Which of the following surgeries use this instrument?
questions.explanation: The instrument shown is a nasal speculum or lacrimal bone punch/forceps used in surgeries like dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) to create the bony ostium into the nose.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify surgical instruments used in dacryocystorhinostomy.
questions.reasoningChain: Kerrison punch / nasal bone rongeur -> Used in Dacryocystorhinostomy for osteotomy creation.
optionExplanations: Evisceration removes intraocular contents while sclera remains.
Enucleation removes the entire globe with part of the optic nerve.
Cataract surgery utilizes phacoemulsification and micro-instruments.
Dacryocystorhinostomy utilizes bone punches/rongeurs to create an opening in the lacrimal bone.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A young lady presented to the ENT OPD with a history of sudden onset unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness following an episode of acute otitis media two weeks back. Rinne test and fistula test were positive. She had refused treatment then and currently came with complaints of worsened hearing loss in the affected ear. On examination, the fistula test was negative. What would be the most likely finding on the Rinne test in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Following severe otitis media with complications like labyrinthitis or fixation, mixed or sensorineural hearing loss develops. When severe sensorineural hearing loss occurs, bone conduction is severely reduced, but skull vibrations can still be perceived by the opposite healthy cochlea, giving a false negative Rinne test result.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the mechanism of a false negative Rinne test.
questions.reasoningChain: Profound unilateral hearing loss -> Bone conduction perceived by contralateral ear -> False negative Rinne test.
optionExplanations: True positive indicates normal hearing or sensorineural loss where air conduction > bone conduction correctly.
True negative indicates standard conductive hearing loss where bone conduction > air conduction accurately.
False positive occurs when the test ear is not properly masked during bone conduction testing.
False negative occurs in profound unilateral sensorineural hearing loss when sound is perceived by the contralateral cochlea.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old man after his retirement party came with the complaint of sudden painless loss of vision in his left eye for the past 2 hours. Fundoscopic examination shows a similar picture given below. What is the most probable cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: Fundoscopic examination showing a pale, edematous retina with a classic 'cherry-red spot' at the fovea is pathognomonic for Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose central retinal artery occlusion on fundoscopy.
questions.reasoningChain: Acute painless vision loss + pale retina with cherry-red spot -> Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).
optionExplanations: BRAO (branch retinal artery occlusion) presents with localized retinal whitening and visual field defect.
BRVO presents with retinal hemorrhages in a localized quadrant.
CRAO presents with sudden painless loss of vision, a pale retina, and a cherry-red spot.
CRVO presents with diffuse retinal hemorrhages ('blood and thunder' appearance).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Identify the structure marked a ‘c’.
questions.explanation: In the sagittal laryngeal diagram, structure 'C' points to the leaf-shaped epiglottis located at the superior entrance of the larynx.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify laryngeal cartilages and structures on anatomical diagrams.
questions.reasoningChain: Superior cartilaginous lid of larynx labeled C -> Epiglottis.
optionExplanations: Epiglottis is correctly identified by label C.
Hyoid bone is located superiorly in the neck above the thyroid cartilage.
Thyroid cartilage forms the prominent anterior wall of the larynx.
Cricoid cartilage forms the inferior complete ring of the larynx.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: What is the Battle sign?
questions.explanation: Battle's sign is ecchymosis over the mastoid process behind the ear, which serves as a classic clinical indicator of a middle cranial fossa skull base fracture.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize Battle's sign in basilar skull fracture.
questions.reasoningChain: Mastoid ecchymosis following head trauma -> Battle's sign.
optionExplanations: Mastoid ecchymosis is defined as Battle's sign.
Periorbital hematoma (raccoon eyes) indicates anterior cranial fossa fracture.
Bezold abscess is a deep neck abscess originating from mastoiditis.
Perichondritis is inflammation of the auricular cartilage.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A patient with a corneal scar has a visual acuity of 6/36, which improves to 6/18 with a pinhole. The most likely reason or this is –
questions.explanation: Improvement in visual acuity through a pinhole indicates that the visual deficit is caused by refractive errors, particularly irregular astigmatism caused by corneal scarring, which disrupts light rays in an uneven manner.
questions.educationalObjective: Interpret pinhole visual acuity testing in corneal scarring.
questions.reasoningChain: Corneal scar + visual improvement with pinhole -> Irregular astigmatism.
optionExplanations: Glaucoma causes optic neuropathy and peripheral visual field loss, not correctable by pinhole.
Malingering shows inconsistent vision without pinhole improvement correlation.
Irregular astigmatism from corneal irregularities is overcome by a pinhole aperture.
Cataract causes scatter and glare, partially corrected by pinhole depending on density.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: At what level does the spinal cord end in infants?
questions.explanation: In neonates and infants, the spinal cord extends lower down the vertebral column, typically terminating at the level of the L3 vertebra, before ascending to the L1-L2 level in adults.
questions.educationalObjective: Know the termination level of the spinal cord in infants.
questions.reasoningChain: Infant spinal cord termination level -> L3 vertebra.
optionExplanations: L1 is the adult termination level of the spinal cord.
L2 marks the conus medullaris lower limit in some adults.
L3 is the vertebral level where the spinal cord terminates in infants.
L4 is below the normal neonatal cord termination level.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: An 18-year-old boy presents with a history of injury to the eye caused while climbing a tree 5 days ago, resulting in pain, photophobia, and redness of the eye for 2 days. Slit-lamp examination reveals a lesion as shown below. Which among the following is a feature of this condition?
questions.explanation: The slit-lamp image shows a fungal corneal ulcer (keratitis) characterized by a dense stromal infiltrate with irregular feathery borders and characteristic satellite lesions surrounding the main ulcer.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify features of fungal keratitis.
questions.reasoningChain: Corneal injury from plant matter + hypopyon + satellite lesions -> Fungal keratitis.
optionExplanations: Reverse hypopyon is seen in certain uveitic or masquerade syndromes.
Dendritic ulcer is characteristic of herpes simplex keratitis.
Ring abscess is typical of Pseudomonas bacterial keratitis.
Satellite lesions are characteristic features of fungal (Aspergillus/Fusarium) keratitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A 5-year-old female patient presented for her first complete eye examination after a school vision screening found unequal visual acuity. Her parents have not noted any eye problems. Visual acuity in the right eye was 20/20 and the left eye was 20/80. The rest of the examination including the Fundus exam was unremarkable, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A child with decreased visual acuity in one eye and a normal fundus exam, discovered during routine screening, most likely suffers from amblyopia ('lazy eye') due to uncorrected anisometropia or strabismus during visual development.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose amblyopia in pediatric vision screening.
questions.reasoningChain: Unequal visual acuity in a child with normal fundus exam -> Amblyopia.
optionExplanations: Brain lesion would present with neurologic signs or distinct optic atrophy.
Retinoblastoma presents with leukocoria and intraocular mass on fundoscopy.
Congenital cataract presents with visible lens opacities and diminished red reflex.
Amblyopia is functional reduction of vision without organic ocular pathology.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: An 80-year-old man developed right-sided calf muscle pain and swelling. He was bedridden following a right inter-trochanteric fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A bedridden patient with fracture and immobility who develops unilateral calf pain and swelling presents with classic signs of deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose deep vein thrombosis in an immobilized patient.
questions.reasoningChain: Bedridden post-fracture patient + calf pain and swelling -> Deep vein thrombosis.
optionExplanations: Chronic osteomyelitis presents with draining sinuses and bone destruction.
Deep vein thrombosis results from Virchow's triad (stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial injury) in bedridden patients.
Compartment syndrome presents with severe disproportionate pain and tense fascial compartments after trauma.
Arterial claudication presents with exertional pain relieved by rest.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is true with respect to the Little’s area?
options: Keisselbach’s plexus is present in the Little’ area
It is situated at the postero-inferior part of the nasal septum
Anastomoses of 7 major arteries occur here
questions.answer: Keisselbach’s plexus is present in the Little’ area
questions.explanation: Little's area is located on the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum (Kiesselbach's plexus), formed by the anastomosis of five major arteries, and is the most common site for anterior epistaxis.
questions.educationalObjective: Describe the anatomy of Little's area.
questions.reasoningChain: Anteroinferior nasal septum vascular plexus -> Kiesselbach's plexus in Little's area.
optionExplanations: Kiesselbach's plexus is situated in Little's area on the anteroinferior septum.
It is situated at the anterior-inferior part, not postero-inferior.
It is the most common site for epistaxis, not the least common.
Anastomosis of 5 major arteries occurs here, not 7.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: Which is the most common cause of preventable childhood blindness?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency remains the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide, leading to xerophthalmia, corneal ulceration, and keratomalacia.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness.
questions.reasoningChain: Nutritional deficiency leading to ocular damage -> Vitamin A deficiency -> Preventable childhood blindness.
optionExplanations: Refractive errors cause visual impairment, but vitamin A deficiency is the leading cause of preventable blindness.
Vitamin A deficiency is the foremost cause of preventable blindness in children.
Retinopathy of prematurity affects premature infants receiving high oxygen therapy.
Injuries are a major cause of monocular trauma blindness, but systemic nutritional deficiency leads bilateral blindness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast and a fever. On examination of the affected side, there is localized erythema, warmth, and point tenderness, the fluctuation test is positive. There is mild axillary lymphadenopathy on the affected side and the contralateral breast is normal. Repeated aspirations under antibiotic cover done were unsuccessful. A USG done showed fluid collection. What is the management plan for this patient?
questions.explanation: A lactating mother with a breast abscess showing fluctuation, failure of repeated aspirations, and persistent infection requires formal surgical incision and drainage along with appropriate antibiotic coverage.
questions.educationalObjective: Manage lactating breast abscess unresponsive to aspiration.
questions.reasoningChain: Lactating breast abscess + failed aspirations + fluctuation -> Incision and drainage.
optionExplanations: Incision and drainage is the definitive treatment for fluctuant breast abscesses unresponsive to needle aspiration.
Antibiotics alone are insufficient once pus has accumulated and formed an abscess cavity.
Breast conservation surgery is reserved for neoplastic tumors.
Punch biopsy is indicated for suspected inflammatory or malignant skin lesions.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: Identify the condition shown in the image.
questions.explanation: The image shows inward turning of the eyelid margin and eyelashes rubbing against the ocular surface, which defines entropion.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify entropion on clinical examination.
questions.reasoningChain: Inward rotation of eyelid margin -> Entropion.
optionExplanations: Entropion is the inward turning of the eyelid margin.
Ectropion is the outward turning of the eyelid margin.
Trichiasis refers to misdirected eyelashes rubbing the eye with a normally positioned lid margin.
Ptosis is drooping of the upper eyelid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: The dermatome of the area marked in the given below image is.
questions.explanation: The dermatome map of the lower limb indicates that the anteromedial aspect of the leg and medial side of the foot correspond to the L4 nerve root dermatome.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify lower limb dermatomes.
questions.reasoningChain: Anteromedial leg / medial foot strip -> L4 dermatome.
optionExplanations: L4 dermatome supplies the medial aspect of the leg down to the medial malleolus and foot.
L5 dermatome covers the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.
S1 dermatome covers the lateral aspect of the foot and sole.
S2 dermatome covers the posterior thigh and calf.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A 23-year-old woman presents to the surgery out-patient with a left-sided breast lump which she noticed on a self-breast examination 3 weeks ago. She has no other complaints. On palpation, the lump seems to be mobile and firm. Mammogram revealed a benign lesion. What is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation: A young patient with a smooth, firm, mobile breast lump confirmed as benign on mammography/biopsy requires reassurance and regular clinical follow-up.
questions.educationalObjective: Manage benign breast lumps in young women.
questions.reasoningChain: Young female + benign firm mobile breast lump -> Reassurance and follow-up.
optionExplanations: Biopsy is already established as benign or unnecessary if imaging is definitively benign.
Reassurance and follow-up is the appropriate management for confirmed benign fibroadenomas in young patients.
Surgical excision is reserved for large, growing, or symptomatic lesions.
Tamoxifen is used for high-risk breast cancer chemoprevention or hormone-receptor-positive cancer.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A 7-year-old boy presented with a white pupillary reflex for which enucleation was done. The histopathological examination of the specimen revealed Flexner Wintersteiner rosettes. What could be the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathology of an enucleated eye with leukocoria in a child is pathognomonic for retinoblastoma.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose retinoblastoma using histopathology.
questions.reasoningChain: Leukocoria + Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histology -> Retinoblastoma.
optionExplanations: Retinoblastoma histology characteristically demonstrates Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.
Medulloblastoma is a pediatric cerebellar tumor showing Homer Wright rosettes.
Rhabdomyosarcoma is a soft tissue sarcoma showing primitive round cells.
Astrocytoma is a glial brain tumor with Rosenthal fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: The neurovascular plane of the abdominal wall lies
options: Between the internal oblique and external oblique
Between the internal oblique and rectus abdominis
Between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis
questions.answer: Between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis
questions.explanation: The neurovascular plane of the anterior abdominal wall is located between the internal oblique muscle and the transversus abdominis muscle, carrying intercostal nerves and vessels.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the neurovascular plane of the abdominal wall.
questions.reasoningChain: Abdominal wall nerves and vessels course -> Between internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles.
optionExplanations: Between external and internal oblique muscles contains no major neurovascular trunk.
Deep to transversus abdominis lies the transversalis fascia and peritoneum.
Between internal oblique and rectus abdominis contains the rectus abdominis muscle and sheath structures.
Between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis is the true neurovascular plane.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A 14-year-old male presented with recurrent epistaxis. There is no history of trauma associated with it. He also complained of nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea. On examination, there is a firm purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A young male adolescent presenting with recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and a firm, purplish vascular mass in the nasopharynx has classic juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA).
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.
questions.reasoningChain: Adolescent male + recurrent epistaxis + vascular nasopharyngeal mass -> Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.
optionExplanations: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma occurs in older adults and is associated with EBV.
Rhabdomyosarcoma presents as a soft tissue sarcoma in younger children.
Pyogenic granuloma is a small vascular lesion, not a large posterior nasopharyngeal mass.
Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign, highly vascular tumor in adolescent males causing epistaxis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: An industrial worker was admitted to the hospital after an eye injury sustained while cutting stone with a hammer and iron chisel. A foreign body was suspected to be impacted in his eye. Which of the following is the best investigation for foreign body localization?
questions.explanation: Computed tomography (CT) scan is the gold standard and best imaging investigation for localizing intraocular metallic or stone foreign bodies following trauma.
questions.educationalObjective: Select the best imaging study for ocular foreign body localization.
questions.reasoningChain: Suspected intraocular foreign body from stone/metal cutting -> CT scan provides superior spatial resolution and localization.
optionExplanations: MRI is contraindicated if the foreign body is metallic due to the risk of magnetic movement and further tissue damage.
CT scan is the imaging modality of choice for accurate intraocular foreign body localization.
X-ray can screen for radiopaque foreign bodies but lacks precise 3D localization compared to CT.
B-mode ultrasound is useful for posterior segment evaluation but avoided if globe rupture is suspected.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: The false statement about cystic masses of the neck is:
options: Type 3 branchial fistula has its internal orifice on cricopharynxgeus
Cystic hygroma is filled with clear lymph
Thyroglossal cyst moves upwards on swallowing and tongue protrusion
questions.answer: Type 3 branchial fistula has its internal orifice on cricopharynxgeus
questions.explanation: Branchial anomalies originate from the persistent remnants of embryonic branchial clefts or pouches. Type 3 branchial cleft anomalies typically have their internal orifice associated with the piriform fossa rather than the cricopharyngeus muscle. Cystic hygromas contain clear lymphatic fluid. Thyroglossal duct cysts characteristically elevate upon swallowing and tongue protrusion due to their attachment to the hyoid bone. Branchial cleft cysts usually demonstrate positive clinical fluctuation.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand the anatomical characteristics and clinical presentations of congenital neck masses including branchial cysts and fistulae.
questions.reasoningChain: Type 3 branchial fistula internal orifice opens in the piriform fossa -> statement 1 is false -> correct answer.
optionExplanations: Incorrect because the internal opening is in the piriform fossa.
Correct anatomical fact regarding cystic hygromas containing clear lymph.
Correct clinical sign characteristic of thyroglossal cysts.
Correct physical sign found in branchial cleft cysts.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the best line of treatment in a 3-year-old child presenting with a recent onset of 15-degree accommodative esotropia?
questions.explanation: In young children presenting with a recent onset of low-angle accommodative esotropia, the underlying etiology is typically uncorrected hyperopia. Accommodation is linked to convergence; thus, focusing to overcome hyperopia triggers excessive esodeviation. Management involves full cycloplegic refraction correction to eliminate the accommodative stimulus and straighten the eyes.
questions.educationalObjective: Treat accommodative esotropia primarily with appropriate refractive correction rather than immediate surgery.
questions.reasoningChain: Accommodative esotropia -> driven by uncorrected hyperopia -> full refractive correction is first-line treatment.
optionExplanations: Orthoptic exercises are not the primary treatment for accommodative esotropia.
Surgery is reserved for non-accommodative deviations or residual angles after glasses.
Relieving prisms are used for persistent diplopia, not primary pediatric accommodative squint.
Refractive correction eliminates the accommodative drive to converge.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.prompt: Given below is a histological section of the thyroid gland. Which of the following is secreted by the cell marked ‘X’ in the image?
questions.explanation: The histological image demonstrates a thyroid section showing thyroid follicles alongside parafollicular cells, also known as C cells, indicated by 'X' within the interfollicular space. Unlike follicular cells that secrete thyroxine (T3/T4), these C cells are derived from the neural crest and are responsible for synthesizing and secreting calcitonin, a hormone involved in lowering blood calcium levels.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify parafollicular C cells of the thyroid and their secretory product, calcitonin.
questions.reasoningChain: Cell 'X' is in interfollicular space -> parafollicular C cell -> secretes calcitonin.
optionExplanations: Thyroxine is secreted by the follicular epithelial cells.
Calcitonin is secreted by the parafollicular C cells marked as X.
Parathormone is secreted by the chief cells of parathyroid glands.
Serotonin is an enterochromaffin or neurotransmitter amine.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A 35 year old woman presents to you with complaints of difficulty in hearing in the right ear which is slowly progressive. She also has tinnitus which is pulsatile in nature. On examination, a reddish mass was seen behind the tympanic membrane and an audible bruit is heard over the mastoid when auscultation with a stethoscope. Her Rinnie test was negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A glomus jugulare or tympanicum tumor characteristically presents with progressive conductive hearing loss, pulsatile tinnitus, a reddish mass visible behind the intact tympanic membrane, and a vascular bruit over the mastoid due to hypervascularity. Rinne test is negative in conductive hearing loss. These clinical findings are classic for a paraganglioma of the middle ear.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation of a glomus tumor featuring pulsatile tinnitus and a vascular retrotympanic mass.
questions.reasoningChain: Pulsatile tinnitus + reddish retrotympanic mass + conductive loss -> Glomus tumor.
optionExplanations: CSOM typically presents with otorrhea and tympanic membrane perforation.
ASOM presents with acute pain, fever, and bulging opaque tympanic membrane.
Mastoiditis presents with postauricular swelling, erythema, and tenderness.
Glomus tumor matches vascular retrotympanic mass and pulsatile tinnitus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A contact lens user presents with the following clinical picture. He had watering, redness, and foreign body sensation in the eye for the past 2 months. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical image demonstrates giant, cobblestone-like papillae on the tarsal conjunctiva of a chronic contact lens wearer. This condition, known as giant papillary conjunctivitis, represents an immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to mechanical irritation and protein deposits on contact lenses, resulting in itching, foreign body sensation, and increased mucous discharge.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose giant papillary conjunctivitis associated with chronic contact lens wear.
questions.reasoningChain: Contact lens history + giant tarsal papillae -> Giant papillary conjunctivitis.
optionExplanations: Acute trachoma shows follicles and scarring with pannus, mainly in endemic areas.
Follicular conjunctivitis presents with multiple small follicles without giant papillae.
Giant papillary conjunctivitis shows large cobblestone papillae, typical in contact lens users.
Spring catarrh (vernal keratoconjunctivitis) occurs seasonally in young males with shield ulcers.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: What is the preferred management of the condition given in the image below?
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates a classic pediatric dermoid cyst, usually presenting as a smooth, painless, subcutaneous mass near the eyebrow. The treatment of choice for a dermoid cyst is complete surgical excision. Incomplete removal can lead to recurrence or chronic sinus tract formation.
questions.educationalObjective: Manage periorbital dermoid cysts with complete surgical excision.
questions.reasoningChain: Periorbital cystic swelling -> Dermoid cyst -> Requires surgical excision.
optionExplanations: Surgical excision is the definitive treatment to prevent recurrence and cyst rupture.
Radiotherapy has no role in the management of benign dermoid cysts.
Antibiotics are ineffective as this is a congenital inclusion cyst, not an active infection.
Intralesional steroids are used for inflammatory lesions like chalazia, not dermoid cysts.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A worried mother brought her son for a vision examination when she noticed him reading a book too closely. She says he also narrows his eyes while watching television. Examination revealed myopia. Which of the following lenses should be prescribed to correct this child’s vision?
questions.explanation: Myopia (nearsightedness) occurs when the optical power of the eye is too great or the axial length is too long, causing light rays to focus in front of the retina rather than directly on it. To diverge incoming light rays and shift the focal point backward onto the retina, concave lenses (diverging lenses) are prescribed.
questions.educationalObjective: Correct myopia using appropriate diverging concave lenses.
questions.reasoningChain: Myopia -> rays focus in front of retina -> corrected with concave lenses.
optionExplanations: Convex lenses converge light and are used to correct hyperopia or presbyopia.
Concave lenses diverge light and are the correct choice for myopia.
Cylindrical lenses are used for correcting astigmatism.
Combination lenses are used for complex mixed refractive errors, not simple myopia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.prompt: A school-going child presents with a history of recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, mouth breathing, and impaired hearing. On examination, a high arched palate is noted. What is the management of this condition?
questions.explanation: Recurrent upper respiratory infections, mouth breathing, impaired hearing (due to conductive loss from serous otitis media), and a high-arched palate are classic signs of chronic adenoid hypertrophy. Management of severe obstruction and associated middle-ear effusion involves adenoidectomy combined with myringotomy and grommet (tympanostomy tube) insertion.
questions.educationalObjective: Manage chronic adenoid hypertrophy with persistent otitis media using adenoidectomy and grommet insertion.
questions.reasoningChain: Adenoid hypertrophy with hearing loss -> adenoidectomy and grommet insertion.
optionExplanations: Tonsillectomy alone does not resolve adenoid-induced nasal obstruction or Eustachian tube dysfunction.
Adenoidectomy alone treats obstruction but fails to drain existing middle ear effusion.
Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion addresses both nasal obstruction and associated conductive hearing loss.
Myringotomy with grommet addresses ear effusion but ignores the primary adenoid source.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old man presents to the casualty with a sudden loss of vision and painful ocular movements. On examination in the affected eye, a relative afferent pupillary defect is seen, however the optic disk was normal. Visual field testing was done which revealed central scotoma in the same eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Optic neuritis classically presents in young adults with acute unilateral vision loss, pain with eye movements, a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), and central scotoma on visual field testing. The optic disc often appears normal initially (retrobulbar neuritis), differentiating it from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy where disc edema is prominent.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose optic neuritis based on painful vision loss, central scotoma, and normal optic disc.
questions.reasoningChain: Painful vision loss + central scotoma + normal disc -> Optic neuritis.
optionExplanations: Optic nerve glioma is a slow-growing tumor presenting with painless progressive vision loss and proptosis.
Optic neuritis matches painful vision loss with a normal optic disc and central scotoma.
Eale's disease is an idiopathic retinal periphlebitis associated with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage.
Neuroretinitis presents with optic disc edema and macular star formation, unlike retrobulbar optic neuritis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A young girl presents with complaints of continuous dribbling of urine. However, she also voids normally. Her parents tell you that she had never been totally dry since her birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Continuous dribbling of urine alongside normal voluntary voiding since birth in a female is pathognomonic for an ectopic ureter. The ectopic ureter typically inserts distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., into the vagina or vestibule), bypassing bladder control while the main bladder fills and voids normally via the orthotopic ureter.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify continuous urinary incontinence with normal voiding in females as a sign of an ectopic ureter.
questions.reasoningChain: Continuous urinary leakage with normal voiding -> ectopic ureter bypassing sphincter.
optionExplanations: Ectopic ureter causes continuous dribbling alongside normal micturition cycles.
Ureterocele typically presents with urinary tract infections or obstruction rather than constant dribbling.
Congenital megaureter presents with dilation and urinary stasis, often causing flank pain or UTIs.
Vesicoureteric reflux causes recurrent febrile urinary tract infections and voiding dysfunction.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A patient who underwent surgery for a lipoma 5 weeks back, now presents with a scar at the incision site that is limited to the original wound boundaries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A hypertrophic scar is characterized by excessive collagen deposition following tissue injury that remains strictly confined within the boundaries of the original wound. Unlike keloids, hypertrophic scars frequently regress over time and do not invade surrounding normal tissue.
questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish hypertrophic scars from keloids by their restriction to original wound boundaries.
questions.reasoningChain: Scar limited to original wound boundaries -> Hypertrophic scar.
optionExplanations: Keloids extend beyond the boundaries of the original wound and rarely regress.
Exuberant granulation represents excessive granulation tissue protruding above the wound surface.
Hypertrophic scar is confined to original wound margins and often improves over time.
Granulation tissue consists of new capillaries and fibroblasts during the proliferative phase of healing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: Which of the following steps in the metabolism of vitamin D requires sunlight?
questions.explanation: Endogenous vitamin D synthesis begins in the skin where ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation from sunlight facilitates the photolysis of 7-dehydrocholesterol to form cholecalciferol (vitamin D3). Subsequent hydroxylation steps occur in the liver (to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol) and kidneys (to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol).
questions.educationalObjective: Describe the sun-dependent cutaneous step in vitamin D synthesis from 7-dehydrocholesterol.
questions.reasoningChain: Sunlight (UVB) acts on skin -> converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol.
optionExplanations: This describes a reversal or misstated pathway, not the physiological direction.
Sunlight converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin into cholecalciferol.
Cholecalciferol is hydroxylated to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol in the liver enzymatically.
25-hydroxycholecalciferol is hydroxylated to active calcitriol in the kidneys via 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: During wound healing, the cells that appear first due to chemotaxis, at the site of the wound are
questions.explanation: During acute inflammation and early wound healing, neutrophils are the first inflammatory cells to be recruited to the injury site via chemotaxis, typically peaking within 24 to 48 hours. They play a critical role in clearing bacteria and debris before being replaced by monocytes and macrophages.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify neutrophils as the earliest cellular responders to acute injury and wound healing.
questions.reasoningChain: Wound occurrence -> rapid chemotaxis -> neutrophils arrive first.
optionExplanations: Neutrophils are the earliest leukocytes to arrive at the site of acute inflammation.
Monocytes migrate into tissues later to differentiate into macrophages.
Macrophages arrive subsequent to neutrophils to orchestrate tissue remodeling and phagocytosis.
Lymphocytes arrive later in chronic inflammation or specific immune responses.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A person was brought to the emergency department with facial swelling, itching, and hypotension following a bee sting. The mentioned clinical features are due to the increase in which immunoglobulin?
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis and allergic reactions following insect stings are mediated by Type I hypersensitivity reactions. This immediate hypersensitivity response is driven by allergen-specific IgE antibodies binding to high-affinity Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils, leading to degranulation and the massive release of vasoactive mediators.
questions.educationalObjective: Connect Type I hypersensitivity reactions and anaphylaxis to elevated IgE levels.
questions.reasoningChain: Bee sting anaphylaxis -> Type I hypersensitivity -> mediated by IgE.
optionExplanations: IgA is the primary immunoglobulin found in mucosal secretions.
IgE mediates immediate hypersensitivity reactions like anaphylaxis and allergic rhinitis.
IgM is the initial antibody produced during primary humoral immune responses.
IgG is the predominant circulating antibody involved in secondary immune responses and opsonization.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: Menke’s disease is due to a deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7A gene, which encodes a copper-transporting ATPase. This defect leads to systemic copper deficiency and impaired activity of copper-dependent enzymes, resulting in kinky hair, developmental regression, and arterial tortuosity.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize Menkes disease as a condition caused by impaired copper absorption and transport.
questions.reasoningChain: ATP7A gene mutation -> impaired copper transport -> Menkes disease.
optionExplanations: Zinc deficiency causes acrodermatitis enteropathica and impaired wound healing.
Menkes disease is characterized by systemic copper deficiency due to defective ATP7A.
Iron deficiency leads to microcytic hypochromic anemia.
Magnesium deficiency manifests as tetany, cardiac arrhythmias, and neuromuscular hyperexcitability.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: 1-month-old child is brought to the OPD for consultation regarding an empty scrotal sac. On examination B/L inguinal masses are palpable. What is the next step of management for this child?
options: Surgical exploration within the next 2 weeks
Wait and watch for spontaneous descent within the next 6 months
questions.answer: Wait and watch for spontaneous descent within the next 6 months
questions.explanation: In full-term infants with congenital cryptorchidism (undescended testes), spontaneous descent typically occurs within the first few months of life, most frequently by 3 to 6 months of age. Therefore, the standard management is to wait and monitor for spontaneous descent until 6 months of age before considering surgical orchidopexy.
questions.educationalObjective: Manage congenital undescended testes by observation until 6 months of age.
questions.reasoningChain: 1-month-old with undescended testes -> spontaneous descent possible -> watch and wait for 6 months.
optionExplanations: Karyotyping is reserved for bilateral cryptorchidism with ambiguous genitalia or dysmorphic features.
Surgical intervention is generally postponed until 6 months of age.
Early orchidopexy is premature at 1 month of life given potential spontaneous descent.
Waiting and watching for spontaneous descent within the first 6 months is the standard approach.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A Rh-negative mother delivered an Rh-positive baby and Coomb’s test was positive for the baby. What is the mechanism of hypersensitivity seen in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Rh incompatibility leading to hemolytic disease of the newborn involves maternal alloantibodies binding to fetal red blood cells, which are subsequently destroyed by cytotoxic mechanisms involving macrophages and Fc receptor-bearing cells. This is classified as a Type II hypersensitivity reaction, often referred to as antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Rh incompatibility hemolytic disease as a Type II hypersensitivity antibody-mediated reaction.
questions.reasoningChain: Rh incompatibility -> maternal antibodies coat fetal RBCs -> antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
optionExplanations: Antigen-dependent cellular cytotoxicity is not the standard classification term.
Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (Type II) describes maternal antibodies destroying Rh-positive fetal red cells.
Immune complex deposition characterizes Type III hypersensitivity reactions.
CD4-T cell-mediated cytokine release describes Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: Classical galactosemia is due to a deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Classical galactosemia is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT). This leads to the toxic accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver, kidneys, and brain, causing jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, and intellectual disability.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose classical galactosemia resulting from galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency.
questions.reasoningChain: Classical galactosemia -> GALT enzyme deficiency -> toxic metabolite accumulation.
optionExplanations: Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol and galactose to galactitol.
Galactokinase deficiency causes non-classical, milder galactosemia characterized by cataracts.
Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency causes classical galactosemia.
UDP-galactose-4-epimerase deficiency causes epimerase deficiency galactosemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: Which of the following molecules helps in the adhesion of the leucocyte to the endothelium during inflammation?
questions.explanation: During acute inflammation, leukocyte adhesion to the vascular endothelium is mediated by selectins (such as E-selectin and P-selectin) which bind to carbohydrate ligands on the leukocyte surface, producing the characteristic 'rolling' phenomenon prior to firm adhesion and transmigration.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify selectins as the adhesion molecules responsible for leukocyte rolling on endothelium.
questions.reasoningChain: Inflammation -> endothelial and leukocyte interaction -> selectins mediate leukocyte rolling and adhesion.
optionExplanations: P-selectin is a specific selectin, but selectins represent the broader class mediating initial rolling.
Platelet-activating factor causes platelet aggregation and bronchoconstriction.
Selectins are the specific family of adhesion molecules mediating leukocyte rolling.
Complement proteins are involved in opsonization, chemotaxis, and membrane attack complex formation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a function of glucagon?
questions.explanation: Glucagon is a catabolic hormone secreted during fasting states to elevate blood glucose levels. It stimulates gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and ketogenesis while inhibiting anabolic pathways such as glycolysis and glycogen synthesis.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize glycolysis as an anabolic/fed pathway inhibited or not stimulated by glucagon.
questions.reasoningChain: Glucagon acts during fasting -> stimulates catabolic pathways -> does not stimulate glycolysis.
optionExplanations: Glycolysis is stimulated by insulin in the fed state, not by glucagon.
Gluconeogenesis is stimulated by glucagon to produce glucose from non-carbohydrate sources.
Glycogenolysis is promoted by glucagon to release stored glucose.
Ketogenesis is promoted by glucagon during fasting to provide alternative fuel for the brain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: A 34-year-old male was on maize as a staple diet for a prolonged period. He presented with pain abdomen, loss of appetite, and diarrhoea. On examination, there was glossitis and a pigmented rash in sun-exposed areas. A lesion over his neck was seen as shown in the image below. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's presentation of diarrhea, dermatitis (Casal's necklace pigmented rash in sun-exposed areas), and glossitis following a maize-based diet is classic for pellagra. Pellagra is caused by a deficiency of niacin (Vitamin B3) or its precursor tryptophan, prevalent where corn is the dietary staple.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose pellagra based on the classic triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia due to niacin deficiency.
questions.reasoningChain: Maize diet + Casal's necklace dermatitis + diarrhea -> Pellagra.
optionExplanations: Pellagra matches the niacin deficiency signs including Casal's necklace and glossitis.
Scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency, presenting with petechiae, gingivitis, and poor wound healing.
Megaloblastic anemia is caused by vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, leading to fatigue and macrocytosis.
Beriberi is caused by thiamine deficiency, presenting with wet (cardiac) or dry (neurological) symptoms.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: Cholesterol is synthesized primarily from:
questions.explanation: Cholesterol synthesis begins in the cytoplasm and endoplasmic reticulum, where the primary precursor is acetyl-CoA derived from mitochondrial metabolism and transported via citrate. Acetyl-CoA molecules are condensed to form HMG-CoA, which is subsequently reduced by HMG-CoA reductase to mevalonate, the rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify acetyl-CoA as the primary precursor for cholesterol biosynthesis.
questions.reasoningChain: Cholesterol synthesis pathway -> initiated by condensation of acetyl-CoA units.
optionExplanations: Malonyl-CoA is primarily utilized in fatty acid chain elongation, not as the primary initiator for cholesterol.
Pyruvate is a glycolytic intermediate, not the direct precursor for cholesterol.
Oxaloacetate is an intermediate in the TCA cycle and gluconeogenesis.
Acetyl-CoA provides all the carbon atoms required for cholesterol synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: Which of the following enzymes is deficient in the autosomal recessive type of severe combined immunodeficiency?
questions.explanation: Autosomal recessive severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is most frequently caused by a deficiency of adenosine deaminase (ADA). ADA deficiency leads to the intracellular accumulation of toxic deoxyadenosine nucleotides, which preferentially impair the development and function of T and B lymphocytes.
questions.educationalObjective: Link adenosine deaminase deficiency to autosomal recessive severe combined immunodeficiency.
questions.reasoningChain: AR-SCID -> ADA deficiency -> purine metabolite toxicity affecting lymphocytes.
optionExplanations: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency causes urea cycle disorder with hyperammonemia.
Phosphomannose isomerase deficiency causes congenital disorder of glycosylation type 1b.
Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes SCID through purine toxicity in lymphocytes.
HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome characterized by self-mutilation and hyperuricemia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following options describes the symptoms seen classically in a patient bitten by the snake shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: The image displays a krait (Bungarus), which is a highly venomous elapid snake. Elapid snake venom contains potent neurotoxins (such as alpha-bungarotoxin) that block postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, classically resulting in progressive descending motor paralysis, cranial nerve palsies, and respiratory failure with minimal local tissue reaction.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify krait envenomation as causing prominent neurotoxicity and neuromuscular paralysis.
questions.reasoningChain: Krait snake identification -> elapid neurotoxin -> neurotoxicity and muscle paralysis.
optionExplanations: Non-poisonous snake bites lack envenomation fang marks and systemic neurological signs.
Severe edema and necrosis are typical of viperid (hemotoxic) snake bites.
Severe muscle necrosis and rhabdomyolysis are characteristic of sea snake envenomation.
Neurotoxicity and muscle paralysis characterize elapid bites such as cobras and kraits.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old woman was diagnosed with a large tumor in the right ovary and histopathology shows it has origin from all three germ layers. Which of the following is the most likely tumor she is having?
questions.explanation: Teratomas are germ cell tumors characterized histologically by the presence of mature or immature tissues derived from all three embryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm). Mature cystic teratomas (dermoid cysts) are the most common benign ovarian germ cell tumors in young women.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose ovarian teratoma based on tissue derivation from all three embryonic germ layers.
questions.reasoningChain: Tumor originating from all three germ layers -> Teratoma.
optionExplanations: Dysgerminoma is a malignant germ cell tumor composed of uniform cells resembling primordial germ cells.
Teratoma consists of elements derived from ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.
Thecoma is a sex cord-stromal ovarian tumor composed of lipid-laden stromal cells.
Theca lutein cyst is a functional non-neoplastic ovarian cyst associated with high hCG levels.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old male complained of fatigue for the past 1 year. Examination revealed massive splenomegaly. His blood workup shows the following findings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? ● Anemia ● Total leucocyte count - 1,50,000/microL ● Peripheral blood smear 60% neutrophils-6% Basophils-4% Eosinophils Myeloblasts, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes Myeloid to erythroid ratio – 18:1
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of massive splenomegaly, extremely elevated leukocyte count (150,000/microL) with a full spectrum of myeloid precursors in the peripheral blood (myelocytes, metamyelocytes, myeloblasts), and basophilia is pathognomonic for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose chronic myeloid leukemia based on marked leukocytosis with myeloid left shift and massive splenomegaly.
questions.reasoningChain: Massive splenomegaly + extreme leukocytosis with myeloid precursors -> CML.
optionExplanations: ALL typically presents with lymphadenopathy and bone marrow blast proliferation in children.
AML presents with cytopenias and high blast counts rather than a full spectrum of mature and immature myeloid cells.
CML presents with massive leukocytosis, basophilia, and myeloid precursors in peripheral blood.
CLL presents with mature-appearing lymphocytes and smudge cells in older adults.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: An 18-year-old male presented to the outpatient department with gum bleeding and fever for the past 2 months. General examination showed a pallor and the systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory examination revealed Hb level-3 gm/dI, TLC-1500/microL, and platelet count- 15000/micro. Peripheral smear shows macrocytes and the reticulocyte count is 0.5. Bone marrow examination revealed fatty streaks and absent megakaryocytes but no immature cells. What is the likely diagnosis? Hb-Hemoglobin TLC-Total leucocyte counts
questions.explanation: The clinical findings of severe pancytopenia (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia), low reticulocyte count, and a hypocellular (fatty) bone marrow with absent megakaryocytes and no abnormal or immature cells are diagnostic of idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose aplastic anemia based on pancytopenia, hypocellular bone marrow, and reticulocytopenia.
questions.reasoningChain: Pancytopenia + hypocellular fatty bone marrow -> Idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia.
optionExplanations: Idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia matches the findings of pancytopenia and fatty bone marrow.
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria presents with hemolytic anemia, thrombosis, and hemoglobinuria.
Myelodysplastic syndrome features hypercellular bone marrow with dysplastic changes and cytopenias.
Tuberculosis does not typically present with isolated hypocellular fatty bone marrow and pure pancytopenia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: A patient was referred by a doctor to a radiologist for a CT scan and the doctor was given money for the referral. What is this unethical act called?
questions.explanation: Dichotomy (fee-splitting) refers to the unethical practice where a physician accepts a financial commission, kickback, or reward from another physician, laboratory, or diagnostic center in exchange for patient referrals. This practice violates medical ethics codes globally.
questions.educationalObjective: Define dichotomy as the unethical financial kickback for patient medical referrals.
questions.reasoningChain: Doctor receiving money for patient referrals -> Dichotomy (fee-splitting).
optionExplanations: Dichotomy refers to fee-splitting or taking kickbacks for diagnostic referrals.
Medical maloccurence refers to adverse therapeutic outcomes without negligence.
Criminal negligence involves reckless disregard for patient safety resulting in injury or death.
Commission is a general term, but dichotomy is the specific medicolegal term for referral kickbacks.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A patient presents with repetitive episodes of heartburn and chest pain. What is the most common condition that causes these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Repetitive episodes of heartburn and retrosternal chest pain are the classic symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The most common underlying structural and inflammatory cause of these chronic symptoms is esophagitis resulting from prolonged acid exposure to the lower esophageal mucosa.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify esophagitis as the most common cause of recurrent heartburn and reflux symptoms.
questions.reasoningChain: Repetitive heartburn/chest pain -> reflux disease -> esophageal mucosal inflammation (esophagitis).
optionExplanations: Barrett's esophagus is a potential long-term complication of chronic GERD, not the most common overall cause.
Pneumonia presents with cough, fever, and consolidation rather than primary heartburn.
Myocardial infarction presents with ischemic cardiac chest pain, though it must be ruled out.
Esophagitis is the most common underlying cause of typical heartburn and reflux symptoms.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old female patient presented with malar rash, recurrent oral ulcers, and multiple joint pain. She has no relevant past history and does not take any medication. On further investigations, thrombocytopenia was seen and the Anti-Sm antibody was positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of malar rash, oral ulcers, and polyarthralgia combined with thrombocytopenia and positive Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibodies is diagnostic of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Anti-Sm antibody is highly specific for SLE.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose systemic lupus erythematosus using specific autoantibodies like Anti-Sm and classic clinical criteria.
questions.reasoningChain: Malar rash + oral ulcers + Anti-Sm antibody positivity -> Systemic lupus erythematosus.
optionExplanations: Scleroderma features skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, and anti-Scl-70 antibodies.
Sjogren's syndrome presents with dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia).
Rheumatoid arthritis features symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis and anti-CCP antibodies.
Systemic lupus erythematosus matches malar rash, cytopenias, and Anti-Sm antibody.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old man presents with an excessive desire for sexual intercourse. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Satyriasis is defined as an excessive, uncontrollable desire for sexual intercourse in males. The corresponding term in females is nymphomania. Both represent hypersexuality disorders categorized under sexual jurisprudence and abnormal psychological conditions.
questions.educationalObjective: Define satyriasis as excessive hypersexuality in males.
questions.reasoningChain: Excessive desire for sexual intercourse in a male -> Satyriasis.
optionExplanations: Satyriasis is the term for excessive sexual desire in males.
Frotteurism is a paraphilic disorder involving touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person.
Nymphomania refers to excessive sexual desire in females.
Masochism involves sexual arousal derived from experiencing pain or humiliation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A baby playing unsupervised was brought with complaints of difficulty in swallowing for the last few hours. The x-ray image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The chest radiograph demonstrates a radiopaque coin oriented in the coronal plane within the upper midline mediastinum, which is characteristic of an esophageal foreign body. In contrast, foreign bodies in the trachea typically present with the coin oriented in the sagittal plane on lateral views due to tracheal cartilage anatomy.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify a radiopaque coin in the esophagus on pediatric radiographs based on its coronal orientation.
questions.reasoningChain: Radiopaque coin seen in anterior-posterior and lateral views in the upper GI tract -> Foreign body in the esophagus.
optionExplanations: Foreign body in the trachea would show sagittal orientation on lateral chest radiographs.
Foreign body in the esophagus is confirmed by the coronal orientation of the coin on AP/lateral views.
Foreign body in the lungs typically localizes to distal bronchial branches with hyperinflation or atelectasis.
Foreign body in the pleura is extremely rare and associated with penetrating trauma.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: Identify the plant shown in the image below.
questions.explanation: The plant depicted in the image is Parthenium hysterophorus (congress grass), an invasive weed known for causing contact dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, and asthma due to its allergenic sesquiterpene lactones (such as parthenin). In forensic toxicology, it is also studied as an irritant weed.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Parthenium hysterophorus from its botanical features and associated allergic contact dermatitis.
questions.reasoningChain: Visual identification of invasive weed with dissected leaves and small white flowers -> Parthenium hysterophorus.
optionExplanations: Parthenium hysterophorus is identified by its distinctive leaves and small white flower clusters.
Datura stramonium features trumpet-shaped flowers and spiny seed capsules containing anticholinergic alkaloids.
Digitalis purpurea displays prominent bell-shaped purple flowers containing cardiac glycosides.
Calotropis gigantea produces milky latex and large grayish-green leaves with waxy flowers.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A middle-aged man working in sandblasting developed hemoptysis, and a productive cough. A chest x-ray is suggestive of tuberculosis. Which of the following is associated with the same?
questions.explanation: Sandblasting exposes workers to crystalline silica dust inhalation. Chronic inhalation leads to nodular pulmonary fibrosis known as silicosis, which significantly increases the susceptibility to mycobacterial infections, presenting with hemoptysis, productive cough, and radiographic findings mimicking tuberculosis.
questions.educationalObjective: Link sandblasting exposure to silicosis and increased tuberculosis susceptibility.
questions.reasoningChain: Sandblasting exposure + upper lobe nodular fibrosis + hemoptysis -> Silicosis.
optionExplanations: Asbestosis is caused by asbestos fiber inhalation, typically producing lower lobe interstitial fibrosis and pleural plaques.
Silicosis results from silica dust inhalation during sandblasting and predisposes to tuberculosis.
Anthracosis is coal worker's pneumoconiosis resulting from coal dust accumulation.
Siderosis is caused by iron oxide particle inhalation, typically benign without significant fibrosis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: In the case of drowning, the following finding is seen at autopsy. What is it called?
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates a hand tightly clutching weeds and mud, a phenomenon known as cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor). This occurs immediately at the moment of death due to severe nervous tension or violent physical activity, locking muscles in place and serving as definitive proof of antemortem drowning when a body is recovered from water.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify cadaveric spasm as an instantaneous stiffening of muscles at death, often seen in drowning victims clutching objects.
questions.reasoningChain: Hand clutching weeds tightly at time of death -> Cadaveric spasm.
optionExplanations: Cadaveric spasm involves immediate muscular contraction persisting postmortem, typical in drowning.
Cutis anserina (goosebumps) results from rigor mortis of arrector pili muscles post-mortem.
Rigor mortis develops gradually hours after death due to ATP depletion, not instantaneously.
Washerwoman's hands refer to skin maceration and wrinkling caused by prolonged immersion in water.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: Which of the following is considered a universal methyl group donor in various biochemical reactions?
questions.explanation: S-Adenosylmethionine (SAMe) serves as the primary and universal methyl group donor in numerous biochemical transmethylation reactions throughout the body, transferring its methyl group to substrates such as DNA, proteins, and lipids, thereby converting into S-adenosylhomocysteine.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify S-Adenosylmethionine as the universal methyl group donor in biochemical reactions.
questions.reasoningChain: Universal methyl group donor in transmethylation -> S-AdenosylMethionine.
optionExplanations: Glucose-6-phosphate is an intermediate in glycolysis and glycogen metabolism.
Acetyl-CoA is a donor of acetyl groups in acetylation and the primary precursor for lipid synthesis.
S-AdenosylMethionine acts as the primary methyl group donor in cellular metabolism.
S-Adenosyl Serine is not the primary physiological methyl donor.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: Identify the odor produced by the change seen in the image below.
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates mummification, a preservation process occurring in hot, dry, and arid environments where tissues undergo severe desiccation, preventing bacterial putrefaction. Because putrefaction and bacterial gas formation are arrested, mummified bodies are characteristically odorless.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that mummification results in a dry, well-preserved body that is odorless due to lack of putrefaction.
questions.reasoningChain: Mummification (desiccation) -> absence of putrefaction -> odorless condition.
optionExplanations: Odorless characterizes mummified remains due to complete tissue desiccation halting bacterial putrefaction.
Pungent odors are associated with chemical poisons or decomposition gases, not mummies.
Putrid odors occur during advanced putrefaction and tissue liquefaction.
Offensive odors are typical of wet decomposition, unlike dry mummification.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: Thermogenin protein is mainly found in…
questions.explanation: Thermogenin (UCP1, uncoupling protein 1) is a specialized mitochondrial inner membrane protein found predominantly in brown adipose tissue. It functions by uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation from ATP synthesis, dissipating the proton gradient as heat in non-shivering thermogenesis.
questions.educationalObjective: Locate thermogenin protein within the inner mitochondrial membrane.
questions.reasoningChain: Thermogenin uncouples oxidative phosphorylation -> located in mitochondria.
optionExplanations: Golgi complex is responsible for protein glycosylation and packaging.
Endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes lipids and proteins.
Mitochondria house thermogenin in the inner membrane for heat generation.
Nucleus stores and replicates genetic material.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and was discharged after removing the drain tube on the first postoperative day. On day two, the patient came back to the hospital with complaints of increasing abdominal pain and was febrile on examination. On ultrasound examination, there was a 5 x 5 cm collection in the subhepatic space. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: Postoperative fever, increasing abdominal pain, and subhepatic fluid collection shortly after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy strongly indicate a bile leak, most commonly from the cystic duct stump or a minor radical duct injury. Fluid collections in the subhepatic space require imaging and potential drainage.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify bile leak as a primary cause of subhepatic fluid collection following cholecystectomy.
questions.reasoningChain: Post-cholecystectomy subhepatic fluid collection + fever/pain -> Bile leak.
optionExplanations: Infection can accompany fluid collections, but the direct surgical cause of subhepatic collection is a bile leak.
Surgical site pain is superficial and does not cause intra-abdominal fluid collections.
Bile leak is the specific etiology of subhepatic fluid accumulation after cholecystectomy.
Retained gallstones typically present with cholangitis or jaundice rather than isolated subhepatic collections.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A 48-year-old patient presented with scrotal swelling. Investigations for testicular tumors revealed that LDH was raised but AFP was within normal limits. Following orchidectomy, the following histological picture was observed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The histological image demonstrates sheets of uniform, clear-to-polyhedral cells separated by delicate fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes, which is classic for a seminoma. Seminomas typically present with elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) while alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) remains strictly normal.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose seminoma based on characteristic histology and normal alpha-fetoprotein levels.
questions.reasoningChain: Testicular tumor with normal AFP + lymphocytic septa and uniform clear cells -> Seminoma.
optionExplanations: Yolk sac tumors typically feature Schiller-Duval bodies and elevated AFP levels.
Teratomas contain mature tissues from multiple germ layers.
Seminoma features uniform clear cells with fibrous septa and lymphocytic infiltration, with normal AFP.
Embryonal carcinoma shows pleomorphic cells forming glandular or papillary structures.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: Identify the post-mortem finding in a patient with a stab wound on the left side of the chest.
questions.explanation: The images demonstrate hemopericardium and a tense, blood-filled pericardial sac (Image B) compressing the heart, which is pathognomonic for cardiac tamponade resulting from a penetrating chest wound or stab injury to the heart or great vessels.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify cardiac tamponade at autopsy following chest trauma.
questions.reasoningChain: Stab wound to chest + blood accumulation in pericardial sac -> Cardiac tamponade.
optionExplanations: Cardiac tamponade is demonstrated by blood filling and distending the pericardial sac, compressing the heart.
Fat necrosis involves saponification of adipose tissue, typically in pancreatitis or breast trauma.
Hemothorax involves blood accumulation within the pleural cavity, not strictly the pericardium.
Pulmonary embolism involves thromboembolic occlusion of the pulmonary arterial tree.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: A young boy presented with fissured tongue, lips, and lesions in the angle of the mouth as shown below. On investigation, he had low RBC glutathione reductase activity. Which vitamin is deficient here?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of angular stomatitis, cheilosis, and glossitis combined with low erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity points directly to a deficiency of riboflavin (Vitamin B2). Erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity serves as a functional enzymatic assay for riboflavin status.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose riboflavin deficiency based on angular stomatitis and decreased red blood cell glutathione reductase activity.
questions.reasoningChain: Cheilosis + glossitis + low RBC glutathione reductase -> Riboflavin deficiency.
optionExplanations: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.
Vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia).
Biotin deficiency causes dermatitis, alopecia, and neurological symptoms.
Riboflavin deficiency manifests with angular cheilitis, glossitis, and low glutathione reductase activity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old lady is found to have a gallbladder polyp of size 5 mm on abdominal USG with no associated gallbladder stones. She appears to be healthy and is asymptomatic. How will you manage this patient?
questions.explanation: According to current guidelines, asymptomatic gallbladder polyps smaller than 10 mm (5 mm in this case) without gallstones or high-risk features carry an extremely low risk of malignancy and should be managed conservatively with regular ultrasound follow-up.
questions.educationalObjective: Manage small (<10 mm) asymptomatic gallbladder polyps with serial ultrasound follow-up.
questions.reasoningChain: Gallbladder polyp <10 mm + asymptomatic -> Regular follow-up USG.
optionExplanations: Regular follow-up every 6-12 months (or per local protocols) is recommended for small benign polyps.
Polypectomy is not performed standalone; cholecystectomy is the surgical approach for high-risk polyps.
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is indicated for polyps >10 mm, symptomatic polyps, or those with gallstones.
Open cholecystectomy is unnecessarily invasive for small, asymptomatic polyps.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most common side effect of cholecystectomy?
questions.explanation: Following cholecystectomy, continuous unregulated bile flow into the small intestine occurs because the gallbladder is no longer present to store and concentrate bile. This can result in fat malabsorption and steatorrhea, which is recognized as a frequent physiological consequence or side effect of the procedure.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize steatorrhea as a common metabolic side effect following cholecystectomy due to loss of bile storage.
questions.reasoningChain: Removal of gallbladder -> continuous bile delivery -> fat malabsorption/steatorrhea.
optionExplanations: Acute kidney injury is not a direct, common complication of routine cholecystectomy.
Osteoporosis is unrelated to gallbladder removal.
Steatorrhea is a recognized consequence resulting from altered bile pool kinetics and delivery.
Colorectal cancer has no direct causal link proven with cholecystectomy.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: Identify the test shown in the image below.
questions.explanation: The microscopic image displays rhomboid or needle-shaped dark brown crystals of hematin chloride (haematin hydrochloride), which form when blood stains are treated with glacial acetic acid and sodium chloride. This confirms the Teichmann test (hemin crystal test) used for forensic blood identification.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the Teichmann test by its characteristic brown rhomboid hemin chloride crystals.
questions.reasoningChain: Microscopic brown rhomboid crystals from blood + glacial acetic acid -> Teichmann test.
optionExplanations: Barberio test is a chemical micro-test used for identifying seminal stains via spermin picrate crystals.
Florence test is another test for semen, producing choline periodide crystals.
Takayama test produces pink feathery crystals of pyridine hemochromogen.
Teichmann test produces brown rhomboid crystals of hematin chloride (hemin).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: An elderly woman presented with symptoms of confusion, thirst, and abdominal pain. On examination, she had pallor and thoracic spine tenderness. Her lab investigations showed the following findings. An x-ray of her skull is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Hb – 6.9g/dL WBC 4000/cm3 with normal differential count Serum calcium 13 mg/dL Creatinine 2.3mg/dL Total protein 9g/dL Albumin 2.4g/dL Urinalysis: positive for Bence-Jones proteins
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of anemia, hypercalcemia, renal impairment, elevated total protein with an albumin-globulin gap, and Bence-Jones proteinuria, along with punched-out osteolytic lesions on skull radiography, is diagnostic of multiple myeloma.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose multiple myeloma based on lytic skull lesions, hypercalcemia, renal failure, and Bence-Jones proteins.
questions.reasoningChain: Osteolytic skull lesions + hypercalcemia + Bence-Jones proteins -> Multiple myeloma.
optionExplanations: Metastatic breast cancer can cause lytic lesions and hypercalcemia, but Bence-Jones proteins point specifically to myeloma.
Multiple myeloma is confirmed by osteolytic lesions, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, and paraproteinemia.
Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia and bone resorption, but lacks monoclonal proteins and Bence-Jonesuria.
Milk alkali syndrome involves hypercalcemia from excessive calcium and alkali intake.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.prompt: A 10 year old boy rapidly develops hypoglycemia after moderate activity. Blood examination reveals raised levels of ketone bodies, lactic acid, and triglycerides. On examination, the liver and kidneys are found to be enlarged. Which of the following would be seen in excess amounts in the liver of this child?
questions.explanation: The clinical vignette describes Von Gierke disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I), caused by a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase. This prevents the liver from releasing free glucose into the blood, leading to severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and massive accumulation of glycogen and glucose-6-phosphate within hepatocytes.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose von Gierke disease resulting from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency and intracellular G6P accumulation.
questions.reasoningChain: Hypoglycemia + hepatomegaly + lactic acidosis (GSD I) -> Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency -> accumulation of glucose-6-phosphate.
optionExplanations: Glucose-6-phosphate accumulates in the liver and kidneys due to glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency in GSD Type I.
Glucose-1-phosphate is an intermediate in glycogenolysis upstream of the metabolic block.
Glucose-1,6-diphosphate is an enzymatic cofactor in glycolysis.
Glycosaminoglycans accumulate in mucopolysaccharidoses, not glycogen storage diseases.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A young man presents to the emergency department with complaints of severe abdominal pain and 3 episodes of vomiting in the past 9 hours. He says that the pain radiates to the back and is partially relieved by bending forwards. The abdominal radiograph of the patient is given below which shows a ‘colon cut-off sign’. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Severe epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back that is relieved by leaning forward, accompanied by vomiting, is characteristic of acute pancreatitis. The abdominal radiograph demonstrating a 'colon cut-off sign' (localized spasm of the descending colon adjacent to the inflamed pancreas) supports this diagnosis.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose acute pancreatitis based on clinical presentation and the 'colon cut-off sign' on abdominal imaging.
