questions.explanation: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) is caused by hypertrophy of the circular smooth muscle of the pylorus, not the longitudinal muscle. It presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and is readily diagnosed by ultrasound.
questions.educationalObjective: Correctly identify that CHPS involves hypertrophy of circular smooth muscle rather than longitudinal muscle.
questions.reasoningChain: Pyloric stenosis is characterized by hypertrophy of the circular muscle layer, leading to gastric outlet obstruction.
optionExplanations: Presents with non-bilious vomiting due to obstruction proximal to the ampulla of Vater.
Caused by hypertrophy of circular muscles, making option B the false statement requested by the prompt.
USG is highly sensitive and specific in measuring pyloric muscle thickness and length.
Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis results from persistent loss of gastric hydrochloric acid.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A chronic-alcoholic presents to the emergency room with acute pain abdomen in the epigastric region radiating to the back with nausea, anorexia, and occasional vomiting. Investigations showed elevated amylase levels and total count. Likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: A chronic alcoholic presenting with acute epigastric pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea, vomiting, and elevated serum amylase, classic for acute pancreatitis. Alcohol abuse is a major etiology of acute pancreatitis.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose acute pancreatitis based on classic epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated amylase in an alcoholic patient.
questions.reasoningChain: Alcoholism precipitates pancreatic enzyme activation, causing acute epigastric pain radiating to the back and hyperamylasemia.
optionExplanations: Acute hepatitis presents with right upper quadrant pain and jaundice rather than severe back-radiating epigastric pain.
Acute pancreatitis presents with acute epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and elevated amylase.
Acute cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain with a positive Murphy's sign, not radiating to the back.
Acute appendicitis starts periumbilical and shifts to the right lower quadrant with localized tenderness.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: In which poisoning is cherry red hypostasis seen on post-mortem examination?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning produces characteristic cherry-red or bright pink hypostasis and post-mortem lividity due to the formation of carboxyhemoglobin, which imparts a bright red color to the blood and tissues.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify cherry-red hypostasis as a classic post-mortem finding in carbon monoxide poisoning.
questions.reasoningChain: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin to form carboxyhemoglobin, creating a cherry-red discoloration of post-mortem hypostasis.
optionExplanations: CO poisoning produces cherry-red hypostasis due to carboxyhemoglobin formation.
Hydrogen sulphide poisoning causes dark or greenish-brown discoloration due to sulfhemoglobin formation.
Yellow phosphorus poisoning causes gastrointestinal irritation and garlic odor, without cherry-red hypostasis.
Hydrogen cyanide poisoning causes bright red venous blood due to cellular hypoxia, but cherry-red hypostasis is classic for CO.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: All of the following changes occur in chronic starvation except?
questions.explanation: In chronic starvation, the body undergoes profound catabolism, metabolic slowdown, and depletion of energy reserves. This leads to hypothermia (not hyperthermia), physical exhaustion, generalized muscle and organ atrophy (including the heart), and hypotension.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that chronic starvation leads to hypothermia rather than hyperthermia.
questions.reasoningChain: Starvation decreases basal metabolic rate and fat stores, resulting in hypothermia and emaciation.
optionExplanations: Hyperthermia does not occur in starvation; instead, basal metabolic reduction leads to hypothermia.
Exhaustion and severe generalized weakness are hallmark clinical features of starvation.
Heart atrophy occurs as cardiac muscle is broken down for energy during prolonged starvation.
Hypotension is common due to decreased cardiac output and intravascular volume depletion.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: The shelf life of copper T 380 A is
questions.explanation: Copper T 380A is an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) approved for long-term use with a designated shelf life and effective duration of 10 years in national family planning programs.
questions.educationalObjective: Recall that the effective duration and shelf life of Copper T 380A is 10 years.
questions.reasoningChain: Copper T 380A provides safe, highly effective contraception for up to 10 years.
optionExplanations: 3 years is incorrect for Copper T 380A (some other IUD models have shorter spans).
5 years is the duration for devices like LNG-IUS or older copper devices, not Copper T 380A.
7 years is incorrect for this specific intrauterine device.
10 years is the approved effective lifespan and usage duration for Copper T 380A.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: All of the following are superior mediastinal tumors except:
questions.explanation: Common masses found in the superior and anterior mediastinum include the '4 Ts': Thymus, Thyroid, Terrible lymphoma, and Teratoma (germ cell tumors). However, parathyroid adenomas or ectopic parathyroid tissue can also be found in the superior/anterior mediastinum, whereas primary lymphomas commonly present in the anterior mediastinum or middle mediastinum nodes, making the classification nuanced. Wait, looking closely at classic anterior/superior mediastinal tumors: thyroid, thymus, parathyroid, and teratoma are typical, while lymphoma typically arises in the anterior mediastinum lymph nodes. Actually, parathyroid tumors are posterior/superior mediastinal, but lymphoma is primarily anterior. Let us review the best distractor: lymphoma is typically anterior, but thymic, thyroid, and parathyroid tumors occupy the superior mediastinum. Wait, lymphadenopathy/lymphoma is anterior mediastinal. Let's verify standard textbook teaching: superior mediastinal tumors include thyroid, thymus, parathyroid, and cysts. Lymphoma is anterior mediastinal. Therefore, lymphoma is correctly identified as the exception.
questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate between superior and anterior mediastinal masses in surgical anatomy.
questions.reasoningChain: Lymphoma predominantly involves the anterior mediastinal lymph node compartments rather than being primarily superior mediastinal.
optionExplanations: Parathyroid tumors and ectopic tissue can occur in the superior/anterior mediastinum.
Lymphoma is primarily classified as an anterior mediastinal mass rather than strictly superior mediastinal.
Thyroid masses (retrosternal goiter) extend directly into the superior mediastinum.
Thymus tumors and thymomas are classically located in the anterior and superior mediastinum.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: A public witness of the incident is asked to attend the court and record his evidence. Which type of evidence is provided by the witness to the court?
questions.explanation: When a witness attends court in person and provides verbal testimony under oath regarding facts they personally observed, this testimony is legally classified as oral evidence.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify witness testimony delivered verbally in court as oral evidence.
questions.reasoningChain: A witness speaking directly in court provides verbal testimony, which is termed oral evidence.
optionExplanations: Oral evidence consists of statements made by witnesses in court under oath regarding direct observations.
Hearsay evidence is second-hand information where the witness reports what someone else said.
Subpoena is a legal writ requiring a person to appear in court, not a type of evidence.
Circumstantial evidence is indirect evidence from which an inference must be drawn to establish a fact.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A 73 yr old male smoker with a past history of coronary artery disease presents with blackening of the toes. An image of the foot is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This elderly patient with cardiovascular risk factors and smoking history presents with toe necrosis. The image shows dry gangrene of the toes. Atherosclerosis leads to chronic peripheral arterial disease, causing progressive luminal narrowing and critical limb ischemia. Buerger's disease typically affects younger male smokers with distal small-to-medium vessel involvement, making atherosclerosis the appropriate diagnosis for this age group.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify atherosclerosis as the leading cause of critical limb ischemia and dry gangrene in elderly patients.
questions.reasoningChain: Smoking and CAD risk factors lead to peripheral arterial disease, causing critical ischemia and dry gangrene in the toes.
optionExplanations: Typically affects younger male smokers presenting with distal extremity ischemia and superficial thrombophlebitis.
Correct answer. Older adults with cardiovascular risk factors develop progressive lower extremity ischemia leading to gangrene.
Characterized by episodic vasospasm of digits triggered by cold or stress, presenting with color changes.
Large vessel vasculitis presenting with headache, jaw claudication, and visual symptoms, not extremity gangrene.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old woman after thyroidectomy comes to you for a 2nd opinion for further treatment of papillary thyroid cancer. What would you recommend for this patient?
questions.explanation: Post-thyroidectomy management of papillary thyroid cancer often involves radioiodine (I-131) ablation or scanning to detect and treat residual thyroid tissue or metastatic disease. Although guidelines vary depending on risk stratification, radioiodine is a cornerstone of surveillance and adjuvant therapy.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the role of radioiodine in the staging and follow-up management of differentiated thyroid cancers.
questions.reasoningChain: Papillary thyroid cancer post-thyroidectomy requires remnant ablation or disease detection, for which radioiodine is utilized.
optionExplanations: External beam radiotherapy is generally reserved for advanced, unresectable, or radioiodine-refractory tumors.
Chemotherapy has very limited role in differentiated thyroid cancer, reserved for refractory cases.
Correct answer. Radioiodine scans and therapy are standard follow-up modalities after thyroidectomy for papillary cancer.
Active surveillance is generally not recommended immediately after surgery for intermediate-to-high risk or incompletely staged disease.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a symptom associated with chronic cocaine abuse?
options: Dilated pupils, rapid pulse and sweating.
Hallucination of insects crawling on the skin (formication).
questions.answer: Dilated pupils, rapid pulse and sweating.
questions.explanation: Chronic cocaine abuse leads to sympathomimetic toxicity, nasal septal perforation, palatal destruction, skin formication, and characteristic dental wear or discoloration. Dilated pupils, rapid pulse, and sweating are acute sympathomimetic manifestations rather than symptoms unique to chronic, long-term abuse alone, though they occur acutely. The question asks for features NOT uniquely associated with chronic abuse.
questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate acute sympathomimetic toxidrome features from chronic complications of cocaine abuse.
questions.reasoningChain: Acute sympathetic overactivity causes dilated pupils and tachycardia, whereas nasal perforation and formication are chronic effects.
optionExplanations: Nasal and palatal perforation are well-known structural complications of chronic intranasal cocaine use.
Correct answer. Autonomic signs like mydriasis, tachycardia, and diaphoresis are acute presentations of toxicity.
Black discoloration of tongue and teeth can be seen with chronic poor hygiene and substance use.
Formication, the tactile hallucination of insects crawling under the skin, is a classic chronic cocaine psychosis symptom.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Confidentiality is maintained in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Counselling is a one-on-one confidential interaction between a healthcare provider and a client, allowing personal concerns to be discussed securely. In contrast, group discussions, panel discussions, and seminars involve multiple participants and audiences where absolute medical confidentiality cannot be guaranteed.
questions.educationalObjective: Understand that medical confidentiality is strictly maintained during individual health counseling sessions.
questions.reasoningChain: Counselling involves private one-on-one communication, ensuring patient privacy and confidentiality.
optionExplanations: Group discussions involve multiple participants, preventing strict individual confidentiality.
Correct answer. Counselling is a private, confidential interaction between counselor and client.
Panel discussions involve a group presenting to an audience, lacking privacy.
Seminars are educational presentations to a larger audience without personal confidentiality.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A patient who was diagnosed with prostate cancer is being investigated. The bone scan is reported as a super scan with increased uptake in the bones and reduced activity in the spleen. What is the reason for this super scan appearance?
options: Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis
Decreased uptake by adrenal glands and kidney
questions.answer: Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis
questions.explanation: A 'super scan' on bone scintigraphy occurs due to extremely high metabolic bone turnover and diffuse skeletal uptake of the radiotracer, leading to high bone-to-soft tissue contrast where renal visualization is absent or severely diminished. In prostate cancer, this reflects widespread osteoblastic metastases replacing normal marrow.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the scintigraphic features and underlying cause of a bone super scan in metastatic prostate cancer.
questions.reasoningChain: Prostate cancer metastasizes to bones, causing widespread osteoblastic activity that absorbs all radiotracer, producing a super scan.
optionExplanations: Correct answer. Diffuse skeletal metastasis results in intense uniform tracer uptake leaving little for renal excretion.
While prostate cancer causes the metastases, the direct physiological mechanism of the image is the widespread metastatic burden.
Normal bone uptake is physiologic; the super scan specifically denotes pathological diffuse skeletal involvement.
Kidney tracer clearance is masked by the overwhelmingly high skeletal avidity for the radiopharmaceutical.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old factory worker was brought to the emergency room with complaints of headache, vomiting, and blurring of vision after he consumed local spirit. Which of the following is used for the treatment of his condition?
questions.explanation: Consumption of illicit local spirit ('hooch') frequently carries the risk of methanol contamination. Methanol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase into toxic formic acid, causing severe metabolic acidosis and blindness. Fomepizole is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase used as the primary antidote.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify fomepizole as the specific antidote for methanol poisoning.
questions.reasoningChain: Local spirit consumption suggests methanol toxicity, which is treated with alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitors like fomepizole.
optionExplanations: Correct answer. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing the formation of toxic methanol metabolites.
Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist used for benzodiazepine overdose reversal.
N-acetyl cysteine is the specific antidote used for paracetamol (acetaminophen) toxicity.
Naloxone is an opioid receptor antagonist used to reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old male patient presents with hematuria and a neovascular mass in the left kidney on a CT scan, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The CT scan demonstrates a well-circumscribed renal mass with macroscopic fat attenuation, which is pathognomonic for renal angiomyolipoma. Angiomyolipomas are benign mesenchymal tumors composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and mature adipose tissue. They can present with hematuria or spontaneous hemorrhage if large.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize renal angiomyolipoma on CT by the presence of internal fat density within the mass.
questions.reasoningChain: CT shows a renal mass containing fat density, characteristic of a benign angiomyolipoma.
optionExplanations: Typically solid enhancing renal masses without internal macroscopic fat density on CT.
Benign epithelial renal tumors that cannot be reliably distinguished from carcinoma on imaging alone.
Correct answer. Presence of macroscopic fat within a renal mass on CT confirms angiomyolipoma.
Simple renal cysts are fluid-filled with water attenuation and smooth walls, lacking solid components or fat.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: An 8 weeks pregnant woman, working in an industry, consults a doctor. According to the ESI act, what is the duration of maternity leave that she can get?
options: 28 weeks, starting from 4 weeks after delivery
26 weeks, starting from 8 weeks before delivery
questions.answer: 26 weeks, starting from 8 weeks before delivery
questions.explanation: Under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act in India, female workers are entitled to paid maternity leave. Recent amendments expanded this duration to 26 weeks, with the provision that it can commence up to 8 weeks prior to the expected date of delivery.
questions.educationalObjective: State the maternity leave provisions under the ESI Act for insured female workers.
questions.reasoningChain: ESI Act maternity benefit grants 26 weeks of paid leave starting up to 8 weeks before delivery.
optionExplanations: 4 months is insufficient compared to the updated statutory maternity leave duration.
The timing and total duration do not align with standard statutory labor regulations.
Correct answer. The statutory maternity benefit provides 26 weeks, starting up to 8 weeks prior to delivery.
9 months corresponds to the gestation period, not the duration of statutory maternity leave.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the best imaging modality to diagnose neuroendocrine tumors (NETs)?
questions.explanation: Neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) express somatostatin receptors, making functional imaging with Gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/CT scan the most sensitive and specific modality for diagnosis, staging, and localizing primary or metastatic lesions compared to conventional anatomical imaging.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify PET imaging using receptor-specific tracers as the best modality for neuroendocrine tumors.
questions.reasoningChain: NETs overexpress somatostatin receptors, allowing PET scans with radiolabeled analogs to achieve superior diagnostic accuracy.
optionExplanations: Ultrasound has low sensitivity for detecting small or deep-seated neuroendocrine lesions.
CT provides anatomical detail but has lower sensitivity for small NET metastases than functional PET.
MRI is useful for specific organs like the liver but is not the primary whole-body modality of choice.
Correct answer. PET imaging targeting somatostatin receptors offers the highest sensitivity for neuroendocrine tumors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 29-year-old male patient presents to the OPD with a 10-year history of coarse facial features and progressive enlargement of the hands and feet. Laboratory evaluation revealed elevated IGF-1 and non-suppressible growth hormone levels after the 75 g glucose challenge test. A diagnosis of acromegaly is made. Which of the following drugs is preferred for the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: Acromegaly is caused by excess growth hormone secretion, typically from a pituitary adenoma. When surgery is not curative or feasible, medical management includes somatostatin analogs such as lanreotide depot or octreotide, which suppress growth hormone release and lower IGF-1 levels.
questions.educationalObjective: Select somatostatin analogs as medical therapy for acromegaly when surgery is insufficient.
questions.reasoningChain: Acromegaly involves excessive growth hormone, treated medically with somatostatin analogs like lanreotide.
optionExplanations: Correct answer. Lanreotide depot is a long-acting somatostatin analog used to lower growth hormone and IGF-1.
Terlipressin is a vasopressin analog used primarily for variceal bleeding and hepatorenal syndrome.
Ketoconazole is an antifungal agent sometimes used off-label for Cushing syndrome, not acromegaly.
Leuprolide is a GnRH agonist used in sex hormone-dependent conditions such as prostate cancer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Genetic testing for BRCA 1/BRCA 2 is indicated for all of the following except:
options: a.Breast cancer diagnosed in a postmenopausal female >50 years of age
questions.answer: a.Breast cancer diagnosed in a postmenopausal female >50 years of age
questions.explanation: Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations is indicated in patients with a strong family or personal history suggestive of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. This includes bilateral breast cancer, male breast cancer, and early-onset breast cancer (typically diagnosed under age 50), whereas postmenopausal breast cancer diagnosed over age 50 without other high-risk features is an exception.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify appropriate clinical indications for BRCA1/2 genetic testing based on age and tumor characteristics.
questions.reasoningChain: BRCA testing is indicated for early onset, bilateral, or male breast cancers, but not typically for sporadic postmenopausal breast cancer.
optionExplanations: Correct answer. Sporadic breast cancer diagnosed after age 50 in postmenopausal women without strong family history is an exception.
Male breast cancer has a high association with genetic mutations, making testing indicated.
Bilateral breast cancer raises suspicion for a hereditary cancer syndrome, warranting genetic evaluation.
The combination of breast and ovarian cancer strongly suggests a BRCA mutation and mandates testing.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Which of the following is a first-line antitubercular drug prescribed in the initial 2 months of treatment?
questions.explanation: Under national tuberculosis guidelines (NTEP in India), the intensive phase standard first-line regimen consists of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (HRZE) for the first 2 months. Ethambutol is thus a key first-line drug prescribed during this initial phase.
questions.educationalObjective: List ethambutol as part of the standard first-line intensive phase regimen for tuberculosis.
questions.reasoningChain: First-line TB treatment includes ethambutol alongside isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide during the intensive phase.
optionExplanations: Streptomycin is used as an injectable second-line or alternative first-line agent, no longer standard in the initial oral intensive phase.
Correct answer. Ethambutol is a standard first-line drug included in the 2-month intensive phase regimen.
Linezolid is a reserve second-line agent used in drug-resistant tuberculosis regimens.
Levofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone used as a second-line drug for drug-resistant tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A 51-year-old lady presents with complaints of a mass in the right breast. On examination, the mass was larger than 5 cm and ipsilateral mobile axillary lymph nodes were present. What is the staging, considering the mass is malignant?
questions.explanation: According to the TNM staging system for breast cancer, a tumor size greater than 5 cm is classified as T3. The presence of clinically mobile ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes is classified as N1. Without evidence of distant metastasis, it is staged as cT3N1M0.
questions.educationalObjective: Determine the clinical TNM stage for breast cancer based on tumor size and lymph node status.
questions.reasoningChain: Tumor > 5 cm corresponds to T3, mobile ipsilateral axillary nodes correspond to N1, yielding cT3N1M0.
optionExplanations: Correct answer. Tumor > 5 cm is T3, mobile ipsilateral nodes are N1, and no distant metastasis is M0.
T4 denotes extension to chest wall or skin, which is not described in the prompt.
cT4N1M0 overestimates the tumor classification since the size given is simply >5 cm without chest wall involvement.
The prefix 'y' is used for staging during or after neoadjuvant therapy, not for primary pretreatment staging.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: The process in the oxidation pond is __
options: Aerobic during day, anaerobic during night
Anaerobic during day, aerobic during night
questions.answer: Aerobic during day, anaerobic during night
questions.explanation: Oxidation ponds utilize natural wastewater treatment via algal-bacterial symbiosis. During the day, sunlight enables algae to perform photosynthesis, producing oxygen that sustains aerobic bacteria in breaking down organic matter. At night, in the absence of sunlight, photosynthesis ceases, and conditions become anaerobic as biological oxygen consumption continues.
questions.educationalObjective: Describe the diurnal metabolic cycle of an oxidation pond involving aerobic and anaerobic phases.
questions.reasoningChain: Sunlight during the day promotes algal photosynthesis and oxygen release (aerobic), while darkness at night results in anaerobic conditions.
optionExplanations: Oxidation ponds are not purely aerobic because microbial activity and cessation of photosynthesis cause nighttime anoxia.
They are not purely anaerobic since active algal photosynthesis oxygenates the water during daytime hours.
Correct answer. Algal photosynthesis makes the pond aerobic by day, whereas respiration without light makes it anaerobic at night.
The reverse cycle is incorrect because photosynthesis requires sunlight available exclusively during the daytime.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Which lymph node is most commonly involved in prostate cancer?
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer lymphatic spread follows a predictable anatomical pathway. The primary echelon of lymph node drainage from the prostate gland is into the pelvic lymph nodes, specifically the obturator and internal/external iliac chains, making pelvic lymph nodes the most commonly involved.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify pelvic lymph nodes as the primary site of metastasis for prostate cancer.
questions.reasoningChain: Prostate lymphatic drainage goes primarily to the pelvic nodes, making them the most frequently involved in malignancy.
optionExplanations: Deep inguinal nodes drain structures of the lower limb and external genitalia, not the prostate.
Correct answer. Pelvic lymph nodes are the primary regional drainage basin and most common site of prostate cancer spread.
Superficial inguinal nodes drain the skin of the lower abdominal wall, perineum, and external genitalia.
Internal iliac nodes are part of the pelvic basin, but pelvic nodes collectively encompass the primary drainage groups.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Which of the following is true regarding the single exposure point source epidemic?
options: Has more than one incubation period
questions.explanation: A single exposure point source epidemic (common-source outbreak) occurs when a group of people are exposed to a common source of infection or toxin over a brief period. This results in a sharp, explosive rise and fall in case numbers, with all cases occurring within a single incubation period.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the epidemiological curve characteristics of a single exposure point source epidemic.
questions.reasoningChain: A single common exposure leads to a simultaneous spike in cases, creating an explosive outbreak curve within one incubation period.
optionExplanations: Cases occur within a single incubation period rather than multiple intervals.
Multiple peaks are characteristic of propagated or continuous source epidemics, not single point source ones.
Correct answer. Single exposure point source epidemics present with an explosive, sharp rise and rapid fall in cases.
A slow rise and fall is typical of propagated epidemics transmitted person-to-person over time.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Which of the following procedures has the highest risk of causing the recurrence of duodenal ulcers?
questions.explanation: Highly selective vagotomy (HSV) divides only the vagal fibers supplying the parietal cell mass while preserving the antral innervation and the nerve of Latarjet. Although it avoids the side effects of truncal vagotomy (such as diarrhea and dumping syndrome), it is associated with the highest rate of duodenal ulcer recurrence among surgical vagotomy techniques.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify highly selective vagotomy as having the highest recurrence rate among ulcer surgeries.
questions.reasoningChain: Preserving extra vagal branches in highly selective vagotomy reduces morbidity but increases the risk of ulcer recurrence.
optionExplanations: Gastrectomy involves resecting acid-producing portions of the stomach, resulting in very low ulcer recurrence.
Correct answer. Highly selective vagotomy has a higher recurrence rate compared to truncal or selective vagotomy with drainage.
Truncal vagotomy completely severs the vagal trunks, providing lower recurrence at the expense of side effects.
Gastro-jejunostomy combined with vagotomy effectively reduces acid exposure and ulcer recurrence.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Elective splenectomy is preferred in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited hemolytic anemia where abnormal red blood cells are destroyed prematurely in the spleen. Splenectomy is curative for hemolysis and prevents complications like symptomatic gallstones, making elective splenectomy the treatment of choice in appropriate age groups.
questions.educationalObjective: Indicate elective splenectomy as the definitive management for hereditary spherocytosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Spherocytes are sequestered and destroyed in the spleen; removing the spleen corrects the hemolytic anemia in hereditary spherocytosis.
optionExplanations: G6PD deficiency involves episodic hemolysis triggered by oxidative stress; splenectomy is generally ineffective and not indicated.
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is a stem cell clonal disorder characterized by complement-mediated hemolysis and thrombosis, not treated by splenectomy.
Correct answer. Elective splenectomy cures the hemolytic anemia of hereditary spherocytosis by removing the site of red blood cell destruction.
Hairy cell leukemia is a hematologic malignancy treated with purine analogs, not primary splenectomy.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: Sickness absenteeism of workers in the industry is used to evaluate
questions.explanation: Sickness absenteeism measures the frequency and duration of work absence due to illness among industrial workers. It serves as an indirect index reflecting the health status of the working population and the impact of the occupational environment.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize sickness absenteeism as a key indicator of worker health in occupational health.
questions.reasoningChain: Tracking worker absence due to illness directly measures the health status of the employed workforce.
optionExplanations: Correct answer. Sickness absenteeism is a standard occupational health metric evaluating the health and morbidity of workers.
Family health is evaluated via household surveys and maternal-child health indicators, not industrial absenteeism.
Industrial environment is assessed using environmental monitoring, air sampling, and safety audits.
Community health relies on vital statistics, disease surveillance, and general population health surveys.

questions.subject: PSM
questions.prompt: The incisors of a child who had white patches on them which later turned brown are due to excessive supplementation of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Dental fluorosis is caused by excessive ingestion of fluoride during tooth development in childhood. It manifests initially as chalky white patches or opacities on the enamel, which can later become stained brown or pitted as the teeth erupt and age.
questions.educationalObjective: Link chronic excessive fluoride intake during childhood to dental fluorosis and enamel mottling.
questions.reasoningChain: Excess fluoride intake during tooth formation disrupts enamel mineralization, causing white patches that later turn brown.
optionExplanations: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia, not enamel discoloration.
Chlorine is used for water disinfection and does not cause tooth mottling or brown patches.
Correct answer. Excessive fluoride intake during tooth development leads to dental fluorosis and characteristic brown staining.
Riboflavin deficiency causes angular cheilitis, glossitis, and corneal vascularization, not dental changes.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: What is the fluid of choice for shock in a child with severe acute malnutrition?
questions.explanation: In severe acute malnutrition (SAM) with shock, standard resuscitation fluids like normal saline or plain ringers can precipitate fluid overload and heart failure due to impaired myocardial function and electrolyte shifts. The fluid of choice is Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose (or half-strength Darrows with 5% dextrose), given cautiously in specific restricted volumes.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose as the preferred resuscitation fluid in severe acute malnutrition with shock.
questions.reasoningChain: SAM patients in shock require cautious fluid resuscitation using dextrose-containing electrolyte solutions to avoid overload.
optionExplanations: Normal saline has high sodium content and can easily cause fluid overload and heart failure in SAM.
Ringer lactate lacks necessary glucose, putting malnourished children at risk of severe hypoglycemia during resuscitation.
10% dextrose lacks electrolytes and is inadequate for treating hypovolemic shock on its own.
Correct answer. Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose provides balanced electrolytes and necessary glucose for malnourished children in shock.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: How much oxygen is given to a term infant with respiratory distress during resuscitation?
questions.explanation: According to neonatal resuscitation guidelines, resuscitation of a term newborn should ideally begin with room air (21% oxygen) rather than 100% oxygen. Supplemental oxygen is titrated based on pre-ductal oxygen saturation targets to avoid the oxidative tissue injury associated with hyperoxia.
questions.educationalObjective: State that term infant resuscitation should be initiated with room air (21% oxygen).
questions.reasoningChain: Current resuscitation guidelines recommend starting term infant resuscitation with room air to prevent hyperoxic injury.
optionExplanations: Correct answer. Room air (21% oxygen) is recommended for initiating resuscitation in term newborns.
Starting with 50% oxygen is excessive and discouraged unless indicated by persistent hypoxemia.
70% oxygen concentration is unnecessarily high for initial neonatal resuscitation steps.
100% oxygen is no longer recommended for routine neonatal resuscitation due to risks of oxidative damage.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication for breastfeeding?
questions.explanation: Inborn errors of metabolism such as classic galactosemia (due to galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase deficiency) represent an absolute contraindication to breastfeeding, as breast milk contains lactose, which breaks down into galactose and causes severe hepatic, renal, and neurological toxicity.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify galactosemia in the infant as an absolute contraindication to breastfeeding.
questions.reasoningChain: Galactosemia prevents the metabolism of milk sugars, making breast milk toxic and rendering it an absolute contraindication.
optionExplanations: HIV is an indication for formula feeding in many settings, but with modern antiretroviral therapy and viral suppression, guidelines have evolved in certain contexts, whereas galactosemia remains an absolute infant-side contraindication.
Correct answer. Galactosemia prohibits the digestion of lactose/galactose present in breast milk, causing life-threatening toxicity.
Hepatitis C is generally not a contraindication to breastfeeding unless nipples are bleeding heavily.
Tuberculosis in the mother is not an absolute contraindication provided appropriate precautions and infant prophylaxis are implemented.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: An 8-year-old child presented with a sudden onset of high-grade fever, seizures, and loss of consciousness. On examination, the child had anemia, hypoglycemia, and no neurological deficits. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A child presenting with high-grade fever, seizures, impaired consciousness, anemia, and hypoglycemia strongly suggests severe Plasmodium falciparum infection, specifically cerebral malaria. Cerebral malaria is a medical emergency characterized by unarousable coma and systemic complications like hypoglycemia and severe anemia.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cerebral malaria as a cause of febrile encephalopathy accompanied by hypoglycemia and anemia.
questions.reasoningChain: Fever, seizures, coma, anemia, and hypoglycemia in an endemic setting point directly to severe falciparum malaria.
optionExplanations: Tubercular meningitis presents with a subacute or chronic indolent course with cranial nerve palsies, not sudden high fever and seizures.
Viral meningitis typically presents with headache, fever, and meningeal signs without profound hypoglycemia and severe anemia.
Correct answer. Cerebral malaria is characterized by acute fever, altered consciousness, seizures, hypoglycemia, and anemia.
Fungal meningitis is usually subacute or chronic and predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: A child who has overdosed on iron tablets comes with nausea and abdominal pain. What is the antidote for this toxicity?
questions.explanation: Deferoxamine is the specific chelating agent used for acute iron poisoning, particularly when serum iron levels are significantly elevated or systemic symptoms like severe vomiting and abdominal pain are present. It binds free iron to form ferrioxamine, which is then excreted in the urine, giving it a characteristic reddish color.
questions.educationalObjective: Treat acute iron toxicity with deferoxamine chelation.
questions.reasoningChain: Iron toxicity -> gastrointestinal irritation and systemic symptoms -> administration of chelating agent deferoxamine.
optionExplanations: EDTA is a chelating agent primarily used for lead and heavy metal poisoning.
Deferoxamine is the drug of choice for acute iron poisoning chelation therapy.
British anti-Lewisite is a chelating agent used for arsenic, mercury, and lead poisoning.
Penicillamine is used for Wilson disease, cystinuria, and severe rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A patient presents with complaints of sudden onset headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating. The patient has had multiple similar episodes in the past. During these episodes, the patient's blood pressure is elevated. A 24-hour urinary metanephrine is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits classic symptoms of a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla (pheochromocytoma), characterized by paroxysmal headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis, and hypertension. The diagnosis is confirmed by elevated levels of urinary fractionated metanephrines or catecholamines.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify pheochromocytoma presenting with paroxysmal hypertension and elevated metanephrines.
questions.reasoningChain: Paroxysmal headache, sweating, palpitations + hypertension -> elevated urinary metanephrines -> pheochromocytoma.
optionExplanations: Addison's disease presents with chronic fatigue, hypotension, and hyperpigmentation.
Renal artery stenosis causes secondary hypertension but lacks the classic paroxysmal triad.
Pheochromocytoma causes episodic headache, palpitations, and sweating due to excess catecholamines.
Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss, heat intolerance, and tremor, not episodic hypertensive crises.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: According to the neonatal resuscitation protocol, below what heart rate are chest compressions initiated?
questions.explanation: According to neonatal resuscitation guidelines, chest compressions are indicated if the heart rate remains below 60 beats per minute despite adequate ventilation with 100% oxygen for 30 seconds. This step is critical to restore systemic perfusion during neonatal arrest.
questions.educationalObjective: Initiate neonatal chest compressions for a heart rate below 60 bpm.
questions.reasoningChain: Inadequate heart rate during neonatal resuscitation -> heart rate drops below threshold -> initiate chest compressions at < 60 bpm.
optionExplanations: A heart rate of 50 bpm is below the threshold, prompting compressions as per protocol.
60 beats per minute is the exact cutoff heart rate for starting chest compressions in neonates.
A heart rate of 80 bpm requires ventilation monitoring but no chest compressions.
A heart rate of 100 bpm is normal or responsive; resuscitative steps focus only on airway.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: Gonadal growth corresponds with _____.
questions.explanation: According to Scammon's curves of postnatal growth, different body tissues grow at distinct rates. The neural tissue (brain and central nervous system) grows rapidly in early childhood and reaches adult size remarkably early, a pattern closely paralleled by the development and growth of the gonads during puberty.
questions.educationalObjective: Relate gonadal growth trajectory to neural growth patterns in Scammon's curves.
questions.reasoningChain: Scammon's curves -> neural system grows early and rapidly -> gonadal growth parallels brain growth timing relative to other tissues.
optionExplanations: Skeletal system follows general somatic growth, increasing steadily through childhood and puberty.
Brain growth curve matches the neural pattern that corresponds closely with gonadal growth timing.
Lymphoid growth peaks in pre-pubertal years and then undergoes involution to adult levels.
Dental growth follows a specific timeline distinct from the neural and gonadal patterns.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 70-year-old patient with a smoking history presents with high-grade fever, cough, confusion, and diarrhea. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates in bilateral lower lung fields. On sputum gram stain, no organisms were detected. Laboratory results reveal Na: 126mEq/L, AST:62, ALT:56, RBS:112 mg/dl, serum bilirubin of 0.8mg%, and a positive HIV test. Which of the following organisms is responsible?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture of high fever, confusion, GI symptoms (diarrhea), hyponatremia, and negative routine sputum gram stain in an immunocompromised patient strongly suggests Legionella pneumophila pneumonia. Legionella typically requires specialized media (BCYE) for visualization, hence its negative standard gram stain.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose Legionella pneumonia presenting with atypical features and hyponatremia.
questions.reasoningChain: Fever, cough, diarrhea, hyponatremia, negative gram stain -> intracellular atypical pathogen -> Legionella infection.
optionExplanations: Streptococcus pneumoniae typically shows positive gram-positive diplococci on sputum stain.
Legionella presents with systemic symptoms, GI manifestations, hyponatremia, and negative sputum stain.
Pneumocystis jirovecii presents with subacute dyspnea and diffuse infiltrates without prominent diarrhea.
Klebsiella causes prominent cavitary pneumonia with thick currant-jelly sputum and positive gram stain.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.prompt: A 6-year-old child is brought for complaints of short stature. His height is comparable with his parent's height and his bone age corresponds to his chronological age. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Familial short stature is characterized by a height below the 3rd percentile that is consistent with the genetic potential of the parents (target height). Importantly, the child's bone age matches their chronological age, and they maintain a normal growth velocity.
questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate familial short stature by matching bone and chronological age.
questions.reasoningChain: Short stature matching parental height + bone age equals chronological age -> familial short stature.
optionExplanations: Familial short stature shows normal bone age matching chronological age with short parents.
Constitutional delay typically presents with a delayed bone age and delayed puberty.
Undernutrition shows weight affected before height, with potential deceleration in growth velocity.
Growth hormone deficiency is characterized by significantly delayed bone age and low growth velocity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old patient with a history of smoking a pack of cigarettes for the past 15 years presents with hemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows a 3cm upper lobe mass near the apex of the lung, What is the next best step for managing this patient?
questions.explanation: A patient with a smoking history and a 3cm upper lobe lung mass near the apex requires tissue diagnosis. For peripheral lung lesions or apical masses where bronchoscopy has lower yield, a CT-guided percutaneous core needle biopsy is the preferred next step for histological confirmation.
questions.educationalObjective: Select CT-guided biopsy for peripheral or apical lung masses.
questions.reasoningChain: Smoking history + apical lung mass -> need for tissue diagnosis -> CT-guided biopsy for peripheral/apical lesions.
optionExplanations: Bronchoscopy has lower diagnostic yield for peripheral apical lung masses compared to central ones.
CT-guided biopsy provides direct tissue access and is ideal for peripheral or apical lung masses.
Sputum cytology has low sensitivity for peripheral lung masses and is rarely definitive.
Sputum for AFB is indicated for suspected tuberculosis, not a primary pulmonary mass lesion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Which of the following is seen in all kinds of shock?
questions.explanation: Shock is fundamentally defined as a life-threatening systemic condition of circulatory failure resulting in inadequate oxygen delivery to meet cellular metabolic demands. Therefore, reduced tissue perfusion is the defining hallmark present across all forms of shock (hypovolemic, cardiogenic, septic, and anaphylactic).
questions.educationalObjective: Identify reduced tissue perfusion as the universal hallmark of all shock types.
questions.reasoningChain: All forms of shock -> circulatory failure -> universally results in reduced tissue perfusion.
optionExplanations: Reduced tissue perfusion is the universal pathophysiological endpoint across all forms of shock.
Increased peripheral resistance is absent in distributive shocks like septic or neurogenic shock.
Decreased respiratory rate is incorrect as tachypnea is typically seen in compensatory phases.
Cold clammy skin is typical of hypovolemic/cardiogenic shock, but warm skin is seen in early septic shock.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A woman presents with a history of headaches for the past 9 months that worsen in a recumbent position and improves as the day progresses. She also gives a history of taking oral contraceptives. Fundal examination shows papilledema. There are no focal neurological deficits. What is the probable cause of her headaches?
questions.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) typically affects young women, is associated with oral contraceptive use, and presents with worsening headaches in the recumbent position due to elevated intracranial pressure. Funduscopic examination characteristically reveals bilateral papilledema without focal neurological deficits.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose pseudotumor cerebri presenting with papilledema and OCP use.
questions.reasoningChain: Headaches worse in recumbency + OCP use + papilledema + no focal deficits -> pseudotumor cerebri.
optionExplanations: Myasthenia gravis causes fluctuating muscle weakness and ptosis, not raised intracranial pressure.
Temporal arteritis affects older adults, causing jaw claudication and elevated inflammatory markers.
Chronic migraine presents with episodic throbbing headaches but does not cause papilledema.
Pseudotumor cerebri causes raised intracranial pressure, papilledema, and headaches worse lying down.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A man came with complaints of recurrent discharge and pain due to lesions around the anus for 3 years. A diagnosis of fistula-in-ano is made. What is the gold standard investigation for this condition?
questions.explanation: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis is the gold standard investigation for evaluating fistula-in-ano. It provides exceptional soft-tissue resolution to accurately map the primary tract, secondary extensions, and involvement of the anal sphincter complex.
questions.educationalObjective: Use MRI as the gold standard investigation for fistula-in-ano.
questions.reasoningChain: Recurrent perianal discharge -> fistula-in-ano -> MRI provides best soft-tissue and tract delineation.
optionExplanations: Fistulogram has largely been superseded by cross-sectional imaging for complex fistulas.
USG (especially endoanal) is helpful but inferior to MRI for mapping complex fistulous tracts.
CECT provides good anatomical detail but inferior soft-tissue contrast compared to MRI.
MRI is the gold standard investigation for mapping fistula-in-ano tracts and sphincter involvement.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most common cause of mortality in diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.explanation: While diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) carries several serious complications, cerebral edema is the most common cause of mortality, particularly in children and young adults. It typically arises from overly rapid fluid resuscitation and osmotic shifts, leading to neurological deterioration.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cerebral edema as the leading cause of mortality in DKA.
questions.reasoningChain: Diabetic ketoacidosis -> fluid resuscitation and osmotic shifts -> cerebral edema as primary mortality cause.
optionExplanations: Acute respiratory distress syndrome is a recognized complication of DKA but not the leading cause of death.
Cardiac arrhythmia can occur due to severe electrolyte imbalances but is not the most common cause of death.
Cerebral edema is the leading and most dreaded cause of mortality in DKA patients.
Acute kidney injury can occur secondary to volume depletion but is rarely the primary fatal event.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following is not included in the Gaisböck syndrome?
questions.explanation: Gaisböck syndrome (stress erythrocytosis) is characterized by relative polycythemia, hypertension, anxiety, and obesity, typically occurring in middle-aged men. Leukocyte and platelet counts remain normal, and plasma volume is contracted, distinguishing it from true polycythemia vera.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify features of Gaisböck syndrome including hypertension and erythrocytosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Gaisböck syndrome -> relative erythrocytosis, hypertension, obesity -> hypotension is not a feature.
optionExplanations: Hypotension is not part of Gaisböck syndrome; hypertension is a defining clinical feature.
Erythrocytosis (relative polycythemia due to plasma volume contraction) is a core finding.
Normal leukocyte counts help differentiate Gaisböck syndrome from primary polycythemia vera.
Obesity is classically associated with this syndrome along with stress and hypertension.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: Identify the given instrument.
questions.explanation: The image displays a surgical linear stapler, which is designed to place multiple rows of staples into tissue and simultaneously divide the tissue between the rows. It is commonly used in gastrointestinal and thoracic resections.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify a linear surgical stapler from visual characteristics.
questions.reasoningChain: Surgical instrument with parallel jaws and stapling mechanism -> linear stapler.
optionExplanations: Linear stapler places parallel rows of staples and divides tissue, matching the visual device.
Skin stapler is a smaller, pistol-grip device used exclusively for cutaneous closure.
Circular stapler has a round head designed for end-to-end anastomoses in the GI tract.
Curved stapler is typically used for low pelvic colorectal anastomoses with a curved jaw.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A patient presents with dyspnea and distended neck veins that increase on inspiration. There is no murmur. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kussmaul's sign—an increase or failure to decrease in jugular venous pressure during inspiration—is a hallmark of constrictive pericarditis. This occurs because the rigid, scarred pericardium prevents normal inspiratory blood flow into the right heart chambers.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose constrictive pericarditis presenting with Kussmaul's sign.
questions.reasoningChain: Dyspnea + distended neck veins increasing on inspiration (Kussmaul sign) -> constrictive pericarditis.
optionExplanations: Constrictive pericarditis causes a non-compliant pericardium, leading to Kussmaul's sign.
Aortic regurgitation causes widened pulse pressure and bounding pulses, not inspiratory JVP rise.
Tricuspid stenosis causes elevated JVP with a prominent 'a' wave but lacks inspiratory rise.
Pulmonary arterial hypertension causes right heart failure with elevated JVP without Kussmaul's sign.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.prompt: Inhalational induction of choice in children is:
questions.explanation: Sevoflurane is the inhalational anesthetic of choice for smooth, rapid mask induction in pediatric patients. It has a low blood-gas solubility coefficient, resulting in fast induction and emergence, and lacks significant airway irritation or pungent odor.
questions.educationalObjective: Select sevoflurane as the preferred inhalational induction agent in children.
questions.reasoningChain: Pediatric inhalational induction -> rapid onset, non-irritating airway -> sevoflurane.
optionExplanations: Sevoflurane is sweet-smelling, non-irritating, and the agent of choice for pediatric mask induction.
Desflurane is pungent and causes severe airway irritation, coughing, and laryngospasm.
Halothane is historical and largely avoided due to the risk of severe hepatotoxicity.
Isoflurane is pungent and can cause breath-holding, making it unsuitable for smooth mask induction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.prompt: A patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. Skin grafting was done wherein the graft was taken from the same person. Which type of graft is it?
questions.explanation: An autograft is a tissue graft harvested from one site and transplanted to another site on the same individual's body. The image shows a meshed skin graft successfully placed on the patient's lower extremity, indicative of autologous grafting.
questions.educationalObjective: Define an autograft as tissue transplanted within the same individual.
questions.reasoningChain: Graft taken from the same person -> autograft by definition.
optionExplanations: Autograft refers to tissue transferred from one location to another on the same patient.
Xenograft involves tissue transplanted from a donor of a different species, such as a pig.
Allograft involves tissue transplanted between genetically non-identical individuals of the same species.
Isograft is a tissue graft between genetically identical individuals, such as monozygotic twins.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.prompt: Which of the following is most suitable for intravenous regional anesthesia?
questions.explanation: Lidocaine is the most suitable and commonly used local anesthetic for intravenous regional anesthesia (Bier block). It provides rapid onset and reliable anesthesia for upper extremity procedures when administered under a pneumatic tourniquet without causing systemic toxicity at standard doses.
questions.educationalObjective: Choose lidocaine for intravenous regional anesthesia (Bier block).
questions.reasoningChain: Intravenous regional anesthesia requirement -> safe intermediate-potency agent -> lidocaine.
optionExplanations: Bupivacaine is avoided in intravenous regional anesthesia due to the severe risk of systemic cardiotoxicity.
Mepivacaine is a local anesthetic but lidocaine remains the standard first-line choice for Bier blocks.
Procaine is an ester-type local anesthetic with a short duration and is rarely used for regional blocks.
Lidocaine is the standard, safest local anesthetic utilized for intravenous regional anesthesia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.prompt: Which of the following airway devices helps maintain Fio2 of 0.25-0.60, irrespective of the patient's breathing effort?
questions.explanation: A Venturi mask uses the Bernoulli principle to deliver a fixed, precise fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) ranging from 0.24 to 0.60, irrespective of the patient's respiratory rate, tidal volume, or breathing pattern. It achieves this by entraining room air at fixed high gas flow rates.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify the Venturi mask for delivering fixed, precise FiO2.
questions.reasoningChain: Precise FiO2 delivery independent of breathing pattern -> Venturi mask.
optionExplanations: Nasal cannula provides variable FiO2 dependent on respiratory rate and minute ventilation.
Simple face mask delivers variable FiO2 ranging from 0.35 to 0.60 depending on patient breathing.
Venturi mask delivers a fixed, reliable FiO2 using high-flow jet mixing via the Bernoulli principle.
Non-rebreathing mask delivers high FiO2 (up to 0.90) but is still subject to breathing variations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 5-year-old child presented with recurrent respiratory infections with thickened sputum. Chest X-ray showed bronchial wall thickening. He has been suffering from steatorrhea since birth. Which of the following is the first differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of recurrent respiratory infections, bronchiectasis/bronchial wall thickening, and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (steatorrhea since birth) in a pediatric patient points directly to cystic fibrosis. It is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene leading to thick, viscous mucus secretions.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose cystic fibrosis presenting with steatorrhea and recurrent pulmonary infections.
questions.reasoningChain: Recurrent respiratory infections + thickened sputum + lifelong steatorrhea -> cystic fibrosis.
optionExplanations: Hyaline membrane disease affects premature neonates acutely with surfactant deficiency, not chronic steatorrhea.
Cystic fibrosis classically presents with chronic respiratory disease and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
Alpha 1 anti-trypsin deficiency causes early-onset panacinar emphysema and liver disease, not steatorrhea.
Malabsorption syndrome causes GI symptoms but does not typically account for chronic bronchial wall thickening.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: What is the most common cause of Cushing's disease in a 60-year-old male?
questions.explanation: Pituitary microadenoma (Cushing's disease) remains the most common endogenous cause of Cushing's syndrome across all adult age groups, including older adults. It involves an ACTH-secreting benign tumor of the anterior pituitary gland driving adrenal cortisol hypersecretion.
questions.educationalObjective: Identify pituitary microadenoma as the most common cause of Cushing's disease.
questions.reasoningChain: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome -> ACTH-dependent -> pituitary microadenoma as most common etiology.
optionExplanations: Small-cell lung cancer causes ectopic ACTH syndrome, which is less common than pituitary adenoma.
Adrenal tumor causes ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome, characterized by low plasma ACTH levels.
Ectopic ACTH syndrome is secondary to neuroendocrine tumors and is less frequent than pituitary adenomas.
Pituitary microadenoma is the single most common cause of endogenous Cushing's disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old woman presented with complaints of bone pain and abdominal cramps. Her family says she has a history of abnormal behavior. The consultant doctor arrived at a provisional diagnosis based on the clinical features. Which of the following would be the best investigation to arrive at a definitive diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's presentation of bone pain, abdominal cramps, and psychiatric symptoms ('pain, groans, and psychic moans') suggests primary hyperparathyroidism. A technetium-99m sestamibi scan is the best functional imaging modality to localize hyperactive parathyroid glands or adenomas before surgery.
questions.educationalObjective: Use a sestamibi scan to localize parathyroid pathology in primary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.reasoningChain: Bone pain, abdominal cramps, abnormal behavior -> primary hyperparathyroidism -> sestamibi scan for localization.
optionExplanations: MRI provides anatomical detail but is not the primary functional scan of choice for parathyroid adenomas.
Ultrasonogram is useful for initial neck imaging but is operator-dependent and less comprehensive than sestamibi.
Sestamibi scan is the gold standard functional imaging test for localizing hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue.
CT scan provides cross-sectional anatomy but lacks the specific functional uptake seen with sestamibi scans.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old woman presented with difficulty in activities like climbing stairs, getting up from a chair, and combing hair. Violaceous erythema of the upper eyelids was noted. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by symmetric proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs or combing hair) and characteristic cutaneous manifestations, including a heliotrope rash and violaceous erythema of the upper eyelids (Gottron's papules or heliotrope rash).
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose dermatomyositis based on proximal muscle weakness and characteristic eyelid erythema.
questions.reasoningChain: Proximal muscle weakness + violaceous upper eyelid erythema -> dermatomyositis.
optionExplanations: Inclusion body myositis typically affects distal muscles (like finger flexors) and older adults.
Dermatomyositis presents with classic proximal weakness combined with distinct cutaneous findings like eyelid erythema.
Polymyositis causes symmetric proximal muscle weakness but lacks the characteristic dermatological signs.
Scleroderma presents with skin tightening, Raynaud's phenomenon, and visceral involvement.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A young male patient presents with ptosis and muscle weakness which reportedly worsens in the evening and improves in the morning. This is relieved by neostigmine. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits classic symptoms of myasthenia gravis, characterized by fluctuating skeletal muscle weakness and ptosis that typically worsens with repetitive activity or toward the end of the day and improves with rest. The condition responds to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors like neostigmine.
questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose myasthenia gravis presenting with diurnal fatigue and ptosis improving with neostigmine.
questions.reasoningChain: Ptosis and muscle weakness worsening in the evening + improvement with neostigmine -> myasthenia gravis.
optionExplanations: Myasthenia gravis causes fluctuating weakness that worsens with fatigue and improves with neostigmine.
Huntington chorea is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by involuntary choreiform movements.
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis involves progressive upper and lower motor neuron degeneration without diurnal fluctuation.
External ophthalmoplegia typically refers to chronic progressive conditions without dramatic acetylcholinesterase response.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Bell's palsy involves
options: Ipsilateral upper and lower halves of the face.
Contralateral upper and lower halves of the face.
Ipsilateral lower half of the face.
Contralateral lower half of the face.
questions.answer: Ipsilateral upper and lower halves of the face.
questions.explanation: Bell's palsy is an idiopathic peripheral facial nerve (CN VII) palsy resulting in weakness or paralysis of all muscles of facial expression on the affected side. Because it is a lower motor neuron lesion, it involves both the upper and lower halves of the ipsilateral face.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that Bell's palsy affects both upper and lower halves of the ipsilateral face.
questions.reasoningChain: Bell's palsy -> peripheral facial nerve lesion -> ipsilateral upper and lower facial paralysis.
optionExplanations: Bell's palsy affects the entire ipsilateral half of the face (upper and lower) due to LMN involvement.
Contradictory involvement of upper and lower halves is incorrect anatomically and clinically.
Sparing of the forehead is characteristic of upper motor neuron lesions, not Bell's palsy.
Contralateral lower facial weakness is a hallmark of central facial palsy (stroke), not Bell's palsy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: Which of the following drugs reduce mortality in a patient with heart failure?
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers like metoprolol, carvedilol, and bisoprolol are guideline-directed medical therapies that significantly reduce mortality in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction by blocking chronic sympathetic stimulation. Furosemide and torsemide are loop diuretics used for symptom relief and volume overload without survival benefit. Prazosin is an alpha-1 blocker not recommended for mortality reduction in heart failure.
questions.educationalObjective: Beta-blockers (metoprolol, carvedilol, bisoprolol) reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
questions.reasoningChain: Heart failure involves sympathetic overdrive -> Beta-blockers block excessive sympathetic tone -> Reduced myocardial remodeling and mortality
optionExplanations: Cardioselective beta-blocker that reduces mortality in heart failure patients.
Loop diuretic providing symptom relief from volume overload without survival benefit.
Alpha-1 blocker that is not beneficial for reducing heart failure mortality.
Loop diuretic used for managing fluid overload rather than improving survival.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.prompt: A 49-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of watery diarrhoea, dehydration, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria. Which of the following neuroendocrine tumour can be responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic Verner-Morrison syndrome (WDHA syndrome: watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria), which is caused by a vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting neuroendocrine tumor known as a VIPoma. VIP stimulates intestinal fluid and electrolyte secretion, leading to severe secretory diarrhea, dehydration, and electrolyte depletion.
questions.educationalObjective: VIPoma secretes vasoactive intestinal peptide, causing watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome).
questions.reasoningChain: Neuroendocrine tumor secretes VIP -> Excessive VIP stimulates intestinal secretion -> Watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA)
optionExplanations: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor characterized by recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia, not watery diarrhea.
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor causing diabetes, steatorrhea, and gallstones.
Neuroendocrine tumor responsible for the classic WDHA syndrome of watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria.
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor associated with necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, and weight loss.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A family pedigree chart is given below. Identify the mode of inheritance of this condition.
questions.explanation: The provided pedigree chart demonstrates an affected individual in every generation, with affected males and females transmitting the trait to both male and female offspring without skipping generations, which is characteristic of an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Vertical transmission and male-to-male transmission are both clearly observed.
questions.educationalObjective: Autosomal dominant inheritance is characterized by vertical transmission across generations with no skipped generations.
questions.reasoningChain: Trait appears in every generation -> Male-to-male transmission present -> Rules out X-linked and recessive patterns -> Autosomal dominant
optionExplanations: Correct inheritance pattern shown by vertical transmission and affected individuals in every generation.
Incorrect, as recessive conditions typically show skipped generations and unaffected carrier parents.
Incorrect, because there is clear male-to-male transmission from father to son.
Incorrect, as X-linked dominant traits would show affected fathers passing the trait to all daughters.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: A woman presents with complaints of greenish-frothy vaginal discharge for 1 month. On examination, vulvovaginal erythema is noticed. On saline microscopy, motile organisms are seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis, presenting with a characteristic greenish-frothy vaginal discharge, vulvovaginal erythema, and strawberry cervix. Saline microscopy (wet mount) easily identifies flagellated, motile protozoan organisms confirming the diagnosis.
questions.educationalObjective: Trichomonas vaginalis causes frothy green vaginal discharge and is diagnosed by motile organisms on wet mount.
questions.reasoningChain: Greenish-frothy discharge and vulvovaginal erythema -> Saline microscopy reveals motile protozoa -> Trichomoniasis diagnosis
optionExplanations: Characterized by frothy green discharge, erythema, and motile flagellated protozoa on wet mount.
Presents with thin, gray discharge, a positive amine whiff test, and clue cells, not motile protozoa.
Usually presents as a mucopurulent cervicitis with chlamydia organisms, not motile protozoa on saline.
Presents with thick, white curd-like discharge and pseudohyphae on KOH mount.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: The given inclusion bodies are characteristic of which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation: The provided image illustrates characteristic large cells with prominent basophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies surrounded by a clear halo, giving the classic 'owl's eye' appearance. These cytomegalic inclusions are pathognomonic for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection.
questions.educationalObjective: Cytomegalovirus infection produces characteristic owl's eye intranuclear inclusion bodies.
questions.reasoningChain: Cells show large intranuclear inclusions with a clear halo -> Owl's eye appearance -> Cytomegalovirus
optionExplanations: Associated with koilocytic changes and wart formation, not large owl's eye nuclear inclusions.
Classic viral pathogen showing large cells with prominent owl's eye intranuclear inclusion bodies.
Associated with atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells) and lymphadenopathy, not owl's eye inclusions.
Characterized by Cowdry A inclusions and multinucleated giant cells rather than owl's eye inclusions.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A 70-year-old male comes with complaints of hip pain. An X-ray of the hip shows lytic lesions and elevated serum calcium levels. Bone marrow plasma cells are 42%, and the cells seen are given in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, renal impairment, and a bone marrow plasma cell infiltration greater than 10% (specifically 42% here) along with characteristic plasma cells containing eccentric nuclei and perinuclear halos establishes the diagnosis of multiple myeloma.
questions.educationalObjective: Multiple myeloma is diagnosed by lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, and bone marrow plasmaocytosis >10%.
questions.reasoningChain: Elderly male with bone pain and lytic lesions -> Elevated plasma cells >10% with eccentric nuclei -> Multiple myeloma
optionExplanations: Malignancy of plasma cells presenting with lytic lesions, hypercalcemia, and characteristic plasma cells.
Characterized by small, mature-appearing lymphocytes and smudge cells in peripheral blood.
Presents with blasts in bone marrow and pediatric predominance, not plasma cells.
Myeloproliferative disorder showing granulocytic precursors in various stages of maturation.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: If the division in the zygote occurs between 9-12 days after fertilization, which of the following twin is expected?
questions.explanation: Division of the zygote occurring between 9 to 12 days after fertilization results in monochorionic monoamniotic twins, because the embryonic disc has already split after the formation of both the chorion and the amnion. Division at earlier timeframes yields dichorionic diamniotic or monochorionic diamniotic twins, while later division leads to conjoined twins.
questions.educationalObjective: Zygotic division between 9-12 days post-fertilization results in monochorionic monoamniotic twins.
questions.reasoningChain: Zygote division at 9-12 days -> Amnion already formed -> Monochorionic and monoamniotic placenta and sac
optionExplanations: Results from zygote division within the first 3 days after fertilization.
Results from incomplete zygote division occurring after 13 days post-fertilization.
Results from zygote division between 4 and 8 days after fertilization.
Correct outcome of zygote division occurring between 9 and 12 days post-fertilization.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: The following picture showed a lymph node biopsy of a 30-year-old male with cervical lymphadenopathy. The diagnosis is
questions.explanation: The histological image demonstrates a classic Reed-Sternberg cell—a large binucleated or multinucleated cell with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli resembling 'owl-eyes' set in a background of mixed inflammatory cells. This finding is diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.educationalObjective: Reed-Sternberg cells in lymph node biopsy are diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Lymph node biopsy with large binucleated cells and prominent nucleoli -> Reed-Sternberg cells -> Hodgkin disease
optionExplanations: Presents with myeloblasts and Auer rods, not binucleated giant cells in lymph nodes.
Malignancy characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells within an inflammatory lymph node background.
Viral infection associated with koilocytes, not neoplastic giant cells.
Lymphoproliferative disorder showing proliferation of small mature lymphocytes in blood and bone marrow.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: What type of cell is shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: The image clearly shows a large binucleated cell with abundant cytoplasm and prominent eosinophilic inclusion-like nucleoli, which is the classic description of a Reed-Sternberg cell seen in Hodgkin lymphoma. The other choices represent completely different hematologic cytomorphologies.
questions.educationalObjective: Reed-Sternberg cells are large multinucleated cells characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.reasoningChain: Binucleated giant cell with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli -> Reed-Sternberg cell -> Hodgkin lymphoma
optionExplanations: Bundles of Auer rods seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia.
Classic large binucleated malignant cell seen in Hodgkin lymphoma histopathology.
Plasma cells with multiple Russell bodies found in chronic inflammation or multiple myeloma.
T-cells with hyperconvoluted cerebriform nuclei seen in Mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old female presents with frequent headaches. Investigation reveals raised intracranial pressure and the presence of a dural-based tumor. Which of the following histological findings correlate with the diagnosis?
options: Psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells
questions.answer: Psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a dural-based tumor causing raised intracranial pressure in an adult female is characteristic of a meningioma. Histologically, meningiomas are classically characterized by the presence of whorled syncytial cell nests and psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concentric structures).
questions.educationalObjective: Meningiomas histologically show whorled tumor cells and psammoma bodies.
questions.reasoningChain: Dural-based brain tumor -> Meningioma -> Characteristic psammoma bodies and whorled cell architecture
optionExplanations: Histological finding typically associated with oligodendrogliomas.
Rosettes seen in retinoblastomas and medulloblastomas.
Characteristic histological findings of meningiomas comprising laminated calcifications and whorled cells.
Perivascular pseudo-rosettes typically seen in central primitive neuroectodermal tumors.

questions.subject: Gynaecology & Obstetrics
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the correct sequence of vaginal discharge during puerperium?
questions.explanation: Lochia, the normal postpartum vaginal discharge, follows a strict chronological sequence as the uterine lining heals.
