questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Identify the lymphatic structure from the histology section given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: D) Thymus
Explanation:
The image shows a distinct lobulated structure with a darker outer cortex and a lighter inner
medulla. This is characteristic of the thymus.
Parts of the Thymus:
1. Cortex:
•
The outer, more densely packed region of the thymus.
•
Filled with immature T cells (thymocytes), undergoing differentiation and
maturation as they move towards the medulla.
•
The cortex contains thymic nurse cells that support the maturing thymocytes.
•
T cells express surface markers (like TCR, CD3, CD4, and CD8) during
maturation.
•
Macrophages are present to phagocytose apoptotic T cells, which fail to mature
properly.
2. Medulla:
•
The inner, less densely populated region.
•
Dominated by epithelial cells with pale-staining nuclei and large cytoplasm.
•
Contains Hassall's corpuscles, concentric structures made of keratinized
epithelial cells, involved in T cell regulation.
•
Dendritic cells and macrophages in the medulla present self-antigens to maturing
T cells, ensuring the elimination of self-reactive cells to prevent autoimmunity.
Histology of the Thymus:
•
Epithelial Framework: Throughout the thymus, epithelial cells provide a structural
scaffold for lymphocyte development and produce hormones like thymopoietin, which
regulate T cell maturation and proliferation.
•
It is divided into lobules by connective tissue septa.
•
A protective blood-thymus barrier prevents antigens from entering, safeguarding T cell
maturation.
With age, the thymus undergoes involution, where lymphoid tissue is replaced by fat, but it
continues to produce mature T cells.
Tonsil (Option A): Tonsils contain lymphoid follicles with germinal centers. The histology of
tonsils features these follicles, unlike the thymus.
Lymph node (Option B):
Lymph nodes also have lymphoid follicles but have a more defined capsule, cortex, paracortex,
and medulla.
Spleen (Option C):
The spleen has a characteristic red pulp (containing blood) and white pulp (containing
lymphocytes)
Reference :
Wheater Functional Histology, 6th Edition, Page: 204- 206.
Inderbir Singh Histology, 9th Edition. Page: 249- 254.
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A person with the H/o long-term sexual relationship presented with painful ulcers on his genitals with tender lymphadenopathy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: D) Chancroid
Explanation: The clinical scenario of a person with a history of a long-term sexual relationship
presenting with painful ulcers on the genitals and tender lymphadenopathy points towards a
diagnosis of Chancroid, typically caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.
Haemophilus ducreyi:
•
Gram-negative coccobacillus
•
Fastidious, requiring X factor but not V factor
•
Forms characteristic "school of fish" or "railroad track" arrangements in Gram stains
•
Safety pin appearance of bipolar staining.
•
Clinical features of chancroid:
•
Painful genital ulcers with ragged edges and a purulent base
•
Painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes)
•
Incubation period of 3-10 days
•
Diagnosis:
•
Clinical presentation
•
Gram stain of ulcer exudate
•
Culture on selective media (challenging and low sensitivity)
•
PCR (most sensitive method)
•
Differential diagnosis includes syphilis, herpes simplex, and lymphogranuloma
venereum
•
Treatment:
•
Azithromycin 1g orally single dose, OR
•
Ceftriaxone 250mg IM single dose, OR
•
Ciprofloxacin 500mg orally twice daily for 3 days, OR
•
Erythromycin 500mg orally three times daily for 7 days
•
Treatment of sexual partners is crucial
Gonorrhea (Option A) typically causes urethritis and discharge, not painful ulcers or
lymphadenopathy.
Chlamydia (Option B) can cause urethritis or cervicitis, but ulcers are rare.
Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) (Option C) presents with painless ulcers and later,
painful lymphadenopathy, unlike the painful ulcers seen in chancroid.
Reference :
Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Page 338, 339
Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 14th Edition, Page 434, 435

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Dehydration is more severe in infants compared to adults. Which of the following is a true statement about infants?
options: Extracellular fluid (ECF) is more than intracellular fluid (ICF)
Intracellular fluid (ICF) is more than extracellular fluid (ECF)
Total body water in infants is more than in adults
questions.answer: Total body water in infants is more than in adults
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: C) Total body water in infants is more than in adults
Explanation:
Infants have a higher total body water (TBW) percentage compared to adults, making them
more susceptible to dehydration.
•
Total body water (TBW) composition:
•
Infants: ~75-80% of body weight
•
Adults: ~55-60% of body weight
•
Higher water turnover: Infants lose water more rapidly due to higher metabolic rates,
increased insensible losses, and immature renal function.
Total Body Water (TBW) Composition:
•
90% of body weight in early fetal life.
•
75% of body weight at birth.
•
60% of body weight by the end of the first year, remaining consistent until puberty.
•
After puberty, males have slightly more TBW compared to females.
Preterm vs. Term Neonates:
•
Preterm neonates have a higher TBW compared to term neonates.
TBW Distribution:
•
TBW is divided into:
•
Extracellular Fluid (ECF)
•
Intracellular Fluid (ICF)
•
The equation is: TBW = ECF + ICF
•
ECF = plasma + interstitial fluid
ECF and ICF Changes:
•
In fetuses and newborns, ECF > ICF volume.
•
After birth, ECF volume decreases and ICF volume increases.
Extracellular fluid (ECF) is more than intracellular fluid (ICF) (Option A) is incorrect
because, while infants have a higher ECF proportion at birth (~40%), ICF eventually exceeds
ECF as they grow.
Intracellular fluid (ICF) is more than extracellular fluid (ECF) (Option B) is incorrect at
birth, but becomes true after the first year. In neonates, ECF is initially greater than ICF.
Extracellular fluid equals intracellular fluid (Option D) is incorrect because ECF and ICF are
not equal at any stage; there is always a shift, with ICF becoming dominant after infancy.
Reference :
Ghai Textbook of Paediatrics, 10th Edition, Page: 55, 56.
Total body water in full-term and preterm newborn
Fluid balance and elimination

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Which drug is preferred for management of diabetes in a patient with cardiac and renal failure?
questions.explanation:
Answer: A) SGLT2 inhibitors
Explanation:
Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) are
preferred for diabetes management in patients with cardiac and renal failure due to their
cardioprotective and renoprotective benefits.
•
Cardiovascular Benefits:
•
Reduce heart failure hospitalisation (especially in HF with reduced ejection
fraction (HFrEF)).
•
Lower major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in high-risk patients.
•
Renal Benefits:
•
Slow progression of diabetic nephropathy.
•
Reduce albuminuria and preserve glomerular function.
Diabetic patients with heart failure best benefit from adding a group of drugs called SGLT-2
(sodium-glucose cotransporter-2) inhibitors, and empagliflozin falls in this group.
By inhibiting the SGLT-2 receptors in the proximal tubule of the kidneys, glucose (and sodium)
reabsorption can be prevented.
Since both sodium and glucose are osmotic molecules, increasing their excretion draws out more
water, making these drugs effective in patients with heart failure.
Drugs:
•
Dapagliflozin.
•
Empagliflozin.
•
Canagliflozin.
•
Ertugliflozin.
Side effects:
•
Infections (vaginal thrush, balanoposthitis, Fournier’s gangrene): Favour the growth
of microbes in the lower urinary tract by providing an environment of excessive glucose.
•
Euglycemic ketoacidosis is due to inhibiting glucose reabsorption and the body’s
preference for ketone bodies as an energy source after excess glucose excretion.
•
Osteoporosis: Rarely due to loss of calcium ions upon inhibition of the SGLT-2
receptors.
Pioglitazone (Option B) is incorrect because pioglitazone (a thiazolidinedione, TZD) causes
fluid retention, worsening heart failure.
Metformin (Option C) is incorrect because although it is the first-line drug for type 2 diabetes,
it is contraindicated in severe renal failure (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m²) due to the risk of
lactic acidosis.
Sulfonylureas (Option D) is incorrect because sulfonylureas (e.g., glibenclamide, glipizide)
increase hypoglycemia risk, especially in renal impairment due to reduced clearance.
Reference :
Goodman & Gillman’s pharmacological basis of Therapeutics, 14th edition, Page 1040
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Which adverse effect of Bleomycin is exacerbated by radiation exposure?
questions.explanation:
Answer: A) Pulmonary toxicity
Explanation:
Bleomycin-induced pulmonary toxicity is the most significant adverse effect, and it is
exacerbated by radiation exposure (a phenomenon known as radiation recall pneumonitis).
•
Mechanism:
•
Bleomycin generates free radicals, leading to oxidative damage and fibrosis in
the lungs.
•
The lungs have low bleomycin hydrolase activity, making them more
susceptible to damage.
•
Radiation exposure further increases oxidative stress and inflammatory
responses, worsening lung injury.
•
Risk Factors:
•
Cumulative bleomycin dose >400 units
•
Concurrent oxygen therapy (risk of oxygen toxicity)
•
Prior or concurrent radiation therapy
•
Older age and renal impairment
•
Clinical Features:
•
Progressive dyspnoea, non-productive cough
•
Interstitial pneumonitis → pulmonary fibrosis
•
Restrictive lung disease with ↓ DLCO (diffusing capacity for carbon
monoxide)
Bleomycin is an antitumor antibiotic that is well-known for its association with pulmonary
toxicity, including pulmonary fibrosis which occurs as follows:
Gastric toxicity (Option B) is incorrect because bleomycin does not significantly affect the
gastrointestinal tract.
Neural toxicity (Option C) is incorrect because bleomycin does not cause neurotoxicity
(unlike vincristine, which affects nerves).
Hepatotoxicity (Option D) is incorrect because bleomycin has minimal liver toxicity compared
to other chemotherapy agents.
Reference :
Goodman & Gillman’s pharmacological basis of Therapeutics, 14th edition, Page 1370
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with gum bleeding, petechiae, poor wound healing, and other related symptoms. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: D) Vitamin C
Explanation:
•
Gum bleeding & petechiae: Classic signs of scurvy, caused by vitamin C deficiency,
due to impaired collagen synthesis leading to fragile capillaries.
•
Poor wound healing: Vitamin C is crucial for collagen formation and connective
tissue repair, and its deficiency results in defective wound healing.
•
Other symptoms of scurvy: Fatigue, corkscrew hairs, anemia, and subperiosteal
hemorrhages.
Vitamin C Deficiency (Scurvy)
Feature
Vitamin C Deficiency (Scurvy)
Poor dietary intake (malnutrition, alcoholism, elderly, infants on cow's
Cause
milk)
Key
Bleeding gums, petechiae, bruising, corkscrew hairs, poor wound healing
Symptoms
Other Signs
Subperiosteal hemorrhage, joint pain, anemia, weakness
Diagnosis
Clinical features, low plasma vitamin C levels
Treatment
Vitamin C supplementation
Vitamin A Deficiency (Option A): Incorrect because it causes night blindness, dry skin, and
keratomalacia, not bleeding gums or petechiae.
Vitamin B6 Deficiency (Option B): Incorrect because it presents with irritability, glossitis,
peripheral neuropathy, and seizures, not connective tissue defects.
Vitamin B3 (Niacin) Deficiency (Option C): Incorrect because it causes pellagra (3 Ds-
diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia) with photosensitive rash, not gum bleeding.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: What is the key difference between Cisplatin and Carboplatin?
options: Cisplatin is less neurotoxic than Carboplatin
Cisplatin causes fewer gastric issues compared to Carboplatin
Carboplatin is more neurotoxic than Cisplatin
Cisplatin has more nephrotoxic side effects compared to Carboplatin
questions.answer: Cisplatin has more nephrotoxic side effects compared to Carboplatin
questions.explanation:
Answer: D) Cisplatin has more nephrotoxic side effects compared to Carboplatin
Explanation:
Cisplatin and Carboplatin are platinum-based chemotherapy agents, but Cisplatin is more
nephrotoxic due to its accumulation in renal tubular cells.
•
Key Differences:
•
Cisplatin:
•
More nephrotoxic → Causes acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and
requires aggressive hydration with mannitol or amifostine to reduce
damage.
•
More neurotoxic and ototoxic → Causes peripheral neuropathy and
sensorineural hearing loss (ototoxicity).
•
More severe nausea and vomiting.
•
Carboplatin:
•
Less nephrotoxic and does not require aggressive hydration.
•
Less neurotoxic compared to cisplatin.
•
More myelosuppressive (causes thrombocytopenia).
Cisplatin is known for its nephrotoxic effects, which can lead to acute kidney injury.
The management of cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity includes
•
Adequate i.v. fluids - Chloride diuresis (Cl inactivates cisplatin)
•
Mannitol - diuresis of inactivated cisplatin
•
Use of nephroprotective agents like amifostine (only i.v.)
•
Cisplatin is less neurotoxic than Carboplatin (Option A): Incorrect because Cisplatin
is more neurotoxic (causing peripheral neuropathy).
•
Cisplatin causes fewer gastric issues compared to Carboplatin (Option B): Incorrect
because Cisplatin causes more nausea and vomiting (highly emetogenic).
•
Carboplatin is more neurotoxic than Cisplatin (Option C): Incorrect because
Cisplatin is more neurotoxic than Carboplatin.
Reference :
Goodman & Gillman’s pharmacological basis of Therapeutics, 14th edition, Page 1352
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient with a history of strenuous exercise skipped a meal and later consumed alcohol at a party. Alcohol inhibits which of the following biochemical processes, potentially leading to hypoglycemia?
questions.explanation:
Answer: A) Gluconeogenesis
Explanation:
•
Alcohol metabolism increases NADH/NAD+ ratio:
•
Ethanol is metabolized in the liver by alcohol dehydrogenase and acetaldehyde
dehydrogenase, leading to excessive NADH production.
•
Inhibition of Gluconeogenesis:
•
High NADH shifts metabolic balance, preventing conversion of lactate to
pyruvate and malate to oxaloacetate, both of which are essential for
gluconeogenesis.
•
Hypoglycemia Risk:
•
After exercise and fasting, glycogen stores are depleted.
•
The body relies on gluconeogenesis for glucose, but alcohol blocks this
pathway, leading to hypoglycemia after drinking.
Alcohol-Induced Hypoglycemia
Feature
Effect of Alcohol
Key Mechanism
↑ NADH inhibits gluconeogenesis
Primary Effect
↓ Glucose production → Hypoglycemia
Clinical Features
Weakness, dizziness, confusion, seizures
Risk Factors
Fasting, exercise, malnutrition, chronic alcoholism
Treatment
IV dextrose, thiamine in alcoholics
•
Glycogenolysis (Option B): Incorrect because alcohol does not directly inhibit
glycogen breakdown. However, after prolonged fasting, glycogen stores are already
depleted.
•
Hexose Monophosphate (HMP) Shunt (Option C): Incorrect because this pathway
primarily generates NADPH for anabolic processes and does not significantly
contribute to blood glucose levels.
•
Ketone Body Formation (Option D): Incorrect because alcohol metabolism can
actually promote ketogenesis, especially in chronic alcoholism, rather than
inhibiting it.
Reference :
Harper’s illustrated Biochemistry 32nd edition, pages 142, 162,163,171, 186, 187
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Scientists administered norepinephrine to guinea pigs, resulting in an increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure and a decrease in heart rate. What mechanism explains this response?
questions.explanation:
Answer: C) Baroreceptor stimulation
Explanation:
The administration of norepinephrine (NE) causes:
•
↑ Systolic and diastolic blood pressure (due to α₁-mediated vasoconstriction).
•
↓ Heart rate (bradycardia) despite norepinephrine’s β₁-stimulatory effects.
This paradoxical bradycardia occurs due to the activation of the baroreceptor reflex in
response to increased blood pressure.
Baroreceptor Reflex:
Aspect
Details
•
Mechanism
Baroreceptors in carotid sinus and aortic arch detect BP changes
•
Increased BP stretches receptors, sending signals to medulla via
glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves
•
Medulla inhibits vasoconstrictor center and stimulates vagal
parasympathetic center
•
Actions
Vasodilation of blood vessels
•
Decreased heart rate and contraction strength
•
Reduced BP due to lower peripheral resistance and cardiac output
•
Importance
Maintains BP stability during activities like standing
•
Fastest acting
•
Tends to reset within 1-2 days for long-term regulation
•
Beta-1 receptor blockade (Option A) is incorrect because norepinephrine stimulates β₁
receptors, increasing contractility, but the reflex bradycardia is due to vagal activation,
not β₁ blockade.
•
Alpha-1 receptor blockade (Option B) is incorrect because norepinephrine activates α₁
receptors, leading to vasoconstriction and increased blood pressure. Blocking α₁
receptors would cause vasodilation and hypotension, the opposite of the observed
effect.
•
Baroreceptor inhibition (Option D) is incorrect because if baroreceptors were inhibited,
heart rate would increase (not decrease) due to unchecked sympathetic activation.
Reference :
1. Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology, Edition 26, Pg 575, 576, 577,578, 579, 582,
583, 585, 586
2. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, Edition 14, Pg 221, 222, 229, 236,
243, 244
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 6 hours after ingesting a large quantity of paracetamol tablets. What is the most likely progression of paracetamol poisoning in this case?
options: Increase in liver enzymes within 24 hours
Paracetamol achieves peak concentration within 4 hours
questions.answer: Increase in liver enzymes within 24 hours
questions.explanation:
Answer: A) Increase in liver enzymes within 24 hours
Explanation:
Paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning follows a predictable progression based on the time
since ingestion. The first 24 hours are usually asymptomatic or present with mild symptoms,
but a rise in liver enzymes (AST, ALT) occurs as hepatotoxicity begins.
Metabolism of Acetaminophen
•
Acetaminophen is mainly metabolized via phase II reactions into harmless sulfate and
glucuronide metabolites.
•
A small portion undergoes phase I metabolism by CYP2E1, forming the hepatotoxic
metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine (NAPQI).
Detoxification of NAPQI
•
NAPQI is neutralized by binding to glutathione, forming water-soluble mercapturic acid,
which is excreted via the kidneys.
Glutathione Depletion
•
When excessive NAPQI is produced, or glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds to
hepatocyte macromolecules, forming acetaminophen-protein adducts, causing hepatocyte
necrosis.
Risk Factors
•
Chronic alcohol use (induces CYP2E1, depletes glutathione).
•
Starvation.
•
Prior use of mixed-function oxidase-inducing drugs (e.g., phenobarbital, INH).
•
Hepatitis C infection increases the risk of liver injury in overdose.
Clinical features
Early Symptoms (4-12 hrs):
•
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, shock.
Delayed Symptoms (24-48 hrs):
•
Hepatic injury becomes apparent.
•
Coagulopathy and encephalopathy.
•
Maximal damage seen 3–5 days post-ingestion with aminotransferase levels >10,000
IU/L.
•
Renal failure and myocardial injury may occur.
Stages of acute acetaminophen poisoning

Description
Ingestion

poisoning is severe.

IV

failure.
•
Liver failure within 24 hours (Option B) is incorrect because severe liver failure
typically occurs at 72–96 hours, not within the first 24 hours.
•
Paracetamol achieves peak concentration within 4 hours (Option C) is incorrect
because while paracetamol reaches peak plasma levels in 30 minutes to 2 hours, this
does not define the course of toxicity.
•
Recovery within 72 hours (Option D) is incorrect because severe toxicity peaks at 72–
96 hours, with either recovery or progression to liver failure afterward.

questions.prompt: A patient with penicillin allergy presents with fever, burning micturition, and hearing problems accompanied by dizziness. Which drug is the most appropriate for the management?
questions.explanation:
Answer: C) Ciprofloxacin
Explanation:
The patient presents with fever, burning micturition (suggestive of a urinary tract infection,
UTI), and hearing problems with dizziness (suggestive of ototoxicity). Given the penicillin
allergy, the most appropriate alternative is Ciprofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone), which is:
•
Effective against common UTI pathogens (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas).
•
Safe in penicillin-allergic patients.
•
Less likely to exacerbate hearing loss compared to aminoglycosides.
Ciprofloxacin
•
Pharmacokinetics
Good oral absorption
•
Bioavailability ~70%,Moderate half-life (~4-5 hours)
•
Widely distributed in tissues and body fluids
•
Renal excretion
•
Uses
Urinary tract infections
•
Prostatitis
•
Pseudomonas aeruginosa (DOC)
•
Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) (DOC)
•
Gastrointestinal infections (e.g., traveller's diarrhoea)
•
Bone and joint infections
•
Side Effects
Gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, diarrhoea).
•
CNS effects (headache, dizziness).
•
Tendonitis and tendon rupture.
•
Photosensitivity.
•
Contraindications
Pregnancy
•
Children (due to potential for cartilage damage)
•
Myasthenia gravis (can exacerbate muscle weakness)
•
Azithromycin (Option A) is incorrect because macrolides are not first-line for UTIs, as
they have poor urinary penetration and limited coverage against Gram-negative
uropathogens.
•
Amikacin (Option B) is incorrect because although aminoglycosides are effective
against UTIs, they are highly ototoxic and nephrotoxic, which is risky given the
patient’s hearing problems and dizziness.
•
Ampicillin-Clavulanic Acid (Option D) is incorrect because the patient has a penicillin

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Which of the following enzymes is typically elevated in prostate cancer?
questions.explanation:
Answer: A) Acid phosphatase
Explanation:
Acid phosphatase, specifically prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP), is an enzyme that is elevated
in prostate cancer, particularly in advanced or metastatic cases. PAP was historically used as a
tumour marker for prostate cancer, though prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is now the preferred
marker.
•
Significance:
•
Elevated in prostate cancer with bone metastases
•
Can be used to monitor disease progression
•
Less commonly used now due to the superior sensitivity of PSA
•
Alkaline Phosphatase (Option B) is incorrect because while alkaline phosphatase
(ALP) is elevated in bone metastases, it is not specific for prostate cancer and can also
be seen in liver disease and bone disorders.
•
Lactate Dehydrogenase (Option C) is incorrect because LDH is a non-specific marker
of cell turnover and is elevated in various malignancies, not just prostate cancer.
•
Alpha-Fetoprotein (Option D) is incorrect because AFP is primarily a marker for
hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumours, not prostate cancer.
Reference :
Robbins Pathology, 10th Edition, Page 976

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A TB patient with HIV begins ART and experiences deterioration in health after 2 months. What is the likely cause?
options: Development of drug resistance to TB drugs
Drug-drug interactions between TB and ART medications
Development of drug resistance to ART
questions.explanation:
Answer: C) Immunological changes in the body
Explanation:
The deterioration of health after starting ART in an HIV-TB co-infected patient is most likely
due to Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS), which is caused by
immunological changes in response to ART.
•
Mechanism:
•
ART restores CD4+ T-cell function and improves the immune response.
•
This leads to a stronger inflammatory response against pre-existing TB
infection, worsening symptoms.
•
IRIS typically occurs 2–12 weeks after ART initiation.
•
Clinical Presentation:
•
Worsening TB symptoms (fever, lymphadenopathy, worsening respiratory
symptoms).
•
New inflammatory lesions (e.g., enlarging TB lymph nodes, worsening pleural
effusions).
•
No evidence of drug resistance.
•
Management:
•
Continue both TB treatment and ART.
•
NSAIDs or corticosteroids may be used for severe cases.
•
HIV-positive individuals face an 8-fold increased risk of developing TB and are prone to
more severe and potentially fatal extrapulmonary TB.
•
To manage co-infection, ATT is initiated first, followed by ART after 2 weeks to
mitigate the risk of Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS), an
exaggerated inflammatory response.
•
Rifampin, a potent CYP inducer in ATT, accelerates the metabolism of certain ART
drugs like nevirapine (NNRTI), dolutegravir (integrase inhibitor), and protease inhibitors
(e.g., Ritonavir, Indinavir, lopinavir), reducing their effectiveness. However, nucleoside
reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) and efavirenz can be safely combined with
Rifampin.
•
Rifabutin, a weaker enzyme inducer, is often used as an alternative to mitigate drug
interactions in ART.
•
All HIV-positive TB patients should also receive cotrimoxazole preventive therapy to
guard against Pneumocystis jirovecii infection.
•
Development of drug resistance to TB drugs (Option A) is incorrect because TB drug
resistance develops over months to years, whereas IRIS occurs within weeks of ART
initiation.
•
Drug-drug interactions between TB and ART medications (Option B) is incorrect
because although interactions (e.g., rifampicin reducing ART levels) are common, they
usually lead to virologic failure, not an inflammatory worsening.
•
Development of drug resistance to ART (Option D) is incorrect because ART
resistance presents with viral load rebound and worsening HIV, not a paradoxical
inflammatory response.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old male experiences headache, nausea, and shortness of breath while trekking. The physician prescribes a drug to alleviate his symptoms. The drug administered primarily acts on which part of the nephron?
questions.explanation:
Answer: A) Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)
Explanation:
The patient is experiencing symptoms of acute mountain sickness (AMS) due to hypoxia at
high altitude. The drug commonly prescribed for AMS is acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase
inhibitor, which primarily acts on the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the nephron.
•
Mechanism of Acetazolamide in AMS:
•
Inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the PCT, leading to:
•
Decreased bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) reabsorption → metabolic acidosis
•
Increased renal excretion of bicarbonate → compensatory
hyperventilation
•
This enhances ventilation and improves oxygenation, helping alleviate AMS
symptoms.
Acetazolamide in AMS Symptom Alleviation
•
Inhibits kidney carbonic anhydrase.
•
Increases urine bicarbonate ions excretion → Metabolic acidosis.
•
Counteracts respiratory alkalosis from high altitude hyperventilation.
•
Improves oxygenation and alleviates AMS symptoms.
•
Loop of Henle (Option B) is incorrect because loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) act
here by inhibiting Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransport, but they are not used for AMS.
•
Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT) (Option C) is incorrect because thiazide diuretics
act here by inhibiting Na⁺-Cl⁻ symport, but they do not correct AMS-related hypoxia.
•
Collecting Duct (CD) (Option D) is incorrect because the collecting duct is the site of
aldosterone and ADH regulation, affected by potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g.,
spironolactone), which do not treat AMS.

Explanation:
Zinc plays a crucial role in wound healing, protein synthesis, and maintenance of skin integrity,
including hair follicle health. The combination of delayed wound healing and alopecia is
particularly characteristic of zinc deficiency, as zinc is essential for both collagen synthesis
and cell division necessary for tissue repair and hair growth.

primary features of copper deficiency include anemia and neutropenia. Copper deficiency
more commonly presents with neurological symptoms and hematological abnormalities.
•

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: An elderly female undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer is experiencing significant hair loss. What is the most likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation:
The most likely cause of significant hair loss in an elderly female undergoing chemotherapy is
Anagen Effluvium. This type of hair loss occurs due to damage to the hair follicle during the
anagen (growth) phase. It is commonly caused by chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or toxic
agents that impair rapidly dividing cells, including hair follicle matrix cells. Hair loss is usually
sudden, diffuse, and non-scarring, occurring within days to weeks after starting chemotherapy.
Other Options:
Telogen Effluvium (Option A): A temporary hair loss condition caused by stress, illness, or
hormonal changes, leading to excessive shedding in the telogen (resting) phase. It is not a
primary side effect of chemotherapy.
Trichotillomania (Option B): A psychiatric disorder characterized by compulsive hair pulling,
leading to patchy hair loss with irregular borders. It is behavioral rather than treatment-induced.
Alopecia Areata (Option C): An autoimmune condition that causes sudden, patchy hair loss
due to immune system attacks on hair follicles. It is unrelated to chemotherapy.
Reference :
Neena Khanna, Textbook of Dermatology, 7th Edition, Page no: 324
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A neonate presents with a growing skin lesion, as shown in the image provided. The mother reports that the lesion has been increasing in size daily. What is the appropriate management?
options: Immediate Biopsy due to Malignancy Risk
questions.explanation:
Infantile hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors that commonly appear within the first few
weeks of life. They typically grow rapidly during the first few months (proliferative phase)
before undergoing spontaneous involution over several years.
Most do not require intervention unless they cause complications such as airway obstruction,
ulceration, or vision impairment.
Other options:
Excision and Laser Therapy (Option B): Reserved for complicated hemangiomas (e.g.,
ulcerated, functionally impairing, or rapidly growing in critical areas like the airway or eyes).
Immediate Biopsy due to Malignancy Risk (Option C): Unnecessary, as infantile
hemangiomas are benign and diagnosed clinically.
Cryotherapy (Option D): Not an appropriate treatment for hemangiomas, as they typically
regress without intervention.

questions.prompt: A patient presents with a history of dysphagia, which is more pronounced for liquids than solids. Which radiological sign is most likely to be seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A) Rat-tail sign
Explanation:
•
Dysphagia that is more pronounced for liquids than solids suggests achalasia, a
motility disorder of the esophagus.
•
Achalasia is characterized by failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to
relax, leading to progressive dilation of the esophagus with tapering at the
gastroesophageal junction.
•
On barium swallow, achalasia classically shows a "Rat-tail sign"—a smooth, gradual
narrowing at the distal esophagus due to the non-relaxing LES.
•

colorectal cancer, not an oesophageal disorder.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Which among the following is pressure epiphysis
questions.explanation:
Pressure epiphysis takes part in joint formation and transmits weight. The head of the humerus is
a pressure epiphysis as it forms the shoulder joint and bears load during movements.
Types of Epiphysis:
1. Pressure Epiphysis – Participates in joint formation and weight transmission (e.g., head
of humerus, lower end of radius).
2. Traction Epiphysis – Non-articular, does not transmit weight (e.g., greater/lesser
trochanter of femur, greater/lesser tubercle of humerus, mastoid process).
3. Atavistic Epiphysis – Once independent but fused for nutrition (e.g., coracoid process of
scapula, os trigonum).
4. Aberrant Epiphysis – Not always present (e.g., head of the first metacarpal, base of
other metacarpals).
The other options (elbow joint, wrist joint, and sternum) are not classified as pressure
epiphyses.
Reference :
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2564388/

questions.prompt: Which findings are suggestive of tubal pregnancy?
options: Ovarian mass with single layer of endometrium
Adnexal mass with empty uterus and fluid in pelvis
questions.answer: Adnexal mass with empty uterus and fluid in pelvis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D) Adnexal mass with empty uterus and fluid in pelvis
Explanation:
Tubal (ectopic) pregnancy occurs when a fertilized ovum implants outside the uterine cavity,
most commonly in the fallopian tube. The characteristic ultrasound findings suggestive of a tubal
pregnancy include:
1. Adnexal mass – Represents the ectopic pregnancy, often seen as a tubal ring or a
gestational sac outside the uterus.
2. Empty uterus – Absence of an intrauterine gestational sac despite a positive pregnancy
test.
3. Fluid in the pelvis – Suggests hemoperitoneum due to rupture or bleeding from the
ectopic site.
Ovarian mass with single layer of endometrium (Option A) suggests an ovarian pathology
(e.g., corpus luteum cyst), not tubal pregnancy.
Adnexal mass with empty uterus (Option B): While this is suggestive, the presence of fluid in
the pelvis increases suspicion of rupture.
Trilayer endometrium without adnexal mass (Option C): A trilaminar endometrium is seen in
normal early pregnancy or luteal phase and does not indicate an ectopic pregnancy.

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), also known as Stein-Leventhal syndrome, is a

sulfate, ANSD—androstenedione.

Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI) or premature ovarian failure (Option B) occurs before 40
years and presents with amenorrhea, estrogen deficiency symptoms (hot flashes, vaginal dryness),
and infertility. Hormonal evaluation shows elevated FSH (>40 mIU/mL) and low estrogen.
Unlike PCOS, which has normal or low FSH with high androgens, POI is characterized by
ovarian failure and lacks polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound.
Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) (Option C)is an acute complication of
ovulation induction (hCG, gonadotropins), leading to fluid shifts, ascites, pleural effusion, and
thrombosis risk. Patients develop rapid weight gain, abdominal distension, and massive ovarian
enlargement (>10 cm) with multiple cysts. Unlike PCOS, which is a chronic condition, OHSS
occurs post-fertility treatment and is associated with hemoconcentration and electrolyte
imbalances.
Theca-Lutein Cysts (Option D) are benign, bilateral, multiloculated ovarian cysts caused by
excess β-hCG stimulation in conditions like molar pregnancy, choriocarcinoma, and multiple
gestations. Unlike PCOS, which is a chronic endocrine disorder, theca-lutein cysts are transient
and regress once β-hCG normalizes.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: What is the likely diagnosis for the given image?
questions.explanation:
Female genital tuberculosis (FGTB) primarily affects the fallopian tubes (M/c) and the
endometrium. It can lead to tubal blockage, infertility, hydrosalpinx, pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian
masses, and pelvic adhesions.
Diagnosis:
•
Definitive: AFB on microscopy/culture or epithelioid granulomas on histopathology (low
sensitivity).
•
Imaging: Ultrasound, CT, MRI, and PET scan aid in diagnosis.
•
Molecular Tests: PCR (high sensitivity, high false positives), Gene Xpert (promising for
extrapulmonary TB).
•
Laparoscopy (Gold Standard): Reveals caseous nodules, tubercles, adhesions, shaggy
areas, straw-colored fluid.
•
Key Signs:
•
Sharma’s Python Sign: Alternating constriction and dilatation of fallopian
tubes.
•
Sharma’s Kissing Fallopian Tubes Sign: Fusion and blockage due to caseous
material and adhesions.
Image showing kissing fallopian tube sign. Nodules are also seen
Normal Fallopian Tube (Option B): The fallopian tube normally appears thin-walled, mobile,
and patent with a uniform lumen. No tubal distortion, adhesions, or nodules are seen in
normal tubes.
Hydrosalpinx (Option C): It refers to fluid-filled, dilated fallopian tubes due to chronic
infection or tubal blockage. The tube appears distended, with a thin wall and no internal
nodules. In contrast, genital TB causes thickened walls with caseous nodules and adhesions, as
seen in the given image.
Endometriosis (Option D): It leads to chocolate cysts (ovarian endometrioma), dense adhesions,
and powder-burn lesions on the peritoneum, uterus, and ovaries. Unlike TB, it does not show
caseous nodules or tubal beading.
Image showing kissing ovaries sign
(sonographic sign of moderate to severe endometriosis)

Shaw’s Textbook of Gynaecology, 17th Edition, Pages 349-352

questions.prompt: A child diagnosed with von Willebrand disease requires an understanding of the role of von Willebrand factor (vWF). What does von Willebrand factor primarily combine with?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A) Glycoprotein Ib
Explanation:
•
Von Willebrand factor (vWF) primarily binds to Glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) on platelets,
facilitating platelet adhesion to damaged endothelium via exposed subendothelial
collagen.
•
vWF also carries and stabilizes Factor VIII, preventing its degradation.
•
Von Willebrand disease (vWD) results in defective platelet adhesion and prolonged
bleeding time.
gp1b-IX is a membrane complex in platelets that facilitates binding to the von Willebrand Factor
which is defective/deficient in von Willebrand disease.
Platelet factor 3 (Option B): PF3 is a phospholipid aiding coagulation but does not directly bind
vWF.
ADP (Option C): ADP is involved in platelet aggregation, not adhesion.
Prothrombin (Option D): Prothrombin (Factor II) converts to thrombin but does not interact
with vWF.

Normal flora of the human body

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male was admitted with respiratory distress. CT showed a nasal polyp with fluid collection in the sinus. Drainage of which of the following is obstructed?
questions.explanation:
The maxillary sinus drains into the middle meatus via the ostium located high on its medial
wall. When a nasal polyp is present, it can obstruct this drainage pathway, leading to fluid
accumulation in the maxillary sinus, as seen on CT.
The maxillary sinus or the Antrum of Highmore, is the largest of the paranasal sinuses,
occupying the body of the maxilla.
•
Shape - Pyramidal
•
Size - 15mL
•
Base - toward the lateral wall of the nose
•
Apex - extends into the zygomatic process of the maxillary bone
Relations:
•
Anterior wall: Formed by the facial surface of the maxilla.
•
Posterior wall: Anterior surface of pterygopalatine fossa.
•
Medial wall: Thin and membranous in some areas, this wall borders the middle and
inferior meatuses and separates the maxillary sinus from the nasal cavity.
•
Roof: Formed by the floor of the orbit
•
Floor: Located approximately 1 cm below the floor of the nasal cavity, it is formed by
the alveolar and palatine processes of the maxilla. Closely related to the roots of the
second premolar and first molar teeth. Cavities in these teeth are associated with oro
antral fistula.
Arterial supply: Branches of the maxillary artery, specifically the infraorbital artery, greater
palatine artery, and the posterior superior alveolar artery.
Venous drainage: Pterygoid venous plexus and the facial vein.
Lymphatic drainage: Submandibular lymph nodes.
Nerve supply: Infraorbital nerve, greater palatine nerve, and the posterior superior
alveolar nerve, which are branches of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V2).
Other Options:
Ethmoidal Sinus (Option A): Drains into the middle meatus (anterior ethmoids) or superior
meatus (posterior ethmoids); obstruction causes ethmoid sinusitis.
Sphenoidal Sinus (Option B): Drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess; obstruction leads to
sphenoid sinusitis, often with deep headaches.
Frontal Sinus (Option C): Drains into the middle meatus via the frontonasal duct; obstruction
causes frontal sinusitis, often with forehead pain.
Reference :
Diseases of Ear, Nose, Throat - PL Dhingra, 8th edition, Pg 233
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 49-year-old female from Nagaland presented with right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. On examination, dull tympanic membrane with lymph nodes in the posterior triangle of the neck was seen. Which of the following is the management for the condition?
questions.explanation:
The patient's symptoms—unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, dull tympanic membrane, and
posterior triangle lymphadenopathy—raise suspicion of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC),
especially considering the geographic location (Nagaland, Northeast India, where NPC is more
prevalent due to genetic and environmental factors, including Epstein-Barr virus association).
Radiotherapy is the primary treatment for NPC, as it is highly radiosensitive.
Other Options:
Grommet insertion + Steroids (Option A): Used for chronic OME but does not treat the
underlying malignancy.
Grommet insertion (Option B): Temporary relief but inappropriate for NPC.
Steroids alone (Option C): May reduce inflammation but will not address the tumor.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: After how long is a patient advised to use alternative contraception following a vasectomy?
questions.explanation:
Sterility after vasectomy is typically achieved within 3 months or after 20 ejaculations,
whichever occurs later. Until then, an alternative method of contraception is required.
Vasectomy is a safe, minimally invasive, and highly effective method of male sterilization.
•
The no-scalpel technique, which involves a small puncture instead of a traditional
incision, is now widely used and associated with fewer complications.
•
The vas deferens, the tube responsible for transporting sperm, is divided during the
procedure.
•
Sperm present in the post-distal ligation area can lead to pregnancy, hence contraception
is required for 3 months or 20 ejaculations, whichever is later.
•
Sterilization is confirmed by semen analysis, with at least 2 analyses showing
azoospermia.
Studies show that 80% of men are sterile after 15 ejaculations or about 6 weeks, and 89% are
sperm-free by 10 weeks. The remaining sperm is gradually cleared, making the safe time period
approximately 3 months.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A total of 2000 patients were assessed for HIV. 200 were diagnosed positive. A new ELISA screening test was tested on the same group. It showed 260 as positive out of which only 130 had the disease. What is the specificity of the test?
questions.explanation:
Specificity is calculated using the formula:
Specificity = True Negatives (TN) / [True Negatives (TN) + False Positives (FP)] x 100
Step 1: Identify the given values
•
Total tested = 2000
•
Actual HIV-positive cases (True Positives + False Negatives) = 200
•
Total test-positive cases (True Positives + False Positives) = 260
•
True Positives (TP) = 130
•
False Positives (FP) = Total test positives - True Positives 260−130=130
•
True Negatives (TN) = Total actual negatives - False Positives (2000−200)−130 =
1800−130 = 1670
Step 2: Calculate Specificity
Specificity = [1670 / (1670 + 130)] x 100 = 92.78%
Rounding to the nearest whole number, specificity = 96%.
Reference :
1. Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (27th edition) Page.155
2. IAPSM textbook of Community medicine (2nd edition) Page.134

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A male presents with a history of vestibular schwannoma and psammoma bodies in the brain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
•
Meningiomas are common extra-axial tumors that arise from the meninges and are often
characterized by the presence of psammoma bodies, which are concentrically laminated
calcifications.
•
These tumors are typically slow-growing and can cause symptoms due to compression of
adjacent brain structures.
•
The association of vestibular schwannoma with meningioma is seen in
Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), a genetic disorder that predisposes individuals to
multiple nervous system tumors, including bilateral vestibular schwannomas and
meningiomas.
Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM (Option B): GBM is the most aggressive primary brain tumor,
typically arising from astrocytes. It is characterized by pseudopalisading necrosis and
microvascular proliferation, not psammoma bodies. Unlike meningioma, which is well-
circumscribed and extra-axial, GBM is an infiltrative intra-axial tumor.
Pilocytic Astrocytoma (Option C): This is a low-grade astrocytoma, most commonly seen in
children and often located in the cerebellum. It is histologically characterized by Rosenthal fibers,
which are eosinophilic, corkscrew-shaped inclusions, but it does not show psammoma bodies.
Additionally, pilocytic astrocytomas are not associated with vestibular schwannomas.
Oligodendroglioma (Option D): These tumors arise from oligodendrocytes and are commonly
associated with calcifications and a "fried egg" appearance of tumor cells due to perinuclear
clearing. However, unlike meningiomas, they do not contain psammoma bodies.
Oligodendrogliomas are also intra-axial tumors, meaning they arise from within the brain
parenchyma, whereas meningiomas are extra-axial.
Reference :
Robbins Basic Pathology, 11th Edition, Page no: 345

questions.explanation:
A woman who had a forceps delivery 24 hours ago presents with perineal pain, hypotension (BP:
80/60 mmHg), and bluish perineal swelling, indicating an actively bleeding postpartum vulvar
hematoma. The presence of hypotension suggests ongoing blood loss and impending shock,
necessitating urgent intervention.
Attempting wound repair in the ward is not suitable, as it fails to achieve adequate hemostasis
and increases the risk of recurrent bleeding and complications. Delaying surgical intervention
can lead to worsening maternal morbidity and mortality.
Postpartum spontaneous vulvar hematoma is a rare but potentially life-threatening
complication, commonly associated with instrumental deliveries such as forceps or vacuum-
assisted births. It occurs due to trauma to the labial branches of the internal pudendal artery,
leading to a localized blood collection in the vulvar or perineal region. If left untreated, the
hematoma can expand rapidly, resulting in severe hemorrhage, anemia, and hemodynamic
instability.
Management Approach
The immediate priority in such cases is:
•
Surgical exploration in the OT for hematoma evacuation and bleeding vessel
ligation(Option C)
•
Blood transfusion for hemodynamic stabilization (Option B)
Involvement of a senior obstetrician for expert management (Option D)

questions.prompt: Which of the following are the changes seen in irreversible cell injury
questions.explanation:
Irreversible cell injury is characterized by severe damage to cellular structures, leading to cell
death via necrosis or apoptosis. The hallmark of irreversible cell injury is damage to
mitochondria, specifically the appearance of amorphous densities within mitochondrial
matrices, which indicates a point of no return in cell injury. This suggests permanent
mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of ATP production, and cell death.
(Option A): This is an early and reversible change in cell injury, where the plasma membrane
forms protrusions due to cytoskeletal disruption.
(Option C): This occurs due to decreased ATP and ionic imbalances but is still reversible unless
nuclear fragmentation (karyorrhexis or karyolysis) occurs.
(Option D): This is also a reversible change caused by failure of ion pumps, leading to
intracellular water accumulation.

Follicular carcinoma of the thyroid is characterized histologically by follicular cells with
abundant pink, eosinophilic cytoplasm. This eosinophilic change is due to the presence of

Hurthle cell changes can also be seen in Hurthle cell carcinoma, a variant of follicular
carcinoma.

nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies. Does not prominently feature eosinophilic cytoplasm in
follicular cells.

Histologically shows amyloid deposits (Congo red positive) and polygonal cells in nests.
Anaplastic CA (Option D): Highly aggressive and undifferentiated. Composed of pleomorphic
giant cells, spindle cells, and high mitotic activity, with no follicular architecture or Hurthle
cell features.

q13, leading to the loss of genes that are normally expressed from the paternal allele. This occurs
due to genomic imprinting, where the maternal allele is normally silenced, and the paternal
allele is essential for normal function.
(Option A): Caused by a maternal deletion of chromosome 15q11-q13 (opposite of Prader-Willi
Syndrome). Features include severe intellectual disability, ataxia, happy demeanor (frequent
laughter), seizures, and microcephaly. UBE3A gene is affected.
(Option C): Caused by a deletion of chromosome 5p (5p- syndrome). Features include high-
pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and distinctive facial features.
(Option D): Caused by MECP2 gene mutations on the X chromosome (affects females almost
exclusively). Features include neurodevelopmental regression, loss of purposeful hand
movements (hand-wringing), ataxia, and seizures.

questions.prompt: In a patient with electric burns and stable vital signs, red-colored urine is observed. What is the most likely finding in the patient's serology?
questions.explanation:
The clinical manifestations indicate Rhabdomyolysis secondary to electrical burns. When
electrical current passes through muscle tissue, it causes extensive muscle damage, leading to the
release of myoglobin, which gives urine its red color (myoglobinuria). The destroyed muscle
cells release their contents, including potassium, creatine kinase, and myoglobin, into the
circulation. Despite stable vital signs, hyperkalemia is a critical concern in these patients due to
massive muscle cell destruction. Rhabdomyolysis is a type of false positive hematuria.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Under IDSP, which diseases are included under sentinel surveillance?
questions.explanation:
Under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) in India, sentinel surveillance is
conducted for specific diseases to monitor trends and inform public health interventions.
According to the IDSP guidelines, the diseases included under sentinel surveillance are:
•
HIV/AIDS: Monitored through designated sentinel sites to track prevalence and trends.
•
Hepatitis B Virus (HBV): Included in sentinel surveillance to assess infection rates and
inform public health strategies.
•
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs): Other STIs are also monitored to understand
their epidemiology and control measures.
HIV + TB (Option B): Incorrect. While HIV is under sentinel surveillance, tuberculosis (TB) is
monitored through regular surveillance mechanisms, not sentinel surveillance.
Malaria + Dengue (Option C): Incorrect. Both malaria and dengue are vector-borne diseases
monitored under regular surveillance, not sentinel surveillance.
Measles + Diphtheria (Option D): Incorrect. These vaccine-preventable diseases are also
monitored through regular surveillance rather than sentinel surveillance.
Reference :
1. About IDSP :: Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme(IDSP)
2. Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27th Edition Pg 824-825

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Following a fight between 2 groups, a boy was brought with severe pain in the chest, distended neck veins, dyspnea, and a BP of 80/50 mmHg. X-ray shows the following findings: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Answer: A) Tension Pneumothorax
Explanation:
1. Clinical Presentation:
•
Severe chest pain, dyspnea, distended neck veins (JVD), and hypotension
(80/50 mmHg) suggest a life-threatening tension pneumothorax.
•
Trauma history (fight) further supports the diagnosis.
2. Increased Intrathoracic Pressure → Impaired Venous Return → Distended Neck
Veins (JVD)
•
As intrathoracic pressure rises, it compresses the superior vena cava (SVC)
and right atrium, obstructing venous return to the heart.
•
This results in jugular venous distension (JVD) due to backed-up blood in the
venous system.
3. Decreased Preload & Cardiac Output → Hypotension (Low BP)
•
The compression of the right atrium and ventricle reduces blood filling
(preload), decreasing stroke volume and cardiac output.
•
This leads to severe hypotension and, if untreated, cardiac arrest due to
obstructive shock.
4. X-ray Findings:
•
Hyperlucency (increased radiolucency) on the right side due to air
accumulation.
•
Mediastinal shift to the left due to increased intrathoracic pressure.
•
Depressed diaphragm on the affected side.
•
Absence of lung markings on the affected side.
5. Management:
•
Immediate needle decompression at the 2nd intercostal space (midclavicular
line) followed by chest tube placement.

Explanation:
The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a tool used to assess a patient’s level of consciousness based
on three parameters: eye-opening, verbal response, and motor response.
•
Each parameter is scored, and the total GCS score ranges from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully
awake).
•

corresponding to a score of 1.
•

a score of 2.
•
Motor response: The patient exhibits abnormal flexion (decorticate posturing) in
response to pain, corresponding to a score of 3.

Thus, the GCS score for this patient is: 1 (Eye) + 2 (Verbal) + 3 (Motor) = 6

questions.prompt: For the diagnosis of typhus, an antigen of Proteus is used. What is this type of antigen called?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: D) Heterophile antigen
Explanation: Proteus antigens are classified asheterophile antigens because they cross-react
with antibodies produced against Rickettsia in the diagnosis of typhus.
Weil-Felix Test:
•
Weil-Felix Test is a heterophile agglutination test that works on the principle of
rickettsial antibodies showing antigenic cross-reactivity with Proteus antigens (OX 19,
OX 2 and OX K strains).
•
It is a tube agglutination test where serial dilutions of a patient's serum are treated with
non-motile strains of P. vulgaris OX 19 and OX 2 and P. mirabilis OX K.
Disease
Agglutination Test Result
Mainly agglutinates with OX19; sometimes
Epidemic and endemic typhus
with OX2

Antibodies to both OX19 and OX2 elevated.
Scrub Typhus
Raised antibodies to OXK
Rickettsial Pox, Q Fever, Ehrlichiosis,
Negative test
Bartonellosis
•
False-positive titer - Due to underlying Proteus infection. Hence, fourfold rise of
antibody titer in paired sera is better than a single high titer.
•
False-negative titer - Due to excess antibodies in the patient's sera (prozone
phenomenon). This can be obviated by testing with serial dilutions of the patient's serum.
Sequestered antigens (Option A)are normally hidden from the immune system due to
anatomical barriers (e.g., myelin basic protein, lens proteins of the eye, sperm-associated
antigens). When exposed after trauma, infection, or inflammation, they may trigger autoimmune
reactions (e.g., sympathetic ophthalmia, multiple sclerosis).
Superantigens (Option B) are highly potent immune activators that bypass normal antigen
presentation by directly binding to MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors, leading to
massive cytokine release and systemic immune activation. Examples include:
•
Staphylococcal enterotoxins (food poisoning)
•
Toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST-1)
•
Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (scarlet fever, toxic shock syndrome)
Isoantigens (or alloantigens) (Option C) are antigens that vary among individuals of the same
species, such as blood group antigens (ABO, Rh) and HLA antigens. These play a role in blood
transfusion compatibility and organ transplantation but are not relevant in the diagnosis of typhus.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old person presented with an ulcer on the medial canthus. The ulcer has rolled-out, beaded margins. Histopathology shows nesting cells with peripheral palisading patterns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer and typically occurs in sun-
exposed areas such as the face, particularly around the medial canthus of the eye.
The classic clinical description includes:
•
Ulceration with rolled-out, beaded margins.
•
A pearly or translucent appearance with visible telangiectasia.
Histopathology findings include:
•
Nesting of basaloid cells.
•
Peripheral palisading of nuclei.
•
Clefting artifact between tumor cells and surrounding stroma.
Other Options:
Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) (Option A): Typically presents with a scaly, keratinized
lesion that may ulcerate but lacks the rolled, pearly margins and palisading pattern seen in
BCC.
Nevus (Option B): A benign lesion that does not typically ulcerate or have invasive histological
features.
Melanoma (Option D): Usually presents with irregular pigmentation, asymmetry, and rapid
growth, rather than a rolled-margin ulcer.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause of lower right abdominal pain and rebound tenderness in a patient with Meckel's diverticulum?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: C) Appendicitis
Explanation:
The clinical manifestations indicate acute appendicitis, despite the presence of Meckel's
diverticulum. Lower right abdominal pain with rebound tenderness is a classic sign of acute
appendicitis, and the presence of a Meckel's diverticulum does not change this presentation.
While Meckel's diverticulum can cause abdominal pain, the specific location and presence of
rebound tenderness strongly suggest appendicitis as the primary pathology.
Perforation (Option A): While perforation of Meckel's diverticulum can occur, it typically
presents with more diffuse abdominal pain and peritonitis rather than localized right lower
quadrant pain. The presentation described is more consistent with appendicitis (Option A ruled
out). Perforation would likely cause more widespread symptoms and signs of peritoneal irritation.
Intestinal obstruction(Option B): Meckel's diverticulum can cause intestinal obstruction, but
this typically presents with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and abdominal distention rather
than localized rebound tenderness (Option B ruled out). The absence of these obstruction
symptoms makes this diagnosis less likely.
Cholecystitis(Option D): Cholecystitis typically presents with right upper quadrant pain and
tenderness, not lower right abdominal pain. The location of pain and the presence of rebound
tenderness in the right lower quadrant is inconsistent with cholecystitis (Option D ruled out).
Murphy's sign would be expected in cholecystitis, which is elicited in the right upper quadrant.
Reference :
Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1297
Learning Outcome :

Correct option: C) Repeat β-hCG after 48 hours
Explanation:
In a hemodynamically stable patient, when β-hCG levels are below the discriminatory zone
(<1,500–2,000 IU/L) and ultrasound findings are inconclusive, the next step is to repeat β-hCG
testing after 48 hours to assess the trend.
•
A doubling β-hCG level suggests a normal intrauterine pregnancy.
•
A plateauing or declining β-hCG raises suspicion of an ectopic pregnancy or early
pregnancy loss.
Investigations for ectopic pregnancy:
•
Blood examination should be done as a routine for:
•
Haemoglobin
•
ABO and Rh grouping
•
Total white cell count and differential count
•
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
•
Estimation of β-hCG: The suspicious find-ings are:
•
Lower concentration of β-hCG compared to normal intrauterine pregnancy
•
Plasma concentration does not double in 48 hours like in normal pregnancy
•
Sonography (TVS): The diagnostic features are:
•
Absence of intrauterine pregnancy with a positive pregnancy test.
•
Fluid (echogenic) in the pouch of Douglas.
•
Adnexal mass clearly separated from the ovary (Blob sign).
•
Rarely cardiac motion may be seen in an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy.
•
Combination of quantitative β-hCG values and sonog-raphy: TVS provides visualization
of a well-formed intrauterine gestational sac as early as 4–5 weeks from the last
menstrual period.
•
The lowest level of serum β-hCG at which a gestational sac is consistently visible using
TVS (discriminatory zone) is ≥ 1,500 IU/L.
•
So if the beta-hCG level is ≥ 1,500 and no intrauterine pregnancy is seen, an ectopic
pregnancy is highly suspected.
•
Laparoscopy offers benefits in cases of confusion with other pelvic lesions.
•
Dilatation and curettage: Identification of decidua without villi structure is suggestive.
•
Serum progesterone: A level greater than 25 ng/mL is suggestive of viable intrauterine
pregnancy whereas a level less than 5 ng/mL suggests an ectopic or abnormal intrauterine
pregnancy.
•
Laparotomy offers benefits when in doubt.
Laparoscopy (Option A) is reserved for cases with significant clinical suspicion of ectopic
pregnancy or instability.
Methotrexate therapy (Option B) is initiated only after a confirmed diagnosis of ectopic
pregnancy.
Dilatation and curettage (Option D) is used when miscarriage is suspected and histological
confirmation is needed.
Reference :
DC Dutta Textbook of Obstetrics, 9th Edition, Page 172
Learning Outcome :

questions.prompt: A patient presents with loss of sensation on the posterior surface of the ear along with a lesion. Which structure is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
The Greater Auricular Nerve is a branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3) and provides sensory
innervation to:
•
The posterior surface of the ear.
•
The skin over the angle of the mandible and parotid gland.
•
Part of the posterior auricular region.
Lesions affecting this nerve can lead to loss of sensation in these areas.
Other options:
Internal Jugular Vein (Option B): A major venous structure that drains blood from the head
and neck but does not contribute to sensory innervation.
External Jugular Vein (Option C): Also a venous structure, responsible for draining
superficial areas of the head, but not involved in sensation.
External Carotid Artery (Option D): A major arterial supply to the face and scalp, but it does
not play a role in sensory innervation.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 35 y/o asthmatic patient is scheduled for a minor surgical procedure. Which induction agent and muscle relaxant combination is safest for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: C) Ketamine and Vecuronium
Explanation:
•
Ketamine is beneficial in asthmatics as it provides analgesia and induces bronchodilation
without significant hemodynamic instability.
•
Vecuronium is a non-depolarizing muscle relaxant that does not release histamine,
making it safe for use in asthmatic patients.
Anaesthesia in Asthmatics
•
IV Induction Agent:
•
Propofol: Preferred for stable patients, promotes bronchodilation.
•
Ketamine: Ideal for hemodynamically unstable asthmatics, promotes
bronchodilation.
•
Muscle Relaxant:
•
Vecuronium, Rocuronium, Cis-atracurium: Safe for use in asthmatics, no
significant histamine release.
•
Pancuronium: Releases low levels of histamine.
•
Inhalational Agent:
•
Sevoflurane, Isoflurane, Halothane: Ideal choices as they depress airway
reflexes and relax bronchial smooth muscle.
•
Desflurane: This should be avoided due to airway irritation and increased
airway resistance.
Propofol and Succinylcholine (Option A): Succinylcholine may provoke bronchospasm.
Ketamine and d-tubocurarine (Option B): d-tubocurarine releases histamine, which can trigger
bronchospasm.
Thiopental and Rocuronium (Option D): Thiopental has slower recovery times and can cause
respiratory depression.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Which of the following is not caused by food adulteration?
questions.explanation:
Fluorosis is caused by excessive fluoride intake, primarily through drinking water, and not
by food adulteration. Fluorosis is a chronic condition resulting from prolonged exposure to high
levels of fluoride, typically from geological sources in groundwater, rather than from any
deliberate or accidental food contamination.
Epidemic dropsy(Option B): This condition is caused by the consumption of mustard oil
adulterated with argemone oil (from Argemone mexicana seeds). The toxic alkaloids cause
widespread edema, cardiac involvement, and glaucoma. This is a classic example of food
adulteration causing significant public health problems.
Neurolathyrism (Option C): This is a neurological disorder caused by excessive consumption of
Lathyrus sativus (grass pea) or when other pulses are adulterated with it, especially during times
of famine. It results in spastic paraparesis of lower limbs. The condition is directly linked to food
adulteration or contamination.
Endemic ascites (Option D): This condition is associated with food contamination or
adulteration with pyrrolizidine alkaloids, typically found in certain plants. It can lead to veno-
occlusive disease of the liver resulting in ascites.
Reference :
Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 25th Edition, Page 624
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old woman comes to the clinic for a routine follow-up. She has a history of mild hypertension, which is well-controlled with medication. She reports no symptoms such as palpitations, dizziness, or chest pain. An ECG of the patient is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the ECG findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B) First-Degree AV Block
Explanation:
•
The ECG shows a prolonged PR interval (>0.20 seconds) but consistently conducts P
waves to QRS complexes, indicating first-degree AV block.
•
There are no dropped beats, ruling out higher-degree blocks.
First Degree AV Block
•
Pathology
First-degree AV block is characterized by a prolonged PR interval
(>0.20 seconds) without disruption of conduction from atria to
ventricles.
•
The delay typically occurs in the AV node, but may also involve the
atria, His bundle, or Purkinje fibers.
•
Etiology
Commonly attributed to increased vagal tone in younger patients.
•
In older patients, often due to fibrotic changes in the cardiac
conduction system.
•
Other causes include coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction,
electrolyte abnormalities, inflammation, infections, certain drugs,
infiltrative diseases, collagen vascular diseases, and idiopathic
degenerative diseases.
•
Lymes disease, Chagas disease, Diphtheria, Rheumatoid arthritis,
Scleroderma.
•
Clinical
Usually asymptomatic; patients are often unaware of the condition
Features
until discovered on an ECG.
•
In cases where the PR interval exceeds 0.30 seconds, symptoms
may resemble "pacemaker syndrome," including dyspnea, malaise,
lightheadedness, and chest pain.
•
ECG
Diagnosis is confirmed by a PR interval greater than 0.20 seconds
Features
on an ECG.
•
PR interval can be marked (>0.30 seconds) in some cases, and P
waves may appear within preceding T waves.
•
Treatment
Generally, no treatment is required; routine observation is sufficient.
•
Pacemaker placement may be considered for symptomatic patients
with PR interval >0.30 seconds or those with coexisting heart
disease.
•
No antiarrhythmic medications are indicated, and surveillance with
routine ECGs is recommended to monitor for worsening.
Second-Degree AV Block (Option A):
•
This block features progressive lengthening of the PR interval followed by a dropped
QRS complex, which is absent in this ECG as there are no dropped beats.
Third-Degree AV Block (Option C):
•
Here, there is complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes.
•
This is absent in the ECG since P waves are consistently followed by QRS complexes.
Bundle Branch Block (Option D):
•
This condition shows a wide QRS complex with characteristic morphology.
•
This feature is absent in the ECG, where the QRS complexes are normal in width and
shape
Reference :
1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 1881
2. First-Degree Heart Block - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
3. 1st degree heart block: Causes, symptoms, and treatment

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient undergoing surgery is administered succinylcholine for muscle relaxation. Shortly after administration, he develops hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B) Dantrolene sodium
Explanation:
The clinical manifestations indicate malignant hyperthermia, a rare but life-threatening genetic
disorder triggered by certain anesthetic agents, particularly succinylcholine. It is characterized by
the rapid onset of hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tachycardia, and metabolic acidosis following
exposure to these triggering agents.
The first-line treatment and specific antidote for malignant hyperthermia is Dantrolene sodium.
It works by inhibiting calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle,
effectively reducing the hypermetabolic state and preventing further temperature elevation.
Immediate administration of Dantrolene is crucial to prevent severe complications and mortality.
Diagnosis of malignant hyperthermia
•
Best screening test: Creatine kinase test
•
Gold Standard Diagnostic test: Halothane-Caffeine Test
Treatment for malignant hyperthermia
1. Discontinue volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine immediately. Notify the surgeon
and call for assistance.
2. Hyperventilate the patient with 100% oxygen at a fresh flow rate of at least 10 L/min.
3. Mix dantrolene sodium with sterile distilled water and administer 2.5 mg/kg
intravenously as soon as possible. Repeat every 5 to 10 minutes until symptoms improve,
with a maximum total dose of 10 mg/kg.
4. Administer bicarbonate to address metabolic acidosis.
5. Implement cooling measures, such as lavage, cooling blankets, and cold intravenous
fluids.
6. For severe hyperkalemia, administer dextrose (25–50 g IV) along with regular insulin
(10–20 units IV for adults).
7. Provide antiarrhythmic medications as necessary.
8. Monitor end-tidal CO2 levels, electrolytes, blood gases, creatine kinase, serum
myoglobin, core temperature, urinary output and colour, and coagulation status.
Neostigmine(Option A) is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used primarily to reverse non-
depolarizing neuromuscular blockade at the end of surgery. It would treat the underlying
pathophysiology of malignant hyperthermia and could potentially worsen symptoms by
increasing acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions. Neostigmine is contraindicated in this
scenario as it may exacerbate the hypermetabolic crisis.
Atropine(Option C) is an anticholinergic medication that blocks muscarinic receptors. It would
not treat malignant hyperthermia and might actually worsen the condition by inhibiting sweating
and further elevating body temperature. Additionally, it could exacerbate the tachycardia already
present in this patient.
Midazolam (Option D) is a benzodiazepine with sedative, anxiolytic, and amnestic properties.
While it might provide some symptomatic relief through sedation, it does not address the
underlying pathophysiology of malignant hyperthermia.
Reference :
1. Miller’s Anaesthesia, 9th Edition, Page 1118, 1123, 1124, 1125
2. Morgan and Mikhail’s Clinical Anaesthesia, 7th Edition, Page 2301, 2302
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient scheduled for elective hip surgery is currently taking aspirin, enalapril, a multivitamin, and metoprolol. The surgery is planned in 5 days. What is the appropriate perioperative management for this patient?
options: Stop aspirin to minimize perioperative bleeding risk
Stop metoprolol to increase cardiac output
Increase aspirin dosage for additional analgesic benefit
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A) Stop enalapril
Explanation:
ACE inhibitors such as enalapril should typically be stopped 24 hours before elective
surgery. This recommendation is based on evidence that continuing ACE inhibitors
perioperatively can lead to clinically significant hypotension during anesthesia, particularly
when combined with the vasodilatory effects of anesthetic agents.

Continued or stopped preoperatively

Continued
Antiepileptic
Continued
Antidepressants
Continued
Aspirin
Continued

Continued

Stop at least 6-8 weeks prior

Continued
Anticonvulsants
Continued

Discontinue 2-3 weeks before surgery
Oral Contraceptive Pill
Discontinue at least 6 weeks before
Herbal Supplements
Discontinue at least 2 weeks before
surgery
ACE Inhibitors (Enalapril)
Stop 24 hours before surgery
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs)
Stop 24 hours before surgery
(Telmisartan)

Stop aspirin to minimize perioperative bleeding risk (Option B) may be considered for
neurosurgery or ocular procedures, but current guidelines generally recommend continuing
aspirin for most orthopedic procedures including hip surgery. The modest increase in surgical
bleeding with aspirin continuation is typically manageable and outweighed by the potential
cardiovascular risks of discontinuation.
Stop metoprolol to increase cardiac output(Option C) would be inappropriate and potentially
dangerous. Abrupt beta-blocker discontinuation perioperatively significantly increases the risk of
sympathetic hyperactivity, tachycardia, hypertension, myocardial ischemia, and mortality.
Increasing aspirin dosage for additional analgesic benefit (Option D) has no supporting
evidence of additional benefit and would unnecessarily increase bleeding risk.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: What is the most common defect in a ventricular septal defect?
options: Non-development of the perimembranous part of the septum
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B) Membranous defect
Explanation
The most common defect in ventricular septal defect (VSD) is membranous defect.
Pathophysiology of VSD:
•
The interventricular septum has two parts: membranous and muscular.
•
VSD occurs due to incomplete development or fusion of septal components during
embryonic cardiac formation.
•
A unified classification system is used to describe VSDs.
Types of VSD:
•
Infundibular (Outlet) VSD:
•
Location: Below semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary), within the outlet
septum of the right ventricle.
•
Perimembranous VSD:
•
Location: Membranous septum, below crista supraventricularis.
•
Characteristics: Most common (80% of cases), may involve muscular septum,
potential for spontaneous closure.
•
Inlet (Atrioventricular Canal) VSD:
•
Location: Below the inlet valves (tricuspid and mitral), in the inlet portion of the
right ventricle septum.
•
Characteristics: Represents 8% of all VSDs, more common in patients with
Trisomy 21.
•
Muscular (Trabecular) VSD:
o Location: Muscular septum (apical, central, outlet regions).
o Characteristics: Can present as multiple defects ("Swiss cheese"), more common
in infants, the tendency to close spontaneously with age.
Gerbode Defects:
•
A distinct defect with a direct connection between the left ventricle and right atrium.
•
Type 1: True Gerbode, congenital deficiency in the membranous septum.
•
Type 2: Subvalvular type, ventriculo-atrial shunting due to central VSD and tricuspid
valve defect.
•
Type 3: Combination of Type 1 and Type 2 characteristics.
Reference :
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470330/
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A baby presents with the clinical features shown in the image, including characteristic perioral and perianal rash along with a history of diarrhea. Which of the following is the most likely deficiency responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer: A) Zinc Deficiency
Explanation:
•
Characteristic rash: The image likely shows acrodermatitis enteropathica, which
presents with perioral, perianal, and acral dermatitis—a hallmark of zinc deficiency.
•
History of diarrhea: Zinc plays a crucial role in intestinal function and immunity; its
deficiency leads to chronic diarrhea.
•
Other symptoms of zinc deficiency: Growth retardation, poor wound healing, alopecia,
and immune dysfunction.
Zinc Deficiency & Acrodermatitis Enteropathica
Feature
Zinc Deficiency
Cause
Congenital (SLC39A4 mutation) or acquired (malnutrition, chronic
diarrhea)
Key Skin
Perioral, perianal, and acral dermatitis with erythematous, scaly
Features
plaques
Other
Growth retardation, diarrhea, alopecia, immune dysfunction
Symptoms
Diagnosis
Low serum zinc levels
Treatment
Zinc supplementation
Niacin Deficiency (Option B) is incorrect because niacin deficiency leads to pellagra,
characterized by the "3 Ds"—dermatitis, diarrhoea, and dementia—but the rash is
photosensitive and occurs in sun-exposed areas, not perioral/perianal.
Selenium Deficiency (Option C) is incorrect because selenium deficiency primarily affects the
cardiovascular system (e.g., Keshan disease, causing cardiomyopathy) and does not cause a
perioral/perianal rash.
Magnesium Deficiency (Option D) is incorrect because magnesium deficiency presents with
neuromuscular symptoms (tetany, muscle cramps, seizures) rather than a characteristic rash.
