questions.prompt: A 1.5-month-old male infant presents to the outpatient department with vomiting after feeding and failure to thrive. On examination, a firm, olive-shaped mass is palpated in the upper abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An infant with post-feed vomiting, poor weight gain and a palpable olive-shaped upper abdominal mass has the classic presentation of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Thickening of the pyloric muscle obstructs gastric emptying. The age and palpable mass distinguish this from uncomplicated gastroesophageal reflux. Ultrasound can demonstrate the thickened pylorus. The source PDF omitted its answer field; option B is supported by the clinical findings.
questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the characteristic age, vomiting pattern and palpable mass of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
questions.reasoningChain: Young infant + post-feed vomiting + olive-shaped mass → hypertrophied pylorus → gastric outlet obstruction.
optionExplanations: A nonspecific intestinal obstruction does not account for the characteristic palpable pyloric olive.
Pyloric muscular hypertrophy causes gastric outlet obstruction and the characteristic olive-shaped mass.
Reflux may cause regurgitation but does not produce an olive-shaped abdominal mass.
Esophageal atresia usually presents immediately after birth with feeding difficulty, choking and excessive secretions.

questions.prompt: A newborn male presents with urinary retention, lethargy and a distended bladder. Antenatal ultrasound showed a "keyhole sign" with a thickened bladder wall. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: C) Posterior urethral valves
Explanation
Posterior urethral valves are characterized by membranous folds in the posterior urethra leading
to urinary obstruction, which matches the "keyhole sign" on ultrasound and the postnatal
symptoms of urinary retention and lethargy.
Posterior urethral valves
Definition
Urinary tract obstruction in male infants from membranous folds in
the posterior urethra.
Complications
Chronic kidney disease, pulmonary hypoplasia from
oligohydramnios.
Classification
Type I: Posterior urethral folds
Type II: Membranes at bladder neck
Type III: Round membrane at verumontanum
Etiology
Congenital, unclear embryological origin.
Pathophysiology
Increased bladder pressure → hypertrophy, vesicoureteric reflux,
renal damage
Diagnostic Tools
Ultrasound, VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram) and Renal
scintigraphy.
Antenatal
Ultrasound: Dilated bladder ("keyhole sign"), thickened walls.
Diagnosis
Postnatal
Urinary retention, infections, lethargy, respiratory distress.
Symptoms
•
Management
Antenatal: Vesicostomy, fetal valve ablation
•
Postnatal: Stabilization, cystoscopic ablation
Prognosis
Depends on severity; long-term care needed for CKD, bladder
dysfunction, recurrent UTIs.
•
Hypospadias involves an abnormal urethral opening and does not present with the
obstructive symptoms described, such as a distended bladder and urinary retention.
(Option A)
•
Vesicoureteral reflux can occur secondary to posterior urethral valves but is not the
primary condition associated with the described ultrasound findings and symptoms.
(Option B)
•
Neurogenic bladder results from nerve damage affecting bladder function, but it is not
typically associated with the "keyhole sign" seen in posterior urethral valves. (Option D)

Explanation:
•
Phyllodes tumors are fibroepithelial breast tumors that exhibit stromal overgrowth
and a leaf-like architecture on histology.
•
They often present as large, bosselated (lobulated) masses with rapid growth.
•
Ulceration of overlying skin suggests an aggressive nature, which is common in
borderline or malignant phyllodes tumors.
•
Histopathology confirms the diagnosis by showing stromal hypercellularity and
cleft-like spaces resembling leaf-like structures.

•
Serial PSA measurements help assess treatment response and early detection
of relapse.
•

•
After radical prostatectomy: A rising PSA suggests biochemical recurrence.
•
During androgen deprivation therapy (ADT): Persistent or rising PSA
indicates treatment resistance.
•
Post-radiotherapy: A gradual PSA rise may suggest local or metastatic
progression.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 38 Y/o woman presents with complaints of heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic discomfort, and frequent urination. On physical examination, her uterus is found to be irregularly enlarged. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: C) Leiomyoma
Explanation:
This patient's symptoms of heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic discomfort, frequent urination,
and an irregularly enlarged uterus are most consistent with a diagnosis of leiomyoma, also
known as fibroids.
Leiomyoma:
Leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle neoplasms that originate in myometrium.
Clinical features:
•
Asymptomatic (75%) - mostly an incidental finding
•
Abnormal uterine bleeding(AUB)(30%): Menorrhagia,metrorrhagia
•
Dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia
•
Subfertility
•
Pressure symptoms
•
Bladder symptoms: increased frequency or retention of urine
•
Rectal symptoms: constipation
•
Lower abdominal or pelvic pain or heaviness
•
Irregularly enlarged lower abdomen.
Endometriosis (Option A) also presents with pelvic pain and abnormal menstrual bleeding but
an irregularly enlarged uterus is not seen.
An ovarian cyst (Option B) most commonly, is asymptomatic but increases the risk of ovarian
torsion and presents with an adnexal mass but not an enlarged uterus.
Polycystic ovarian syndrome (Option D) is usually seen in obese women and presents with
irregular menstrual bleeding along with hormonal symptoms such as hirsutism and acne.
Reference :
Williams Gynaecology, 4th Edition, Pages 205, 206
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old female presents with irregular menstrual cycles, acne, and excessive hair growth. An ultrasound reveals multiple ovarian cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A) Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
Explanation:
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), also known as Stein-Leventhal syndrome, is a
heterogeneous, multisystem endocrinopathy in women of reproductive age with ovarian
expression of various metabolic disturbances.
Components of PCOS:
•
Increased androgens
•
Ovulatory dysfunction
•
Polycystic ovaries
Clinical features:
•
Usually present in young women
•
Central obesity (BMI > 30kg/cm2), waistline> 88cm.
•
Oligomenorrhea, amenorrhoea
•
Infertility
•
Hirsutism
•
Acanthosis nigricans due to insulin resistance
Endometriosis (Option B) involves the growth of endometrial tissue outside the uterus and
presents with pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea and infertility.
•
While it can cause irregular menstrual cycles, it does not typically cause acne, hirsutism,
or multiple ovarian cysts.
Hypothyroidism (Option C) can cause menstrual irregularities, weight gain, and fatigue.
•
However, it does not commonly present with acne, hirsutism, or multiple ovarian cysts.
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) (Option D):
•
This condition can occur as a complication of Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART),
particularly in individuals who have undergone ovulation induction with medication.
•
The ultrasound may reveal multiple ovarian cysts, but the clinical presentation is
typically characterized by acute abdominal pain rather than irregular menstrual cycles,
acne, or hirsutism.
Reference :
Shaws textbook of Gynaecology, 17th Edition, Page 315
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old female presents with complaints of a yellowish-green, foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She reports painful urination and pain during intercourse & no itching. On speculum examination, her vulva and vaginal walls appear inflamed. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A) Trichomonas vaginalis
Explanation:
Trichomonas vaginitis is the most common cause of vaginitis in women of reproductive age.
Symptoms include :
•
Sudden, profuse, yellowish-green, frothy, foul-smelling discharge
•
Irritation and itching in and around the vaginal opening
•
Painful urination
•
Pain during intercourse
•
Recurrent infections
•
Inflamed vulva
•
Inflamed vaginal walls with small, punctate hemorrhages ("strawberry cervix")
Candida albicans (Option B):
•
Characterized by a scanty, white, curdy vaginal discharge
•
Intense vulvovaginal itching present leading to erosions causing splash dysuria and
dyspareunia
Gardnerella vaginalis (Option C):
•
Characterized by a foul-smelling, thin, gray-white, or green-yellow vaginal discharge
•
Absence of itching, dysuria, or dyspareunia
Neisseria gonorhhea (Option D):
•
It does not typically cause vaginitis alone.
•
It can cause cervicitis, whose symptoms can overlap with that of vaginitis.
Reference :
DC Dutta Textbook of Gynaecology, 8th Edition, Pages 135, 125, 126
Learning Outcome :
Most common causes of vaginitis:
•
Trichomonas vaginalis
•
Candidal vaginitis
•
Gardnerella vaginalis

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 33 weeks gestation presents for a routine prenatal visit. She reports decreased fetal movements over the past two days. She has a history of gestational diabetes, and her pregnancy has been otherwise uneventful. The doctor decides to perform antepartum fetal surveillance. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial test to assess the fetal well-being in this scenario?
options: Biophysical profile Contraction Stress test Non Stress test
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: D) Non Stress test
Explanation:
•
The NST is a non-invasive, quick, and reliable method to assess fetal heart rate response
to fetal movements, which is crucial given the reported decrease in fetal movements.
•
During an NST, the mother is placed in a comfortable position, and external monitors are
attached to her abdomen to record the fetal heart rate and any fetal movements for 20
minutes.
•
A reactive NST (presence of accelerations in fetal heart rate with movements) indicates
good fetal health, while a non-reactive NST (lack of sufficient accelerations) may
necessitate further testing or intervention.
Antepartum fetal surveillance:
Fetal movement
Maternal observation and recording of fetal movements to assess fetal
well-being and activity levels.
Non-stress test
Monitors fetal heart rate acceleration in response to fetal movements to
(NST)

Biophysical
Assesses fetal well-being based on fetal heart rate accelerations, fetal
profile (BPP)

volume
(Option B ruled
out)

Uses ultrasound to assess blood flow in fetal vessels like umbilical
velocimetry
artery,middle cerebral artery (MCA), and ductus venosus aiding in the
evaluation of fetal well-being and placental function

Measures the depth of amniotic fluid to assess fetal well-being and
index (AFI)
detect potential complications like oligohydramnios or polyhydramnios
(Option A ruled
out)
Contraction
Evaluates fetal heart rate response to uterine contractions to assess fetal
stress test (CST)
well-being and uteroplacental function under controlled stress
conditions.
(Option C ruled
out)
BPP, CST, AFI are not the initial tests that are performed as they are either invasive (CST) or
time consuming (BPP) or do not properly tell us about fetal movements (AFI).

Williams Obstetrics, 26th Edition, Pages 386-391

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: During the active management of the third stage of labor, which intervention is recommended to prevent postpartum hemorrhage primarily due to uterine atony?
options: Immediate administration of 20 units of undiluted oxytocin intravenously
Vigorous fundal massage combined with a uterotonic agent
Controlled cord traction with immediate removal of the placenta
questions.answer: Vigorous fundal massage combined with a uterotonic agent
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: C) Vigorous fundal massage combined with a uterotonic agent
Explanation:
•
Vigorous fundal massage helps to maintain uterine tone and prevent uterine atony, a
common cause of postpartum hemorrhage.
•
Combining it with a uterotonic agent like oxytocin further enhances uterine contraction,
reducing the risk of excessive bleeding.

delivery.

During immediate PPH, perform uterine massage
while evaluating for other bleeding sources and

prophylactic treatment for postpartum
hemorrhage.

crystalloid solution intravenously at 10 mL/min
for a dose of 200 mU/min.
•
Never administer oxytocin as an undiluted bolus
due to risks of severe hypotension or cardiac
arrhythmias.(Option A)

Intravenous oxytocin is also a first-line treatment
for uterine atony.

Oxytocin 10 units can be given IM with the
delivery of the anterior shoulder (Option B)

If the placenta is not separated, perform manual

Delivery of the placenta by cord traction before

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most likely abnormality in a patient of recurrent vomiting with pH 7.5, pCO2 48mm Hg, and HCO3- 33?
questions.explanation:
The clinical manifestations indicate metabolic alkalosis secondary to recurrent vomiting. The
elevated pH (7.5), elevated HCO3- (33 mEq/L), and elevated pCO2 (48 mmHg) are consistent
with metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation. The vomiting causes
loss of H+ ions from the stomach, leading to increased serum bicarbonate concentration.
•
Metabolic
Metabolic alkalosis is characterized by an increase in arterial pH,
Alkalosis:
elevated serum bicarbonate [HCO3−], and increased PaCO2
due to compensatory hypoventilation.
•
Often presents with hypochloremia and hypokalemia.
•
Occurs as a mixed disorder with respiratory or metabolic acidosis
or alkalosis.
•
Causes:
Exogenous Bicarbonate Loads
•
Acute alkali administration
•
Milk-alkali syndrome
•
Effective ECFV Contraction (Normotension, K+ Deficiency,
Secondary Hyperreninemic Hyperaldosteronism)
•
Gastrointestinal Origin: Vomiting, gastric aspiration,
congenital chloridorrhea, gastrocystoplasty, villous
adenoma
•
Renal Origin: Diuretic use (thiazides, loop diuretics),
posthypercapnic state, hypercalcemia/hypoparathyroidism,
recovery from acidosis, non-resorbable anions (e.g.,
penicillin), Mg²⁺ deficiency, K⁺ depletion, Bartter's
syndrome, Gitelman's syndrome
•
ECFV Expansion, Hypertension, K+ Deficiency, and
Mineralocorticoid Excess
•
High Renin: Renal artery stenosis, accelerated
hypertension, renin-secreting tumor, estrogen therapy
•
Low Renin: Primary aldosteronism (adenoma, hyperplasia,
carcinoma), adrenal enzyme defects (11β-hydroxylase,
17α-hydroxylase deficiency), Cushing’s syndrome,
substances like licorice, carbenoxolone
•
Genetic Sodium Channel Mutation (Liddle's Syndrome)
•
Gain-of-function mutation in the distal convoluted tubule,
causing ECFV expansion, hypertension, K⁺ deficiency,
and hypo-reninemic-hypoaldosteronism
•
Clinical
Neurological: Mental confusion, obtundation, potential seizures
Features:
•
Peripheral Nervous System: Paresthesias, muscle cramps, tetany
(similar to hypocalcemia effects)
•
Cardiovascular: Aggravation of arrhythmias, particularly in COPD
patients
•
Electrolyte
Potassium (K⁺): Hypokalemia, especially in cases involving
Imbalances:
secondary hyperaldosteronism or diuretic use.
•
Chloride (Cl⁻): Hypochloremia, frequently accompanying
alkalosis, especially in cases of vomiting or diuretic use.
•
Calcium (Ca²⁺): Symptoms may mimic hypocalcemia despite
normal levels.
Metabolic acidosis(Option A): Metabolic acidosis is characterized by a decreased pH and
decreased HCO3- level, which is opposite to the findings in this case. Additionally, vomiting
typically causes alkalosis, not acidosis.
Respiratory acidosis(Option C): Respiratory acidosis is characterized by an elevated pCO2 and
decreased pH, neither of which is present in this case. Also, the clinical context of vomiting
supports metabolic rather than respiratory disorders.
Respiratory alkalosis(Option D): Respiratory alkalosis is characterized by a decreased pCO2
and elevated pH. The elevated pCO2, in this case, rules out respiratory alkalosis. Furthermore, the
history of vomiting points to a metabolic rather than respiratory cause.
Reference :
1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 365-367
2. Arterial Blood Gases - Physiopedia
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with unilateral throbbing pain, photophobia, nausea, and vomiting. The symptoms improve after taking sumatriptan. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The clinical manifestations indicate classic migraine headache.
The combination of throbbing pain, photophobia, nausea, and vomiting represents the typical
presentation of migraine. The positive response to sumatriptan, a selective 5-HT1B/1D receptor
agonist specifically used for migraine treatment, further confirms the diagnosis. These
medications work by constricting cranial blood vessels and inhibiting neurogenic inflammation.
Clinical Features of Migraine
•
Premonitory
Neck discomfort
(Prodromal) Phase
•
Cognitive impairment (brain “fog”)
•
Mood changes
•
Fatigue
•
Yawning/sleepiness
•
Increased urination and thirst
•
Food cravings
•
Aura
Neurologic disturbances (e.g., visual disturbances like
scintillating scotoma)
•
Due to Cerebral vasoconstriction. Therefore prevention
is by Vasodilators.
•
Headache Phase
Pain
•
Nausea/vomiting
•
Sensory sensitivities:
•
Photophobia (sensitivity to light)
•
Phonophobia (sensitivity to sound)
•
Osmophobia (sensitivity to smells)
•
Allodynia (pain from non-painful stimuli)
•
Vertigo
•
Due to cerebral vasodilation. So treatment is
Vasoconstrictors
•
Postdrome
Tiredness
•
Weariness
•
Impaired concentration
Diagnostic Classification:
Simplified Diagnostic Criteria for Migraine by International Headache Society
Repeated attacks of headache lasting 4–72h in patients with a normal physical examination,
no other reasonable cause for the headache, and:
At least 2 of the following features:
Plus at least 1 of the following features:
•
Unilateral pain
•
•
Throbbing pain
Nausea/vomiting
•
•
Aggravation by movement
Photophobia and phonophobia
•
Moderate or severe intensity
Tension headache (Option B): Tension headaches typically present with bilateral, pressing or
tightening pain without associated symptoms like photophobia, nausea, or vomiting. They do not
typically respond to triptans. The pain is usually described as a band-like pressure rather than
throbbing.
Cluster headache(Option C): Cluster headaches are characterized by severe unilateral pain
around the eye, with autonomic symptoms such as lacrimation, rhinorrhea, and conjunctival
injection. While triptans can be effective, the absence of these distinctive autonomic features
makes this diagnosis unlikely. Additionally, cluster headaches typically occur in cyclical patterns.
Sinus headache(Option D): Sinus headaches are typically associated with nasal congestion,
purulent drainage and facial pressure. They do not typically present with photophobia or respond
to triptans. The pain is usually worse with bending forward and improves with decongestants or
antibiotics if bacterial sinusitis is present.
Reference :
Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 3361
Learning Outcome :

questions.explanation:
Fluorosis is caused by excessive fluoride intake, primarily through drinking water, not by
food adulteration. It leads to dental and skeletal fluorosis due to long-term fluoride
accumulation.

questions.prompt: A patient with a history of pneumonia develops pleural effusion. What is the expected finding in the pleural analysis for parapneumonic effusion?
options: Pleural protein/plasma protein ratio less than 0.5
Pleural LDH less than 2/3rd of plasma LDH
Pleural LDH less than 0.6 of plasma LDH
questions.explanation:
A pleural pH of less than 7.2 is a key diagnostic indicator of complicated parapneumonic
effusion, an exudative pleural effusion associated with pneumonia.This acidic pH develops due
to increased glucose metabolism by bacteria and inflammatory cells in the pleural space, resulting
in lactic acid accumulation. A low pleural fluid pH is an important indication for chest tube
drainage.
Light’s Criteria for Differentiating Exudative and Transudative Effusions:
•
Exudative Effusion: Meets at least one of the following criteria
•
Transudative Effusion: Meets none of the criteria
1. Pleural protein /serum protein >0.5 (Option A ruled out)
2. Pleural LDH /serum LDH >0.6 (Option C ruled out)
3. Pleural LDH > ⅔ upper normal serum limit LDH (Option B ruled out)
Parapneumonic effusion
•
Definition:
A parapneumonic effusion is a pleural effusion that occurs in
association with bacterial pneumonia, lung abscess, or
bronchiectasis.
•
These effusions develop in about 40-60% of patients with
bacterial pneumonia.
•
Types:
Parapneumonic effusions can be categorized into three stages:
simple (uncomplicated), complicated, and empyema.
•
Simple parapneumonic effusions, the pleural fluid is
sterile and can resolve with antibiotic therapy alone.
•
Complicated parapneumonic effusions contain
bacteria and require drainage in addition to antibiotics.
•
Empyema represents the most advanced stage where
frank pus is present in the pleural space.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 72 y/o woman presents with severe chest pain and shortness of breath after a stressful argument. She is post-menopausal with no history of heart disease. O/E, she is slightly tachycardic with normal blood pressure. An echocardiogram shows left ventricular ballooning during systole, and cardiac enzymes are minimally elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B) Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy
Explanation:
•
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, also known as broken heart syndrome, is characterized by
transient left ventricular dysfunction often triggered by emotional or physical stress.
•
The patient’s recent stressful event, post-menopausal status, ballooning of the left
ventricle, and minimal elevation of cardiac enzymes align perfectly with this diagnosis.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (Gebrochenes-Herz syndrome)
•
About
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, also known as broken-heart
syndrome or stress-induced cardiomyopathy, is a non-ischemic
condition primarily affecting post-menopausal women.
•
It features temporary left ventricular dysfunction that resembles
a heart attack but with minimal cardiac enzyme release and no
significant obstructive coronary artery disease.
•
The name "Takotsubo" is derived from Japanese, meaning
octopus trap, reflecting the ballooning shape of the left ventricle
during contraction.
•
Pathophysiology
Catecholamine Hypothesis: Elevated catecholamines
(norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) indicate stress-
induced sympathetic overdrive, leading to microvascular
spasms and myocardial injury.
•
Microvascular Dysfunction: Impaired function is suggested
by abnormalities in coronary flow reserve and microvascular
resistance.
•
Inflammation: Imaging may show myocardial oedema,
necrosis, and fibrosis, with conditions like myocarditis and
autoimmune diseases potentially triggering TC.
•
Estrogen Deficiency: Exaggerated vasoconstriction and
increased sympathetic activity in post-menopausal women
contribute to TC.
•
Clinical features
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy often mimics acute coronary
syndrome.(MI)
•
Common Triggers:
•
Emotional Stress: Events like the unexpected death of
a loved one, domestic abuse, or financial loss.
•
Physical Stress: Serious medical diagnoses or natural
disasters.
•
Symptoms: Chest pain, dyspnea, and syncope. Some patients
may have signs of heart failure, such as tachyarrhythmias or
bradyarrhythmias.
•
A late-peaking systolic murmur may be present due to LVOTO.
•
About 10% of patients may develop cardiogenic shock.
Hypertensive Heart Disease (Option A):
•
Caused by chronic high blood pressure, leading to left ventricular hypertrophy.
•
This patient's history does not indicate long-standing hypertension.
Coronary Artery Disease (Option C):
•
Involves plaque buildup in coronary arteries, causing reduced blood flow.
•
The absence of obstructive disease on angiography and minimal enzyme release suggests
this is unlikely.
Pulmonary Embolism (Option D):
•
Occurs when a blood clot blocks a pulmonary artery, leading to sudden shortness of
breath and chest pain. History of long term immobilization/ DVT is present.
•
The patient's findings indicate a cardiac issue, not a pulmonary one.
Reference :
1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 1966
2. Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 68-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department in acute distress. He is diaphoretic, tachycardic, and complains of severe chest pain. His ECG is given below. Given the patient's condition, what is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: D) Synchronized cardioversion
Explanation:
The patient's clinical presentation of acute distress, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and severe chest
pain, along with the ECG showing saw-tooth flutter waves indicative of atrial flutter, suggests
he is hemodynamically unstable.
•
This necessitates immediate synchronized cardioversion to restore normal sinus rhythm
and stabilize his condition.
Atrial Flutter
•
Features
Atrial flutter is characterized by a large re-entry circuit, usually within
the right atrium, encircling the tricuspid annulus originating from the
cavotricuspid isthmus.
•
The atrial rate is approximately 300 beats per minute.
•
It is typically associated with 2:1, 3:1, or 4:1 AV block, resulting in
ventricular rates of 150, 100, or 75 beats per minute.
•
ECG
The ECG shows saw-tooth flutter waves, often referred to as "F-
Features
waves."
•
With a 2:1 AV block, flutter waves may be buried in QRS complexes
and T waves, making them difficult to identify.
•
Diagnosis
Atrial flutter should be suspected in narrow-complex tachycardia at a
rate of 150 beats per minute.
•
Carotid sinus pressure or intravenous adenosine may help reveal flutter
waves by temporarily increasing the degree of AV block.
Manageme
1. Rhythm Control:
nt
•
Acute Management:
•
Hemodynamically Unstable Patients: Synchronized
cardioversion.
•
Stable Patients:
•
Electrical cardioversion (if no intracardiac thrombus).
•
Pharmacological cardioversion:
•
Antiarrhythmic drugs:
•
Amiodarone
•
Class IA: Procainamide, Quinidine,
Disopyramide
•
Class IC: Flecainide, Propafenone
•
Calcium Channel Blockers: Verapamil,
Diltiazem
•
Beta-Blockers: Metoprolol, Carvedilol, Esmolol
•
Long-Term Management:
•
Radiofrequency catheter ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus.
2. Rate Control:
•
First-Line Agents:
•
Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., Verapamil, Diltiazem)
•
Beta-Blockers (e.g., Metoprolol, Carvedilol, Esmolol)
•
Digoxin (use cautiously due to toxicity).
•
Goal: Heart rate < 110 beats per minute.
3. Anticoagulation:
•
Assess stroke risk using the CHADS2-VASC score:
•
Anticoagulation Recommendations:
•
2 or more points: Strong recommendation for anticoagulation.
•
1 point: Consider either aspirin or full anticoagulation.
Reference :
1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 1899-1902
2. Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 470
3. Atrial Flutter - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
Learning Outcome :

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old woman with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with increased breathlessness, cough, and sputum production over the last two days. She appears distressed and has a respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute. Her oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Which of the following management strategies is most appropriate for her immediate treatment?
options: Initiate high-flow oxygen therapy to maintain oxygen saturation above 95%
Start nebulised bronchodilator therapy with salbutamol and ipratropium
Order a chest X-ray before any treatment is provided
questions.answer: Start nebulised bronchodilator therapy with salbutamol and ipratropium
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B) Start nebulised bronchodilator therapy with salbutamol and
ipratropium
Explanation:
•
Nebulised bronchodilator therapy with salbutamol and ipratropium is the most
appropriate immediate treatment for this patient experiencing an acute exacerbation of
COPD.
•
This therapy helps relieve bronchospasm and improve airflow, which is critical given her
increased breathlessness and distress.
Treatment of Acute Exacerbation of COPD:
Initial Management and Assessment:
•
Symptoms: Increased breathlessness, cough, sputum production; deterioration in lung
function and health status.
•
Triggers: Usually bacterial or viral infections, or changes in air quality.
•
Home management: Increased bronchodilator therapy, short course of oral
glucocorticoids, and possibly antibiotics.
•
Hospital referral indicators:
•
Cyanosis
•
Peripheral oedema
•
Altered consciousness
•
Comprehensive assessment upon admission:
•
Level of consciousness (response to commands, ability to cough)
•
Signs of CO2 retention (warm peripheries, bounding pulse, flapping tremor)
•
Airway obstruction assessment (wheeze, prolonged expiration)
•
Signs of cor pulmonale (peripheral oedema, raised JVP)
•
Background functional status and quality of life
•
Precipitating causes (e.g., infection, environmental factors)
Investigations:
Investigation

maintain PaO2 > 8 kPa (60 mmHg) or SaO2 > 90%.

(Option A ruled out)
•
Regular arterial blood gas monitoring to adjust therapy.
•
Use nebulised short-acting β2-agonists (e.g., salbutamol,
terbutaline) with anticholinergics (e.g., ipratropium).
Bronchodilators
•
If oxygen sensitivity is a concern, use compressed air for
nebulisation.

Antibiotic Therapy

Use simple regimens (aminopenicillin, tetracycline,

•
Safe for mild to moderate respiratory acidosis; helps
Non-Invasive

Not suitable for patients unable to protect their airway.

Consider if there is a reversible cause, no prior respiratory

Ventilation

Decisions should involve the patient, family, and GP.

Diuretics for peripheral oedema.

Doxapram may be used short-term for low respiratory
rates.
Discharge and Follow-Up:
•
Discharge criteria:
•
Clinically stable on maintenance medication.
•
Off nebulised therapy for at least 24 hours.
•
PEF reaches 75% of predicted or personal best.
•
Post-exacerbation follow-up:
•
Identify and avoid trigger factors.
•
Provide asthma education and a written self-management plan.
Begin intravenous glucocorticoids immediately (Option C) is not the first-line treatment in the

Her serum creatinine and potassium levels are normal, but she has microalbuminuria and an HbA1c of 8%. questions.prompt: A 38-year-old male presents with a one-week history of fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, and myalgia. Skin examination reveals multiple purpura and petechiae on the left shoulder, trunk, and legs. Similar cases have been reported linked to increased incidence of mosquito breeding. What is the most common neurological complication associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A) Encephalopathy
Explanation:
•
The clinical presentation including fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, and the
presence of purpura and petechiae, suggests a viral infection consistent with dengue
fever.
•
The association with increased mosquito breeding further supports this diagnosis.
•
Encephalopathy is the most common neurological complication associated with this
condition.
Dengue complications
•
Neurological
Dengue encephalopathy is most commonly encountered
neurological complication of dengue virus
•
linked primarily to dengue hemorrhagic fever and
dengue shock syndrome
•
EEG may show abnormalities such as burst
suppression and seizures
•
CSF profiles typically remain normal.
•
Neuroimaging can be normal or reveal diffuse
cerebral edema.
•
Encephalitis
•
GBS
•
Stroke
•
Cardiomyopathy
Dengue virus-induced dilated cardiomyopathy should always
be considered if a dengue fever patient has refractory shock
and signs and symptoms of congestive heart failure.
•
Hepatic injury
Liver involvement in dengue is a crucial feature
•
The effect ranges from an asymptomatic rise in liver enzymes
to the development of ALF
•
The most common atypical manifestation reported was
hepatitis
•
Pneumonia
Staphylococcus pneumonia is an important accompanying
problem seen in dengue patient
•
co-infection between dengue and influenza can result in
exacerbation of pneumonia
•
Orchitis
Orchitis usually occurs together with epididymitis
•
Commonly seen in men between 14 and 35 years of age.
Dengue
All of the following:
Hemorrhagic
•
Acute onset of fever
Fever
•
2-7 days duration
•
Hemorrhagic manifestations
•
Positive tourniquet test/Petechiae
•

etc

Hemoconcentration >20%
•
Pleural effusion, ascites/Hypoproteinemia)

pulse/Lethargy/Restlessness
•

(e.g. 100/80)

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: An alcoholic patient presents with palpitations, dizziness, and syncopal attacks. On examination, irregularly irregular pulse is seen. What will be seen on JVP?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Absent a wave:
Explanation:
The patient’s irregularly irregular pulse suggests atrial fibrillation (AF), which is common in
chronic alcoholics (so-called holiday heart syndrome). In AF, the atria do not contract
effectively → no coordinated atrial systole → no a wave is produced in the jugular venous pulse
(JVP). Therefore, the finding will be absent a wave.
Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP) reflects right atrial pressure changes during the cardiac cycle.
•
The a wave corresponds to atrial contraction (just before S1).
•
In AF, there is complete loss of organized atrial contraction → a wave disappears.
•
Chronic alcoholics are prone to AF due to atrial dilation, electrolyte imbalance, and direct
myocardial effects.
Atrial fibrillation:
Feature
Details
1
ECG
Irregularly irregular RR intervals, absent P waves, fibrillatory baseline
Causes
Hypertension, valvular heart disease (esp. mitral), alcohol (holiday heart),
thyrotoxicosis
Complications
Stroke, heart failure, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy
Management
Rate control (β-blockers, CCBs), rhythm control (amiodarone, cardioversion),
anticoagulation (CHA₂DS₂-VASc score)
JVP Waveform:
•
Positive waves in JVP:
•
a, c and v
•
a wave - Atrium Contraction (Lat Rapid Filling Phase)
•
c wave - Cusp bulging (tricuspid valve cusp bulging towards the atrium) v wave -
Venous return
•
Negative waves in JVP:
•
x wave - Atrium relaxation
•
x' wave - Tricuspid valve pulling towards the ventricle
•
y descend - Opening of tricuspid valve
JVP finding
Cause
Absent a wave
Atrial fibrillation
Large a wave
Tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary hypertension
2
Cannon a wave
Complete heart block, VT (atria contracting against closed tricuspid valve)
Steep y descent
Constrictive pericarditis
Incorrect Options:
Large a wave (Option B) – Seen when the right atrium contracts against high resistance, e.g.,
tricuspid stenosis or pulmonary hypertension.
Canon a wave (Option C) – Occurs when atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve, e.g.,
complete heart block, VT.
Steep y descent (Option D) – Seen in constrictive pericarditis and severe tricuspid regurgitation.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old female with a previous history of rheumatic fever. Examination shows a loud S1 and mid-diastolic murmur is having which of the following valvular heart disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option C - Mitral Stenosis (MS):
Explanation:
•
The patient has a history of rheumatic fever and presents with a loud S1 and mid-
diastolic murmur, which are classic findings of mitral stenosis. Rheumatic fever is the
most common cause of MS worldwide.
•
Mitral stenosis results from thickening and fusion of the mitral valve leaflets, most often
due to rheumatic heart disease. The loud S1 occurs because the stiff valve closes
forcefully, and the mid-diastolic murmur is due to turbulent flow across the narrowed
mitral orifice during diastole. Other features may include an opening snap and signs of
pulmonary congestion.
Mitral stenosis:
•
Cause: Rheumatic fever (most common), congenital, calcific degeneration (elderly).
•
Pathophysiology: Narrowed mitral orifice → ↑ left atrial pressure → pulmonary venous
hypertension → right heart strain.
•
Clinical features: Dyspnea, orthopnea, hemoptysis, atrial fibrillation.
•
Auscultation: Loud S1, opening snap after S2, low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the
apex (best heard with the patient in the left lateral position).
•
Complications: Pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure, thromboembolism.
•
Treatment: Medical (diuretics, rate control for AF) or surgical (percutaneous balloon
mitral valvotomy, valve replacement).
5
Incorrect Options:
Tricuspid Stenosis (TS) (Option A) – Mid-diastolic murmur increases with inspiration; usually
occurs with MS but isolated TS is rare.
Mitral Regurgitation (MR) (Option B) – Produces a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating
to the axilla, not a mid-diastolic murmur.
6
Aortic Regurgitation (AR) (Option D) – Produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the
left sternal border, not associated with loud S1.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents to the ER with central chest pain. He has a past medical history of heart disease. ECG is shown below. What is the diagnosis? 7
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A. - Anterolateral MI:
Explanation:
ECG Findings:
•
ST-segment elevation:
•
Anterior leads: V2–V4
•
Lateral leads: I, aVL, V5, V6
•
Reciprocal ST-segment depression: leads III and aVF (inferior leads)
Interpretation:
8
•
This combination indicates acute injury involving both the anterior wall (supplied by the
LAD) and the lateral wall (supplied by the LCX or diagonal branches of LAD) — hence,
anterolateral MI.
•
Reciprocal changes (ST depression in inferior leads) strengthen the diagnosis of acute MI
and help differentiate from pericarditis.
MI location vs. ECG leads
MI Location
Leads with ST Elevation
Likely Artery
Anterior
V1–V4
LAD
Lateral
I, aVL, V5, V6
LCX or diagonal branch
Anterolateral
V2–V6, I, aVL
LAD + LCX/diagonal branch
Inferior
II, III, aVF
RCA or LCX
Inferolateral
II, III, aVF, I, aVL, V5, V6
RCA + LCX
Posterior
V7–V9 (or tall R in V1–V2)
RCA or LCX
Incorrect Options:
Inferolateral MI (Option B):
•
Inferolateral MI would have ST elevation in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) plus lateral leads
(I, aVL, V5, V6).
•
Here, inferior leads show ST depression, not elevation → rules out this option.
Acute pericarditis (Option C):
•
Pericarditis usually has diffuse ST elevation across almost all leads without reciprocal ST
depression (except in aVR/V1) and PR segment depression.
•
This ECG shows localized ST elevation with clear reciprocal changes — typical of MI,
not pericarditis.
Constrictive pericarditis (Option D):
•
Constrictive pericarditis is a chronic condition; ECG may show low voltage QRS or
nonspecific changes, not acute ST elevation patterns.
•
It presents with signs like Kussmaul’s sign, pericardial knock, and right heart failure —
not acute chest pain + STEMI pattern.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A study was conducted among nursing staff to analyze the time spent on different aspects of patient care, such as bed preparation, monitoring vital signs, attending the doctor’s rounds, blood sampling, and drug administration. Which of the following management techniques is most appropriate for this type of analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Work Sampling
Explanation:
•
The study in the question focuses on estimating how much time nursing staff spend on
various activities across the day, but not by continuously timing each task from start to
finish. Work Sampling is the appropriate method here because it involves taking
observations at random intervals to determine the proportion of time spent on different
activities.
Work Sampling:
•
Definition: A statistical technique for determining the proportion of time spent on various
activities by making observations at random intervals.
•
Purpose:
•
Assess workload distribution.
•
Identify major time-consuming activities.
•
Provide data for staffing and scheduling decisions.
•
Applications in Healthcare:
10
•
Studying nurse-patient interaction time.
•
Determining how much time doctors spend in direct patient care vs. paperwork.
•
Evaluating efficiency in diagnostic labs.
Critical Path Method (Option A): Project management technique for scheduling dependent
tasks; not for estimating activity time proportions.
System Analysis (Option B): Studies entire systems and processes; too broad for specific
activity-time proportion studies.
Time and Motion Study (Option D): Continuous observation of each step of a task; gives
detailed task timings but is more intrusive and detailed than required for this study.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient after MI develops a broad QRS complex tachycardia. His BP is 120/85 mm Hg. ECG is given below. Best management?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Amiodarone IV:Explanation:
Step 1: Recognising the rhythm
•
Broad QRS (>120 ms)
•
Regular tachycardia
•
Monomorphic appearance
•
Post-MI patient → high risk of ventricular tachycardia (VT)
•
Diagnosis: Sustained monomorphic VT
Step 2: Assessing stability
•
BP = 120/85 mm Hg → patient is hemodynamically stable (no shock, syncope, severe
hypotension, or heart failure).
•
In stable VT, first-line pharmacologic management = IV amiodarone (or procainamide in
some guidelines).
Class III antiarrhythmic that prolongs repolarisation and suppresses ventricular
ectopy. Preferred in structural heart disease post-MI because other agents (like
some beta-blockers) may worsen VT in the acute setting.
Stable vs. unstable broad complex tachycardia (VT)
Status
First-line management
Stable VT
IV amiodarone (or procainamide)

Immediate synchronized DC cardioversion

Immediate defibrillation + CPR

Labetalol IV (Option B):
•
Labetalol is an alpha- and beta-blocker used for hypertension, not for acute VT
management.
•
Giving it here will not terminate VT and can worsen instability.
Metoprolol IV (Option C):
•
While beta-blockers are used post-MI for arrhythmia prevention, they are not the first
choice for terminating sustained VT in the acute phase.
•
Risk of worsening hypotension or bradyarrhythmia once VT resolves.
Nitroglycerin IV (Option D)
•
Used for angina or heart failure due to ischemia.
12
•
Has no role in terminating VT.
•
May cause hypotension in this context.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with weight gain, thinning of hair, and dry skin. Diagnosis is Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Which antibody is seen in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Anti-TPO antibody:
Explanation:
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas,
and it is strongly associated with anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies. These
antibodies cause autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland.
Anti-TPO antibodies target the enzyme thyroid peroxidase, which is essential for thyroid
hormone synthesis (oxidation and iodination of iodine, coupling of iodotyrosines). Their presence
confirms autoimmune thyroid disease, especially Hashimoto’s. Other antibodies, like anti-
thyroglobulin, may also be present but anti-TPO has the highest diagnostic relevance.
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis:
•
AKA Chronic autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis.
•
Epidemiology: More common in women, especially middle-aged.
•
Pathogenesis: Autoantibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin) → chronic inflammation →
fibrosis → hypothyroidism.
13
•
Clinical features: Weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair thinning, constipation,
menstrual irregularities.
•
Lab findings: High TSH, low free T4, positive anti-TPO antibodies.
•
Histopathology:
•
Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration
•
Formation of germinal centers
•
Hurthle cells (large oxyphilic epithelial cells with granular cytoplasm) replacing
follicular epithelium
•
Atrophic thyroid follicles with dense fibrosis in late stages
•
Treatment: Lifelong levothyroxine replacement.
•
Complications: Increased risk of thyroid lymphoma.
Incorrect Options:
Anti TSH (Option B) – Not seen in Hashimoto’s; would interfere with TSH action, not a
diagnostic marker.
Anti TBG (Option C) – Antibodies against thyroxine-binding globulin are rare and not relevant
for Hashimoto’s diagnosis.
Long-acting thyroid-stimulating antibody (Option D) – Seen in Graves’ disease, causes
hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: An RTA patient has received 4 packed RBC within a few hours. Which of the following will be seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option C – Hypocalcemia:
Explanation:
•
Stored packed RBCs contain citrate as an anticoagulant. Rapid transfusion leads to
citrate binding ionized calcium in the recipient’s blood, causing acute hypocalcemia.
•
Citrate toxicity is more likely when large volumes of blood are transfused rapidly, as in
massive transfusion protocols. The liver normally metabolizes citrate, but in shock or
hypothermia this clearance is impaired.
•
Clinical signs: Perioral numbness, paresthesia, muscle cramps, tetany, hypotension, and
prolonged QT interval on ECG.
Massive Blood Transfusion:
•
Definition: Replacement of blood volume exceeding patient’s total blood volume within
24 hrs (or >10 units of PRBC).
•
Acute complications:
•
Metabolic: Hypocalcemia (citrate toxicity), hypomagnesemia, hyperkalemia
(from hemolysis), hypothermia, metabolic alkalosis.
•
Coagulopathy: Due to dilution of platelets and clotting factors.
•
Volume overload & ARDS.
15
•
Prevention: Warm blood before transfusion, monitor electrolytes, give calcium
gluconate if needed, replace platelets & FFP in balanced ratios.
Key electrolyte changes in massive transfusion:

Cause
Change
Calcium
Citrate binding
↓ (Hypocalcemia)
Potassium
Leakage from stored RBCs
↑ (Hyperkalemia)
Magnesium
Citrate binding
↓ (Hypomagnesemia)
Sodium
Usually normal; slight ↑ if using older preservatives
—
Incorrect Options:
Hypernatremia (Option A) – Not a major finding; sodium content in stored blood is minimal.
Hyponatremia (Option B) – Not typically caused by transfusion.
Hyperkalemia (Option D) – Possible in prolonged storage, but acute citrate-induced
hypocalcemia is more characteristic in rapid large transfusions.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A young female presents with ptosis showing diurnal variation. CT chest shows an anterior mediastinal mass identified as thymus gland cancer. Which receptor is affected in this patient?
options: Voltage-gated calcium channels at the NMJ 16
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B.- Post-synaptic ACh Receptor:
Explanation:
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies target post-synaptic
nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, impairing neuromuscular
transmission. Thymic abnormalities (hyperplasia or thymoma) are common in MG.
In MG, antibody-mediated blockade and destruction of post-synaptic ACh receptors reduce the
number of available receptors, leading to muscle weakness. Weakness worsens with activity
and improves with rest (diurnal variation). The association with thymoma is due to aberrant
immune activation in the thymus.
Key features: Ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, proximal muscle weakness, preserved reflexes, and
response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.
Myasthenia Gravis:
•
Epidemiology: More common in young women and older men.
17
•
Pathophysiology: Autoantibodies against post-synaptic nicotinic ACh receptors at NMJ
→ impaired depolarization of muscle fibers.
•
Association: Thymic hyperplasia (65%) and thymoma (15%).
•
Diagnosis: Edrophonium (Tensilon) test, anti-AChR antibody assay, repetitive nerve
stimulation showing decremental response.
•
Treatment: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine), immunosuppressants,
thymectomy (if thymoma present), plasmapheresis/IVIG for crisis.

Presynaptic ACh receptor (Option A) – No such pathology in MG; presynaptic issues are rare
in autoimmune NMJ disease.
Voltage-gated calcium channels at NMJ (Option C) – Targeted in Lambert–Eaton myasthenic
syndrome, not MG.
Acetylcholinesterase (Option D) – This enzyme breaks down ACh in synaptic cleft; it is
inhibited pharmacologically in MG treatment, not attacked by antibodies.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old female with progressive limb weakness for the past 1 year. On examination, muscle fasciculations and hypertonia are noted, and the sensory system is intact. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis)
Explanation:
ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder involving both upper motor neurons (UMN)
and lower motor neurons (LMN), leading to weakness, hypertonia, and fasciculations, while
sparing the sensory system. The presence of UMN signs (hypertonia) and LMN signs
(fasciculations) together is characteristic.
ALS affects motor neurons in the motor cortex, brainstem, and spinal cord.
•
UMN involvement → spasticity, hyperreflexia
•
LMN involvement → muscle atrophy, fasciculations, weakness.
•
Sensory pathways are usually preserved, helping differentiate from other neuropathies.
•
Onset is insidious and relentlessly progressive, leading to respiratory failure.
ALS:
•
Epidemiology: Usually presents in middle age; more common in men.
•
Pathophysiology: Degeneration of corticospinal tracts (UMN) and anterior horn cells
(LMN).
•
Clinical features: Combination of UMN + LMN signs in multiple regions, no sensory
loss.
•
Diagnosis: Clinical (exclusion of mimics), EMG shows denervation and reinnervation.
•
Prognosis: Progressive; most patients die within 3–5 years from respiratory failure.
•
Treatment: Riluzole (glutamate inhibitor) modestly prolongs survival; supportive care is
key.
LMN and UMN signs in ALS:
Feature
UMN signs
LMN signs
Tone
Spasticity
Hypotonia
Reflexes
Hyperreflexia, Babinski+
Hyporeflexia
Muscle bulk
Normal initially
Atrophy
19
Fasciculations
Rare
Common
Incorrect Options:
Spinal muscular atrophy (Option B) – Pure LMN disease; no UMN signs like hypertonia.
Multifocal motor neuropathy (Option C) – Pure LMN weakness, usually asymmetric, often
with conduction block on nerve studies.
Becker muscular dystrophy (Option D) – Genetic myopathy with proximal weakness, no UMN
signs or fasciculations, and onset typically in adolescence or early adulthood.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with symmetrical leg weakness and areflexia. He had developed diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. He was diagnosed as having GBS. What is the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Demyelination of A, B-fibers:
Explanation:
Guillain–Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy, most often
triggered by infections like Campylobacter jejuni. It primarily affects myelinated large-
diameter motor and sensory fibers (A and B fibers), leading to weakness and areflexia.
A- and B-fibers are myelinated nerve fibers responsible for motor function and some sensory
modalities. In GBS, autoantibodies and immune cells attack the myelin sheath, impairing
conduction. This demyelination disrupts both motor signals (causing weakness) and reflex arcs
(causing areflexia).
20
Guillain–Barré Syndrome:
•
Trigger: Often post-infectious (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma).
•
Pathophysiology: Autoimmune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves and nerve
roots.
•
Clinical features: Symmetrical ascending weakness, areflexia, minimal sensory loss;
may involve cranial nerves (bilateral facial palsy).
•
Complications: Respiratory muscle involvement → respiratory failure; autonomic
instability.
•
Diagnosis: CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation (↑ protein, normal cell count);
NCS shows slowed conduction velocity.
•
Treatment: IVIG or plasmapheresis; avoid steroids.
•
Prognosis: Most recover fully, but some have residual deficits.

Myelinated
Preganglionic autonomic
C fibers
Unmyelinated

Demyelination of B-fibers (Option B) – B-fibers are affected, but not in isolation; A-fibers are
also involved.
Demyelination of the spinal cord (Option C) – GBS is a peripheral neuropathy, not a central
spinal cord disorder.
Cord inflammation (Option D) – Suggestive of myelitis, which presents with UMN signs and
sensory level, not typical in GBS.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient has developed a cough and weight loss for the last 3 months. Biopsy of lung mass shows expression of chromogranin and synaptophysin. Which paraneoplastic syndrome will most likely occur in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option D – SIADH:
Explanation:
Chromogranin and synaptophysin positivity suggests a neuroendocrine tumor, such as small
cell carcinoma of the lung. These tumors often produce ectopic ADH, leading to syndrome of
inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH).
In SIADH, excessive ADH secretion causes water retention without corresponding sodium
retention, resulting in dilutional hyponatremia and low plasma osmolality. Small cell lung
carcinoma is notorious for secreting ectopic hormones, particularly ADH and ACTH. The
presence of neuroendocrine markers confirms the tumor’s secretory nature.
Small Cell Carcinoma:
•
Origin: Neuroendocrine Kulchitsky cells in the lung.
•
Markers: Chromogranin, synaptophysin, neuron-specific enolase (NSE).
•
Paraneoplastic syndromes: SIADH (ADH), Cushing syndrome (ACTH), Lambert–
Eaton myasthenic syndrome (autoantibodies against presynaptic calcium channels).
•
Histology: Small cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, high mitotic count.
•
Prognosis: Aggressive, early metastasis; often unresectable at diagnosis.
•
Treatment: Combination chemotherapy ± radiotherapy; surgery rarely indicated.
22

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with palpitations, headache, and sweating. His BP is 180/100 mmHg. 24-hour urinary metanephrine values are elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B – Pheochromocytoma:
Explanation:
•
Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla. Classic
symptoms are episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations with hypertension. Elevated
24-hour urinary metanephrines confirm catecholamine excess.
•
Pheochromocytomas arise from chromaffin cells derived from neural crest tissue.
Excess secretion of epinephrine and norepinephrine causes paroxysmal hypertension and
sympathetic overactivity. Metanephrines are catecholamine metabolites, and their
measurement in a 24-hour urine sample or plasma is the most sensitive test for diagnosis.
Pheochromocytoma:
•
Origin: Chromaffin cells (adrenal medulla).
•
Rule of 10s: ~10% bilateral, 10% malignant, 10% extra-adrenal (paraganglioma), 10% in
children.
•
Associations: MEN 2A, MEN 2B, von Hippel–Lindau disease, NF1.
•
Treatment: α-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) before β-blockade, then surgical resection.
•
Histology: Zellballen pattern (nests of cells with rich vascular stroma).
25
Incorrect Options:
Carcinoid tumor (Option A): Presents with flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm; diagnosis by
urinary 5-HIAA, not metanephrines.
26
Carcinoid crisis (Option C): Severe complication of carcinoid tumor with profound hypotension
and bronchospasm; unrelated to catecholamines.
Neuroblastoma (Option D): Pediatric tumor of adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain; elevated
HVA/VMA (dopamine metabolites), not metanephrines in adults.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient with osteoarthritis, for the last 3 months, has been taking ibuprofen and has developed occult GI bleeding. Which is correct about the cause?
options: PGE-2 and prostacyclin production were reduced
PGE-1 and prostacyclin production were reduced
Mucosal injury due to inhibition of COX-2
questions.answer: PGE-2 and prostacyclin production were reduced
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - PGE-2 and prostacyclin production were reduced:
Explanation:
•
NSAIDs like ibuprofen inhibit COX enzymes, reducing prostaglandin (PGE₂) and
prostacyclin synthesis. These mediators normally maintain gastric mucosal protection
by increasing mucus and bicarbonate secretion and promoting mucosal blood flow.
•
Loss of PGE₂ and prostacyclin leads to impaired gastric mucosal defense, making the
mucosa susceptible to acid-induced injury and bleeding. This is the primary mechanism
for NSAID-induced gastritis and peptic ulcers. COX-1 inhibition is particularly
responsible for GI side effects, as it is involved in constitutive prostaglandin synthesis for
mucosal protection.
NSAID-induced GI injury:
•
Mechanism: COX-1 inhibition → ↓ PGE₂, ↓ prostacyclin → ↓ mucus, ↓ bicarbonate, ↓
blood flow.
27
•
Risk factors: High-dose/long-term NSAID use, elderly, alcohol, corticosteroids, H.
pylori infection.
•
Prevention: Co-prescription of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) or misoprostol (PGE₁
analog).
•
Histology: Superficial mucosal erosions with inflammatory infiltrates.
•
Complications: Peptic ulcers, GI bleeding, perforation.
Incorrect Options:
Increased acid production (Option B): NSAIDs do not significantly increase gastric acid
secretion; the main issue is reduced mucosal defense.
PGE-1 and prostacyclin production reduced (Option C): The main gastric protective
prostaglandin is PGE₂, not PGE₁.
Mucosal injury due to inhibition of COX-2 (Option D): COX-2 inhibition is more linked to
anti-inflammatory effects and cardiovascular risk, not primary GI mucosal damage (which is
COX-1–mediated).
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

The technical platform under India’s National Tele Mental Health Programme (NTMHP)
designed specifically for delivering mental healthcare services through telephone, digital

Launched by: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India.

Provide accessible, affordable, and quality mental health services across India.

Reduce stigma and bridge the treatment gap for mental illnesses.

Structure:

Tier 1: State Tele-MANAS cells with trained counsellors and mental health
professionals answering calls via a toll-free helpline.

Tier 2: District-level mental health facilities for in-person follow-up and
advanced care.

Key Features:

Toll-free 24×7 helpline.

Multi-language support.

Integration with digital platforms and online portals for follow-up care.

questions.prompt: Who is primarily responsible for registering eligible couples for family planning and maintaining their records under the national health system?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Multipurpose Worker (Female)
Explanation:
•
Under India’s national health system, the Multipurpose Worker (Female), often
synonymous with the Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM), is responsible for registering
eligible couples for family planning and maintaining their records.
•
This includes updating the Eligible Couple Register, tracking contraceptive use, and
ensuring follow-up services. ASHAs and Anganwadi Workers assist in community
mobilization and education but do not maintain the official eligible couple records.
Multipurpose Worker (Female) / ANM in Family Planning:

Role in Family Planning:
•
Maintain Eligible Couple Register (ECR) at the sub-centre level.
•
Identify eligible couples (married women aged 15–49 years).
•
Record contraceptive choices and follow-up dates.
•
Distribute contraceptives (condoms, OCPs) and counsel couples.
•
Refer for IUCD, sterilization, or other services as required.
•
Coordination: Works with ASHAs, Anganwadi Workers, and Medical Officers for
outreach.
ASHA (Option A): Assists in identifying eligible couples, motivating them for family planning,
and distributing contraceptives, but does not maintain the official ECR.
Village Health Guide (Option C): Works in basic health education and minor treatment at the
village level; not involved in formal family planning registration.
Anganwadi Worker (Option D): Focuses on nutrition, child care, and preschool education
under ICDS; not responsible for maintaining eligible couple records.
