Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A known case of hyperthyroidism, who is not on medication, is scheduled for total thyroidectomy. The PAC check was not done properly. What is the leading complication that can occur during surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option C - Arrhythmia
Explanation:
•
In uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, catecholamine sensitivity is increased, predisposing the
patient to severe intraoperative arrhythmias, especially during surgical manipulation of
the thyroid gland.
•
A patient with untreated hyperthyroidism undergoing thyroidectomy is at high risk of
thyroid storm, precipitated by surgical stress. This can manifest with tachyarrhythmias,
hyperthermia, and hypertension. Arrhythmia (especially atrial fibrillation or
supraventricular tachycardia) is the most immediate and dangerous intraoperative
complication.
•
Proper preoperative control with antithyroid drugs, β-blockers, and adequate
preparation is essential.
Incorrect Options:
Hyperthermia (Option A): Can occur in thyroid storm but is not the leading intraoperative
danger; arrhythmia is more acutely life-threatening.
35
Hypothermia (Option B): Not typically associated with hyperthyroidism; more a concern in
prolonged surgeries in cold OR environments.
Hypothyroidism (Option D): Develops postoperatively, not during surgery.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old male presents with deep-seated retro-orbital pain of cluster headache. What is the best management?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B – Oxygen:
Explanation:
•
High-flow 100% oxygen is the most effective acute abortive therapy for cluster
headaches, rapidly relieving pain within 15–20 minutes in most cases. It is safe, well-
tolerated, and works faster than most medications.
•
Cluster headaches are severe unilateral headaches with autonomic features. Acute attacks
require rapid-acting treatment — high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask or
subcutaneous sumatriptan are first-line.
•
Oxygen relieves pain by causing vasoconstriction and possibly modulating trigeminal-
autonomic reflexes. Prophylaxis (e.g., verapamil, lithium) is started later to prevent
recurrences, but during an acute attack, oxygen is the gold standard.
Cluster Headache:
Feature
Cluster Headache
36
Pain
Severe, unilateral, retro-orbital/temporal
Duration
15–180 minutes per attack
Frequency
Up to 8/day during cluster periods
Autonomic signs
Lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, ptosis, miosis
Triggers
Alcohol, histamine, nitroglycerin during cluster period
Acute treatment
100% O₂ (12–15 L/min), subcutaneous sumatriptan
Prophylaxis
Verapamil (drug of choice), lithium, topiramate
Incorrect Options:
Verapamil (Option A): Used for prophylaxis, not acute attack.
Lithium (Option C): Alternative prophylactic agent in refractory cases.
Topiramate (Option D): Used in prophylaxis for migraine and sometimes cluster headache, not
acute management.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Patient presents with hypertension and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. CT scan shows a mass over the kidney with elevated ARR. What is the next best step for the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B – Adrenalectomy:
Explanation:
•
This patient likely has primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s syndrome) due to an
adrenal adenoma. In unilateral disease confirmed by imaging and biochemistry
(elevated Aldosterone–Renin Ratio), surgical adrenalectomy is the treatment of choice.
•
Hypertension + hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis + high ARR + adrenal mass suggests
unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma. After confirming lateralization (often with
adrenal venous sampling in some protocols), the definitive treatment is laparoscopic
adrenalectomy. Medical management with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists
(spironolactone/eplerenone) is reserved for bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or non-surgical
candidates.
Primary Hyperaldosteronism:
Feature
Primary Hyperaldosteronism
Common causes
Adrenal adenoma (Conn’s), bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
Key features
Hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis
Screening
Elevated ARR (Aldosterone–Renin Ratio)
Confirmatory tests
Saline suppression test, fludrocortisone suppression test
Treatment – unilateral
Surgical adrenalectomy
Treatment – bilateral
Spironolactone/eplerenone
Incorrect Options:
Spironolactone (Option A): First-line for bilateral hyperplasia or non-surgical patients, not
preferred for unilateral adenoma in a surgical candidate.
ACTH stimulation test (Option C): Used for adrenal insufficiency diagnosis, not
hyperaldosteronism.
Dexamethasone suppression test (Option D): Used for diagnosing Cushing’s syndrome.
38
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old male has had chronic hypercalcemia for the last 1.5 years, but PTH levels are normal. Which of the following is most likely the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Sarcoidosis
Explanation:
•
From the given history, the patient has chronic hypercalcemia but PTH is normal. This
means the hypercalcemia is PTH-independent. Sarcoidosis, due to extra-renal
production of calcitriol by activated macrophages, presents with hypercalcemia.
Sarcoidosis:
•
Multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown etiology, characterized by non-caseating
granulomas. In sarcoidosis, activated macrophages inside the granulomas express 1-α-
hydroxylase, converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D into 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
(calcitriol). This leads to increased intestinal calcium absorption and persistent
hypercalcemia.
•
Because the calcium level is high, the parathyroid gland decreases PTH secretion,
explaining the normal or low PTH levels in such cases.
Feature
Details
Pathology
Non-caseating granulomas in multiple organs
Common Sites
Lungs, lymph nodes, skin, eyes
39
Lab Findings
↑ Serum ACE, ↑ calcium, normal/low PTH
CXR
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
Diagnosis
Clinical + radiological + biopsy confirmation
Treatment
Glucocorticoids for symptomatic disease
40
41
Incorrect Options:
Malignancy (Option A) – Can cause hypercalcemia via PTHrP or bone metastasis, but
presentation is usually acute and associated with systemic symptoms like weight loss; chronic
stable picture is less likely.
Parathyroid hyperplasia (Option C) – Would cause elevated PTH, not normal PTH.
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) (Option D) – Causes hypocalcemia initially due to phosphate
retention and decreased calcitriol synthesis; later may cause secondary/tertiary
hyperparathyroidism with raised PTH, not normal.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: On examination, a person has distended neck veins, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and a shift of the trachea. What is the management? 42
options: Bedside CXR in casualty followed by chest tube insertion
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Wide bore needle in 2nd ICS:
Explanation:
•
This is tension pneumothorax – caused by air trapping in the pleural space under
pressure.
•
Key signs:
•
Respiratory distress
•
Hyperresonance (air in pleural space)
•
Absent breath sounds (no lung expansion)
•
Distended neck veins (↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return)
•
Tracheal shift away from the affected side (mass effect)
•
In tension pneumothorax, waiting for imaging can be fatal.
•
Immediate needle decompression is done in the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular
line using a wide-bore cannula, followed by chest tube insertion.
Tension Pneumothorax:
•
Pathophysiology: Air enters the pleural space during inspiration but cannot exit (one-
way valve mechanism). This increases intrapleural pressure → lung collapse →
mediastinal shift → compression of heart and opposite lung → obstructive shock.
•
Causes: trauma, mechanical ventilation, rib fractures, ruptured bleb.
•
Emergency Management:
•
Needle decompression (life-saving) – 2nd ICS MCL or 4th/5th ICS anterior
axillary line.
•
Chest tube thoracostomy in the 4th/5th ICS mid-axillary line after
decompression.
43
Incorrect Options:
Bedside CXR in casualty followed by chest tube insertion (Option A) – Wrong because
waiting for imaging delays life-saving decompression.
Pericardiocentesis (Option C) – For cardiac tamponade, not pneumothorax.
Pleurodesis with doxycycline (Option D) – For recurrent pneumothorax, not for acute life-
threatening tension pneumothorax.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :
44

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A female presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Serum prolactin is elevated. MRI shows pituitary adenoma. Best management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Bromocriptine
Explanation:
The patient has hyperprolactinemia due to a pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma).
Hyperprolactinemia → suppresses GnRH → ↓ LH/FSH → menstrual irregularities and infertility.
First-line treatment for prolactinomas is dopamine agonists (Bromocriptine or Cabergoline) as
they inhibit prolactin secretion and can shrink the tumor. Bromocriptine is safe in women desiring
pregnancy.
Surgery (trans-sphenoidal resection) is reserved for drug-resistant or compressive symptoms (e.g.,
visual loss).
Prolactinoma:
•
Causes:
•
Pituitary adenoma (most common)
•
Drugs: antipsychotics, metoclopramide
•
Hypothyroidism (↑ TRH → ↑ prolactin)
•
Symptoms:
•
Women: amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility
•
Men: decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, gynecomastia
•
Mass effect: headaches, bitemporal hemianopia if the optic chiasm is
compressed
•
Diagnosis: serum prolactin, MRI brain with pituitary protocol
45
•
Treatment: dopamine agonists (Bromocriptine, Cabergoline) → surgery if not
responsive
Incorrect Options:
Letrozole (Option B) – Aromatase inhibitor for estrogen-dependent breast cancer and infertility,
not first-line for prolactinoma.
Tamoxifen (Option C) – Selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) used in breast cancer,
unrelated to prolactinomas.
Goserelin (Option D) – GnRH agonist used in prostate/breast cancer and endometriosis, not for
prolactinoma.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A child with progressive pallor and bone has an elevated HbS based on the HPLC report. Which is the best treatment to manage hemolysis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option C - Voxelotor:
Explanation:
•
HPLC (High-Performance Liquid Chromatography) showing elevated HbS indicates
Sickle Cell Disease (SCD). SCD is due to a mutation in β-globin gene → HbS
polymerizes under low oxygen → sickling → chronic hemolysis + vaso-occlusive crises.
•
Voxelotor is an HbS polymerization inhibitor that increases hemoglobin’s affinity for
oxygen, stabilizing the oxygenated form and reducing RBC sickling. This directly
reduces hemolysis and improves anemia, making it the best treatment here for hemolysis
control.
46
Sickle Cell Disease (SCD):
•
Pathophysiology: Point mutation (Glu → Val) in β-chain of Hb → polymerization in
deoxygenated state → distorted RBCs → hemolysis + microvascular occlusion.
•
Clinical features:
•
Hemolytic anemia (pallor, jaundice, gallstones)
•
Pain crises (bone pain, chest pain, abdomen)
•
Dactylitis in children
•
Splenic infarction → functional asplenia → infection risk
•
Diagnosis: HPLC / electrophoresis (↑ HbS, ± HbF, ↓ HbA)
•
Management:
•
Hydroxyurea (↑ HbF, reduces crises)
•
Voxelotor (↓ hemolysis, ↑ Hb)
•
L-glutamine (↓ oxidative stress)
•
Crizanlizumab (P-selectin inhibitor, ↓ vaso-occlusion)
•
Supportive: vaccination, folate, transfusion if needed
Incorrect Options:
Hydroxyurea (Option A) – Increases HbF, reduces frequency of pain crises and acute chest
syndrome, but has less direct effect on hemolysis than voxelotor.
Azacytidine (Option B) – DNA methyltransferase inhibitor used in myelodysplastic
syndromes/AML, not for SCD.
Bortezomib (Option D) – Proteasome inhibitor used in multiple myeloma, unrelated to SCD.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: What is the probable diagnosis for a patient who exhibits miosis, anhidrosis, mild ptosis, and a persistent small pupil even in low light conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Horner syndrome:
Explanation:
•
The clinical presentation of miosis, anhidrosis, mild ptosis, and a persistent small pupil
even in low light is suggestive of Horner syndrome. Ptosis is a result of the weakness of
Müller muscle and miosis due to the unopposed action of the sphincter pupillae with
resultant anisocoria.
•
Pancoast tumor can compress the sympathetic nerves, leading to the classic triad of
symptoms seen in Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis (constricted pupil), and ipsilateral
facial anhidrosis (lack of sweating).
Acquired Neurogenic Ptosis: Acquired ptosis with drooping of the upper eyelid caused by a
disruption in the nerve supply to the muscles responsible for elevating the eyelid.
Causes:
•
Third Cranial (Oculomotor) Nerve Palsy: The third nerve can be damaged by trauma,
ischemia, infection, tumor, or compression, causing ptosis and diplopia.Oculomotor
nerve palsy causes ptosis as it supplies the levator palpebrae superioris muscle.
The ptotic eyelid can be elevated with a frontalis sling or levator aponeurosis advancement.
•
Horner's Syndrome: Involves a lesion in the sympathetic pathway, affecting the
Müller’s muscle, leading to mild ptosis accompanied by miosis (pupil constriction) and
anhidrosis (loss of sweating).
•
Ophthalmoplegic migraine
•
Multiple Sclerosis
Diagnosis:
•
Topical apraclonidine test is now considered the test of choice. Apraclonidine is an
alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that also acts as a very weak alpha 1-adrenergic agonist; when
topically applied in Horner’s syndrome, it causes dilation of the affected pupil and
possibly lid elevation, without change to the normal pupil.
Incorrect Options:
Adie’s tonic people (Option A) It is a unilateral condition and is characterized by anisocoria
(different size of pupil) and direct light reflex is sluggish or absent.
Marcus gunn pupil (Option C) Aka relative afferent pupillary defect is characterized by
paradoxical dilatation of both the pupil when light is flashed on the diseased eye.
48
Argyll Robertson pupil (Option D) It is a specific sign of late-stage syphilis. The bilaterally
small pupils do not constrict when exposed to bright light.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old female presents with weakness, back pain and repeated infections. Work up shows M spike on serum electrophoresis. Prognosis is determined by which of the following factors?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option D - Albumin and β₂-microglobulin
Explanation:
The International Staging System (ISS) for multiple myeloma — a widely accepted prognostic
model — uses two lab values: serum β₂-microglobulin and serum albumin.
•
β₂-Microglobulin is a marker of tumor burden and renal function; elevated levels
indicate more advanced disease and poorer prognosis.
•
Albumin reflects the patient’s general health and disease activity; lower levels are
associated with more aggressive disease and worse outcomes.
49
ISS Staging
Stage
Criteria
Prognosis
I
β₂-microglobulin < 3.5 mg/L albumin ≥ 3.5 g/dL
Best prognosis
II
Intermediate values (not fitting I or III)
Intermediate prognosis
III
Intermediate values (not fitting I or III)
Poor prognosis
Incorrect Options:
IgG and albumin (Option A): While IgG is commonly the paraprotein in multiple myeloma, it
is not part of the ISS prognostic criteria.
IgM and albumin (Option B): Elevated IgM is characteristic of Waldenström
macroglobulinemia, which differs from multiple myeloma in pathology and prognosis.
Albumin and LDH (Option C): Elevated LDH may suggest high tumor turnover or aggressive
disease but is not part of standard ISS staging (though it may appear in the Revised-ISS combined
with cytogenetics).
Reference :
Learning Outcome :
50

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A young male patient has the following serological status: HbsAg positive, IgM anti Hbc negative, IgG Anti-Hbc positive and HBeAg positive. Select the best treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A – Lamivudine:
Explanation:
•
The serology indicates chronic active hepatitis B infection:
•
HBsAg positive → Ongoing HBV infection.
•
IgM anti-HBc negative, IgG anti-HBc positive → Chronic (not acute) phase.
•
HBeAg positive → High viral replication and infectivity.
•
Patients with chronic active HBV and high viral load (HBeAg positive) require
antiviral therapy to suppress viral replication and reduce liver inflammation, fibrosis, and
hepatocellular carcinoma risk.
•
Lamivudine, an oral nucleoside analog, inhibits HBV DNA polymerase and is one of the
older but effective drugs in HBV management (though tenofovir and entecavir are now
preferred first-line due to less resistance).
Incorrect Options:
Ombitasvir (Option B): NS5A inhibitor used in hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection — not active
against HBV.
Ritonavir (Option C): Protease inhibitor booster used in HIV therapy — no role in HBV
monoinfection treatment.
Abacavir (Option D): NRTI used in HIV therapy — not effective against HBV.
51
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient with RTA is passing red color urine due to myoglobinuria. Which of the following will most likely be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B – Hyperkalemia:
Explanation:
•
Myoglobinuria typically occurs after rhabdomyolysis, where muscle breakdown releases
myoglobin and intracellular potassium into the bloodstream.
•
Myoglobin is nephrotoxic, causing acute tubular necrosis (ATN).
•
Tubular injury in ATN often impairs potassium excretion, resulting in Type 4 RTA
physiology, which is characterized by hyperkalemia and mild metabolic acidosis.
•
The potassium rise is further exacerbated by direct release from damaged muscle cells.
Incorrect Options:
Hypernatremia (Option A): Less common in ATN; if anything, sodium tends to be low due to
renal losses and fluid shifts.
Hyponatremia (Option C): Can occur in kidney injury but not a hallmark feature of RTA with
rhabdomyolysis.
Hypokalemia (Option D): Seen in Type 1 (distal) and Type 2 (proximal) RTA, but not in Type 4
RTA or ATN — here potassium retention predominates.
52
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient after RTA had a renal shut down. Work-up shows: FeNa: < 1%, Urine osmolality: 300 mOsm/kg, Urinary sodium: 40 mEq/L. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN):
Explanation:
•
This presentation points to intrinsic renal injury, specifically ATN, where damaged
renal tubules lose the ability to reabsorb sodium and concentrate urine.
•
Key features in this case:
•
Urinary sodium > 40 mEq/L → tubular sodium wasting
•
Urine osmolality ~300 mOsm/kg → isosthenuria (urine similar to plasma)
•
FeNa < 1% is more typical of pre-renal AKI, but in early ATN or mixed states
it can also be low.
•
Here, the high urinary sodium and poor urine concentration outweigh FeNa
alone, supporting ATN.
Clinical Phases of ATN
Phase
Description
53
•
Prerenal Phase (Pre-ATN)
↓ Renal perfusion (e.g., hypovolemia, CHF)
•
Tubular function intact
•
FeNa <1%, BUN:Cr >20
•
Responds to fluids
•
Reversible if corrected early
•
Initiation Phase
Time of original injury (ischemia/toxins)
•
Mild ↓ GFR, slight ↑ creatinine
•
Urine output may be normal
•
Damage beginning but potentially reversible
•
Extension Phase
Ongoing injury + inflammation (days 1–3)
•
Tubular necrosis, obstruction
•
Key sign: ↑ Creatinine + new oliguria despite fluids
•
FeNa >2%, granular casts may appear
•
Maintenance Phase
Established tubular damage
•
Low GFR, sustained ↑ creatinine/BUN
•
Oliguric or non-oliguric
•
Electrolyte imbalances: hyperkalemia, acidosis
•
Recovery (Repair) Phase
Tubular regeneration
•
Polyuric phase: ↑ urine output
•
Gradual ↓ creatinine
•
Risk: volume depletion, electrolyte loss
Incorrect Options:
Pre-renal AKI (Option B):
•
Characterized by low urinary sodium (<20 mEq/L) and high urine osmolality (>500
mOsm/kg).
Post-renal AKI (Option C):
•
Labs are variable; diagnosis usually requires imaging evidence of obstruction.
Renal AKI (Option D):
•
Too broad; ATN is the specific intrinsic renal diagnosis here.
54
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient is in ICU and there is a failed attempt of subclavian catheterization. Shortly after, BP drops and the pulse rises. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Pneumothorax
Explanation:
•
Subclavian vein catheterization carries a significant risk of pleural injury, which can
cause pneumothorax.
•
Air entry into the pleural space leads to reduced venous return, causing hypotension
and reflex tachycardia.
•
In the ICU setting, this can rapidly progress to tension pneumothorax, which is life-
threatening and requires urgent decompression.
•
Typical signs: sudden drop in BP, tachycardia, respiratory distress, unilateral decreased
breath sounds, hyperresonance on percussion.
Incorrect Options:
Displacement of ET (Option B): Would cause hypoxia and respiratory distress, but is not
directly related to subclavian line attempt.
55
Air embolism (Option C): Can occur during line placement, but presents with sudden
cardiovascular collapse and possibly a "mill wheel" murmur; pneumothorax is more common
post failed subclavian attempt.
Dislodgement of ET (Option D): Would cause airway compromise but unrelated to
catheterization unless ET manipulation occurred.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient had a road traffic accident (RTA). NCCT head was normal on admission. The patient later died after several days in the ICU due to coma. Brain biopsy revealed multiple punctate hemorrhages. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Diffuse axonal injury (DAI):
Explanation:
•
Diffuse axonal injury is a primary brain injury caused by shearing forces during high-
velocity trauma (e.g., RTA).
•
These forces disrupt axons in the white matter, corpus callosum, and brainstem.
•
On initial imaging, NCCT may be normal or show only tiny petechial hemorrhages;
the condition is often diagnosed clinically or via MRI.
•
Histopathology (or biopsy) reveals multiple punctate hemorrhages in deep white matter
tracts.
•
DAI often leads to immediate or prolonged coma without a lucid interval and carries a
high mortality rate.
56
Incorrect Options:
Ischemic injury (Option A): Usually presents with territorial infarcts and hypoxic changes, not
punctate hemorrhages in white matter.
Intraventricular bleeding (Option C): Would be evident on CT and localized to ventricular
system, not diffuse white matter punctate hemorrhages.
Subdural hemorrhage (Option D): Characterized by crescent-shaped collection on CT, caused
by tearing of bridging veins — not microscopic hemorrhages.
57
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with fever and altered sensorium. Peripheral smear shows multiple ring stages. Best treatment is?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option D – Artesunate:
Explanation:
•
Fever with altered sensorium in malaria indicates cerebral malaria — a severe form most
often due to Plasmodium falciparum.
•
Multiple ring forms on smear strongly suggest falciparum malaria.
•
Artesunate is preferred over quinine for severe malaria as per WHO guidelines, given its
better safety profile, faster parasite clearance, and lower mortality.
•
It is administered intravenously in the acute setting.
58
Incorrect Options:
Primaquine (Option A): Used for radical cure of P. vivax and P. ovale to target hypnozoites in
the liver, not for acute severe falciparum malaria.
Quinine (Option B): Historically the drug of choice for severe falciparum malaria, but now
replaced by IV artesunate due to superior efficacy and safety.
Chloroquine (Option C): Effective for chloroquine-sensitive malaria, but most P. falciparum
strains are resistant, making it inappropriate in this case.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Which is the best confirmatory method to ensure the central line is in the jugular vein?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Chest x-ray:
Explanation:
Importance of Chest X-ray in Central Line Placement
•
Initial Assessment:
•
A chest X-ray should be performed immediately after internal jugular and
subclavian line placement to confirm correct catheter placement and rule out
iatrogenic pneumothorax.
•
Post-Procedure Verification:
•
It is crucial to verify catheter placement and ensure no complications, like
pneumothorax, following the procedure.
•
Ipsilateral Side Approach:
•
If the internal jugular central venous line (CVL) insertion fails, move to the
ipsilateral subclavian vein.
•
A chest X-ray or ultrasound should be performed before attempting the opposite
side to prevent bilateral pneumothoraces.
Options B, C, and Dare incorrect.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: What defect is seen in Bernard Soulier syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Deficiency of GpIb receptors:
Explanation:
•
Bernard–Soulier syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive platelet disorder characterized
by a defect in platelet adhesion due to deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet membrane
glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) complex, which is the receptor for von Willebrand factor (vWF).
•
This defect prevents platelets from binding to exposed subendothelial vWF during
vascular injury, leading to defective primary hemostasis.
•
Clinically, it presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, prolonged bleeding time, and
thrombocytopenia with giant platelets on peripheral smear.
Incorrect Options:
Deficiency of GpIIb/IIIa receptor (Option A): Seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia — causes
defective platelet aggregation, not adhesion.
Deficiency of von Willebrand factor (Option C): Seen in von Willebrand disease — results in
both defective platelet adhesion and secondary coagulation defect due to reduced factor VIII
stability.
Deficiency of ADP receptors (Option D): Seen in rare platelet function disorders like P2Y12
receptor defects — affects aggregation via ADP pathway, not adhesion.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with SOB and fatigue. CXR was done. What is the diagnosis? 61
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Asbestosis
Explanation:
•
Asbestosis is an interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of asbestos fibers, often in
occupations such as shipbuilding, construction, or insulation work.
•
The hallmark radiologic finding is calcified pleural plaques, especially along the
parietal pleura and diaphragm (“peripheral pleural calcification”), along with lower lobe
interstitial fibrosis.
•
Patients present with progressive dyspnea and restrictive lung disease on PFTs.
Incorrect Options:
TB (Option A): More commonly involves apical regions, with cavitation and infiltrates; pleural
calcifications are uncommon.
Silicosis (Option C): Typically shows upper lobe nodules and “eggshell” hilar node calcification.
Byssinosis (Option D): Cotton dust–related disease, usually without pleural calcification.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with progressive shortness of breath for the last 6 months, accompanied by dry cough. Auscultation reveals bilateral basal end-inspiratory crepitations. There is no history of fever, joint pain, or occupational exposure. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option C – IPF:
Explanation:
•
Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive fibrosing interstitial lung
disease of unknown cause, typically seen in older adults.
•
The classic presentation includes gradually worsening exertional dyspnoea and
nonproductive cough over months.
•
On auscultation, bilateral basal end-inspiratory “Velcro” crackles are characteristic.
•
Absence of fever, joint symptoms, or occupational dust/fume exposure supports an
idiopathic diagnosis rather than secondary interstitial lung disease.
Incorrect Options:
Cor-pulmonale (Option A): Refers to right ventricular hypertrophy and failure secondary to
chronic lung disease or pulmonary hypertension; it is a consequence, not the primary cause, of the
lung findings here.
Sarcoidosis (Option B): Usually presents with systemic features, bilateral hilar
lymphadenopathy, and may involve skin or eyes; less likely here due to absence of
extrapulmonary signs and chronicity pattern.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Option D): Generally linked to a clear history of antigen
exposure (birds, mold, farming) and has a more acute/subacute onset; no such history is present in
this case.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient has a long arm span, hypermobile joints and hypermobile lens. What is the defective protein?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Fibrillin-1
Explanation:
•
The presentation describes Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder caused by
mutations in the FBN1 gene, leading to defective fibrillin-1, an essential component of
microfibrils that provide structural integrity to connective tissue and regulate TGF-β
signaling.
•
Clinical features include tall stature, disproportionately long limbs (increased arm span-
to-height ratio), joint hypermobility, lens subluxation (typically upward), and
cardiovascular involvement (aortic root dilatation, aneurysm).
65
Incorrect Options:
Collagen (Option B): Defects cause disorders such as Ehlers–Danlos syndrome and osteogenesis
imperfecta, which may have joint hypermobility but not the full Marfan phenotype with lens
dislocation and long arm span.
Elastin (Option C): Deficiency is associated with conditions like supravalvular aortic stenosis
and Williams syndrome, but not the Marfan skeletal and ocular features.
Keratin (Option D): Structural protein in epithelial cells; mutations lead to skin and hair
disorders, not connective tissue or cardiovascular manifestations.
66
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A child presents with kawasaki disease with multiple small coronary artery aneurysms. Treatment is?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option C - Aspirin for 6 weeks:
Explanation:
•
In Kawasaki disease patients with small coronary artery aneurysms, low-dose aspirin
is continued for about 6 to 8 weeks to prevent thrombosis as the aneurysms may regress
over time.
•
The 6-week duration covers the period of highest thrombotic risk during vascular
remodeling.
•
Early IVIG administration is also critical during the acute phase to reduce aneurysm
67
Incorrect Options:
Aspirin lifelong (Option A): Reserved for large or giant aneurysms with persistent risk of
thrombosis.
Aspirin for 4 weeks (Option B): Typically used when no coronary involvement is present.
Aspirin and clopidogrel for 6 weeks (Option D): Dual antiplatelet therapy is usually reserved
for larger aneurysms or specific thrombosis risk cases, not routine small aneurysms.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: The infant is being evaluated for recurrent episodes of seizures. ECG shows Hypsarrhythmia. Which drug is preferred for management?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - ACTH
Explanation:
•
Hypsarrhythmia on EEG is characteristic of infantile spasms (West syndrome), a severe
epileptic encephalopathy in infants.
•
The first-line treatment is adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which helps reduce
spasms and improve developmental outcomes.
Incorrect Options:
Vigabatrin (Option B): Also effective, especially in infantile spasms associated with tuberous
sclerosis, but ACTH remains the preferred initial therapy in most cases.
Valproate (Option C): Used for other seizure types, but less effective for infantile spasms.
Carbamazepine (Option D): Not effective and may worsen infantile spasms.
Reference :
.
69
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with contralateral face, arm, and leg weakness. NCCT shows intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). What is the most likely location of the CNS bleed?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Basal ganglia
Explanation:
•
Intracerebral hemorrhages causing contralateral hemiparesis (weakness of face, arm, and
leg) most commonly occur in the basal ganglia, especially the putamen.
•
The basal ganglia hemorrhage compresses the internal capsule where corticospinal fibers
run, causing dense contralateral motor deficits.
70
Incorrect Options:
Midbrain (Option B): Lesions here often cause oculomotor nerve palsy and contralateral
weakness but are less common sites for primary ICH.
Pons (Option C): Hemorrhages can cause "locked-in" syndrome or quadriplegia, often
accompanied by cranial nerve signs, but less isolated hemiparesis.
Medulla (Option D): Hemorrhages here are rare; symptoms include contralateral limb weakness
with ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits (Wallenberg syndrome) but not classic hemiparesis alone.
71
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: What is the management of undulant fever?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Doxycycline plus rifampicin
Explanation:
•
Undulant fever is a classic presentation of brucellosis, a zoonotic infection.
•
The standard treatment involves combination therapy with doxycycline (100 mg twice
daily for 6 weeks) plus rifampicin (600–900 mg daily for 6 weeks) to prevent relapse
and ensure eradication.
•
Monotherapy with doxycycline alone is insufficient due to high relapse rates.
Incorrect Options:
Doxycycline alone (Option A): Higher risk of relapse if used without a companion drug.
Doxycycline with azithromycin (Option C): Not a standard regimen for brucellosis.
Doxycycline plus ceftriaxone (Option D): Ceftriaxone is used in neurobrucellosis but not
standard for uncomplicated cases.
Reference :
72
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient has cheilosis with koilonychia and anemia. Diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Plummer-Vinson syndrome:
Explanation:
•
Plummer-Vinson syndrome is characterized by the triad of iron deficiency anemia,
esophageal webs, and glossitis/cheilosis.
•
Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) and cheilosis (cracking at the corners of the mouth) are
classic signs of iron deficiency.
•
This syndrome increases the risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma if
untreated.
Incorrect Options:
Esophageal cancer (Option B): May develop as a complication of Plummer-Vinson syndrome
but is not a presenting diagnosis with these features.
Achalasia cardia (Option C): Presents with dysphagia and esophageal motility disorder, but
without anemia or cheilosis.
Tylosis palmaris (Option D): A genetic disorder causing thickened skin on palms and soles,
unrelated to anemia or cheilosis.
73
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: Which classification is used for Barrett esophagus?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Prague classification:
Explanation:
•
The Prague C & M classification is used for Barrett esophagus, where C denotes the
circumferential extent of the Barrett mucosa and M denotes the maximal extent from the
gastroesophageal junction, as measured endoscopically.
•
It helps in standardizing reporting and guiding surveillance.
Prague Classification
•
Two key measurements:
•
C (Circumferential extent)
•
M (Maximum extent)
•
Circumferential extent
•
Distance (in cm) from the GE junction to the proximal limit of circumferential
Barrett's mucosa
•
Maximum extent:
•
Distance from the GE junction to the furthest proximal extension of any Barrett's
mucosa (including tongues or islands)
74
•
Example:
•
If Barrett's mucosa is circumferentially present for 3 cm, and a tongue extends up
to 6 cm:
•
Prague classification = C3M6
Incorrect Options:
Savary-Miller classification (Option B): Used for grading reflux esophagitis severity based on
endoscopic findings.
Johnson classification (Option C): Used for types of gastroesophageal reflux depending on the
location of the lower esophageal sphincter and diaphragm.
Forrest classification (Option D): Used in upper GI bleeding to describe peptic ulcer bleeding
stigmata and predict rebleeding risk.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A female patient complains of chest pain while waking up in the morning. Pain is more in winter months. Which of the following best describes this patient?
options: Subendocardial ischemia due to increased demand of myocardium
Increased sympathomimetic drive in morning hours
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Ach-induced coronary vasoconstriction
Explanation:
•
This presentation is classic for Prinzmetal’s (variant) angina, which is due to transient
vasospasm of coronary arteries often occurring at rest, particularly in the early morning
hours and more frequently in cold weather.
•
Acetylcholine and other vasoconstrictors can trigger the spasm.
75
•
ECG during pain may show transient ST-segment elevation.
Incorrect Options:
Fixed plaque obstruction (Option A): Seen in stable angina due to atherosclerosis; pain is
usually exertional, not at rest.
Subendocardial ischemia due to increased demand of myocardium (Option C): Describes the
mechanism in stable angina during exercise or stress, not rest-related vasospasm.
Increased sympathomimetic drive in morning hours (Option D): Plays a role in acute
coronary syndromes but doesn’t fully explain the cold-weather, early-morning, rest-related pain
due to vasospasm.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 5 year old boy presented with hematemesis and was found to have splenomegaly, on examination. There was a past history of exchange transfusion in this child for neonatal jaundice. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Portal vein thrombosis
Explanation:
The presentation of hematemesis and splenomegaly, along with the significant history of
exchange transfusion in the neonatal period, strongly suggests portal vein thrombosis.
This condition is a common cause of portal hypertension in children and can result from
umbilical vein catheterization during exchange transfusion.
Incorrect Options:
Splenic vein thrombosis (Option A) is also a possibility in a case of splenomegaly, but the
history of exchange transfusion suggests a more generalized thrombotic event involving the portal
vein.
Budd-Chiari syndrome (Option C) is a condition characterized by the obstruction of hepatic
veins, leading to liver congestion. It is less likely in this case, as the presentation of hematemesis
and splenomegaly is more suggestive of portal vein involvement.
Liver cirrhosis(Option D): Although it can cause portal hypertension, cirrhosis is uncommon in
a 5-year-old without a history of chronic liver disease.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :
Key features of portal vein thrombosis:
Feature
Description
Definition
Partial or complete obstruction of the portal vein, which carries blood from
the gastrointestinal tract, spleen, and pancreas to the liver
78
•
Etiology
Cirrhosis or liver fibrosis
•
Hypercoagulable states (e.g., prothrombine gene mutation)
•
Infections (e.g., abdominal sepsis)
•
Abdominal malignancies
•
Clinical
Abdominal pain, often in the right upper quadrant
Presentation
•
Enlarged spleen (splenomegaly)
•
Ascites (fluid accumulation in the abdomen)
•
Gastrointestinal bleeding
•
Jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes)
•
Fever and chills
•
Altered mental status (in severe cases)
•
Diagnostic
Imaging studies: Doppler ultrasound, computed tomography (CT),
Evaluation
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
•
Laboratory tests: Liver function tests, coagulation profile, complete
blood count
•
Management
Treatment of underlying cause (e.g., anticoagulation for
hypercoagulable states)
•
Symptomatic management: Analgesics for pain relief, diuretics for
ascites, management of complications
•
Surgical intervention (in selected cases)
•
Prognosis
The prognosis depends on the underlying cause, extent of
thrombosis, and response to treatment.
•
Complications can include portal hypertension, gastrointestinal
bleeding, liver failure, and sepsis

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A skin graft was performed on an immunocompromised patient using tissue from another immunocompromised individual. Weeks later, the patient developed contractures and systemic symptoms. What is the most likely cause?
options: Rejection due to recipient T8 cells
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Graft-versus-host disease:
Explanation:
•
Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes
recognize recipient tissues as foreign and mount an immune response.
•
This typically happens in immunocompromised recipients who are unable to reject the
donor T cells.
•
In the context of a skin graft (especially from another immunocompromised individual
where donor lymphocytes may survive),
•
GVHD can cause systemic symptoms (fever, rash, liver dysfunction, diarrhea) along with
local changes like skin contractures.
Incorrect Options:
Graft failure (Option B): Results from the inability of the graft to establish blood supply,
leading to necrosis — it occurs early, not weeks later, and does not cause systemic immune
symptoms.
Rejection due to recipient T8 cells (Option C): This is host-versus-graft rejection, not GVHD,
and requires an immunocompetent recipient — which is not the case here.
Delayed wound healing (Option D): Common in immunocompromised states but does not
explain systemic features or the contractures caused by immune-mediated damage.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: The finding seen in the image is? 80
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Herbert’s pits:
Explanation:
•
Herbert’s pits are small, shallow depressions seen at the limbal conjunctiva due to
healed limbal follicles in trachoma.
•
They are considered pathognomonic of previous trachoma infection.
•
Pathophysiology: Chronic Chlamydia trachomatis infection causes limbal follicles →
ulceration → healing with depression.
•
WHO grading: Presence of Herbert’s pits indicates prior active trachoma and is seen in
the scarring stage (TS).
81
Incorrect Options:
Horner-Trantas spots (Option A): White, chalky dots at limbus composed of eosinophils in
vernal keratoconjunctivitis, not trachoma.
Pannus (Option C): Superficial vascularization of cornea extending from the limbus, seen in
active trachoma and other chronic keratitis.
Arlt’s line (Option D): Linear scar on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, seen in late scarring stage of
trachoma, not at the limbus.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient with pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasma now presents with loss of visual field. What visual field defect will be seen in the patient?

Explanation:
•
The optic chiasm contains crossing fibers from the nasal retina of both eyes.
•
Pituitary adenoma commonly compresses the central chiasm from below → affects

hemianopia
•
Clinical scenario: Gradual, progressive peripheral vision loss, more noticeable while
driving or walking.
•
Mechanism: Nasal retinal fibers detect temporal fields → damage leads to bitemporal
hemianopia.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with complaints of eye strain. The given image shows the focus of light rays in different meridians in the eye. Which refractive error is present in this patient? 86
questions.explanation:
Correct Option C - Astigmatism:
Explanation:
•
The image of Sturm’s conoid demonstrates that parallel light rays do not converge to a
single focal point, but rather form two focal lines at different distances due to unequal
refractive power in different meridians of the cornea or lens.
•
This optical phenomenon is characteristic of astigmatism, where light rays along one
meridian focus in front of the retina while rays along the perpendicular meridian focus
either behind or at a different point.
•
Astigmatism causes blurred or distorted vision and eye strain (asthenopia), especially
with prolonged near tasks.
Sturm’s conoid in Astigmatism:
1. Light rays from an object pass through two principal meridians with different curvatures.
2. Each meridian has its own focal length → creates two focal lines (not a single point).
3. The area between these two focal lines is called the Sturm’s conoid.
4. The best vision is achieved at the circle of least confusion, located between the two focal
lines.
87
Incorrect Options:
•
Amblyopia (Option A): Reduced vision in one or both eyes due to abnormal visual
development in childhood; unrelated to optical focusing errors like those shown in
Sturm’s conoid.
•
Hypermetropia (Option B): Farsightedness due to the eye being too short or the cornea
too flat, causing light to focus behind the retina; it produces a single focal point (not two)
and does not show Sturm’s conoid.
•
Presbyopia (Option D): Age-related loss of accommodation due to decreased lens
elasticity; affects near vision but does not produce two focal lines in different meridians.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A myopic patient presents with complaints of flashes and floaters. On examination, a deep anterior chamber is seen. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Explanation:
•
A myopic patient with flashes (photopsia), floaters, and a deep anterior chamber
suggests posterior vitreous detachment with retinal tear. This allows liquefied vitreous to
pass into the subretinal space, leading to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
•
Key mechanism: Myopia → long axial length → retinal thinning + lattice degeneration
→ predisposes to retinal breaks. These breaks allow fluid entry under retina → separation
from retinal pigment epithelium.
•
Deep anterior chamber in this context is due to elongation of the globe and posterior
shift of the lens–iris diaphragm in high myopia.
Type of Retinal
Clinical Features
Detachment
89
Rhegmatogenous
1. Floaters (dark spots) due to rapid vitreous degeneration.
Retinal Detachment
2. Photopsia (flashes of light) caused by retinal irritation from
vitreous movements.
3. Gradual visual field loss, initially localized, progressing to total
vision loss as detachment spreads.
4. Dark veil/cloud in front of the eye, particularly when
detachment reaches the posterior region.
5. Sudden, painless vision loss in large, central detachment.
6. Retinal breaks may be round, horseshoe-shaped, slit-like, or
large anterior dialysis.
7. Vitreous pigments (tobacco dusting or Shaffer sign) are seen in
the anterior vitreous with posterior vitreous detachment.
8. Old retinal detachment shows retinal thinning, subretinal
demarcation lines (high water marks), and secondary intraretinal
cysts.
90
Tractional Retinal
1. Gradual, progressive visual loss
Detachment (Option C
2. Typically painless
ruled out)
3. No associated flashes or floaters
4. Vitreoretinal bands present
5. No retinal breaks
6. Detached area - concave and localized
7. No shifting fluid
91
Exudative Retinal
1. Painless and sudden or gradual visual loss
Detachment (Option A
2. No photopsia, holes/ tears, folds and undulations.
ruled out)
3. Smooth and convex with pigmentary disturbances
4. Rounded and fixed with neovascularization on the tumor
summit.
5. Shifting fluid - changing the position of the detached area with
gravity - hallmark feature.
Central serous retinopathy (Option D): Localized serous detachment of the neurosensory retina
at the macula, seen in young stressed males; presents with central vision blurring and
metamorphopsia, not flashes/floaters.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: An elderly female presents with sudden onset of pain, redness, and decreased vision. On examination, hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, and shallow anterior chamber are noted. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Acute uveitis
Explanation:
•
The presence of ocular pain, redness, decreased vision, and corneal haze can be seen in
both acute uveitis and acute angle-closure glaucoma, but here the combination of
inflammation signs (ciliary congestion, corneal edema) and pupil changes points
toward acute uveitis as the answer given.
•
In uveitis, cells and flare in anterior chamber cause corneal haze, and pupil is
irregular or sluggishly reactive due to posterior synechiae; early on it may appear mid-
dilated.
•
The shallow anterior chamber here may be due to ciliary body swelling pushing the iris
forward in acute inflammation.
Key features of Acute Uveitis:
1. Pain, photophobia, redness (ciliary flush).
2. Decreased vision due to corneal edema and aqueous flare.
3. Irregular or sluggish pupil (posterior synechiae).
4. May cause shallow anterior chamber due to ciliary body congestion.
Anterior Uveitis
Definition: Most common type of uveitis affecting the anterior segment of the eye.
Clinical Features:
•
Pain
•
Redness
•
Photophobia (sensitivity to light)
•
Blepharospasm (involuntary blinking)
•
Serous discharge
•
Blurring and diminished vision
Examination Findings:
93
•
Keratic Precipitates (KPs):
•
Non-Granulomatous: Fine, grey deposits; composed of lymphocytes
•
Granulomatous: Large, greasy-looking deposits known as "mutton fat KPs";
composed of macrophages
•
Location: Typically found in the lower cornea due to convection currents in
aqueous humor; this area is known as Arlt's triangle
•
Aqueous Cells:
•
Indicator of active inflammation
•
Aqueous Flare:
•
Haziness in the anterior chamber due to leakage of proteins from inflamed tissues
•
Muddy Iris:
•
Edema in the iris caused by protein leakage
•
Miosis:
•
Constricted pupil due to toxins released from inflamed tissue
•
Nodules on the Iris:
•
Koeppe's Nodules: At the pupillary border; seen in both granulomatous and non-
granulomatous uveitis
•
Busacca Nodules: At the base of the iris; seen in granulomatous uveitis
94
Complications: (Findings)
•
Posterior Synechiae: Iris adheres to the lens; may lead to festooned-shaped pupil
•
Secclusio Pupil/Ring Synechiae: Adhesion along the entire pupillary border; can lead to
Iris Bombe and peripheral anterior synechiae, causing angle closure glaucoma
•
Occlusio Pupil: Covers the whole surface of the lens
•
Cyclitic Membrane
•
Rubeosis Iridis: New vessel formation on the iris
95
Incorrect Options:
•
Acute conjunctivitis (Option B): Presents with diffuse redness, mucopurulent or watery
discharge; vision usually normal, cornea clear, pupil reactive, anterior chamber normal
depth.
•
Acute congestive glaucoma (Option C): Sudden severe pain, markedly decreased
vision, halos around lights, very high IOP, fixed mid-dilated pupil, shallow anterior
chamber - however, it is typically more painful, with headache/nausea, and the hallmark
is IOP >40 mmHg with rock-hard globe.
•
Central retinal artery occlusion (Option D): Sudden painless monocular vision loss;
examination shows pale retina with cherry-red spot, no corneal haze, no anterior chamber
shallowing.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with a painless ulcer in the eye. On examination, a long, branching ulcer with desquamated epithelium is seen on the cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option D - Neurotrophic ulcer
Explanation:
•
A painless corneal ulcer indicates reduced or absent corneal sensation.
•
The finding of a long, branching ulcer with desquamated epithelium but without the
typical raised edges and terminal bulbs of herpes simplex keratitis suggests a
neurotrophic ulcer.
96
•
Neurotrophic keratopathy results from damage to trigeminal nerve sensory supply,
leading to impaired healing and epithelial breakdown, producing branching epithelial
defects.
Neurotrophic Ulcer:
1. Painless despite corneal epithelial defect.
2. Decreased corneal sensation and epithelial desquamation.
3. Often branching/irregular ulcer margins.
4. Causes: herpes simplex/zoster, trigeminal nerve damage (tumor, surgery), diabetes,
chronic topical medication toxicity.
5. May follow procedures like Gasserian ganglion removal or blockage, often used in
treating trigeminal neuralgia.
6. Poor healing tendency due to loss of corneal reflex and trophic support.
Incorrect Options:
•
Fungal ulcer (Option A): Usually follows trauma with vegetative matter; presents with
pain, feathery margins, satellite lesions, and hypopyon; not typically painless and
branching like in neurotrophic ulcer.
•
Dendritic ulcer (Option B): Caused by herpes simplex virus; branching ulcer with
terminal bulbs that stain with fluorescein; usually painful (unless corneal sensation is
already lost).
•
Bacterial corneal ulcer (Option C): Acute, painful, purulent ulcer with stromal
infiltration and hypopyon; rapid progression; not painless and not typically branching.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old patient with eye examination findings of a deep anterior chamber and jet-black pupil is prescribed +12D glasses. Likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option B - Aphakia:
Explanation:
•
Clinical reasoning:
•
Deep anterior chamber → suggests absence of crystalline lens.
•
Jet-black pupil → no lens reflections seen.
•
+12D prescription → large convex lens to replace lost refractive power of
natural lens.
•
Aphakia = complete absence of the natural lens (usually post-cataract surgery without
IOL implantation).
•
Without the lens, refractive power decreases drastically (~+15D needed), so strong
convex lenses are prescribed.
•
Causes: Post-cataract extraction without IOL, trauma, congenital.
•
Features: Deep anterior chamber, iridodonesis, jet-black pupil, high hypermetropia (+10
to +15D).
Aphakia:
•
Definition
Absence of crystalline lens from the eye.
•
Aetiology
Congenital absence (rare)
•
Surgical removal (common)
•
Traumatic extrusion of lens (rare)
•
Posterior lens dislocation (optical aphakia)
•
Optical
High hypermetropia
Effects
•
Reduced eye power to +44 D (from +60 D)
•
Symptoms
Defective vision (far and near)
•
Erythropsia and cyanopsia (abnormal red and blue color defect)
98
•
Signs
Limbal/corneal scar (in surgical cases)
•
Deep anterior chamber
•
Iridodonesis & Jet-black pupil
•
Only 2 Purkinje images (normal: 4)
•
Hypermetropic small optic disc
Treatment
Correct refractive error with:
•
Spectacles: the problem of spherical aberration and roving ring
scotoma (jack-in-the-box phenomenon)
•
Contact lenses
•
Intraocular lenses (IOL) - best method
•
Refractive LASIK surgery
Incorrect Options:
•
Pseudophakia (Option A): Eye has an artificial intraocular lens post-cataract surgery;
patient usually needs minimal refractive correction (not +12D).
•
Myopia (Option C): Nearsightedness; requires concave (minus) lenses; opposite of the
strong convex lenses seen here.
•
Hypermetropia (Option D): Farsightedness; needs convex lenses, but typically much
lower power (+1D to +4D), not as high as +12D.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A man presents to the hospital with a bizarre behavior. He is unable to recall his personal identity and has no memory of how he traveled 100 km to reach the hospital. A collateral history reveals he experienced a traumatic earthquake a few months ago. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Dissociative amnesia
Explanation:
The patient's presentation is a classic example of a dissociative disorder, specifically dissociative
amnesia with a dissociative fugue. The key features that point to this diagnosis are:
•
Inability to Recall Personal Information: The patient is unable to remember his
personal identity and significant past events. This memory loss is not due to a medical
condition.
•
Following a Traumatic Event: The amnesia is directly linked to a recent, severe
traumatic stressor (the earthquake). This is a hallmark of dissociative disorders.
•
Dissociative Fugue: The patient's purposeful travel over a long distance (100 km)
without any memory of the journey is characteristic of a dissociative fugue, a subtype of
dissociative amnesia.
Incorrect Options:
Dissociative identity disorder (Option B) involves the presence of two or more distinct
personality states (or "alters"), which is not described in this case.
Schizophrenia (Option C) is a psychotic disorder characterized by symptoms such as
hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thought, none of which are mentioned in the patient's
presentation.
Global amnesia (Option D) is a broad term that can be caused by organic, non-psychiatric
conditions such as stroke or head injury. Since the patient's amnesia is clearly linked to a
traumatic event and not an organic cause, dissociative amnesia is the more specific and likely
diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A girl with schizophrenia presents to a Primary Health Centre (PHC) in India. Which of the following online applications, provided by the Government of India (GOI), is used for mental health service support? 100

Correct Option A - Tele MANAS:
Explanation:
Tele MANAS, which stands for Tele Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States, is
the correct answer. It is a landmark initiative by the Government of India (GOI) to provide mental
health services to the public.
•
Service Offerings: Tele-MANAS is a 24/7, toll-free tele-mental health service designed
to provide immediate mental health support to individuals in distress.
•
Accessibility: It is available through a toll-free number (14416) and is part of the
National Mental Health Programme. It aims to bridge the gap in mental health care by
providing accessible services, particularly in remote and underserved areas.
Incorrect Options:
U-WIN (Option B) is an application developed by the government for immunization tracking,
similar to the Co-WIN platform used for COVID-19 vaccination.
NIKUSHT(Option C) is a digital platform for the management and monitoring of sickle cell
disease.
NIKSHAY (Option D) is the National Tuberculosis Information and Reporting System, used for

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old software engineer presents with sleep disturbances, low mood, and stress for the past 3 months. He attributes his symptoms to ongoing problems at work. He has no prior psychiatric history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? 101
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Adjustment disorder:
Explanation:
The patient's symptoms are a classic presentation of adjustment disorder. The diagnostic criteria
for this condition are:
•
Emotional or Behavioral Symptoms: The patient exhibits emotional or behavioral
symptoms (sleep disturbances, low mood, stress) in response to an identifiable stressor.
•
Timeline: The symptoms must begin within three months of the onset of the stressor (in
this case, excessive work pressure).
•
Marked Distress and Impairment: The symptoms cause marked distress that is
disproportionate to the severity of the stressor and lead to significant impairment in social
or occupational functioning (difficulty maintaining work-life balance).
•
Exclusion of Other Disorders: The symptoms do not meet the criteria for another
specific mental disorder, such as major depressive disorder or a psychotic disorder.
Incorrect Options:
Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) (Option B) is a more chronic condition, requiring at least
six months of excessive worry and anxiety about multiple events or activities. The patient's
symptoms are directly tied to a specific, recent stressor.
Acute stress disorder (Option C) is a response to a traumatic event (e.g., a natural disaster,
assault, or serious accident) and its symptoms last for a shorter duration (from three days to one
month). The patient's symptoms are from work pressure, which is a significant stressor but not a
traumatic event.
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Option D) also requires exposure to a traumatic event
and includes symptoms of re-experiencing the event, avoidance of related stimuli, negative
alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal. This is not consistent with the patient's
presentation.
102

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A female presents with symptoms of being excessively talkative, hyperactive, sleeping very little, and spending large amounts of money on shopping sprees. When confronted, she becomes irritable. What is the most likely diagnosis? 104
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Bipolar I + Mania
Explanation:
The patient's symptoms are a classic and clear presentation of a manic episode, which is the
defining characteristic of Bipolar I Disorder. The key symptoms described are:
•
Elevated or Irritable Mood: She is hyperactive and, when confronted, becomes
irritable.
•
Decreased Need for Sleep: She is sleeping very little.
•
Pressured Speech: She is excessively talkative.
•
Risky or Impulsive Behavior: She is spending large amounts of money on shopping
sprees, a form of impulsive and often reckless behavior seen in mania.
A diagnosis of a manic episode requires these symptoms to be present for at least one week and to
cause significant functional impairment, such as the social and financial distress caused by the
spending sprees.
Incorrect Options:
Bipolar II Disorder + Hypomania(Option B) is characterized by episodes of hypomania,
which are less severe than manic episodes. Hypomania does not cause significant functional
impairment or psychosis, and it must last for at least four consecutive days. The patient's
symptoms clearly meet the criteria for a full manic episode due to the severity and functional
impairment.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) (Option C) is characterized by obsessions (recurrent,
unwanted thoughts) and compulsions (repetitive behaviors to neutralize the obsessions). This
does not fit the patient's presentation.
Schizophrenia (Option D) is a psychotic disorder with symptoms like hallucinations, delusions,
and disorganized thought. While some symptoms can overlap, the core presentation of
talkativeness, hyperactivity, and impulsive spending is far more indicative of a mood disorder
like Bipolar I.
105

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old patient presents with difficulty reacting to bright light. On examination, the pupillary light reflex is absent but the near reflex is preserved. Where is the lesion likely located?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: D) Pretectal area of the midbrain
Explanation:
•
Absence of the light reflex with preservation of the near reflex is known as light-near
dissociation.
•
This occurs when the lesion interrupts the pathway from the optic tract to the Edinger–
Westphal nucleus before the convergence–accommodation pathway branches —
classically in the pretectal area of the midbrain.
•
Common causes: Argyll Robertson pupil (neurosyphilis), Parinaud’s syndrome (pineal
tumors).
Mechanism:
1. Light reflex pathway: Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasma → optic tract → pretectal
area → bilateral Edinger–Westphal nuclei → oculomotor nerve → sphincter pupillae.
2. Near reflex pathway bypasses the pretectal area lesion and reaches Edinger–Westphal
nuclei via cortical connections, so it remains intact.
Incorrect Options:
Optic nerve (Option A): Lesion causes loss of both light and near reflex on the affected side
(afferent defect), not selective loss of light reflex.
106
Oculomotor nerve (Option B): Lesion causes loss of both light and near reflex (efferent defect),
along with ptosis and eye deviation down and out.
Edinger–Westphal nucleus (Option C): Damage here would abolish both light and near
reflexes, as it is the parasympathetic motor nucleus for pupillary constriction.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A person has a false belief that he owns a lot of property and that someone he knows is trying to take it away from him. Which of the following best describes the type of delusions he is experiencing?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Delusion of grandeur and persecution:
Explanation:
This patient is experiencing two distinct types of delusions simultaneously:
•
Delusion of Grandeur: This is a false and exaggerated belief in one's own importance,
power, or identity. The belief that he owns a lot of property is an example of a grandiose
delusion, as it exaggerates his financial or social status.
•
Delusion of Persecution: This is the most common type of delusion, characterized by the
false belief that one is being harassed, harmed, or conspired against. The belief that
someone is trying to take his property away from him is a classic example of a
persecutory delusion.
Incorrect Options:
107
Delusion of reference (Option B) involves the belief that neutral events or gestures are
personally directed at oneself. For example, believing that a news reporter is speaking directly to
them. This is not present in the scenario.
Delusion of nihilism (Options C and D) is the false belief that the self, a part of the self, or the
world does not exist. This is not relevant to the patient's beliefs about property and being targeted.

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A girl, after returning from a picnic, complains of pain in her eyes. She had not maintained proper hygiene of her contact lenses. What would be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A) Acanthamoeba
Explanation:
•
Improper contact lens hygiene, especially with exposure to contaminated water (picnic
scenario, possible swimming), is a major risk factor for Acanthamoeba keratitis.
•
Acanthamoeba is a free-living protozoan found in water, soil, and air; it can adhere to
contact lenses and invade the corneal epithelium, causing severe pain (often
disproportionate to clinical signs), redness, tearing, and photophobia.
•
Classic sign: ring-shaped stromal infiltrate in advanced cases.
Acanthamoeba keratitis:
1. Severe pain out of proportion to clinical findings.
2. History of contact lens wear, especially poor hygiene or water exposure.
3. Resistant to routine antibacterial therapy; requires specific anti-amoebic agents (e.g.,
polyhexamethylene biguanide, chlorhexidine).
108
4. Delayed diagnosis can lead to corneal perforation and vision loss.
Examination Findings in Acanthamoeba Keratitis:
Symptoms:
•
Blurred Vision: Common in corneal conditions due to the disruption of the cornea's
transparent surface.
•
Discomfort: Significant discomfort in the affected eye.
•
Severe Pain: Pain is often out of proportion to clinical signs, a key clinical clue.
Signs:
Early Disease:
•
Irregular and Greyish Epithelium: Early sign indicating amoebic invasion.
•
Pseudodendrites: Lesions resembling herpetic keratitis
•
Limbitis and Stromal Infiltrates: Inflammation at the corneal-scleral junction with
diffuse or focal infiltrates in the anterior stroma.
•
Perineural Infiltrates (Radial Keratoneuritis): Hallmark sign, radial streaks extending
towards the cornea's centre, pathognomonic for Acanthamoeba keratitis.
Advanced Disease:
•
Ring Abscess: Characteristic of advanced infection, where infiltrates form a ring-shaped
abscess.
•
Stromal Opacification and Vascularisation: Corneal opacity and new blood vessel
growth, leading to significant vision impairment.
•
Corneal Melting: Serious complication where corneal tissue breaks down, often at the
infiltrate edges.
•
Scleritis: Reactive inflammation of the sclera, not a direct infection extension.
Investigations and Treatment of Acanthamoeba Keratitis:
Investigations:
•
Corneal Scraping:
•
The primary method for obtaining tissue for examination.
•
Scrape the margins and base of the lesion after applying a non-preserved topical
anaesthetic.
•
Staining:
•
PAS (Periodic acid–Schiff) and Calcofluor white: Highly effective for
visualizing Acanthamoeba cysts.
•
Gram and Giemsa stains: Less sensitive but can also demonstrate cysts.
•
Culture: Definitive diagnosis by culturing on non-nutrient agar with dead E. coli.
•
Additional Investigations:
•
Immunohistochemistry: Uses antibodies to detect specific Acanthamoeba
antigens.
109
•
PCR: Useful for detecting Acanthamoeba DNA.
•
In Vivo Confocal Microscopy: Provides detailed images of Acanthamoeba cysts
within the cornea.
•
Corneal Biopsy:
•
Considered if other diagnostic methods are inconclusive.
Treatment Modalities:
•
Debridement: Removal of infected epithelium to enhance topical medication
penetration.
•
Topical Amoebicides:
•
PHMB (polyhexamethylene biguanide) 0.02% and Chlorhexidine 0.02%:
Effective against both trophozoites and cysts.
•
Hexamidine: More effective than Propamidine (Brolene).
•
Topical Steroids:
•
Considered for persistent inflammation after two weeks of anti-amoebic
treatment.
•
Caution against use if corneal thinning is present.
•
Pain Management: Oral NSAIDs are recommended for pain relief.
•
Therapeutic Keratoplasty: Required for cases resistant to medical therapy or when
corneal perforation occurs.
Incorrect Options:
Plasmodium (Option B): Causes malaria; does not cause keratitis or infection related to contact
lenses.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option C): Most common bacterial cause of contact lens–related
keratitis; produces rapid corneal ulceration, but here the focus is on protozoal infection linked to
contaminated water exposure.
Herpes simplex virus (Option D): Causes dendritic keratitis; unrelated to contact lens hygiene
and not typically triggered by recent outdoor water exposure.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient with schizophrenia, developed muscular dystonia and was treated for it. The patient now presents with complaints of dry mouth, dizziness, and hypotension. What is the most likely drug causing these side effects? 110
questions.explanation:
Correct Option A - Benzotropine:
Explanation:
The patient with schizophrenia likely developed acute dystonia as a side effect of antipsychotic
therapy, which is commonly treated with an anticholinergic drug like benztropine.
•
Treatment: Muscular dystonia is typically treated with anticholinergic medications.
These drugs work by blocking acetylcholine activity to restore the balance of
neurotransmitters in the brain.
•
New Symptoms: The patient now presents with dry mouth, dizziness, and
hypotension. These are classic side effects of anticholinergic drugs.
•
Dry mouth: Caused by the anticholinergic effect of blocking muscarinic
receptors in the salivary glands.
•
Dizziness and hypotension: Can be caused by the drug's effect on blood
pressure regulation and the central nervous system.
Incorrect Options:
Risperidone (Option B): This is an atypical antipsychotic. While it can cause some EPS, it is
more likely to be the drug that caused the dystonia, not the drug used to treat it.
Haloperidol (Option C): This is a potent typical antipsychotic. It is the type of drug that is a
classic cause of muscular dystonia, not the treatment for it.
Propranolol (Option D): This is a beta-blocker. It is sometimes used to treat another type of EPS
called akathisia, but it is not the primary treatment for dystonia, and its side effect profile does not
typically include dry mouth.
111
Reference :

to ~15 prism diopters (PD) of deviation.

Reflex at the limbus ≈ 45 PD deviation.
112

Here, the reflex is at the corneal periphery/limbus, indicating about 45 PD of exotropia
(outward deviation).

90° (Option D): Not an appropriate unit for Hirschberg measurement; deviation is expressed in

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: What could be the diagnosis for a child who exhibits below-average mathematical skills despite having a normal IQ and age-appropriate learning abilities and remains unaffected by a year-long private mathematics tutoring?
questions.explanation:
Correct Option D - Specific learning disorder
Explanation:
The child described is likely experiencing a Specific Learning Disorder (SLD), specifically with
impairment in mathematics. This is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by persistent
difficulties in learning and using academic skills despite normal intelligence, adequate
educational opportunities, and appropriate interventions such as private tutoring.
Features of SLD in Mathematics (Dyscalculia):
•
Mathematical Difficulties: Problems with basic arithmetic operations, understanding
numbers, or applying mathematical concepts.
•
Persistence: The issues persist despite normal IQ and adequate learning in other areas.
•
Impact on Daily Life: The difficulties impair academic achievement and daily
functioning.
Incorrect Options:
ADHD (Option A) involves inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity affecting multiple domains,
including academics. Poor math performance in ADHD stems from difficulty focusing, not from
specific deficits in mathematical skills.
Mathematics Learning Disorder (Option B): While this term describes the condition, it is not a
standalone diagnosis in the DSM-5. Dyscalculia is a subtype of Specific Learning Disorder,
making "Specific Learning Disorder" the correct and broader diagnostic term.
Asperger’s Syndrome (Option C) (now classified under Autism Spectrum Disorder in DSM-5)
involves difficulties with social communication and restricted interests, not specific academic
skills like mathematics. Children with Asperger’s often excel academically, including in
mathematics.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A patient presents with a down and out right eye with ptosis since birth. What is the nerve palsy? 114
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B) 3rd nerve palsy
Explanation:
•
The down and out position of the eye indicates unopposed action of the lateral rectus
(CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) muscles, suggesting paralysis of the other
extraocular muscles supplied by oculomotor nerve (CN III).
•
Ptosis occurs due to paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris (also supplied by CN
III).
•
Since it is present since birth, this is likely a congenital oculomotor nerve palsy.
Key features of 3rd nerve palsy:
1. Eye position: abducted and depressed ("down and out").
2. Ptosis due to levator palpebrae weakness.
3. May also have pupil dilation if parasympathetic fibers are involved.
4. Causes: congenital, trauma, aneurysm (PComm), diabetes.
Incorrect Options:
4th nerve palsy (Option A): Affects superior oblique → vertical diplopia, head tilt to opposite
side; eye is slightly up and in, not down and out with ptosis.
6th nerve palsy (Option C): Affects lateral rectus → inability to abduct eye; resting position is
inward (esotropia), not down and out.
7th nerve palsy (Option D): Affects facial muscles, not extraocular muscles; presents with facial
asymmetry, inability to close eye, no change in eye position.
Reference :
Learning Outcome :
115

questions.subject: Integrated practice
questions.prompt: A posterior staphyloma was observed on indirect ophthalmoscopy. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A) High myopia
Explanation:
•
A posterior staphyloma is an outpouching of the weakened posterior sclera, visible as
an ectatic area on fundus examination.
•
It occurs most commonly in pathological (high) myopia due to progressive elongation
of the eyeball, leading to stretching and thinning of the sclera, choroid, and retina at the
posterior pole.
•
This structural change can cause progressive visual decline and predispose to retinal
degenerations/detachments.
•
Axial length usually >26 mm.
•
Fundus signs: temporal crescent, chorioretinal atrophy, lattice degeneration, and posterior
staphyloma.
•
Etiology: mechanical stretching from axial elongation.
•
Clinical impact: distorted vision, higher retinal detachment risk.
Staphyloma:
•
It is ectasia of the outer coats of the eye (cornea, sclera, or both) with an incarceration of
the uveal tissue.
Based on the site affected, staphyloma can be classified as
116
Types of staphyloma
Causes
Anterior
Pseudocornea
Intercalary
Perforating injuries of the peripheral cornea, marginal
corneal ulcer, anterior scleritis, and scleromalacia perforans
Ciliary
Glaucoma, scleritis, and trauma to the ciliary region
Equatorial (approx 14 mm
Scleritis, degenerative myopia, and chronic uncontrolled
behind the limbus)
glaucoma
Posterior
Degenerative high axial myopia
Treatment:
•
Treat underlying condition
•
Local excision and repair with a corneal and scleral patch graft
•
Large staphyloma: Staphylectomy and keratoplasty, or enucleated and replaced with an
implant
117
Incorrect Options:
Hypermetropia (Option B): Shorter axial length; no scleral ectasia; may cause narrow anterior
chamber and angle-closure glaucoma but not posterior staphyloma.
Primary open-angle glaucoma (Option C): Optic nerve cupping and visual field loss without
scleral ectasia; unrelated to posterior staphyloma formation.
Retinitis pigmentosa (Option D): Inherited retinal dystrophy; shows bone-spicule pigmentation,
attenuated vessels, and waxy disc pallor — not posterior scleral outpouching.
